SpaceX no longer needs NASA, and that’s a problem for America’s space agency

Ars Technica Long form October 29, 2026

“NASA desperately needs SpaceX, and SpaceX knows it, and Elon knows it.”

For nearly a quarter of a century, Elon Musk and his essential partner at SpaceX, Gwynne Shotwell, viewed the United States government as El Dorado, the mythical city of gold.

Like machete-wielding treasure hunters, Musk and Shotwell hacked through a tangled jungle filled with lurking carnivores such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin, as well as bean counters and regulators. Over time, against long odds, the pair cleared a path for SpaceX to contracts at NASA and the US military. They sued when things did not go their way. They hollered about unfair playing fields. Most importantly, they delivered quality space products to the US government for less.

And so, after a while, SpaceX found El Dorado and a city of contracts.

Then they started winning everything. So much so that the relationship between the customer and contractor began to change. Slowly at first, but ever more quickly, SpaceX went from needing the US government as an indispensable customer to becoming an indispensable contractor for the nation.

The pendulum has swung so far now that SpaceX seems increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services, such as Starshield for military communications and observations.

“I guess I am still in denial that there is a divorce pending,” said Lori Garver, a deputy NASA administrator during the Obama White House years who was instrumental in expanding the agency’s use of commercial contracts with companies like SpaceX. “I literally cannot wrap my head around a future yet where SpaceX stops flying Dragon and Falcon. Not yet.”

But the signs point to at least a partial breakup. Consider the following data points:

To be clear, SpaceX is still fulfilling its existing contracts with NASA, the US Space Force, and other government entities. And it continues to do so at a lower cost and generally higher level of reliability than pretty much anyone else.

But the company is no longer signing many large new contracts for spaceflight services, at least in the traditional launch and in-space flight domains. The shift comes after 15 years in which the US government has grown accustomed to lower costs and rapid innovation that has revitalized the nation’s access to space.

For SpaceX and its shareholders, as shocking as it may seem for a US company to leave billions of dollars on the table in government contracts, this may be the right decision. SpaceX sees the vast bulk of its future revenue coming from artificial intelligence. However, SpaceX’s retreat from the public square comes as both NASA and the Space Force confront growing challenges from a rising space program in China and an aging but still dangerous Russia in space.

So what does it mean if the halcyon days of SpaceX riding to the rescue for America in space—such as in the saga of Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams—seem to be ending?

In the early days, Musk and Shotwell sought revenue from various sources as SpaceX developed the scrappy Falcon 1 rocket. But it was NASA that stepped in at two crucial moments in the company’s first decade.

The first came in 2006, with a $278 million award to develop a cargo delivery spacecraft for the International Space Station. It helped SpaceX expand rapidly when it was struggling to develop the Falcon 1 rocket. An even more consequential award arrived in December 2008, $1.6 billion for a dozen Dragon cargo flights to the space station. The funding arrived as SpaceX struggled to meet payroll. Both Musk and Shotwell have said this award probably saved SpaceX from bankruptcy.

NASA and SpaceX then fell into an increasingly warm and mutually beneficial relationship. During the last two decades, NASA has awarded contracts to SpaceX worth approximately $20 billion, and Musk has been deeply appreciative. In 2017, he revealed that the online password for some of his accounts was “ILoveNASA.” In return, NASA got reliable cargo, eventually crew services into low-Earth orbit, and a revolution in US spaceflight capabilities.

Musk and Shotwell fought to extend their relationship with the federal government in the mid-2010s. In 2014, they filed a lawsuit against the US Air Force for the right to bid for national security launch contracts. Musk contended that United Launch Alliance had a monopoly and said SpaceX should be eligible to bid. “We’re just protesting and saying these launches should be competed,” he said at the time. “And if we compete and lose, that’s fine, but why were they not even competed?”

The effort proved successful. SpaceX won national security contracts, and launch costs for the military plunged. Over time, SpaceX became the dominant player. Even today, with United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin struggling to bring their large Vulcan and New Glenn rockets into service, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets have become a single-point failure for national security launches. If the US military needed to get a dozen large satellites into orbit during the next 12 to 18 months, there is only one company that could credibly pull that off.

The bottom line is that SpaceX, far more often than any other competitor over the last 15 years, delivered spaceflight services to the US government when other contractors were late or overbudget or simply failed. That no other commercial space company has risen alongside SpaceX during this period is a problem. NASA, certainly, sought to support competitors such as Blue Origin, Sierra Space, Rocket Lab, Orbital Sciences, Boeing, and others. The US military supported development of United Launch Alliance’s rocket with $2 billion in funding as an alternative to Falcon.

And still, none have yet come remotely close to matching what SpaceX has done in launch, spacecraft, and in-space data services.

The relationship dynamic began to change about half a decade ago.

At the height of the pandemic, in mid-2020, SpaceX delivered a huge win for NASA by safely flying astronauts Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken to the space station. It is difficult to overstate the importance of this achievement for NASA. Since 2011, the space agency had swallowed its pride and gone, hat in hand, to Russia for transportation to the space station. Its astronauts spent months in Russia learning the language and training to ride the Soyuz spacecraft into orbit. With a single successful 64-day mission, SpaceX ended all of that.

Less than a year later, NASA again turned to SpaceX. The space agency needed a Moon lander. But Congress had only appropriated beer money for a champagne project. NASA had three options for a privately developed lunar lander. None were ideal. SpaceX’s $2.89 billion proposal to develop Starship as a lunar lander and fly two missions was the only bid that fit NASA’s budget profile. Yes, Starship presented a complicated, oversized, and technically demanding solution. But in 2021, SpaceX was NASA’s only spaceflight contractor consistently delivering big results.

Almost overnight, then, NASA’s two most important and costly programs, the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon and the International Space Station, became utterly dependent on SpaceX.

This power imbalance continued to grow, breaking into wider public view in June 2025 amid a temporary falling out between Musk and the president he helped elect. After Trump threatened to “terminate” SpaceX’s governmental contracts and subsidies, Musk’s response was essentially so what? In return, Musk threatened to decommission the Dragon spacecraft. He knew—correctly, it turns out—that SpaceX’s role in US government space programs could not be easily replaced. A Pentagon review in July 2025 found most of the company’s contracts with the US Department of Defense were essential.

Trump could still have hurt Musk’s businesses through regulatory review, particularly with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Aviation Administration. And the two made up. But one indisputable takeaway from this brouhaha is that the US government now needed SpaceX more than SpaceX needed the US government.

“The dust-up with President Trump, when Musk threatened to take away Dragon, was utterly irresponsible,” said Chris Davenport, a professor at Arizona State University and author of Rocket Dreams. “If Falcon and Dragon go away, that is a huge disservice to the US government. NASA desperately needs SpaceX, and SpaceX knows it, and Elon knows it.”

This represented a truly remarkable shift for everyone who watched SpaceX fight so hard, for so long, to get its foot in the door at NASA and the Space Force. But as jarring as it is, this shift is no longer deniable.

Around the time of his dispute with Trump, Musk came to fully believe that artificial intelligence was not just the next big thing. Rather, it was the industrial revolution of his lifetime. He began vectoring his two biggest companies, Tesla and SpaceX, toward dominating AI software, AI hardware, and computing power on the ground and in space to run it all.

This largely explains SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI and its subsequent IPO. It is also behind the potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla. This will give Musk more direct control over Tesla, something he values. But more critically, it gives him an immense pool of assets to deploy toward building data centers terrestrially and in space, autonomous vehicles, robots, massive rockets, and more.

No other company on Earth has the potential, at least in the near term, to own an entire stack of artificial intelligence. Elon Musk wants to manufacture the chips and electricity infrastructure for data centers, he wants to build the data centers that will power the AI revolution, he wants to develop and train the AI models that will provide its intelligence, and he wants to build physical products that he believes will become the shaping force of the 21st century.

He wants it all.

Such a future, in his mind, does not include a dead-end technology like the Dragon spacecraft—even though Dragon is the only reliable way to get humans into space outside of China and Russia, and only took flight with humans six years ago. He does not want to fly the partially reusable Falcon 9 rocket—even though it is the best, cheapest, and only Western vehicle capable of expanding to meet the growing demand from government and commercial customers for access to space right now.

Musk believes the government moves too slowly and simply isn’t ambitious enough when it comes to space. Often, in meetings at SpaceX, he will describe working with the US government as “like wearing lead shoes and walking through molasses.”

Instead, Musk wants to build bigger things, like Starship. He wants to move fast and break things when necessary. This explains why he has invested something like $15 billion in the development of the Starship rocket, from its engines to a growing number of launch sites in Texas and Florida, to get the massive, fully reusable vehicle off the ground.

For a time, this looked like a win-win situation for the US government and a growing commercial space industry counting on frequent, low-cost access to space. NASA built its Artemis Program around Starships landing on the Moon. The commercial space industry looked forward to abundant, cheap launches. The general sense was that pulling Dragon and Falcon 9 off the market would cause temporary upheaval, but these problems would soon be ameliorated by Starship and its promise of lower cost and even greater capability.

That was the hope, at least.

In March 2020, SpaceX published its first “Starship Users Guide,” which included a 9-meter payload fairing with a “clamshell” structure that would open once in space to deploy payloads. The company said it would support Falcon-compatible payload adapters.

But in recent years, there has been little evidence that SpaceX is actually developing such a deployment mechanism. Rather, the company has implemented a Pez-like dispenser that releases flattish satellites from a narrow door in the middle of the Starship vehicle. This serves SpaceX’s internal payloads of Starlink and future Starmind (data center) satellites. But it’s unsuitable for deploying more traditional satellites or big NASA payloads, such as large space telescopes.

Multiple people Ars spoke with for this story said it would be incredibly beneficial if SpaceX publicly committed to developing a large payload door and provided a timeline for its readiness. Ars offered SpaceX the opportunity to make such a commitment, but the company didn’t take it.

And it doesn’t have to. The reality is straightforward. This year’s IPO gave SpaceX a laser-like focus on its core business plan. Reaching stratospheric financial targets requires launching incredible numbers of Starlink and Starmind satellites, all of which can be dispensed like Pez candy into space. Launch services for third parties, which include NASA and other Moon Base customers, represent a rounding error in SpaceX’s revenue in the post-IPO world.

In its recent third-quarter 10-Q financial filing, the company references these launch priorities for Starlink and artificial intelligence: “We allocate a significant amount of launch capacity to our Connectivity segment and expect to allocate a significant amount to our SI segment in the future.”

An argument often made about SpaceX’s decision to end the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rocket is that these programs—which operate with unprecedented efficiency in the history of launch—consume valuable engineering time. This talented team pushed Falcon 9 above 150 launches a year and helped make SpaceX globally dominant. Musk has said he would like to redirect these talented engineers to bring similar launch-operation efficiency to the Starship program.

Great engineers are certainly a finite resource. And SpaceX faces fierce competition in the US space industry for talented engineers, with higher salaries offered by Blue Origin, and attractive alternatives such as Stoke Space, Rocket Lab, Firefly, and Relativity Space all recruiting.

The question is whether Musk would devote his Falcon engineering team solely to Starship. Perhaps not. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call in October, Musk made a striking comment while musing about how the company aimed to deploy 10 GW of compute (on Earth) in 2027.

“What we’ve done at SpaceX is we’ve taken a team that has been able to achieve a market share in mass to orbit that is almost 90 percent,” Musk said. That team, he added, “has been able to achieve results that are an order of magnitude greater than the rest of all competitors in space combined.” Now, he said, SpaceX was applying that same team to the deployment of terrestrial compute. They would not be sent to Starbase for Starship, in other words, but to places like Memphis, Tennessee.

“This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League,” Musk said. “It’s not fair. But the net result is being able to deploy power, cooling, and infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than anyone else and may at some point be faster than everyone else combined.”

So yeah.

SpaceX can do what it wants. But there are consequences, and some people at NASA are starting to wonder how serious SpaceX is about the Human Landing System contract it won from NASA in 2021. Landing on the Moon is wholly tangential to the company’s near-term AI future, and fulfilling the contract will almost certainly be a net negative from a financial perspective.

SpaceX, of course, says it is working assiduously on a lunar lander. And publicly, NASA officials say the company is a good partner. In an interview with Ars last week, the manager of the Artemis Program for NASA, Jeremy Parsons, said he regularly visits SpaceX facilities in Hawthorne, California, and Starbase, Texas. “Their management team is definitely committed to the lunar missions,” he said. Parsons credited the SpaceX engineers working on Starship as “some of the smartest individuals” he had ever met.

No one I have spoken to at NASA, both on and off the record, says SpaceX has given them a reason to believe the company will not eventually meet its Human Landing System commitments. And to date, SpaceX has had a remarkably good track record of delivering for NASA on its contracts. Nevertheless, the road ahead may be rocky in an era when SpaceX is pulling back from government involvement.

SpaceX has consistently told NASA it must get Starship flying orbital missions regularly. It has to get to full reusability, or nothing else matters. It has to do propellant transfer. All of that must come before finalizing the lander. And sure, it’s totally fair to say that the most important thing SpaceX can do for NASA right now is getting Starship to a very high flight rate. In SpaceX’s view, in a few years, Starship will be flying so often—the company recently told the Federal Aviation Administration it plans to launch 10,000 Starships a year by the 2030s—that fueling depots for missions to the Moon and Mars will be trivial.

Such a launch cadence surely would change everything, but nothing in aerospace ever happens as fast as one thinks or wants. And for now, the real issue is just how committed SpaceX is to the lander project and NASA’s competition with China. At SpaceX, projects deemed most important by leadership get the most resources. That is, the best engineers, the most software support, the most funding, and so on. Those projects are currently things like Starmind, the Colossus data center project in Memphis, and Starship engineering. It’s not the Human Landing System, multiple sources told Ars.

As SpaceX has struggled through the Starship test flight program, NASA has been waiting for an in-space fueling test, which has slipped its schedule many times. Testing propellant transfer and storage at a large scale is critical, and it has never been done in space. Successfully completing this test would reduce much of the risk for the kinds of refueling operations needed to send a fully loaded Starship to the Moon.

The latest target for such a test is “early” 2027, according to NASA and SpaceX. But this date seems aspirational. According to Parsons, the test requires one Starship to launch from Starbase in Texas and another to launch from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Starship has not yet flown from there. Presently, a debut Florida launch is not expected until at least January. According to Parsons, the in-orbit fueling test is the third launch planned from Florida.

Once SpaceX demonstrates in-orbit refueling, it could begin planning a campaign to send an uncrewed Starship to land on the Moon as a demonstration. How many tanker launches would this take? The internal estimate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center is “about 22” Starship launches, Ars reported last week. Musk followed that up by saying the actual number “will be more like 6 to 8.”

So what’s the truth? In the near term, given Starship’s lift capacity, a lunar landing will probably require about 20 launches, which is the most current publicly disclosed government planning figure. With improvements to Starship and Raptor engine performance, and as SpaceX gets a better handle on in-space refueling operations, that number will assuredly come down. So at some point in the future, it could be as low as six. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman appeared to confirm this last week when he characterized Musk’s estimate of six to eight refueling flights as the “ultimate potential end state” of Starship.

Unfortunately, to beat China back to the Moon by 2030, NASA can’t wait for Starship to reach its final form. If SpaceX were to fly a lunar demonstration in the next year or two, a necessary precursor to human landings, it probably would take something like 20 Starship launches. Starship has flown 14 times in the last three and a half years. Its flight rate will undoubtedly accelerate in the coming months, but even at a weekly launch cadence, fueling a Starship for a lunar landing would still require more than four months of dedicated launches.

Frankly, it’s difficult to envision SpaceX dedicating 20 Starships to a NASA mission anytime soon. The opportunity cost is enormous. Those same rockets could launch hundreds of revenue-generating Starlink V3 satellites into orbit. A single Starlink launch on Starship delivers the same amount of bandwidth as 10 Falcon 9 launches—bandwidth SpaceX can sell to customers for years to come. And as SpaceX expands into artificial intelligence, the company has even greater incentives to reserve Starship’s capacity for its own growing constellation of satellites.

And then there’s the financial burden. Let’s assume an unoptimized launch cost of $100 million for early Starship flights—still a phenomenally low number for a super heavy lift vehicle. At that price, a lunar landing campaign requiring 20 launches would cost approximately $2 billion in launch expenses alone. Recall that SpaceX’s original Human Landing System contract was valued at $2.89 billion and included both an uncrewed demo and crewed landing.

The actual cost of a single lunar landing mission remains uncertain, and some of the investments needed to fulfill the contract will benefit Starship more broadly. But the larger point is clear: NASA is asking SpaceX to devote substantial resources to a program that offers comparatively little financial upside at a time when the company’s own commercial ambitions are growing exponentially.

Imagine a world where SpaceX had gone all in on developing a lunar lander. Would the company be taking a different approach to the immense technical challenges of getting Starship to the Moon, perhaps with a stubby Starship variant? Would it be devoting more of its best engineers to the program? Would it consider using an expendable tanker Starship to reduce the total needed?

SpaceX very well might still get to the Moon in the next five years, and the company has enormous technical capacity. Its history suggests that when Musk makes something an overriding priority, things happen quickly. All it would take for SpaceX to go full throttle on a lunar Starship would be for Musk to text a technical leader at the company something like, “Do HLS.”

Last year, Ars asked Musk if it mattered to him that China gets back to the Moon before NASA with the Artemis Program.

“I think the United States should be aiming for Mars, because we’ve already actually been to the Moon several times,” he replied. “Yeah, if China sort of equals that, I’m like, OK, sure, but that’s something that America did 56 years ago.”

In November of last year, Ars posed a similar question to Blue Origin’s chief executive, Dave Limp. “We just want to help the US get to the Moon,” he said. “If NASA wants to go quicker, we would move heaven and Earth, pun intended, to try to get to the Moon sooner.”

Multiple NASA sources said Blue really is doing whatever it takes to help NASA and that what once appeared as a rocky relationship is now flourishing.

After SpaceX won a sole-source contract for the Human Landing System in 2021, Blue Origin sued NASA. This pressure, along with NASA’s desire for a second provider, led Congress to eventually add funding for a second lander. As with Starship, Blue Origin’s original design under this new contract also involved refueling operations in low-Earth orbit for the large Blue Moon Mark 2 vehicle.

As it became increasingly clear that China was on course to land humans on the Moon by or before 2030, Blue Origin’s large and ambitious Blue Moon lander did not serve NASA’s more immediate needs. It would take too long.

In 2025, Ars was first to report that Blue Origin might be able to develop a lunar landing system that involved a smaller version of the Blue Moon Mark 2 vehicle and multiple transfer stages based on the existing Mark 1 lander. This involved a significant redesign to the Blue Moon program, but critically, it removed the need for in-space refueling. Eventually, this became the new plan. Blue Origin, without any guarantee of new funding, changed its design when NASA needed something faster.

“I will tell you, they are absolutely fantastic partners,” Parsons, NASA’s Artemis manager, said of Blue Origin. “They have leaned forward at every step, and they are all in on the mission.”

NASA’s upcoming Artemis III mission is illustrative of the differences.

The mission is intended to test both Blue Origin and SpaceX’s lunar landers in space. Blue Origin is building a special “test” version of its Blue Moon lander to demonstrate a host of capabilities for NASA. After docking, the crew will exit the Orion spacecraft and spend time aboard the Blue Moon vehicle. By contrast, SpaceX is pulling a “ship off the line” of its Starship program for the flight. Orion will rendezvous and dock with Starship, but there will be no ingress into the vehicle and hence no life support equipment.

Earlier this year, NASA revealed a major new initiative to develop a Moon Base. Not long after, New Glenn exploded on its launch pad. In the aftermath, Blue Origin has moved with uncharacteristic speed to repair its launch pad to get New Glenn flying again, while investing $3 billion in Florida facilities to support a much higher launch cadence.

This matters because New Glenn is superseding Starship as the essential rocket powering NASA’s lunar ambitions.

Beyond the Human Landing System, there are myriad robotic elements of the Moon Base that need to get to the surface, and NASA has contracted with a host of US space companies to develop smaller cargo landers. Some of these providers are growing nervous about launch. At least two of these companies had “rough order of magnitude” estimates and other types of launch agreements with SpaceX for Falcon 9s to deliver elements of NASA’s Moon base later this decade. But in the last several weeks, SpaceX, the only company that can offer reliable launch dates, has told them it will no longer sell rides to the Moon.

This has sent shockwaves through the Artemis community. It is not the behavior of a partner being broadly supportive of NASA’s lunar efforts. These smaller lander companies now must hope that New Glenn can pick up the slack or a company like Relativity Space can bring its Terran R rocket to readiness quickly.

Ars pressed Parsons on how committed SpaceX really was to NASA’s lunar activities. For example, did he really believe SpaceX would be willing to sideline its profitable Starlink and Starmind launches for the extended period to support an Artemis landing? “It’s a fair question, especially as they have gone public,” he acknowledged.

For more than a decade, NASA more or less turned its spaceflight fortunes over to one billionaire. That partnership now appears to be unraveling, and there seems to be a growing sense that if the space agency is to achieve its considerable lunar ambitions in the next decade, it may need another billionaire to bail it out.

“This could end up being a very big opportunity for Blue Origin and Jeff Bezos, who would absolutely relish the role of coming to the country in its time of need,” said Davenport, the author who has written about the rocket billionaires. “Bezos has been public in saying he wanted to serve his country, particularly if it meant in doing it instead of SpaceX and Elon.”

Bezos, of course, is not doing this out of the goodness of his heart or because he bleeds red, white, and blue. He stands to gain Artemis customers, national security launch contracts, and commercial business. He is chasing SpaceX’s enormous valuation with his own space company. But no one thinks Bezos would pull his rockets off the market if NASA were desperate to get to the Moon.

The real question is whether Blue Origin can succeed. The company has a long, long list of things to achieve to make Artemis a reality, from rockets to landers to in-space operations. And for all the many billions of dollars Bezos has invested, Blue Origin has a short track record of execution. It has only ever launched three orbital missions.

Now it is being called on to spearhead the landing of humans on the Moon. On a rocket that recently blew up. Aboard a lander that doesn’t yet exist. At the 11th hour.

Meta shocked by $25B fine after N. M. refused to join multistate settlement

Ars Technica Long form October 22, 2026

Meta will appeal a ruling imposing the largest fine Mark Zuckerberg has ever seen.

Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws.

The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an $18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this year with attorneys general in nearly all states.

In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”

New Mexico had asked the court to impose even higher fines, up to $40 billion. The entire state of 2 million people were harmed by Meta’s conduct, Torrez argued, and it seemed dubious that Meta would make meaningful changes unless the penalty impacted Meta’s stock price.

Mathew found that the trial record—which showed that top leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, were aware that the company, then known as Facebook, was making misleading public representations—supported “the highest level of penalty allowed by the NM Unfair Practices Act.”

“The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public” and “took advantage of the public’s lack of knowledge respecting Facebook’s practices to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote.

To Mathew, it seemed that Meta made a choice to avoid transparency with users in a bid to capitalize on data they didn’t realize they were sharing and better compete with one of its main rivals, the platform then known as Twitter.

“The violations the jury found were not the product of a single misleading statement or isolated incident,” Mathew noted. “They arose from repeated public representations over more than 11 years, concerning multiple core aspects of Facebook’s platform and business.”

Meta had hoped that New Mexico’s penalty would be more in line with a $5 billion settlement the company made with the Federal Trade Commission to address the Cambridge Analytica fallout. At most, they expected to pay $3.4 billion, while arguing that anything more would be “unconstitutional,” AP News reported.

But Mathew said that the FTC settlement “cannot be viewed in a vacuum” while noting that so far, “penalties, consent agreements, and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices” since the Cambridge Analytica scandal was first exposed.

“To induce users to provide their personal information to Facebook, Facebook made many false promises respecting the security and control of that data over the course of more than a decade,” Mathew wrote.

In a press release, Torrez celebrated the ruling, calling it “a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country.”

“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said. “A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

A Meta spokesperson confirmed to Ars that the company plans to appeal. Legal experts told Reuters the company has a decent chance at slashing the fine on appeal based on constitutional claims. On top of likely claiming that the penalty is unconstitutional, Meta also feels that “this ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” the spokesperson said.

The eye-popping fine following the multistate settlement appears to be making the company uncomfortable, despite critics claims that New Mexico’s penalty is just a “drop in the bucket” for a company that makes $200 billion annually. On Thursday, the Verge highlighted Meta’s third-quarter earnings report, which showed the company paid close to $10 billion for the multistate settlement. Without that expense, Meta’s income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, the report said.

The high penalties come as Meta attempts to reboot its struggling AI strategy, and Meta appeared to signal to Donald Trump’s administration to possibly support its appeal by nodding to its AI wing in its statement opposing the ruling.

“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Meta’s spokesperson said. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”

Nidhi Hegde, executive director of a watchdog nonprofit called the American Economic Liberties Project, told AP News that Meta users want more enforcers willing to take the company to trial rather than settle matters in ways that the FTC settlement suggested weren’t genuine.

In his opinion, Mathew noted that the jury found that Meta internal messages and investigation results showed that “rather than seek to educate Facebook’s users… Zuckerberg chose instead to capitalize on that lack of understanding in order to manipulate users into sharing more of their personal information publicly.” In one message, Zuckerberg was found laying out a plan to deceive users, saying, “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”

The company also failed to notify users when apps misused their data, only flagging two of 2,000 unique apps associated with data misuse, Mathew said. Following its investigation, Meta’s “decision was deliberately made to narrow Facebook’s internal definition of data misuse so that Facebook would not have to notify as many people due to the operational burden of doing so,” he wrote.

Additionally, Facebook continued knowingly profiting off of pages with misinformation and hate speech, Mathew wrote. Internal research found “substantial amounts of misleading, false, and possibly false political, health, and science content,” with Meta documenting a “greater concentration of false content in top performing advertising content than in top performing Facebook content.”

Rather than share that research, Meta buried it, while also deceiving users in dozens of other ways, including by misrepresenting that the average Facebook users gets “equal treatment” to celebrities and influencers. While Meta claimed everyone was treated the same, one class of users received warning to remove violating content before strikes were applied and frequently got harmful or sketchy content decisions overturned in cases where most users would not.

Hegde told AP News that she thinks as Meta and other company’s AI products grow more popular, it will be increasingly important for states to remain watchful and protect residents from unknown harms.

“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” Hegde said. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”

Torrez vowed to keep watch in New Mexico and to continue using the blueprint from the Meta case to enforce consumer protection laws and prevent tech giants’ misuse of data.

“This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,” Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law. This outcome reinforces a fundamental principle, companies that do business in our state must follow our laws and respect the rights of our people.”

Review: Apple’s M6 iMac is pricey, but it’s still a good choice for a clean desk

Ars Technica Long form November 12, 2026

Apple’s M6 keeps the iMac current without shaking things up much.

The Apple Silicon iMac got its fourth refresh this month.

Every other Apple Silicon Mac has found a way to move forward over the last half-decade—we’ve gotten a more Pro design for the MacBook Pro, a mini-er design for the Mac mini, and a Mac Studio that has finally made Apple admit it doesn’t want to make the Mac Pro anymore.

But the Apple Silicon iMac has always been more interested in looking backward. It’s the thin, screen-on-a-stand iMac design by way of the original Bondi Blue G3 iMac. It’s a clean and pretty desktop computer, one I see all the time in small offices and on TV shows that depict small offices. We’re long past the days when it was Apple’s primary workstation computer.

So I wanted to write about this new iMac from the perspective of that entry-level iMac buyer, who chooses the iMac because it’s simple and then uses it until it breaks. What does a new iMac get you if you’re stepping up from the M1 model or comparing it against an older refurbished M4 model? Without any real external updates, what makes this iMac iteration interesting?

If you haven’t used an Apple Silicon-era iMac before, here’s a brief primer.

The new iMac is much thinner than the older aluminum Intel models. Its front is mostly one big 24-inch screen, surrounded on all sides by a relatively thick white bezel (I still wish black were at least an option, but Apple apparently doesn’t agree).

White bezel aside, it’s by far Apple’s most colorful computer. The iMacs ship with color-matched fronts, backs, stands, keyboards, mice, trackpads, and cables. Apple has tweaked the color offerings and changed the tints of each specific color a few times over the years, but the M6 iMac uses the same six color tints (plus silver) that the M4 iMac did.

The basic $1,499 iMac is essentially a MacBook Air in terms of ports—it has two Thunderbolt ports on the back and a headphone jack on the left side. Choosing this model also locks you into a lesser version of the Apple M6 with 10 CPU cores and 10 GPU cores instead of 12 of each, a maximum of 24GB of RAM, a minimum of 256GB of storage, and a maximum of 1TB. Its default keyboard doesn’t have Touch ID support, and the only way to get it is to buy the version with the built-in number pad, an $80 upsell.

The $1,699 version is the one to get if you still intend to use the iMac as a workstation. It includes the full-speed version of the M6 with all its CPU and GPU cores intact (though there are performance caveats here we’ll talk about later), plus options for 32GB of RAM and up to 2TB of storage. This version also includes four Thunderbolt ports on the back for connecting additional accessories. Both available keyboards on this version have Touch ID.

A 2.5 gigabit Ethernet port can be added to any iMac for $30. This port is located on the desktop’s power brick rather than the iMac itself, an elegant solution that keeps even a wired Internet connection hidden beneath your desk with the other cables. All iMacs also offer a VESA mount adapter option in place of the default stand at no extra charge.

I still really like the effect created by the color-matched keyboard, mouse/trackpad, and cables—even the white bezel complements the white keycaps and mouse. Just know you’re paying quite a lot for how the desktop looks. The $899 Mac mini is $800 cheaper than the iMac with the same chip, the same amount of RAM, and the same amount of storage. Sure, it would cost something to add a nice-looking 4K monitor, but not $800, even if you go for extra frills like a high refresh rate.

It’s fine that the iMac upcharges you for style and convenience. That’s the point of the computer. Just make sure that’s what you want to pay for.

Here are the basic specs for every entry-level iMac Apple has shipped, going all the way back to the last of the Intel models.

The iMac’s evolution has been slow and gradual during the Apple Silicon era. The computer has never gotten a base storage upgrade, and the base M4 and M6 models still only support a single external display (the upgraded models support two external displays, finally surpassing the old Intel model).

If you have any kind of Apple Silicon iMac and you’re happy with how it’s performing and you’re not hankering for more RAM or more displays, I don’t think the M6 model really adds anything worth upgrading for. It’s definitely faster, but even six years on, the Apple M1 remains perfectly serviceable for daily use, especially when it’s attached to 16GB of RAM.

And if you’re in the market for an iMac now, I think the M4 model still gets you the best bang for your buck if you can find one refurbished or on sale. That one still gets you a minimum of 16GB of RAM, Thunderbolt in all four ports for the four-port model, the 32GB RAM option, the nano-texture display option, and support for multiple external displays (again, in the four-port model).

The M6 iMac builds on that, and it comes with real performance benefits (more on that shortly). But the brightest dividing line in the Apple Silicon iMac model history is between the M3 and M4 model, not the M4 and M6 model. And that’s true despite the two-generation silicon upgrade.

A quick recap on the M6: a total of 12 CPU cores (two super cores, four performance cores, six efficiency cores), either 10 or 12 GPU cores, 16/24/32GB RAM options, and a doubled Neural Engine NPU with 32 cores instead of 16. For the iMac, the M6 also introduces some of the architectural tweaks introduced with the Apple M5, including the addition of neural accelerator hardware to the GPU cores. This boosts the speed of some kinds of local AI workloads compared to the M4, including MetalFX upscaling and frame generation in games.

The M6 in the Mac mini and the M6 in the 14-inch MacBook Pro both perform similarly within a roughly 28 W sustained power envelope. The version with 16GB of RAM will perform slightly worse in games and other workloads sensitive to memory bandwidth—the 16GB M6 offers 153 GB/s of memory bandwidth, and the 24GB and 32GB versions offer 170 GB/s. But that’s a pretty minor difference.

The iMac is slower than either of those two Macs, particularly in multi-core CPU benchmarks and graphics benchmarks, and the HandBrake video encoding test shows the likely culprit. The iMac’s M6 consumes an average of 18 W of power under sustained heavy load. It won’t throttle its speeds as aggressively as a MacBook Air because the iMac still includes an active cooling fan, but the reduced power envelope does mean that the Mac mini or MacBook Pro are 5 to 8 percent faster than the iMac in heavy multi-core CPU tasks and about 8 to 12 percent faster in graphics benchmarks.

One benefit of the smaller power envelope is that the iMac’s chip is even more power-efficient than the regular M6 and the iMac’s version of the M4, using much less power to do the same amount of work.

That still makes it a solid upgrade over the M4. The iMac’s M6 is 15 to 20 percent faster in our single-core CPU benchmarks, between 20 and 30 percent faster in multi-core CPU benchmarks, and between 20 and 40 percent faster in graphics benchmarks (the Blender GPU benchmarks do even better—they seem to like the neural accelerators in the M5 and M6 GPUs). Especially with 24GB or 32GB of RAM, it’s perfectly capable of being the heart of a multi-monitor workstation setup or a light photo/video editing rig.

The M6 iMac changes almost nothing about who the iMac is for, its position in Apple’s lineup, or what it’s technically capable of. It’s a box-ticking upgrade, and the box being ticked is “keep the insides up to date.”

That means today’s iMac is best for the same kinds of computer users it was good for in 1998: people who don’t want a laptop, people who need a friendly and approachable kiosk or office computer, and people who just want something pretty that doesn’t require a lot of fussing with screens or cables.

That’s the main thing I miss about being an iMac user. I like how my current Mac Studio desktop works, and I need flexibility and complexity in my specific setup to get the Mac and a gaming PC connected to all the same stuff. But despite my best efforts, the cable situation has always been a barely managed mess.

If someone you know has a cable management problem and doesn’t need the complexity, congratulations, you’ve found someone the iMac is for. I just wish Apple would use these kinds of pretty, saturated colors in a laptop or desktop that meets my needs, you know?

2026 iPad mini review: Maximizing the mini

Ars Technica Long form November 05, 2026

It’s more compelling than ever, but also more expensive.

The iPad mini has long felt like a niche product. It has earned a reputation as a quality tablet for people who want something small, comfortable, and portable, but its small screen and comparatively limited processing power have restricted its appeal, making it best suited to watching media or playing games.

With the 2026 version, the iPad mini is more competitive than ever. Its chip is current, its speakers are better, and, most impressively, it trades its 8.3-inch IPS screen for an 8.5-inch OLED that can hold its own against other premium tablets. There isn’t much more you can ask of an iPad this small.

But at just $50 less than the larger, more powerful iPad Air (11-inch), the iPad mini still has a hard time making a case for itself.

The most immediately noticeable change to the 2026 iPad mini is its display. At 0.2 inches larger than the 2024 iPad mini’s screen, the difference might not sound like much, but it has a meaningful impact on a tablet this small. Beyond providing a bigger view of photos, video content, and lengthy documents, the extra space makes it easier to work with multiple windows, giving you more room to view them and adjust their size and location.

One of our biggest complaints about the prior mini was its bezels, which felt large for a tablet of its size. This time, Apple managed to fit a larger screen in a slightly smaller tablet (7.69 × 5.22 × 0.21 inches and 0.56 pounds for the 2026 mini versus 7.69 × 5.3 × 0.25 inches and 0.65 pounds for the 2024 mini) by reducing the bezels by 24 percent. The result is a streamlined viewing experience that feels more modern and appropriate for a new Apple product.

And you’ll certainly want to watch content on the 2316 × 1512 OLED display, which packs 326 pixels per inch. OLED displays often lack the brightness of their LCD-LED counterparts, but the gap has narrowed in recent years. The new mini is brighter than its IPS-based predecessor, with Apple claiming full-screen brightness of up to 600 nits, compared to 500 nits on the previous model. It’s also much better suited to HDR content, with peak HDR brightness reaching 1,200 nits for highlights and a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1.

Since content consumption is arguably the mini’s strongest use case, it makes sense for Apple to focus on changes that enhance the viewing experience. Watching shows and movies feels as luxurious as possible on a screen this size, and the mini maximizes its display in nearly all the ways that matter.

I say “nearly” because the mini still has a 60 Hz refresh rate; 120Hz is limited to the iPad Pro. A 120 Hz refresh rate makes little difference when watching most shows or movies, but it can make some tasks, such as scrolling through long documents, look smoother. Still, the difference is less noticeable on a smaller screen.

Overall, the refresh rate didn’t feel like a drawback during regular use. Apple has gone a step further, noting that OLEDs typically have faster response times than IPS displays. That’s generally true when discussing gray-to-gray (GtG) response times. However, moving picture response time (MPRT) can be a better indicator of potential persistence-related motion blur, including during scrolling, because it measures how long an image remains visible on the display, contributing to blur as your eyes track moving content. GtG, by contrast, measures how quickly individual pixels transition between shades. Slower pixel transitions can create motion artifacts such as ghosting.

According to Blur Busters’ MPRT Indicator, the mini has an MPRT of about 17 ms, about what I’d expect from a 60 Hz IPS display. Anyone who needs a high-refresh screen will still want to look at the Pro series.

One feature the mini borrows from the iPad Pro but that other iPads lack is the option for nano-texture glass, which is designed to reduce glare. It costs an extra $100 and is only available on the 256GB and 512GB versions of the mini.

The 2024 mini debuted with a year-old chip, but this year’s model sports Apple’s latest mobile processor. The 2026 mini makes a considerable jump from the A17 Pro, a 3-nanometer, iPhone 15 Pro-era chip from 2023, to the A20 Pro, a 2-nanometer chip that debuted in the new iPhone 18 Pro.

The newer chip has 50 percent more memory bandwidth, which significantly boosts graphics performance. It’s also up to 60 percent faster.

I tested the 512GB version of the iPad Mini, which, like the 128GB and 256GB versions, features a seven-core integrated GPU. The 512GB model, however, gets a bump from five CPU cores to six and doubles the number of 16-core Neural Engines from one to two, promising better performance in on-device AI applications, such as image generation.

I don’t expect many people to run particularly intensive workloads on a tablet this small. Still, tasks such as photo editing, light video editing, and juggling many open applications felt smooth. The performance boost makes the iPad mini much more powerful than the standard iPad 11, which uses an A16 processor. The iPad Pro (M5) and the iPad Air (M4), however, remain better equipped for demanding workloads such as video editing and 3D rendering.

Siri AI is still in beta, so we won’t cover that in this review. But the tablet supports features under the Apple Intelligence umbrella, including various generative AI capabilities. Tasks like removing objects from photos, changing a photo’s perspective, or extending a photo’s borders should take roughly the same amount of time on the 512GB iPad mini as they do on the iPhone 18 Pro. In my experience, that’s usually about 20 seconds.

The mini is surprisingly loud. Its speakers are powerful enough to make TV dialogue easy to hear, even with my noisy heater running in the background.

The tablet has two woofers designed to deliver higher volume and stronger bass than the prior mini. A pair of custom-designed tweeters between the tablet’s glass and aluminum enclosure are intended to improve the clarity of higher frequencies.

You won’t get the deepest bass or the crispest high notes, but the speakers surpassed my expectations when playing music. I didn’t immediately feel the need to connect the iPad to dedicated speakers.

And the mini pulls this off without any visible speaker holes in its chassis.

That detail helped the mini earn the first IP67 rating for an iPad. The Ingress Protection rating means the device is “dust-tight” and “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water,” according to the International Electrotechnical Commission.

The 2026 mini has the same 12 MP front and back cameras as its 2024 predecessor, but the front-facing camera has moved from one of the shorter sides to one of the longer sides. This took some getting used to for FaceTiming and selfies. Holding the tablet in portrait orientation now places you off-center in the frame, while holding it in landscape mode to FaceTime on the go quickly became uncomfortable. The new location was fine when I could sit down and prop the tablet on a stand.

Another addition is the back camera’s Adaptive True Tone flash, which Apple markets as a way to quickly scan documents. When the Camera app identifies a document, such as a piece of paper or a book, it automatically adjusts which of the camera’s LEDs light up to minimize shadows and produce clearer text.

When I used the tablet’s camera to photograph text on both a piece of paper and a book, it quickly used machine learning to identify them as documents. A pop-up appeared, offering the option to “Scan Document”; selecting it allowed me to automatically take a picture of just the document. It’s not a feature many people will use regularly, but when the need arises, it makes capturing a sharp, detailed image of text considerably easier.

Additional upgrades include a move from Wi-Fi 6E to Wi-Fi 7 and from Bluetooth 5.3 to Bluetooth 6. These capabilities come from the introduction of Apple’s N1 wireless networking chip, which also adds Thread support. Apple launched the N1 last year with the iPhone 17-series and iPhone Air.

The iPad mini also has the C2 cellular modem that Apple unveiled last month in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. For those who rely on cellular service, it’s reassuring that the tablet uses the same technology here as some of Apple’s best phones.

Although it’s not an upgrade, it’s impressive that the new mini has the same battery life as its predecessor, despite having a smaller chassis and a larger screen. The mini also gains support for fast charging.

With the 2026 model, the iPad mini feels less like a compromise. Its larger OLED screen, current-generation processor, more durable build, and better speakers make it feel more modern and competitive than the 2024 version.

These improvements come with a pricing predicament, though. Today, the iPad mini starts at $699 for the 128GB version, putting it just $50 below the 11-inch iPad Air (M4) at its lowest configuration. The 512GB mini I tested, which came with a more powerful A20 Pro chip, is $999. In 2024, the iPad mini started at $499, and the iPad Air 11-inch (M2) started at $599.

The mini’s OLED screen is a standout, but the Air remains a better choice for those seeking a balance between power and portability. Its more capable processor and still-excellent, larger IPS display make it more versatile. It also offers comparable battery life, though it lacks fast charging. Meanwhile, the Pro series remains the best option for demanding workloads and extensive multitasking. The Mini is much more capable of handling serious work, multitasking, and editing than it was before, but it still isn’t the best iPad for these purposes.

Despite narrowing the gap with other tablets, the mini is still a niche product. The biggest reason to pick it over other iPads is if you truly want the smallest device, primarily for content consumption. My preference for devices that are easy to handle without straining my smaller hands or weighing me down, combined with my appreciation of high-end displays, love of streaming, and interest in using secondary screens to boost productivity, confirms that this niche has an audience. Many of Apple’s improvements make the mini more enjoyable for these users.

Beyond comparisons with the rest of the iPad lineup, though, the mini makes the most of its small design. Apple fit just about everything it could into a device that’s somehow even smaller than its predecessor.

For anyone looking for an ultraportable tablet primarily for enjoying content on an excellent, high-end display, the mini is a markedly better device than it used to be.

From impulse purchase to pocket studio: The M-Vave FM-1

Ars Technica Long form October 26, 2026

M-Vave’s cheap FM-1 pocket synth has exploded as a community firmware playground.

The M-Vave FM-1 is exactly the kind of device I have a weakness for. I may not have an intended use for the frequency-modulation synthesizer, but when a low price meets a high coolness factor, I’m powerless to keep it out of my cart.

Initially billed as a pocket cousin of the famous Yamaha DX7 synthesizer, the FM-1 is a bargain at only $59.72 after fees. At release, it was a cool device that did what it said on the box, but not much else.

But in July, some intrepid tinkerers on Reddit’s r/synthdiy board began reverse-engineering the FM-1’s stock firmware to expand the device’s abilities. By September, custom firmware began appearing. We’re not even through October, and there are already more community firmware projects available to install on the FM-1 than I could ever hope to cover.

I decided to check a few of them out. And just in case you were wondering: Yes, it plays Doom.

On October 17, M-Vave announced FM1 Open, a software package that encourages FM-1 owners to develop custom firmware for the synth-turned-whatever-else-you-can-imagine. Alongside the FM1 Open package came an SDK, a browser-based workbench, and version 15 of the stock firmware, now an open platform you can flash and build on. The unit’s 27 physical piano keys and modest 1.54-inch TFT display lend themselves well to a host of projects, musical or otherwise.

Normally, when an enthusiast community reverse-engineers a closed device, an official patch quickly follows. M-Vave has taken the opposite approach, though. The application source is published under GPLv3, and the company even includes an in-browser emulator to test custom firmware prior to flashing actual hardware. There’s a caveat, however: The underlying synth engine that powers the stock FM-1 package is still distributed as a closed binary, so it’s the application layer of the stack that’s actually open. I don’t think that diminishes M-Vave’s gesture toward the community, but it’s worth noting.

Before you rush to AliExpress, be aware that flashing custom firmware comes with risks. The JieLi chip powering the FM-1 keeps firmware in a single flash bank, so an interrupted update can leave the device in a difficult-to-recover state. As long as the flashing process completes without interruption, you should be fine. But nothing is foolproof, and there’s always a risk of bricking a device if something goes wrong.

Flashing will also wipe all information on the device. Before you try to load a new firmware package on the synth, back up your saved projects and settings because they will disappear. I was starting from a blank stock canvas, so there was no real risk.

The unit I received was running stock v14 firmware, and community guides repeatedly warn users to update to the stock v15 firmware before attempting to install custom firmware. Guess who didn’t listen? I blindly assumed that since I’d just received my FM-1, it would be running the latest firmware package (v16 now). I was wrong.

Caught in the excitement, I tried to flash Doom directly onto the v14 firmware package, and the installation failed about 80 percent through. Still, it wrote something. The synth worked, but the device stopped speaking the same language as the installers. Thankfully, M-Vave anticipated careless users like me and thoughtfully included a “force-flash” tool in the FM1 Workbench. It restored my unit to stock v15 in about 10 seconds, saving me a huge headache.

The lesson is simple: Always check your current firmware version.

The development scene around the FM-1 is exploding, and new options are appearing all the time. You can browse the listings to see what you might like to try, and a community tip from the fm1-custom-fw GitHub offers some good advice:

While not an absolute hard rule, there is a prominent community recommendation to avoid flashing one custom firmware directly over another. To minimize bricking risks, some users suggest rolling back to the official stock firmware (v15) via M-VAVE’s official updater first, and only then flashing the next custom firmware build. Alternatively, you can use TransitFM1—a dedicated lightweight bridge firmware by Quixotic7 designed with crash-guarded boot stubs and stock V15 identity emulation to safely transition between custom builds.

Some other tips I picked up along the way from community discussions and my own mistakes:

Here are some projects to try.

What better way to measure the value of any electronic device than asking, “will it run Doom”?

The FM-1 already has several Doom-related projects up and running. Playing on a 240 x 240 display with mini piano keys will never be my preferred way to take down demons with a shotgun, but that doesn’t make it any less cool to see the game running on a $60 synthesizer clone. It’s a novelty, but the clone version played surprisingly well. The short draw distance means enemies occasionally pop out of nowhere, but who doesn’t love a jump scare while demon hunting?

You can explore community Doom options through the fm1-editor directory.

While the stock firmware aims to re-create the Yamaha DX7 experience, Melodee takes its cues from the mid-’80s Casio CZ-1, a full-featured synthesizer that uses phase distortion to create a sound modern artists are still chasing. Melodee comes with four engines: a CZ-1 emulator, a DX7-style engine, a percussion engine for the 808s, and my personal favorite, a Commodore 64 SID sound chip emulator.

As a child of the 8-bit era, I’ve always had a soft spot for the amazing soundtracks built around the technological limits of the day. Composing chiptunes always seemed like an interesting hobby, but I never had the right tools. Now, thanks to Melodee, I have a pocketable chiptune keytar I can take anywhere.

Want to re-create that classic Cash Money sound on a $60 budget? The FM-1 now has you covered—this could be your chance to become the next Mannie Fresh.

This is where a capable device becomes the deal of the year. Felucca is the foundation for many other community firmware projects, transforming the FM-1 into a true multi-engine synth. The stock firmware lets you select different instruments, but you can play only one at a time. Felucca runs independent instruments simultaneously, letting you create a full-band sound all by yourself.

Felucca includes more than a dozen sound engines, from phase distortion to virtual analog, plus a built-in sampler. Other highlights include a RAW in-browser web editor that makes arranging tracks less painful than working on the FM-1’s tiny screen, and a full multi-track pattern sequencer built into the device. If you want to make music, this is a great place to start.

SLOOP is the FM-1’s groovebox solution. Cards on the table: Before writing this article, I wasn’t familiar with what a groovebox was. In a nutshell, it’s a self-contained music studio that can be operated without a PC. SLOOP turns the FM-1 from an instrument you play into one you compose with. You program drums and bass on a grid, chain loops together, and let the machine keep the beat going while you layer other sounds on top.

SLOOP adds drum machines and synth layers to the FM-1, running on Felucca’s sound engines. The result is a legitimate eight-track, battery-powered beat maker that fits in your pocket. Unlike Felucca, SLOOP is designed more for live performance, letting you build and stack layers of sound as you go. I didn’t always fully understand how I arrived at the results I produced in SLOOP, but I was having too much fun to care.

After exploring some of the available custom firmware packages, I decided to take my own advice and try Felucca as a starting point for actual recording. I connected the FM-1 to my PC using the same USB connection I’d previously used for flashing. Audacity recognized Felucca immediately, and I was able to select it as a recording device. From there, I could select any instrument or effect on the device and record it live over USB to Audacity tracks.

That’s all well and good if you’re sitting at a desk with a PC, but what if inspiration strikes while you’re out and about? That’s where Felucca’s self-contained recording process shines.

Creating music entirely on the FM-1 was more intuitive than I expected. Once I pulled up the Felucca controls cheat sheet, the process was smooth: use the Algorithm knob to switch between recording tracks and Presets to switch instruments. From there, I could build and layer my creation track by track.

I put together a four-track beat loop after about 15 minutes of fiddling with the firmware. I just felt my way around in the dark, auditioning sounds and slipping them in wherever I thought they fit. It was about as simplistic as it gets, but with some time and practice, I think I could churn out something worthwhile. If it was this straightforward for me, just imagine what someone with actual musical talent could achieve.

I’ll admit that my fingers were occasionally too big for the task. The FM1’s soft-touch keys feel great, but my index finger sometimes slipped off the intended note and onto an adjacent key. It’s not a dealbreaker, but there were a few times I had to retry a part due to hitting a wrong note.

Since there doesn’t appear to be an on-device export function, transferring the track to my PC was as simple as opening Audacity and hitting record while playing a beat on the FM-1. I retained live control throughout recording, too. Toward the end of the sample below, you can hear me fading out the audio by turning down the master volume knob. The same approach would let you weave any number of live modulations into a recording. You can hear my modest attempt at a quick beat below.

The FM-1 is the type of technology I love. I’m the furthest thing from a professional musician, but the price is low enough and the device is versatile enough that I can play around without feeling guilty about a $1,500 synth setup gathering dust in the corner.

My 10-year-old has been taking piano lessons for a few years now and has clearly inherited my urge to tinker with tech. The FM-1 could be the perfect holiday gift he never knew he needed. I’ll probably order another one for him since I still want to play with mine. At this price, I don’t have to sweat it.

M-Vave didn’t send this unit for review; checkout curiosity just got the better of me. I’ve since ordered the company’s SMC-PAD sampler, too, but that’s another article for another day.

Would I buy the FM-1 again tomorrow? In a beat.

DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won’t want to

Ars Technica Long form October 19, 2026

A primer on the joys and pains of building your own head-mounted display.

Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro.

But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.

That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.

I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.

As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)

That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150. The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines, I thought it sounded kind of fun.

That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.

The best starting place is Relativty VR. This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.

But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD, Project North Star, and the full-body tracking SlimeVR. There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.

A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.

The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders—Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.

Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.

Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.

The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.

Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.

You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.

My total spend for all that came to just under $180.

Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.

I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.

You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.

Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.

Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.

Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.

Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.

As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.

Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.

You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.

That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.

This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in there.

This is not what you should do. The exposed LCDs are extremely fragile, and by clipping them in, I managed to break both. The small amount of pressure required was enough to shatter them, and the damage was invisible until I turned them on.

Given that, I highly recommend modifying those boxes, either by printing them without the clips or by breaking them off after the print is complete. I used a few strips of thin painter’s tape to hold mine in place.

With all the wires jammed into place, I screwed the headset together, stuck on the face pad, threaded on the head strap, and proceeded to spend about five minutes trying to get a comfortable fit. I never quite succeeded.

I booted into SteamVR’s living lounge space and was immediately discombobulated. For one thing, I was staring straight at the floor. For another, turning my head just sent the view spinning in different directions in a way that quickly threatened nausea.

I had forgotten to recalibrate the headset after mounting all the components, and my cut-rate IMU was now oriented differently than it had been when it was on my workbench.

After recalibrating and a little more firmware fiddling, I got back into SteamVR’s setup room and could tell I still had a problem. Holding my head perfectly still, I could see the perspective slowly spinning.

Additionally, the IMU axes seemed slightly crossed, so the perspective change didn’t quite match my head movement. I verified the IMU was mounted correctly in the case and recalibrated a few times with no improvement.

I soldiered on, booting into iRacing, my favorite SteamVR-compatible racing sim. Before I was even out of the pits, my perspective was drifting. I mapped the recenter view command to a button on my steering wheel, and had to reach for it quite often.

Still, the image quality was not nearly as bad as I expected. Those cheap plastic lenses work surprisingly well, and though I could make out the pixels on the displays (the dreaded “screen door” effect of VR), it didn’t bother me. Brightness and contrast were more than adequate, and the refresh rate of 60 Hz was enough for casual practice.

But sensor drift and headset comfort were real issues. Without a proper cable-routing solution, the headset kept tugging to one side, and despite the padding, it was smashing my nose and cheeks.

I’ve done hourslong endurance races in multiple mass-market VR headsets. After 15 minutes in this one, I was ready to quit.

My total outlay for this project was $239.93. But that includes the extra $62 I had to spend on a second set of displays. Avoid that expensive gaffe, and you’re looking at around $180 in components.

That makes it roughly half the cost of a Meta Quest 3S, one of the cheapest headsets on the market right now. That’s a substantial savings, but I’d certainly recommend that most people pay the extra. The tracking issues in my headset are maddening, the image quality is middling at best, and this is far and away the least comfortable headset I’ve ever worn.

All that can be fixed, though. Some projects use a MinIMU-9 IMU, which looks miles more accurate and is less likely to be faked, but it’s also substantially more expensive at $35. You can also step up to higher-quality LCDs or even tiny OLED panels that come with all the color and contrast you could ever want. There are options for onboard battery packs, wireless adapters, and of course you can spend as much time as you like designing an ultra-comfortable housing for it all.

But even if you ignore the time commitment, once you start adding those upgrades, you’re not far from the cost of that Quest, a far-from-perfect headset that still works effortlessly and comfortably out of the box.

As always with these projects, it depends on what you want. If you just want a cheap, easy, reliable headset for your next-gen immersive gaming fix, this probably isn’t it.

If, however, you want a fun project that will help you appreciate the industrial design required to make a good-looking and comfortable wearable device, this could be it. I learned a lot and, despite the frustrations, I’m glad I embarked on this journey.

That said, while I’ll keep tinkering and likely throw a few more upgrades at this thing, I can’t see it replacing my other headset for regular racing duties, deprecated though it may be.
