Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:34:58 GMT

At least 74 countries were affected by the Microsoft outage which was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, all experienced "connectivity problems", the company said.

As of early Friday afternoon (GMT), Microsoft was reporting improvements, with email queues "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, the disruption was widespread. Here is what happened around the world.

In the US, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico their work had been halted by the outage.

"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems.

OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.

Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.

Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.

The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.

"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."

In Canada, a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.

The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.

Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.

Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers might not be able to receive emails about their trips because of the outage.

Disruptions were also reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.

In Japan, some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.

"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times.

The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.

Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".

Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.

In the Philippines, the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".

In India, the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.

People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.

"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.

Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.

Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.

China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.

Australia's spy and federal police agencies were affected by the outage, though officials suggested the impact was minimal.

"The impact that they are dealing with is very much on email system," the head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, Mike Burgess, told reporters.

Other Australian public service providers also confirmed they had been affected by the outage, but similarly said this was mostly limited to emails, and the BBC understands there were no major impacts across New South Wales' primary services in health, education, transport, and emergency services.

European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.

Speaking to the same news agency, the head of Germany's BSI cybersecurity agency, Claudia Plattner, said the country's authorities had not been affected because they did not rely on Microsoft 365 services.

However, Reuters reported that Germany's national rail operator, Deutsche Bahn, was having difficulties sending out timetables for diverted trains due to the outage.

Plattner added the disruption was "affecting the whole world". "It is a global disruption that spans a vast number of data centres – stretching from Asia right across to the US, via Europe," she said.

In Antalya, Turkey, advisers and officials attending the UN Climate Change Conference, Cop31, were left frustrated by the outage.

James Young, a climate change adviser at the Inuit Circumpolar Council, the organisation which represents around 180,000 Inuit people living in the Arctic, told Reuters the council relied on emails and Microsoft Teams to communicate across several countries.

"It's just been really frustrating and challenging to maintain contact with our colleagues and to be able to effectively participate here," he said. "I think our dependence on technology leaves us vulnerable to situations like this."

In the UK, GPs, police and pharmacies were among services affected.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.

Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.

"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."

Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa were unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.

However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.

One winemaker in South Africa said almost his entire business had been brought to a "standstill" by the Microsoft outage.

"It's incredibly frustrating," Peter Pentz added. "We export a lot, so communication with exporters in Europe has come to a standstill."

Order processing, dispatch, communications and even "critical production work" were halted, he said, as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Eight sentenced to jail over Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili brawl

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:15:52 GMT

Merab Dvalishvili (left) has won 21 of his 27 professional fights

Eight people have received prison sentences for their part in a mass brawl involving MMA fighters Usman Nurmagomedov and Merab Dvalishvili at a hotel in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.

A video of the incident appeared to show Russian Nurmagomedov slapping former UFC bantamweight champion Dvalishvili after approaching the Georgian from behind.

Fighting then broke out between the two and members of their teams, with Abu Dhabi police later confirming the incident led to 10 arrests being made.

According to a social media post by Abu Dhabi's judicial department, all 10 defendants have been convicted for their part in the brawl.

A report by Abu Dhabi news outlet the National, external went into more detail, adding that six of the defendants were sentenced to six months in prison, fined £62,000 each and ordered to be deported after completing their sentences.

It added they have been convicted for "disturbing public security, causing panic and endangering lives".

Two others were given the same punishment, but for "violating privacy by using information technology to film and publish footage of the brawl".

The remaining two defendants were fined £10,200 each for "disturbing public security and assaulting others".

None of the defendants have yet been named, but Real American Freestyle (RAF) co-founder Chad Bronstein says Dvalishvili has been released from custody.

"I'm pleased to share that Merab Dvalishvili is back with us in Abu Dhabi," Bronstein said in a statement.

"We would like to express our sincere appreciation to the relevant authorities in Abu Dhabi for their professionalism and support.

"We remain focused on moving forward and are pleased to have Merab back with us."

BBC Sport has asked Abu Dhabi's judicial department for confirmation.

Dvalishvili, 35, is scheduled to compete at the RAF event in the United Arab Emirates on Saturday against Brazilian Marlon Moraes.

Dvalishvili released a video after the incident calling Nurmagomedov, 28, and his team "snakes" as he received treatment on his bloodied face.

Nurmagomedov is in Abu Dhabi to support his brother Umar, who was set to compete against American Urijah Faber at Saturday's event.

However, Umar has been replaced in the bout by Dvalishvili's team-mate Saba Lazishvili, who was also involved in the mass brawl but appears to have been released from custody.

Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili's teams had a previous altercation at a RAF event in July, which UFC champion Islam Makhachev - a close friend and training partner of the Nurmagomedovs - suggested led to Wednesday's brawl.

Nurmagomedov is the PFL lightweight champion but is out of contract after winning his last bout with the organisation in July.

He has been heavily linked with a switch to the UFC but on Friday the promotion's president Dana White said he had not spoken to the Russian.

White then called the altercation "ridiculous" and "stupid", and referred to the participants as "a bunch of idiots".

Man jailed for grooming at least 70 girls online

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:10:27 GMT

A man who groomed at least 70 girls and manipulated them into sending sexually explicit videos and images of themselves has been sentenced to 30 years in prison.

Bilal Kazi, 27, targeted his victims - aged between 10 and 17 - using apps including Snapchat, Wink and Roblox between August 2021 and August 2025.

Kazi, a student from India who was studying at the University of Chester, posed as a 14-year-old white British teenage boy and made his victims believe they were in a relationship with him.

He was jailed after pleading guilty to 37 charges including making indecent images, blackmail and inciting a child to engage in sexual activity.

Kazi must serve a minimum of 20 years in prison before being eligible for parole and will be on the sex offenders register for life.

Once eligible for parole he will be on licence for eight years.

In a personal impact statement read out at Chester Crown Court earlier, one victim said she had struggled with anxiety as Kazi, who later moved to Birmingham, had "taken away a sense of privacy and security".

"I am doing my best to move forward but the effects are still with me," she said.

"The harm caused is not limited to the time events took place - they continue to affect my daily life."

The court heard that some of the victims had attempted suicide, struggled with anxiety and developed eating disorders.

One victim, who was 13 years old when Kazi first contacted her, said he took her "innocence away".

"I hope one day I can get on with my life," she said.

The court heard how Kazi often used the fake name of "Reece" and provided a false photograph of a boy - who has not been identified - to aid his deception.

He would then demand they sent him progressively more intimate content.

The court heard if any of the victims were reluctant to send images he would tell them it was "what people do when they love each other".

If the victims refused, he would then threaten to "leak" the images that had already been sent to him or recorded by himself covertly on Snapchat to their friends and family.

In some cases, Kazi hacked into victims' social media accounts, shared the content with their friends and published the pictures on social media.

In one exchange, a victim said she felt "uncomfortable" sharing explicit photographs of herself, adding: "I don't want to do it again."

Kazi replied: "That's fine w me" - before revealing to the victim that he had a secret "back up" of images she had already sent him.

In another exchange with a victim over Snapchat, Kazi posed as "Reece" to ask for photographs of a victim in her underwear.

Kazi then sent a follow-up message asking the victim to share her live location with him on the app.

The investigation into Kazi's crimes began after a victim came forward to Derbyshire Police in December 2021.

The victim explained that she started speaking to Kazi on Snapchat when she was 13, believing him to be the same age.

In May 2022, the investigation was passed to Cheshire Constabulary, which said 180 possible victims had been identified in the initial investigation.

Kazi had left Chester - and the university - but was later arrested at Heathrow Airport when he was re-entering the country on 21 July 2023.

He was subsequently charged with 39 offences and pleaded guilty in July 2026 to 37 of the charges, with two left to lie on file.

He has also been charged by West Midlands Police with a further eight offences committed while on police bail for the Cheshire investigation.

Cheshire Police said these offences were considered as part of his overall sentence.

Judge Stephen Everett said Kazi was a sexual predator who took advantage of "what appears to be a lack of proper security on social media sites".

"It is incomprehensible to me why any person would do what you did to those little girls," the court heard.

"This was bad enough, but when one learns of all the other images you demanded for your deviant sexual desires, we will never know how many victims there were.

"Children who believed they were safe in their own homes - and by your gross misuse of social media - you took away all of that safety, all of that comfort."

The judge said it was difficult to find any mitigating factors and said he doubted Kazi's remorse.

"You are a very dangerous person," he said.

"In a sophisticated way, you got into the minds of young people and got them to do things that were totally alien to them."

Talking about one victim, Everett said: "She won't look back on her childhood with any great pleasure - she will look on it totally blighted at what this fiend did to her."

He added: "These are not just pictures on a computer these are young lives that have been blighted."

Det Con Georgia Hughes, from Cheshire Police, said Kazi had not shown any remorse.

"The girls targeted by Kazi were young and vulnerable," she said.

"For many, their interactions with him were their first experience of what they believed to be a romantic relationship.

"Exploiting that trust, Kazi manipulated them into believing that his behaviour was normal.

"Many lived in constant fear of what he would do if they failed to comply with his demands, and some have carried that fear with them for years.

"What should have been important formative years have instead been overshadowed by the trauma of Kazi's abuse."

Speaking on online safety, Sgt Ross Peel said the force's message to parents was to "speak to your children and take an interest in the apps and platforms they are using".

"The potential for online offending is vast," he said.

"And offenders can target children from anywhere in the world.

"By educating yourselves and your children about online safety and the risks associated with communicating with people they do not know online, you can help protect them."

Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:53:50 GMT

The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:40:31 GMT

Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".

That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.

But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.

"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.

"Our proposals were almost laughed at.

"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."

Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.

Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.

This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.

After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.

But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

And what of Putin?

At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.

You can see why.

The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.

And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.

And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.

Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.

But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of UK knife attack

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:51:24 GMT

A former Hamas bodyguard, wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to murder Jewish people, has been found guilty of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his UK home.

Mohammed Alfatih, previously known as Mohammed Naim, was regularly seen acting as a bodyguard for a former leader of Hamas in 2006. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.

The 40-year-old was found guilty by majority verdict of unlawfully wounding a bailiff who had come to repossess his wife's car, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of wounding with intent.

Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terror unit at the moment he attacked the bailiff in Birmingham last year.

The son of a senior Hamas official, he could not be named during his trial due to reporting restrictions.

During the trial, footage was shown of Alfatih brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in the suburb of Kings Heath and trying to stab the bailiff as he drove away.

He told the court he chased the victim across the street to scare him away after his wife was asked to settle her debts of more than £2,250 linked to unpaid parking fines.

Her car had been clamped by the enforcement officer, who was involved in a struggle inside Alfatih's terraced home.

Jurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group Hamas or his work as a bodyguard to its now-deceased former leader Ismail Haniyeh.

But it can now be revealed that while detained for the attack in Birmingham, he was re-arrested when authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged gun plot to attack Jewish targets there.

It is alleged Alfatih was an organiser and was involved in the movement of weapons.

German authorities also allege he had pre-recorded a video wearing a balaclava and sunglasses claiming the attack was planned on behalf of the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of Hamas. The alleged attack was prevented after a tip-off from the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad.

Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK.

During his evidence, Alfatih did not mention Hamas but told the court he had been tortured for 25 days while detained in Egypt in 2010.

The father-of-four, an IT worker, failed in a legal application to try to get the wounding charges thrown out on the grounds of prejudicial media coverage about the investigation in Germany.

During the two-week trial at Birmingham Crown Court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.

Bailiff Kevin Bucknall was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment, but the defendant had pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.

Alfatih told jurors it had happened a day after he had learned one of his brothers had been killed in Gaza.

He also said while giving evidence that traumatic experiences in his past included being shot and injured on two different occasions.

"I just want to be as honest as I can," he told the jury.

"I don't think I was even in my full mind. I didn't intend anything other than him moving away.

"I wasn't anything more than terrified."

Defence barrister Kate O'Raghallaigh said Alfatih had a heightened perception of danger, triggered by fear and desperation he had previously experienced.

Jurors deliberated for more than six hours over three days before convicting him, with Alfatih heard mumbling to himself as the verdicts were returned.

He has been in custody since the knife attack and now faces sentencing in Birmingham on 11 January, as well as separate extradition proceedings at Westminster Magistrates' Court.

The BBC understands that when Alfatih went by the name of Naim, he enrolled in a VIP protection course and was selected to accompany Haniyeh on trips to Egypt and other countries between 2006 and 2008. However, he was later removed from the role due to his behaviour.

The second son of former Hamas health minister Bassem Naim, he later spent time in Malaysia, Qatar and Turkey before arriving in Britain.

Following his conviction, a government source said it was "staggering" that he was granted asylum and later given citizenship.

A Home Office spokesperson added Hamas was a proscribed terrorist organisation and the government condemned "those who choose to support its activities and further its aims".

Additional reporting by Josh Sandiford

Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:49:30 GMT

This video can not be played

England become world champions for third time

Sharks and ladders played their part in England's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup success.

As they chased success in Australia, they had a ladder in team meetings to help them visualise their route to the trophy - spray painting a rung gold with each victory.

And they spent time comparing themselves to lifeguards and sharks.

It was all part of coach Tom Coyd's masterplan, which boiled down to one thing - taking an aggressive approach.

It worked. On Friday, they beat France 50-38 in the World Cup final in Wollongong, to defend the trophy they won in Manchester four years ago.

Not that Coyd ever used the word 'defend'. He has steered clear of that term since England lifted the trophy in November 2022. For four years, he has wanted his team to have a more attacking mindset in the pursuit of back-to-back world titles.

His team were positive from the off at this tournament, amassing 386 points across the group stage and semi-finals while conceding just 68.

And his approach ultimately ensured that England became the first nation to win the Wheelchair World Cup three times.

"I think your reality is the story that you tell yourself," Coyd said. "And the narrative that we felt might be upon us coming in was that we are here to defend and we are here to retain.

"We found that framing to be defensive, to be a bit passive - and knowing that we've been world number one since November 2022, we wanted to come in with an attacking mindset and with a hunter's mindset.

"If we had not spent the last four years talking about defending the World Cup, we weren't going to spend the last three weeks [at this tournament] talking about it either.

"We wanted to prime the group to be forward thinking, to attack the attack when we didn't have the ball - and when we did have the ball, to be a shark smelling blood in the water."

Across the World Cup finals of 2013, 2017 and 2022, the game's two powerhouse nations had been separated by a total of only 10 points - two in the first match, and four in the following two.

However, on the western coast of Australia - around 70 miles south of where England won the inaugural competition in Sydney back in 2008 - Coyd's group of players served up an exceptional display.

Having initially forged ahead, England then fought back from a 22-10 deficit before powering to victory against Cyril Torres' uncompromising French side.

"I think the way they executed tonight was just outstanding," Coyd added.

"I don't think France have moved backwards. If anything, they looked hungrier than I've ever seen them.

"But the rate of which these 10 lads have moved on just blew my mind. I'm so proud of them."

England win Wheelchair World Cup for third time

The brothers and their dad driving England's World Cup bid

This video can not be played

Brown and Coyd on England's World Cup win

Thirty minutes into the final, England were in danger of disappointment. France, having trailed 10-0, had responded with 22 unanswered points to take control.

However, that dominance was fleeting. By the break, tries from Rob Hawkins - recently crowned the world's best player for a third time - and Jack Brown had restored order.

And when captain Lewis King led a short half-time huddle, it delivered a moment of reassurance for the group that quietly helped lay the platform for success.

"Lewis' presence is everything for this team," added Coyd.

"He always finds the right words at the right time. That's before, during and after games.

"Even in those moments during the match today, where we've been calling it a riptide - continuing on a surfing theme, when it feels like the waves are going against you, even though you feel like you don't deserve that.

"The steadiness and the composure that Lewis just lives and breathes so innately - the boys feed off of it. He's without the doubt the talisman for this group."

Joe Coyd - the head coach's younger brother, who scored four of England's nine tries - added: "We don't need a massive rousing 'let's all go together' type of speech.

"We've got such confidence in each other and we've all seen the work we're doing and we challenge each other in such a good, positive way.

"Tom's not even [been] in the changing room in the last messages today and hasn't been all tournament."

Jack Brown, playing at his fifth World Cup and earning his third winner's medal, added: "I don't think the team missed that [not having a rousing speech] because we saw it as a confidence in the team.

"We knew what we had to do and we knew that we had so many leaders in our team."

German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:42:52 GMT

Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.

But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.

The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.

For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.

In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.

This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.

Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.

That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.

Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.

They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.

The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.

"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."

In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.

German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.

The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.

And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".

The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era.

"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."

"It's difficult to talk now," he said. "I'm a very emotional guy. It's a very sad decision.

His first match in charge will be an away match against Liverpool on 22 November.

Pochettino's arrival at Old Trafford marks the end of a decade-long courtship.

Thriving during an 18-month stint at Southampton, he led the Saints to eighth place during his only full season on the south coast.

Tottenham moved quickly to appoint one of the most promising young coaches in Europe in 2014, and it was in north London that his reputation rocketed.

The club had finished in the top four just twice in the 22 years before his appointment, but Pochettino led them there four times in his five full seasons.

It was two years into his time in the capital that United first considered a move for Pochettino.

The Argentine dined with legendary former United boss Sir Alex Ferguson in Mayfair, London just weeks before Louis van Gaal was sacked as Red Devils boss.

The club ultimately decided to appoint Jose Mourinho, and Pochettino was again overlooked when the Portuguese departed in 2018, with Ole Gunnar Solskjaer impressing so much in an interim role that he was given the job more permanently.

In 2022, it was between Pochettino and Erik ten Hag for the United job but the board opted for the Dutchman, who had led Ajax to the semi-finals of the Champions League in 2019, when they were beaten by Pochettino's Tottenham.

Pochettino was interviewed by United again in 2024 following his exit from Chelsea, but the board opted instead to hire Ruben Amorim from Sporting to replace Ten Hag.

Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania.

"Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."

Owain was undertaking his second challenge for the BBC charity fundraiser, following his 24-hour drumathon in 2021.

During the ride Owain received a heartwarming message of support from his primary school teacher Cath Adams.

Speaking to his parents on Radio 2, he recalled having a pink Care Bears lunch box while in reception because he loved the programme.

He added: "I remember Cath Adams bringing it out and telling the other kids that this is alright.

Speaking to Kay, he spoke about the gruelling nature of the challenge.

"You train so hard, me and Shania Chain going around the streets, but the reality of it, it's so hard.

"It's been amazing every step of the way and that's been super emotional as well."

Owain previously admitted he "never enjoyed exercise at school" because of bullying, ahead of his four nations biking challenge.

The broadcaster also expressed his gratitude for the support of Radio 2 listeners.

His messages of support from public figures included one from the Princess of Wales, who recorded a message for him in Welsh, saying: "Hi Owain, it's Catherine, you're doing so well. Keep going. Wishing you all the very best."

Shania Twain was so impressed that the bike had been named after her that she sent a message of good luck before the challenge.

"On behalf of all the Radio 2 listeners as well as the thousands of children and families who will benefit from his Herculean fundraising efforts we simply can't thank him enough. Diolch Owain! "

Evans began his broadcasting career in Welsh-language television when he presented the children's news programme Ffeil.

He later presented the weather on BBC Wales Today and began hosting BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show in 2023.

Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:34:21 GMT

Conservative MP Chris Philp and Reform UK's Zia Yusuf had a blazing row at a joint press conference, as they joined villagers protesting against asylum accommodation plans.

The pair clashed when sharing a platform in Piddington to oppose converting a former military site at MoD Bicester into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers.

The two politicians were invited to make speeches about the plans, but things became heated after Yusuf asked Philp to apologise for the Conservatives' record on immigration.

Philp, the shadow home secretary, told Yusuf to "calm down" and accused him of "cheap politics", an assertion Reform's home affairs spokesman dismissed.

A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.

The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.

In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire.

Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.

Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.

Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.

He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government.

"So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"

Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.

He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".

Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."

Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.

Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."

Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.

As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."

Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".

McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."

While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.

Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives, and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.

Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels.

Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.

Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.

Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".

He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military, again after it was attached to the base of the car and detonated remotely.

The man targeted in the attack is yet to be named officially, but reputable sources suggest he was a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army.

Overnight into Friday, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.

How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:22:30 GMT

How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The answer is very.

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.

But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?

That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.

A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.

Other senior officials wanted a tougher response.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

On Friday, Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce for not blacklisting the company, telling CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

There have also been questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.

Now the political pressure is building.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.

And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.

Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.

The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.

It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".

That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?

The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.

This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

The programme included an interview with a woman referred to as Emily, not her real name, who said she was in a relationship with Brand when she was in her twenties.

On one occasion, she said she "literally begged" Brand to stop after he refused to wear a condom during sex.

Surfing speedster Beardman gives a glimpse of Ashes future

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 11:39:43 GMT

Beardman was player of the match in the 2024 Under-19 World Cup final but has only played 26 matches in professional cricket across formats

How would you celebrate after posting record bowling figures on a debut aged just 21?

If you're Mahli Beardman, now the most exciting fast bowler in Australian cricket, it's easy: "Try and get down to the beach!"

In his maiden one-day international, which was also his first match for Australia on home soil, Beardman took 6-24 - the best figures by an Australian on a one-day debut.

In doing so, the man who loves surfing swept aside England and set up a crushing victory in Perth.

"I would love to live my life like him - pretty carefree, loves the ocean and loves to learn about fast bowling," beamed proud captain and fellow Western Australian Mitchell Marsh.

With the nonchalance of youth and a flash of the future, Beardman was the perfect antidote during this moment of crisis for Australia.

To him, sandpaper is merely used to clean up his surfboard.

However, he has been made to wait for this moment and has had his troubles.

Two years ago, and with only one professional match to his name, he toured England with Australia's white-ball teams after an impressive Under-19 World Cup.

He did not play but bowling spells during intervals - his blond hair billowing behind him - felt like a glimpse into Australia and England's Ashes future.

Watching Mitchell Johnson tear apart England in the 2013-14 Ashes inspired Beardman to take up cricket, while he has worked with Dennis Lillee, another Australian Ashes legend, since his teenage years.

Add in accuracy, zip and effortless pace, and all of the ingredients appear to be there.

But in 2025 he suffered the first of two stress injuries in his back – the scourge of the young fast bowler.

The second of those came after his one previous Australia appearance to date – a T20 in Pakistan in January, in which he returned figures of 2-33.

Two weeks earlier he had dismissed and unsettled Australia great Steve Smith in a Big Bash play-off match which had built momentum further.

"There is always doubt," he said after his match-winning performance on Friday.

"I don't think I ever lost my love for the game, it was more 'Will I come back and be able to bowl the same and will the air speed be there?'"

After a carefully managed return, those questions were emphatically answered in Perth – where he has played all of his domestic cricket to date.

Across 7.4 overs, Beardman averaged 86.5 mph – his quickest match on record. His fastest delivery was clocked at 90.6mph, again his best effort on record.

Most impressive was his control of line and length, however. Rarely was there a ball there for England to hit.

He moved the ball in and out, not a lot but enough – enough to find Harry Brook's outside edge for his first ODI wicket at the start of his second over.

"After I got the first wicket, Zamps [spinner Adam Zampa] ran up, tapped me on the back and said 'keep a level head, mate'," Beardman said.

"That helped calm the adrenaline a little bit."

After that, Joe Root edged a drive and Jordan Cox tentatively nicked off. A bouncer to Sam Curran, which the England all-rounder hooked to fine leg, showed Beardman has the skills to unsettle a batter too.

"He bowled lively, got it to swing both ways, and his control was immaculate," former Australia all-rounder Tom Moody told BBC Test Match Special. "I don't think his heart rate went up much."

It points to Beardman's inexperience that Friday's ODI was the first time Moody – as astute an operator as there is in franchise cricket – had watched the young quick in the flesh.

This international was his 12th professional 50-over game to go along with 14 T20s. His first-class debut remains much anticipated.

"I've seen him in the Big Bash and he just has that persona," said former England captain Michael Vaughan.

"Sometimes you look at sportspeople and say 'yes, they have got it'.

"It's hard to explain what they have got. It's the way he strolls around. He is playing the game like it's his club side.

"If he stays fit, he has an incredible career ahead of him."

Beardman bowled an immaculate line and length against England, dismissing Harry Brook, Joe Root, Jordan Cox, Sam Curran, Liam Dawson and Jofra Archer

Australia are not afraid of accelerating the progression of young quicks – Glenn McGrath famously played only eight first-class matches before his Test bow – but his injuries mean Beardman's immediate future is in white-ball cricket.

"It's just a game-by-game thing at the moment," he said earlier this year on the prospect of a red-ball debut for Western Australia. "There hasn't been a set date."

Talk is now inevitable after this breakout showing.

Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc have been brought into the centre of the sandpaper storm by Usman Khawaja's book but debate over who will replace Australia's trio of Ashes and World Cup winners has been going on far longer.

Starc is 37, Hazlewood 35 and Cummins 33, while their current back-up Scott Boland turns 38 in April.

"He offers something quite different to those guys, slightly wider on the crease," former England bowler Steven Finn said on TNT Sports.

"He gets similar movement to Cummins, where he angles the ball into the right-handers, forces them to play and at the last second gets it to zip away.

"That's what the best bowlers in the world do."

In giving England another pounding in Perth, Beardman has moved himself towards the front of a queue of Australia's quicks in waiting.

The line also includes 20-year-old left-armer Harry Hoekstra, who has taken 20 wickets in his past three matches in his debut domestic season, and Lance Morris - once dubbed The Wild Thing and who caught the eye of England coach Brendon McCullum last week.

"We've been crying out to see what the next generation looks like. Ladies and gentlemen, this is what it looks like," Moody said.

Australia needed something to be excited about, even if the man himself, the surfer, speedster and star of the future, is treating it as another day on the beach.

England thrashed by Australia in first ODI

Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'

Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 08:20:28 GMT

As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.

Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.

"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."

A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.

Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."

"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.

There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.

"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.

"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."

Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.

In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.

"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."

However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.

David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.

But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.

And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.

Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".

"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.

"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."

He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.

He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.

"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.

Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.

"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."

Few people think he'll get his wish.

"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.

"I don't know what the outcome will be."

My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw me

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 06:22:12 GMT

As a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates.

At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it.

Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years.

As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable".

"Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said.

Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts".

"I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down.

The condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness.

Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions.

Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years.

The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times".

But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years.

It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits".

If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery.

But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age.

Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety".

"It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon."

That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment.

A breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience.

Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities.

What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17.

"I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said.

"It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied.

"It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus."

McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case.

"There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said.

"If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services.

"But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead."

McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding.

Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions.

She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister.

"I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said.

Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it.

A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow.

It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years.

One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards.

It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity.

Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood.

In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum".

It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery".

"The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically."

Last month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition.

Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term.

"If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future."
