Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 06:12:20 GMT

Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?

If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.

A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.

Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?

Someone, somewhere, knows something.

This video can not be played

The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.

Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.

"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.

"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."

His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.

They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.

"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.

"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."

Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.

The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.

Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.

What happened next, though, was not part of the script.

There was huge media interest in the appearance of the Hollywood stars

While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.

The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.

Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.

Jaguar were given two different types of diamond for the weekend - one for promotional purposes (on the left) and one to be welded into the cars (on the right)

Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.

Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.

In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.

Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.

It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.

"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.

He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.

"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.

"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."

By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.

But there were plenty of theories.

Theory: it was not a real diamond

Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.

"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.

"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.

"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."

Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.

"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.

"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.

"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."

Theory: someone pocketed it

"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.

"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].

"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.

"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."

There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.

Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.

"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.

"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.

"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.

"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."

Theory: Klien crashed on purpose

Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.

And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.

"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.

Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.

"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.

"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.

"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."

While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.

His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.

"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.

"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."

In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.

"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.

"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."

Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."

Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.

"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.

Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

The school where white working-class pupils defy the odds

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 00:53:49 GMT

Two years ago, I stood in a school hall in Sunderland on GCSE results day and watched the pride and surprise in the faces of teenagers as the envelopes were opened.

Even after years of covering results days, I was emotional to see a set of outstanding results in a school facing so many challenges. Almost half of the school's pupils receive free school meals, meaning their parents are on low incomes. In fact, the results in the ex-mining town of Hetton-le-Hole were as strong as the most affluent parts of southern England.

This summer, Hetton Academy hit another milestone, with 80% of its pupils getting a pass of at least a grade 4 in maths and English. A grade 4 is roughly equivalent to a 'C' under the old system, and is seen as a passport to jobs and further education.

Another striking detail about Hetton is that almost all of its pupils are from a white, working-class background, a group that's been in the spotlight for some time. This week saw the launch of the second phase of an independent inquiry, led by former Cabinet minister Baroness Morris, into why children from those communities lag behind their peers at school. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "Right now, too many white, working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education."

But Hetton Academy seems to have defied the odds. The school's principal, Vicky Pinkney, refuses to accept low incomes should mean low results. "I don't think we should be accepting less just because of the community you work in," she says.

The stellar results have won Hetton a place among an elite group of schools: mainstream secondaries that don't select pupils academically, and where 80% of pupils get that all-important grade 4 in maths and English.

In fact, there were only 339 non-selective schools in England that hit an average 80% pass rate in maths and English for the three years to 2025, out of around 3,000 that published the relevant data. High achieving schools have been the focus of some political attention recently, with MPs in several parties arguing that we should study them closely.

What can they tell us about how to raise standards? And could other schools facing the same challenges as Hetton achieve equally impressive results?

From a quick glance of those 339 high-achieving schools, it becomes clear that some of their success comes from things that are difficult to shift.

In particular, the economic profile of the pupils clearly matters. Schools that hit the average 80% pass rate have fewer children from the lowest-income families than average, and are less likely to be in deprived areas. They also have fewer children with special educational needs.

Analysts say we shouldn't be surprised by the huge role played by family finances in determining a school's outcome.

Prof John Jerrim, an academic at University College London who researches education systems in different countries, says that England's system is failing poorer pupils.

Since 2010, even while an overhaul of GCSEs has been widely seen as raising standards, the likelihood of the children from the poorest families passing these key exams has barely changed, he says.

"It's really hard to move the dial," says Prof Jerrim.

Seamus Murphy, CEO of Turner Schools, which runs schools in financially deprived areas, thinks the push for higher academic standards under Michael Gove from 2010 instilled "vision and challenge" into the system. But it doesn't work for all pupils, he says.

Especially in places where families are struggling with the cost of living, he says, an 18-year-old earning the minimum wage was "a big deal", and it might be tempting for some parents to push their children towards work rather than education.

The high-performing schools on our list also have a lower proportion of pupils from a White British background than other schools. Earlier this year, Baroness Morris's inquiry found that many white, working-class families have simply lost faith in the school system and increasingly believe it does not guarantee future success.

So it's clear that a school's fortunes are shaped in part by factors outside its control.

But there's a complication. When you zoom in on particular schools, some of them do seem to be able to defy gravity, achieving high results despite seemingly being on the 'wrong' side of those demographic factors.

So back to that school in Sunderland. It stands out as something of an exception: it has a mostly white, working-class population, and lots of pupils from poor families. In fact, if you just look at the very highest grades, the region in which Hetton sits came bottom of the English league table this year. Just 3% of GCSEs in the North East were given the top mark (a grade 9) this summer, versus 8% in London, according to exam watchdog Ofqual. (On other measures of GCSE performance, the North East ranked more favourably.)

So, what is the school doing right?

After opening in the 1960s under the name Hetton School, it struggled for years with low performance. Hetton-le-Hole town was hit hard by the closure of the Eppleton mine in the 1980s. It became common for families to send their children elsewhere in search of a good education. An Ofsted report in 2021 ranked the school as "requires improvement". That was the last report before it converted into an academy.

But by 2024, Ofsted said it was "rapidly improving". This year's 80% pass rate for maths and English GCSEs ranks the school high within the Sunderland local authority, and well above the average for England, where 57% passed maths and 60% passed English.

It's now the "school of choice" for local families, says the principal, Pinkney.

The school also says it aims to have a warm, welcoming ethos.

For Year 11 pupils, there is a separate entrance path which is lined each morning by teachers who stop a few and quiz them about their subject, problem solving on the spot with a whiteboard.

While it's done in a good-humoured way, the decision on who to stop for this brief intervention is discussed at regular review meetings.

There is more structured support for everyone in the form of an hour of extra study four days a week after school. If maths is where you are stuck, you might do two of these hours on that subject.

Over the run-up to exams, the school holds 'Revision Sundays', when the Year 11 pupils can come in for a top-up session and eat a roast lunch together.

It's all designed to foster a feeling of inclusion in the classroom, which in turn can boost exam grades, the school thinks. And it seems to be working. When reviewing the school in 2024, Ofsted praised the "positive relationships" enjoyed between pupils and staff.

And a government-commissioned study, published this year by the University of Cambridge, found that pupils who say they "belong" in school see "significantly higher attainment" in their GCSEs.

Around this time of year at Hetton, parents of Year 11 pupils, who will sit exams next summer, receive an invitation to a 'Fish and Tips' evening at the school. They'll get advice on what they can do as parents to support learning and a bag full of revision resources. Booklets and stationery are tailored to each pupil.

Afterwards Pinkney and the other staff sit down with them for fish and chips in the canteen, paid for by the school. The parents see her as "just another Mam", she says, who wants their children to do their best. She says some of the parents may have had a poor experience of school, or simply been able to get into work without many qualifications themselves.

It's a community that mostly "stays in the area", Pinkney says, and it's the school's task to "open their horizons".

But still, challenges remain. It certainly won't be easy for every school in a white, working-class area to emulate Hetton's success.

Prof Lindsey Macmillan, an expert in how education shapes life chances, was involved in the recent inquiry into white working-class children.

The pupils start school already behind, she says, and that gap only widens through secondary school due to a growing disengagement with education.

The inquiry found "telling" evidence that the connection with school "falls off a cliff" for white working-class families at the point of moving to secondary school, leading to poor attendance.

Parents told the inquiry things like, "I didn't need qualifications" to get into work - the same message as Pinkney hears from some parents in Hetton-le-Hole. (In reality, Macmillan says, formal qualifications are now more important for getting a job than they were in previous decades, when there were more routes into well-paid industrial work, and more on-the-job training.)

That's a point supported by Prof Jerrim, who thinks schools should get families to buy-in on education by clearly explaining to them how qualifications can help their children find work.

The inquiry also reported a sense of white working-class parents not wanting their children to leave their area, with its strong sense of connection. England's education system was described as being out-of-step with the values of white, working-class communities. Parents in those areas are ambitious for their children, the inquiry found, but often prioritise happiness and life-readiness alongside or above high grades.

But Macmillan, an education professor at University College London, also says that high grades shouldn't be seen as the only route into successful adult life. To suggest that sounds "demeaning" to some parents who didn't achieve high grades themselves, she thinks.

"Why have we created a structure where getting those maths and English GCSEs is so important to your life chances?" she says.

She wants the government to think about more entry-level apprenticeships and other on-the-job learning, so children with lower academic grades can still thrive.

Back in Sunderland, the 700 or so pupils at Hetton Academy have just arrived back in school after their half-term.

Does the principal think other places could replicate its success?

Absolutely, Pinkney says. And for her, it's personal: she points out that she too was raised by a single mother with little money, and still thrived academically.

"I feel really strongly about that. My school helped me to be able to achieve."

Additional reporting: Phil Leake.

The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?

BBC News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 00:13:35 GMT

Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?

Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.

From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.

But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".

So how much AI enhancement is too much?

Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.

But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.

"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."

For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.

It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.

But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.

"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."

All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.

Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.

It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.

According to a recent survey of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.

Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.

He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.

But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.

"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."

He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.

Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.

In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.

In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.

Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.

"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.

A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".

"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."

Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.

But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.

He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.

"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages

New Scientist November 12, 2026

A decades-old, vastly influential conjecture about quantum computing has finally been proven – by AI. It confirms that a whole class of mathematical problems wouldn’t be more easily solved by quantum computers.

In 1999, Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin got stuck on a question about when exactly quantum computers could excel over their conventional counterparts.

At this time, researchers knew of at least one example of a problem where the quantum approach outshone all others: Shor’s algorithm for factoring numbers. But they suspected that this hinged on the specific mathematical structure that underlies the factoring problem.

Advertisement

Aaronson wondered whether quantum computers could also win in the opposite case, when the problem contains little to no structure and lots of randomness instead. In 2011, he and Andris Ambainis at the University of Latvia formally conjectured that, in at least one case, the answer was negative – but they couldn’t prove it.

AI refutes 30-year-old mathematical assumption in computer science

Now, David Turturean at the start-up Physical Superintelligence (PSI) and his colleagues have used Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to provide that proof. This eliminates a whole class of problems from the race to understand what quantum computers are best at.

“It’s a very crisp mathematical question that has consequences for quantum computing, and it has been very hard to solve, to the degree that I had given up on it my myself,” says Ambainis.

“This might be one of the [few] remaining long-standing open questions that are worth pursuing,” says Turturean.

The problem at the heart of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture requires a computer to answer a “yes” or “no” question after being fed a huge but random string of bits, or 1s and 0s. Could a quantum computer get an answer by looking at the string significantly fewer times than a conventional computer would have to? The pair conjectured that a conventional computer could approximate the quantum computer’s performance for most strings and without having to take much longer. More simply, you could get away with not using a quantum computer at all.

Free newsletter

Importantly, Aaronson and Ambainis translated the statement at the core of their conjecture into the language of polynomials, recasting it as a problem in a different field of pure mathematics. “We didn’t think it would catch on like it did. People who were powerhouses in their own fields and didn’t care about quantum computing got interested,” says Aaronson.

PSI’s breakthrough builds on the work of such mathematicians. Turturean says it took about four days for Fable 5.2, which wasn’t publicly available at the time, to complete the proof, improve and refine it twice, then verify the final version with the proof-checking software Lean. The PSI team then shared the proof with Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan at Stanford University in California, who studied it and wrote an exposition that unravelled its key ingredients.

In a joint statement to New Scientist, they wrote that the new proof meaningfully surpasses all studies that it draws upon. “The proofs are entirely different – and substantially more difficult. Everything is also woven together in a novel way,” they wrote.

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Three days after PSI made their proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture public, Supartha Podder at Stony Brook University in New York and his colleagues put forward another, shorter proof of the same thesis, developed with the aid of ChatGPT 5.6 and 6. After four months of building out the framework for their proof, one part of the work by Turturean and his colleagues “supplied the missing ingredient that allowed this approach to succeed”, the researchers wrote in their paper, which was only about seven pages long.

Shachar Lovett at the University of California, San Diego, whose work was one of the key ingredients in the PSI proof, says that this exposition reveals tricks that mathematicians can now learn from and reuse. “This helps us guide our research. What I think is going to come from these AI tools is that now we can maybe ask more ambitious questions,” he says.

But Lovett is cautious about the impact this new work might have on quantum computing, as it is more mathematical than practical, he says. In Aaronson’s view, the weight of the practical implications is also unclear. “This rules out a potential direction where you could look for quantum speed-ups, but it wasn’t a plausible direction anyway,” he says. The glaring question now is where to look for new problems that quantum computers are uniquely positioned to take on.

Determining how useful different quantum computers are has been a long running challenge – now researchers appear to have the answer

“This is far from the end of quantum speedups. Instead, it informs us on what types of problems we should consider,” wrote the Stanford team. A similar problem with a shorter or less random input string, or one for which the quantum computer doesn’t give just a “yes” or “no” answer, could still benefit from the quantum approach, they wrote. This leaves tremendously many problems, including simulating industrially relevant molecules and some optimisation problems.

Aaronson says that many of the questions related to quantum information science that are best tackled with mathematics have already been answered by AI, so it is time to formulate some new ones. Matthew Pines at PSI says he and his colleagues now also want to use AI to explore new ideas, instead of just knocking down famous problems. The future will show how successful this can be. “There is some major creative leap needed. I think that’s something where AI is not good yet,” says Ambainis.

A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time

New Scientist November 12, 2026

A robot has built a structure in space without any help of astronauts. The first-of-its-kind achievement is a step towards autonomous in-orbit manufacturing and assembly of structures such as space stations and data centres, which will be crucial if we want to develop an orbital economy.

Sergio Pellegrino at the California Institute of Technology and his team developed their robot as part of a US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) initiative to explore new ways to build in space. Large orbiting structures in the past have either been assembled with the help of astronauts or launched pre-assembled and folded up, spring-loaded to unfold upon release from their capsules.

But unfolding doesn’t work for more complex structures, and sending astronauts to build space stations isn’t cost-effective. “We’ve been unfolding things in space, there’s been a lot of unfolding,” says Pellegrino. “The big picture is how are we going to transition from unfolding in space to building in space.”

Advertisement

Putting data centres in space isn’t going to happen any time soon

The robot that he and his team built is essentially a sophisticated arm that picks up parts and clicks them together in a process similar to putting up a tent or playing with a toy construction set. The precision involved in the movements makes this more difficult than one might expect, especially because the researchers only had 18 months to take the whole project from idea to execution in orbit.

Since its March launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the robot has been working on building a radio antenna, 1.4 metres in diameter, from a set of tubes, joints and reflective nets. As it went along, images of each step were beamed back to Earth, where the researchers checked them and troubleshot any problems with an identical robot in their lab. Construction of the antenna hasn’t quite been completed and the mission ends in December, but work has proceeded far enough to prove that this is a viable approach, says Pellegrino.

Free newsletter

Now that it has had its first test, Pellegrino hopes that other researchers and space-flight businesses get onboard to accelerate development of faster, larger assembly systems. “I think our objective should be that in the next 5 years we start doing some of this, and in 10 years, there is the beginning for a real maturing infrastructure,” he says.

Eventually, the goal is to build much larger structures, with less troubleshooting from the ground.

Taking space-based construction out of human hands could accelerate the development of businesses and science in orbit enormously, and putting together one radio antenna in space is just the beginning.

Economics, not climate summits, will dictate the net-zero transition

New Scientist November 12, 2026

The stench of hypocrisy is in the air at the COP31 summit in Turkey. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to show British leadership on climate action. Meanwhile, his government just green-lit the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which will emit up to 36 million tonnes of carbon dioxide without noticeably reducing energy prices, and it is considering approving the Rosebank oilfield and weakening its electric vehicle mandate.

The summit’s joint hosts, Turkey and Australia, are pushing for a clean energy revolution, but this week Turkey announced two new oilfields that would help boost production 30 per cent, while promising to double natural gas production. Australia has recently approved fossil fuel projects including a “climate bomb” coal mine extension that will emit enough carbon to kill an additional 15 million Great Barrier Reef coral colonies during every bleaching event. Meanwhile, the second biggest emitter, the US, is again boycotting the annual climate summit.

How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

While the world shaved more than 1°C off the warming trajectory after the 2015 Paris Agreement, “collective climate action has effectively stalled”, and current policies put the world on track for a catastrophic 2.7°C rise by 2100, according to Climate Action Tracker.

Advertisement

But there is one piece of good news. The Global Carbon Budget also just announced that fossil fuel emissions are expected to slightly decrease in 2026 – something that has only previously happened during the covid-19 pandemic, the 2008 financial crisis and the break-up of the Soviet Union. Granted, the 0.4 per cent decline wouldn’t have happened without the Iran war oil crisis. But the growth in cheap solar, wind and electric vehicles has offset more emissions than the spike in oil prices.

If clean tech can keep accelerating, “a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away”, the Global Carbon Budget report said. This means that economics, not politics, is pushing the clean energy transition forward, despite the failed leadership on display at COP31.

Free newsletter

“Policy was never the main driver,” says Auke Hoekstra at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. “These technologies are simply superior.”

Hoekstra is known for his graphs showing how solar panel production has repeatedly outperformed International Energy Agency expectations. Solar is now providing 10 times more energy than when the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015, making it the fastest-growing electricity source ever, followed closely by wind.

Money talks, and electricity from solar and wind costs less on average than from natural gas or coal. In the US, the top oil-producing state, Texas, where climate denier Donald Trump won a landslide, has also become the top producer of both solar and wind power. In low-income countries like Nigeria and Pakistan, rather than waiting for governments to update expensive and unreliable fossil fuel-based power grids, people are simply installing cheap Chinese solar panels on their roofs, “leapfrogging” hydrocarbon-fuelled development altogether.

The one drawback had been that solar and wind don’t generate much energy in the evening during peak demand. But cheap batteries are quickly solving that problem. Utility and home battery storage is now growing even faster than renewable power generation.

An ambitious form of climate modelling aims to pin the blame for disasters – from floods to heatwaves – on specific companies. Is this the tool we need to effectively prosecute the world’s biggest carbon emitters?

Of course, early subsidies and regulations by governments like China and Germany created the market conditions for renewables to start coming down the cost curve. While economics is driving the energy transition, policy can speed it up or, as in the case of Trump cancelling electric vehicle subsidies, slow it down. Governments still provide more than $900 billion of annual support for fossil fuels.

The target proposed at COP31 of increasing energy use from electricity to 35 per cent by 2035 would send a positive signal. The biggest bottleneck to this is expanding the grid, something governments could accelerate at home by cutting red tape and offering subsidies and loans.

Kingsmill Bond at think tank Ember Energy thinks the economics of clean tech will let the world limit warming to much less than the projected 2.7°C by 2100. Exactly how much less depends on politics. He proposes that energy-importing countries start their own COP, where fossil fuel-exporting countries can’t delay progress.

“The old system is just being propped up by legacy policy and ignorance,” he says. “We’ve just got to tear that down.”

Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss

New Scientist November 12, 2026

Brief bursts of ‘pink noise’ played while people with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease sleep might give them a slight memory boost, a small study suggests.

Pink noise is best described as a low-pitched hiss. There is some evidence that exposure to pink noise during sleep may help clear waste products from the brain. As such, researchers are beginning to assess whether pink-noise therapy has benefits for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.

Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s?

An international team of researchers has explored this possibility. They worked with 37 people, each with diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and experiencing mild cognitive impairment affecting memory. On two occasions, 14 days apart, the 37 participants were invited into the lab in the evening and asked to memorise 30 word pairs. They then slept in the lab while the researchers monitored their brain activity.

Advertisement

Javier Mínguez at Elevvo Therapeutics in Spain, and a member of the research team, says slow brainwaves and brief bursts of neural activity known as sleep spindles help the brain consolidate memories, a process Alzheimer’s can disrupt. The researchers used a system developed by Spanish neurotechnology company Bitbrain that can identify when slow brainwaves are approaching their peak. Throughout the first night in the lab, the researchers played a 50-millisecond-long pulse of pink noise to the sleeping participants each time these peaks occurred.

“Timing is critical, because the useful window is only about 200 milliseconds wide,” says Mínguez.

On the second night in the lab, the study participants were not exposed to pink noise as they slept.

Free newsletter

After both nights, the participants were asked to recall the word pairs they had learned the evening before. They remembered slightly more word pairs after exposure to pink noise than after the night without pink noise: 0.88 word pairs more, on average, after the pink-noise exposure. This is equivalent to about a 19 per cent improvement in memory, the researchers say. The clinical significance of this result remains uncertain.

“These results are meaningful theoretically and fit with an increasingly strong set of findings linking memory storage with overnight brain activity,” says Ken Paller at Northwestern University in Illinois, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study hasn’t yet been peer-reviewed. Several authors have commercial connections to Bitbrain or its spin-off Elevvo Therapeutics, and three are inventors on a pending patent covering the method, says Mínguez.

Mínguez sees the study as a proof of concept. To find out whether the benefits can last, the researchers are now expanding their experiments. They have given study participants equipment to use at home that offers pink noise stimulation during sleep, and they will assess the effects of continued exposure over a 6-month period.

Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere

New Scientist November 13, 2026

If you listen closely to an underwater seagrass meadow, you can hear the actual sound of photosynthesis. During the day, tiny bubbles of oxygen float from the blades of the seagrass to the ocean’s surface. The popping sound these bubbles make when they burst is like “tinkling bells”, according to Carlos Duarte, a keen scuba diver and expert on ocean noise at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia.

“As long as the meadows are more than 2 metres beneath the ocean surface, when the bubbles break they generate a vibration that is in the same sound frequency as bells,” he says. “If you have a hydrophone and you quantify this, then you could even calculate photosynthetic rates.”

But most of the time, this remarkable acoustic phenomenon is drowned out by human-caused noise pollution. There is barely a habitat on Earth that isn’t subjected to anthropogenic noise pollution from boats, cars, aeroplanes or any number of other noisy human activities. In the oceans, ambient noise levels are about 10 times higher than they were in 1950. “To understand the impact of noise on the marine environment, we need to imagine ourselves living in a great party, 24/7, throughout our entire lifespan. It is really a persistent and chronic impact,” says Duarte.

Advertisement

Human noise pollution drives monkeys to rely on communication by scent

Now, scientists are learning more about how serious and widespread the impact of noise pollution is on wildlife subjected to it – and the results are disturbing. A meta-analysis published in the journal Science earlier this month looked at 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species, spanning six continents. It concluded that noise pollution altered at least one physiological, developmental or behavioural trait in 80 per cent of the species studied, with the effects occurring in every habitat. In short, noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of a huge range of animals across land and sea.

“Every ecosystem, or every major habitat, is affected by noise,” says Hansjoerg Kunc at Queen’s University Belfast in the UK, who conducted the analysis with his colleague Rouven Schmidt. “We looked at a lot of different physiological responses [in wildlife] and basically nearly all of them found an effect for noise.”

In general, noise forces predators to work 2.5 times harder to catch 25 per cent less prey overall, reported Kunc and Schmidt. Creatures like bats expend more energy and are less successful at hunting when subjected to ambient noise, while noise from ship engines disrupts communication and disorientates marine life such as whales and dolphins.

Free newsletter

Animals also learn to avoid noisy habitats, which shrinks their available area and therefore limits their population size. Dolphins, for example, actively avoid noisy coastlines, while bats have been shown to avoid roads that were noisy during a motorcycle rally long after the vehicles had left the area.

In noise-polluted areas, mortality among animals studied jumped by 138 per cent, on average. Sometimes, the death is instantaneous: underwater explosions from oil and gas exploration, for example, can cause a fish’s bladder to explode. Other times, it is slower and more painful, such as gradual starvation from reduced hunting success.

Not every animal suffers a negative impact from noise pollution, Kunc notes. Some predators might benefit from noise – enjoying increased hunting success when human noise flushes their prey out of its hiding place, for example.

But even though some animals might benefit in the short term, the overall effect is negative on the ecosystem, he says, because its natural dynamics are being warped by external stress. “If you think about an ecosystem, all species in this ecosystem have adapted to the way it should be,” he says. “So, from my point of view, it doesn’t really matter who is more affected or less affected. It is changing, and that is what we want to avoid, because we want to protect a functioning ecosystem.”

Powerful new book explores how noise has taken over the world

Kunc wants more thought to be given to protecting the soundscape of the natural world, alongside the conservation of physical habitats. “We know that the acoustic environment is a strong evolutionary force, and we have shown that it really changes the physiology, development and behaviour [of wildlife],” he says.

Some efforts are already under way. In the US, national parks such as Yellowstone have designated quiet zones, which reduce the amount of noise made by visitors by 3 to 5 decibels according to Rachel Buxton, formerly of the US National Parks Service and now at Carleton University in Canada.

She thinks more can be done to reduce noise pollution, especially in protected areas, such as by closing roads to traffic during certain periods or re-routing aircraft to shadow busy road networks and avoid wilderness areas.

“Think of the Grand Canyon. We wouldn’t dream of building a giant building in the middle of the Grand Canyon, and yet there are overflight tours that pass over the airspace all the time, polluting the whole space with noise,” she points out.

Pitcairn Island, one of the remotest places on Earth, was once home to mutineers. Today it’s a trailblazer in biodiversity protection with lessons for us all

We also need to tackle noise pollution at sea, says Duarte. He argues for enforcing acoustic limits in marine protected areas, which could include setting noise limits for ships and other marine activities.

New technologies also give hope for a quieter future. Emerging evidence suggests that electric vehicles are quieter and therefore less disturbing to most wildlife. Similarly, electric motorboats and ferries could lead to quieter shorelines for marine life, says Duarte. “Moving to electric mobility, which we’ve done largely on land, to the ocean will immediately reduce noise around the shorelines,” he says, pointing out that countries such as Sweden are leading the way in creating a market for electric boats.

The covid-19 pandemic offers an insight into what happens in the natural world when the noise stops. Noise pollution across oceans dropped by 20 per cent during the crisis, says Duarte, and led to extraordinary sightings of marine life returning to busy waterways and city shorelines, and the sound of birdsong filling cities.

Unlike pollutants that linger in the atmosphere, shutting off the noise immediately removes the problem, Duarte points out. “As soon as the noise stops, then animals claim back their ancestral territory and home,” he says.

Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?

New Scientist November 13, 2026

The polar vortex has suffered an unprecedented early breakdown, threatening Europe with cold and snow, and some scientists think the record super El Niño is to blame.

The polar vortex, a high-altitude band of westerly winds circling the Arctic that bottles up cold air over the north pole, typically strengthens through the winter and weakens in the spring.

Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?

The El Niño climate phase, which has already warmed surface waters in the tropical Pacific to record temperatures and continues to heat up, tends to keep the vortex strong in autumn and early winter. Then, in late winter, it often weakens the vortex, allowing that cold air to spill southwards into Europe and sometimes North America.

Advertisement

But on 10 November, the polar vortex weakened to the point that it broke down, with the winds reversing direction to blow weakly from the east. While these collapses happen every few years, they almost never occur in November. This is the earliest it has happened since weather balloon records began in the 1950s, beating the old record by 18 days.

This may have been due to random fluctuations in the atmosphere. It is also possible, however, that the extremely strong El Niño could have sped up the weakening of the polar vortex that typically happens later in the winter, though that isn’t proven, according to Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s weather service.

Free newsletter

“There probably is some kind of El Niño influence on it,” he says. “That would be my suspicion, but we don’t know that for sure.”

As east-to-west trade winds weaken during El Niño and the warm water they built up in the western Pacific washes back eastwards, a low-pressure centre of warm, rising air moves eastwards with it. This causes extra waviness in the jet stream, another band of strong westerly winds that circles the globe, except further south and lower in the atmosphere than the polar vortex. The jet stream meanders further southwards around Alaska, deepening a low-pressure system there called the Aleutian low.

But the El Niño-linked wave doesn’t just propagate side to side in the jet stream. It can also propagate upwards into the stratosphere, where the polar vortex is. As the air gets thinner, the wave’s amplitude gets bigger until it crashes into the polar vortex like a wave crashing onto a beach, says Scaife. And while the polar vortex is westerly, these waves carry easterly momentum.

“When they dump that momentum, they push the polar vortex against its flow, and they weaken it,” he says.

5 graphs that show how the record-breaking El Niño will affect the world

But another reason for the polar vortex breakdown could be a high-pressure “blocking” system that developed over Scandinavia in recent weeks, which blocked the jet stream and caused large meanders in it. This waviness could also have weakened the polar vortex through the same wave-breaking process, regardless of El Niño.

“I would be wary of saying it was caused by El Niño,” says Andrew Charlton-Perez at the University of Reading, UK. “I would say the blocking high is probably more important.”

The reversal of the polar vortex isn’t related to the current cold weather in the UK. But it could bring even more cold, snowy weather in the coming weeks.

A polar vortex breakdown is also known as a sudden stratospheric warming event. As the winds weaken, high-level air rushes in over the north pole, increasing atmospheric pressure and raising temperatures, just as pumping up a bike tyre warms it up.

Meanwhile, over the following weeks, cold surface-level air can descend from the Arctic into northern Europe. A polar vortex breakdown preceded the “Beast from the East” cold snap in 2018, when blizzards covered much of the UK in snow and killed 10 people.

While the polar vortex is expected to strengthen towards the end of November, bringing warmer weather, it could break down again this winter, Scaife warns.

“The risk of cold easterlies this winter is increasing,” he says.

Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight

New Scientist November 13, 2026

For the first time, researchers have built a quantum clock that uses light from the sun as a key component. It could be used to diagnose shifts in the sun’s velocity or probe processes on its surface.

This is not your mother’s sundial. People have known that they can keep track of time with sunlight ever since antiquity. But contemporary record-breaking timekeepers, which are called optical clocks, derive their accuracy from quantum mechanical effects and typically have atoms that have been isolated from the external world at their core. Now, Scott Diddams at the University of Colorado, Boulder, and his colleagues have built an optical clock that relies on sunlight instead.

In a typical optical clock, an electron within an atom is made to oscillate between two energy levels, and an ultra-stable laser is tuned, or locked, to the frequency of that oscillation. Next, these oscillations – the ups and downs of the light waves that comprise the laser beam – are translated into usable ticks of a clock. To do this, researchers use a device called a frequency comb, which turns visible light into microwaves that can be processed by standard electronics.

Advertisement

First working nuclear clock heralds a new era in timekeeping

In the new experiment, the researchers still used a laser and a frequency comb to build their clock, but the role of the atom was played by a process that happens near the sun.

Specifically, instead of locking their laser to an electron’s jumps within an atom, the researchers locked it to a process where sunlight causes similar jumps as it hits iron atoms in our star’s atmosphere. This process leaves a signature in the spectrum of colours that comprise sunlight, so the team collected sunlight into a special fibre and fed it into the rest of the clock. This type of solar optical clock has never been built before.

While the new clock doesn’t rival the best atomic optical clocks in accuracy, the researchers showed that it could possibly be used as a tool for studying stars. During the partial solar eclipse in 2024, they observed a signature shift in the sunlight’s spectrum due to the moon passing in front of the star. If the clock was fed light from a faraway star in place of sunlight, similar shifts could indicate the presence of orbiting exoplanets, which raises the possibility of the new clock design becoming a tool for astronomical discovery. In this case, however, starlight would have to be collected through large telescopes, sometimes over long periods of time.

Researchers have designed a quantum version of a pendulum clock. It could shed light on timekeeping in the quantum realm

Piet Schmidt at the National Metrology Institute of Germany says that the new work is interesting because it demonstrates an optical clock design that leverages light from the stars rather than being based exclusively on objects under tight control in the lab.

But as an astronomical instrument, it doesn’t yet surpass existing methods for studying light from stars, and for very distant stars, the new clock’s usefulness would be seriously limited by how faint their light is, says Schmidt.

There may, however, be advantages in studying the properties of our sun, he says. For example, the clock could probe eruptive events, sunspots and the effects of solar “wind” made from streams of charged particles in the outer layers of the sun’s atmosphere.

Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?

New Scientist November 13, 2026

New Scientist has always been interested in science fiction and its attempts to imagine the future. In 1958, when the magazine was 2 years old, it published an article by Ian S. Menzies in which he wrote: “Like every other form of literature, s. f. ranges from excellent to awful. But the best of science fiction today is far superior to much other fiction.” Elsewhere in the feature, Menzies talked about the risks of the “rapid catching up of reality with fiction”.

It’s true that some of the sci-fi he was reading then was rapidly overtaken by events and, in the process of that, rendered redundant. What Menzies couldn’t know was that other works from that same period would still be regarded as prescient, important or relevant, or even all three, decades later.

So, which sci-fi stories, published over the seven decades of New Scientist’s history, have proved to be both prophetic and enduringly pertinent as the world has changed around them? Here are some of my personal picks.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

The Death of Grass by John Christopher (1956) is an English period piece, with all the particular social politics of its era on display (sexism included). Yet somehow it manages to foreshadow a host of modern-day crises, from pandemics and the fragility of food supply lines to the befouling and stripping of the land by big agriculture.

The book opens with the news that a virus is killing grasses; eventually that comes to include all cereal crops. Abruptly, the country’s food reserves are gone, and no more food is coming. The novel’s main characters are mostly middle-class professionals who do a few things “right” early on. They are quick to acquire guns and flee London; also, quick to gun down anyone who tries to stop them. They make their way in convoy through a brown land, heading towards a Cumbrian valley where one of their group has a relative. The valley is gated; one way in, one way out. They think they could be safe there.

First they have to survive their journey, though, and England, within hours, is lawless. I finished the book wishing that I could buy a remote valley and build a wall across the bottom of it.

The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress by Robert A. Heinlein (1966) is the story, set in 2075, of a group of lunar residents who plot to overthrow their overlords on Earth. It’s a great premise rendered quite dull in execution; much of the book reads like the minutes from a local council meeting. In addition, the sexual politics of the colony are filtered through male 1960s sensibilities, adding cringeworthy moments.

The reason this remains a classic is that one of the characters in the book, Mike, is an AI. Not just some 60s idea of what an AI might be, but our idea of an AI. On the very first page, our narrator Mannie (who speaks a futuristic version of English) writes: “Mike was a fair dinkum thinkum, sharpest computer you’ll ever meet… Not that Mike would necessarily give right answer; he wasn’t completely honest.” Remind you of anything?

Ursula K. Le Guin’s astonishing novel The Dispossessed (1974) remains daisy fresh. Le Guin, as her fans will know, could do it all: character, politics, ideas, exquisite writing… and, in this case, spaceships too.

Our hero, Shevek, is a brilliant physicist and also a good man (what a wonderful creation he is!) trying to do right in a future where the human colonies have gone different ways – one into anarchy, for example, another into the rule of an elite – as they struggle with climate change, moral exhaustion, repression, inequality… and much else that we struggle with today. If you’ve never read this one, I highly recommend it.

I’m going to cheat for the 80s and pick two books, because I can’t choose between Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) and William Gibson’s Neuromancer (1984).

In Atwood’s masterwork, the US has been captured by a radical right-wing group and is now called the Republic of Gilead. Women’s rights have been scrapped. Our hero, named Offred by the new regime, is assigned as a handmaid to a family of loyalists. Her job is to produce a baby for the commander who is her new master. She is, in short, a womb with arms and legs, and nothing more, to Gilead.

I don’t think I need to draw any lines for you, straight or otherwise, from this book written 40 years ago to current events.

Atwood aside, I didn’t want to leave out Neuromancer because its vision of our digital future is so weirdly prescient. Gibson, famously, was no computer expert and wrote the book on a typewriter. Yet he foresaw what cyberspace would actually be like.

Case, our chief protagonist, is a former hacker trying to make ends meet in Japan after his ability to access cyberspace has been taken from him. Then a woman called Molly approaches him, asking him to get involved in a heist. Cue a high-stakes drama in and out of cyberspace. The book is a bit dense to start with, but it’s well worth sticking with.

Is Neuromancer’s cyberpunk dystopia still thrilling in 2025?

Octavia E. Butler’s Parable of the Sower (1993) is a barnstormer of a novel that remains as relevant today as when it was first published. Our hero, Lauren Olamina, is a young woman living in a gated community in a United States that is rapidly falling apart.

Climate change is escalating and the streets are full of desperate people forced into savagery simply to survive. Lauren’s community is hanging on, but soon the chaos is going to come through that gate.

Lauren, still a teenager, develops her own religion and names it Earthseed. Its divine purpose is for humans to colonise the stars. Such a bold vision is preposterous amidst the horror of the world Lauren is forced to make her way through, and yet it sustains her.

N. K. Jemisin on the prescience and brilliance of Parable of the Sower

The book is a hymn (I think) to the power of taking full responsibility for your life and facing up to the fact that everything changes. Let us hope, as with The Death of Grass, that this version of the future remains in some parts fictional.

Butler wrote a follow-up, Parable of the Talents, in which Lauren sees her dreams begin to come true. A third book in the series remained unfinished when Butler died.

One does need some time to pass before being able to decide if a book has truly got the future right. However, I am reasonably confident that The Three-Body Problem by Cixin Liu (2008) is going to prove to be so.

3 Body Problem review: Cixin Liu’s masterpiece arrives on Netflix

The story is a brilliant one. Aliens are heading for Earth, and they’re not friendly, but it’s going to take them hundreds of years to arrive. Can the scientists of Earth band together and push science forward so hard that humans will survive the coming invasion? Yes, Liu wrote a book all about physics, but made it gripping!

So, in the case of the book, the science push is all about aliens. But it doesn’t take a big leap of the imagination to suggest that there might be some important real world parallels here. This is the first of a trilogy. The two follow-up novels are also fantastic.

I’m going to take a chance on two very different novels from recent times that might, in the future, be viewed as accurate visions.

First, Station Eleven (2014) by Emily St. John Mandel, which essentially predicted the covid-19 pandemic. Except in Mandel’s pandemic, the world was left in ruins.

We follow a travelling group of actors and musicians as they journey between communities in this future world. The book explores the idea that “survival is insufficient”; that humanity needs art, culture and history to truly live. Its ideas still feel extremely relevant 12 years later.

Second, Kim Stanley Robinson’s chronicle of the near future, The Ministry for the Future (2020). Clear-eyed, but essentially optimistic, it describes humanity’s efforts to deal with climate change in the decades to come.

This is a very untraditional book in structure, and although you could say the main character is Mary Murphy, the head of the titular ministry, parts of the book are devoted to (fictional) witness accounts of future events. It’s not an easy read, but then it’s not an easy subject, and this is a massively ambitious work.

Despite the horrors contained in the book, we may end up wishing, in the future, that it had been more prescient, rather than less.

So those are my picks. You may have better ones. In terms of Ian S. Menzies’s central argument seven long decades ago, I think that what he said still holds true. Science fiction continues to range from excellent to awful. But the best of sci-fi today is still far superior to much other fiction. It’s where the big ideas are, simple as that.

Did Emily get it right? Come and join the discussion about the sci-fi novels that have best predicted the future

Emily H. Wilson is author of the Sumerians series and is working on her first sci-fi novel. She is a former editor of New Scientist, and is now the magazine’s science-fiction columnist

Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop

New Scientist November 13, 2026

The Queen of Christmas, Mariah Carey, has declared “It’s time!!!!”, which can only mean one thing: the holiday season is officially upon us, with all the extra spending that entails.

If past years are anything to go by, I suspect that many of my impulse purchases will spark more guilt than joy, as they gather dust in the corners of my home. So, I was extremely interested to read a copy of Influenced: The science of why we buy by Aarron Atkinson-Toal, published last week.

An assistant professor in marketing at Durham University in the UK, Atkinson-Toal has spent much of his career studying the forces that influence consumer decision-making. Like many before him, he argues that our judgements are often driven by cognitive shortcuts called heuristics that help the brain to appraise a situation without consciously deliberating over every piece of data it receives.

Advertisement

The late Nobel prizewinning psychologist Daniel Kahneman described this intuitive thinking as System 1, as opposed to the conscious, careful calculations of System 2. Leaning on System 1 can save us a lot of time and effort in the information overload of daily life. Unfortunately, this efficiency comes at the cost of accuracy and logic, since it can be easily swayed by our emotions and tends to bypass our self-control.

“It is believed that up to 95 per cent of daily decisions are made in this subconscious and reactive way,” writes Atkinson-Toal. “That is a lot of decisions being made without full awareness of actions and consequences.”

In Influenced, he sets out the many ways that marketing schemes have been designed to exploit this – and highlights some of the most important errors that may influence our shopping – and describes our feelings after we have made our purchases.

How rethinking your relationship with time could give you more of it

In the run-up to Black Friday, we’ll see many time-limited deals that promise huge savings. When we are rushed, we are especially likely to fall into System 1 thinking, as we prioritise speed over accuracy.

Imagine you see a new phone, discounted from £1000 to £800. Under time pressure, you will be more easily swayed by your fear of regret for missing out on the bargain, since you know that you can save £200 if you buy it now. If you had more time to decide, however, you might conclude that £800 is still too much to spend for a relatively minor upgrade.

Devices like countdown timers on online retailers’ websites when you put something in your virtual cart “are attempts to make the fast decision-making process of shoppers even faster,” writes Atkinson-Toal.

To make matters worse, these limited-time offers promote the idea of scarcity, which we tend to associate with a higher value, leading us to believe that we’re getting a better deal, argues Atkinson-Toal.

In one classic experiment, Stephen Worchel, then at the University of Virginia, and his colleagues asked participants to test various goods in the lab, including a jar of cookies. The scientists found that the participants gave consistently higher ratings if there were only two cookies in the jar, compared with 10 – even though the cookies were identical in each condition. The effect was even greater if the participants were told that the cookies were running low due to high demand from other students.

When you see a “low stock alert” on a website, or an emptying shelf in a physical shop, you are primed to make a similar judgement – compelling you to buy the product.

The anchoring effect was one of the first cognitive biases that Kahneman and his colleague the late Amos Tversky documented. In one study, they asked participants to spin a “wheel of fortune” containing the numbers 0 to 100 before estimating the percentage of African countries in the UN. They found that the random number chosen by the wheel of fortune “anchored” the participants’ answers: the higher the random number, the bigger their estimate.

Anchoring is prevalent in sales. If you are first recommended a high-priced product, you will be more inclined to pay more for whatever you finally choose to buy, because the luxury good has anchored your judgement of what is reasonable.

How to build powerful microhabits for your wellbeing – and keep them

Despite our amazing capacity for mental time travel, we tend to be pretty poor at estimating how decisions today will affect our feelings in the future. We prioritise immediate rewards over our future wellbeing, a habit known as temporal discounting. We also struggle to predict how we will feel about future stresses, which are known as errors in affective forecasting.

Imagine you have been putting money aside for a trip next year. When you see that advert for a new phone, you focus on the instant excitement of unwrapping the shiny new product and forget the disappointment that may arise from finding your piggy bank empty when you come to book your holiday. “It is easier to write off today’s decisions as tomorrow’s problem,” Atkinson-Toal says in the book.

The sheer array of options available can leave us feeling bamboozled – a phenomenon that is sometimes called choice overload. Studies show that the more offers available, the less satisfied we may feel after having made our decision. “After the rush of Black Friday, or any purchase made under time pressure, reality often kicks in about just how much has been spent on things that were not needed, fuelling a feeling of regret and likely leading to more product returns,” writes Atkinson-Toal.

All of which is certainly going to encourage me to exercise my critical thinking before I start my holiday shopping – especially when I feel rushed to make a quick choice. Simple awareness of the forces shaping our decision-making is likely to help. From my own writing on rational thinking, I know that a good rule of thumb is to actively argue with your intuitions. If you feel the impulse to buy something super expensive, give yourself enough time to list two or more reasons why it might be a bad idea. Maybe you will still conclude that you have found the ideal bargain, but at least you will have engaged some System 2 thinking to curb some of System 1’s excesses.

I’ll also be bearing in mind two reliable findings from the broader psychological literature. Spending money on experiences tends to bring greater happiness than buying physical things; and spending money on others tends to bring greater happiness than spending money on ourselves. Hosting a generous festive party, in other words, is more likely to leave me full of good cheer than any new device.

David Robson’s latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 social strategies that will transform your life. If you have a question that you would like answered in his column, please send him a message at davidrobson. me/contact
