Concerns raised over children’s safety in Family Court

New Zealand Herald November 13, 2026

Concerns have been raised about whether children's fears and safety are being considered in Family Court decisions involving family violence. Photo / 123rf

When children say they are scared and don’t want to return to a parent’s care, is the Family Court listening? Rafaella Melo reports.

A 10-year-old told adults they had been hurt at a parent’s home and did not want further contact. Supervised visits continued.

Other children reported being hurt by a parent, only for their concerns to be interpreted by legal professionals as possible influence from the other parent.

In another case, two children who had witnessed family violence were required to spend time in a home where violence was still occurring.

These are among the experiences described by Canterbury family violence organisation Aviva, which says children’s fears are not always given enough weight in Family Court proceedings.

Aviva’s principal clinical adviser Gwenda Kendrew told the Herald the organisation had encountered many families facing similar situations.

“It’s quite frequent,” she said.

Kendrew said requiring children to return to someone’s care despite expressing fear could undermine their trust in the people and institutions meant to protect them.

“What we hear is that they’re not believed, they’re not heard, so then they don’t speak.”

She warned that children who experience this may grow up viewing abuse as normal, potentially perpetuating harm in the wider community.

“I think that it’s ongoing unless the system begins to work together, and the voice of the children is strongly heard.”

Kendrew questioned whether some lawyers appointed to represent children meet children frequently enough and whether some could make assumptions based on information provided by adults.

She wondered if some lawyers and judges could not sufficiently understand psychological abuse, coercive control and the dynamics of family violence.

The organisation was also concerned about the length of Family Court proceedings, which could leave families living with uncertainty and distress.

“The whole system needs to have a complete overhaul,” Kendrew said.

“Our feedback would be that the children’s experiences of family violence and their views about safety are not being heard and given meaningful weight.”

Under the Care of Children Act, a child’s welfare and best interests are the paramount consideration in parenting decisions, and children must be protected from violence.

Changes that came into force in August 2023 also strengthened the emphasis on children’s participation in decisions about their care and required judges to consider family violence.

Kendrew said the problem was not whether protections existed, but whether information about children’s experiences was shared and properly understood across the system.

She described situations where protection orders were in place, but subsequent contact arrangements created fresh concerns for families.

She also said disagreements between parents could prevent children from participating in healthy relationship education programmes, even when intended to help them recover from exposure to violence.

A Christchurch mother who spoke to the Herald knows all too well the impact of the Family Court not listening to children.

Despite court findings of family violence, her children were required to continue spending time in their father’s care.

“Sometimes she has not been able to give clear reasons or examples, because of how frightened she has been,” she said.

“That inability to explain herself has been treated as though it meant there was nothing wrong.”

Contact was later suspended after a judge viewed new evidence of the father’s behaviour.

She said the experience had also damaged the children’s trust in the institutions meant to protect them.

“That is the part I find hardest to bear, that people whose job is to protect children were made the means of harming mine.”

Research published in 2025 by University of Auckland law scholar Associate Professor Carrie Leonetti examined two High Court appeals involving children who challenged Family Court parenting orders.

In one case, an 11-year-old was ordered to have extensive unsupervised overnight contact with his father, despite the Family Court finding the father had physically and psychologically abused him and caused him to be afraid.

The child later developed post-traumatic stress, anxiety, panic attacks, insomnia, stomach problems, and a racing heartbeat.

The High Court eventually set aside the parenting order.

In another case, a teenager was ordered to leave his mother’s care in New Zealand and live with his father in Australia, despite objecting to the arrangement.

He ran away and spent weeks in juvenile detention before being allowed to return to New Zealand following an appeal.

Leonetti said older children were often treated as incapable of making decisions about where they lived, despite being able to make important decisions in other areas of life, including medical treatment.

She estimated about 80% of Family Court care and contact disputes involved family violence.

Leonetti believed sexism and outdated attitudes towards children contributed to the problem.

“I think we still have really antiquated views of children as being the property of their parents,” she said.

Leonetti said stereotypes about women fabricating abuse allegations also influenced decisions.

She pointed to findings from an upcoming study suggesting the Family Court disbelieved allegations of family violence about 57% of the time.

For her, risks were sometimes underestimated after separation, when the danger of further violence could increase.

Leonetti called for the reinstatement of stronger legal safeguards against unsupervised contact for perpetrators of family violence unless risks had been addressed.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Ministry of Justice deputy secretary, policy, Caroline Greaney said the Care of Children Act requires children to be given reasonable opportunities to express their views – either directly or through a representative – which judges must take into account.

Greaney said a lawyer for child was appointed in about 90% of Care of Children Act cases.

Lawyers representing children undertake role-specific training overseen by the New Zealand Law Society, including training on family violence.

The ministry also funds additional family and sexual violence response training for court-related professionals.

Between July 2023 and September 2026, 1697 participants attended foundational training, while 247 completed advanced training.

“While participation is strongly encouraged, it is not currently a mandatory training requirement,” Greaney said.

She said judicial education included family violence, coercive control, psychological abuse and child-centred approaches, supported by a Family Violence Bench Book.

The ministry was also progressing initiatives aimed at reducing delays and improving court administration.

Greaney said the courts were independent and the ministry could not comment on individual judicial decisions.

Rafaella Melo is a multimedia journalist with more than 10 years’ experience in Brazil. She spent nearly two years reporting for Hawke’s Bay Today before joining the NZ Herald’s Christchurch team in 2026.

Christopher Luxon at Apec: Why New Zealand must navigate US-China trade rivalry – Fran O’Sullivan

New Zealand Herald November 13, 2026

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is headed to Apec. Photo / Annaleise Shortland

Christopher Luxon is heading to Shenzhen next week for an Apec summit that will put the world’s most powerful political and corporate players in the same rooms.

United States President Donald Trump is bringing American Inc to town. Among the business heavyweights are Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Mastercard chief executive Michael Miebach.

Google and Boeing representatives will be there, but Jensen Huang, who had been expected to join the cavalcade, has been pushed out of Nvidia.

For the American companies, it’s all about opening doors, protecting market access, securing commercial opportunities and ensuring they are not shut out of the world’s second-largest economy, China.

New Zealand has a different but no less important focus.

The Prime Minister arrives at a critical moment. The global trading system is under pressure from Trump’s tariffs, strategic competition between Washington and Beijing, and the growing willingness of major powers to weaponise economic relationships.

Apec’s 21 economies account for 61% of global GDP and more than 75% of New Zealand’s exports. China is our largest trading partner.

The United States is a major export market and an essential security partner.

We cannot afford to be squeezed by their rivalry.

But alongside other smaller but influential economies such as Singapore, Canada and Australia, Luxon can make the case for the Asia-Pacific to stay open.

The US interest is direct: Musk has a substantial manufacturing presence in Shanghai through Tesla and wants to protect his commercial interests.

Mastercard wants opportunities in financial services and cross-border payments. Boeing seeks a major commercial prize in securing Chinese aircraft orders and rebuilding market share against Airbus.

Google has its own complicated relationship with Beijing, while Nvidia’s access to China’s artificial intelligence (AI) market remains entangled in Washington’s semiconductor export restrictions – hence the impact of Huang’s downfall will weigh heavily on the company’s prospects.

These companies want access, regulatory certainty, customers and supply-chain security. Their interests do not always align with Washington’s national security agenda.

But they understand that presidential diplomacy can create commercial opportunities.

New Zealand should take note.

We have internationally competitive businesses in food, agritech, technology, aviation, renewable energy and specialist services. Yet we have nothing like America’s corporate firepower.

That makes effective political and economic diplomacy even more important and underscores why Luxon must have a voice at the table on New Zealand’s behalf.

China is hosting Apec for the first time in 12 years. President Xi Jinping will be keen to position Beijing as a champion of regional co-operation and open trade at a time when Trump’s tariff policies are unsettling established relationships.

China remains fundamental to the fortunes of our dairy, meat, horticulture, forestry and tourism industries. But the next phase of the relationship must be about more than selling greater volumes of traditional commodities.

Already, Luxon has reinforced his relationship with New Zealand’s largest trading partner during a recent call with the Chinese Premier Li Qiang.

In their October conversation, Li signalled interest in expanding co-operation in services trade, electric vehicles, solar and wind technologies. He also raised progress on negotiations over services trade under the existing free trade agreement.

These are opportunities worth pursuing. New Zealand has expertise in agritech, education, financial services and technology. We should look for ways to turn those capabilities into higher-value commercial relationships.

This is likely to be the focus of discussions between Trade Minister Todd McClay (who is also travelling to Apec) and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao.

But Luxon cannot ignore the big strategic risks.

The Kiwi PM needs to be clear that New Zealand’s interests include stability in the Taiwan Strait, freedom of navigation in the South China Sea and peaceful management of disputes across North Asia.

The Korean Peninsula and the security relationships involving Japan and South Korea are also important to regional stability.

Other middle-sized nations like Singapore, Canada and Australia are likely to be on Luxon’s dance card.

All four countries have a strong interest in preserving open trade, predictable rules and a regional order that does not simply reflect the preferences of Washington or Beijing.

They cannot dictate the behaviour of superpowers, but they can build coalitions around shared interests.

The four-country grouping was first pioneered at Apec in Korea in 2025. Whether it meets again remains to be confirmed.

The other big contest playing out in Shenzhen is technological.

China has achieved enormous scale in electric vehicles, batteries and solar manufacturing. America retains major strengths in AI, software, research and capital.

Both recognise that the next industrial revolution will be shaped by control of computing power, data, critical minerals and energy.

New Zealand needs to be part of that conversation. AI adoption, data centres and advanced technology investment will all require reliable electricity. Yet our own energy security debate remains unresolved.

We cannot promote New Zealand as an attractive investment destination while leaving businesses uncertain about long-term power supply and infrastructure.

Supply security also extends to shipping and fuel. Any disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has consequences for energy markets and the availability of essential supplies. The same applies to the major maritime routes through Asia.

Luxon’s programme is compressed. He is expected at Wednesday’s welcome banquet and Thursday’s leaders’ session, departing Shenzhen that afternoon.

McClay will support him and pursue trade priorities, while Foreign Minister Winston Peters is handling a separate East Asia Summit programme.

The world is moving into a more transactional era. Trump is bringing his corporate champions to China to secure commercial advantage. Xi wants to reinforce China’s centrality to the regional economy.

New Zealand cannot match their scale or influence. But we can be smart, ambitious and clear about what we want.

Microsoft outage: ‘Broad recovery’ for Outlook and other services around globe

New Zealand Herald November 13, 2026

Microsoft says that it is seeing “improvements” for Outlook email and other services. Photo / Getty Images

Microsoft has apologised for a global outage that disrupted public services and businesses around the world, as it reported a “broad recovery” for Outlook email and other services.

The company ruled out any malicious “cyber or AI” activity as the cause of the outage, which affected several Microsoft products and disrupted healthcare services, delayed corporate earnings reports and left schools struggling to communicate.

“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” Microsoft said on X, adding full services were still being restored after the outage started yesterday.

“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.”

The disruption knocked out Microsoft products in 74 countries and territories, affecting users across the Americas and parts of Europe, Asia and Africa, according to the outage tracker Downdetector.

New Zealand said the outage forced a halt in the processing of all visa applications. Property settlements, courts and other services were also disrupted.

A top UK trade union said the disruptions were having a “serious impact” on the country’s healthcare service.

National Health Service staff receiving emergency calls were “unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos”, said Rachel Harrison, public services head at the GMB union.

As the outage dragged on for hours, airlines in India warned that customer queries may not be getting through.

IndiGo and Akasa Air both said on X that their email support services had been affected and that they may not be able to receive customers’ emails.

Japan’s Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa warned of a “significant impact” of the outage as the Microsoft products were used by a “vast number of people”.

In London’s financial district, several people interviewed by AFP said the outage exposed their dependence on Copilot, Microsoft’s AI assistant.

“I think one of the biggest things is Copilot not working,” said Yashmit Sharma, 26, an auditor. “I think this was the main bummer. And Outlook as well, of course.”

Sheera, 40, a risk manager at a mid-sized bank, said businesses needed to be better prepared for unexpected technology failures.

“I think we need to be a little bit more careful,” said Sheera, declining to give her last name. “Anything can happen: you wake up and Outlook is not working and it’s the main communication we use for our global team.”

The Australian Computer Society (ACS) called for a national review of sovereign IT risk, with chief executive Prins Ralston saying that small businesses may not have a workaround when Outlook fails.

“We need to know the systems that keep this country running won’t simply fall over without notice,” Ralston said, according to ACS publication Information Age.

On Thursday, Microsoft attributed the disruption to “elevated load” on its infrastructure.

In an updated statement on Friday, it said the “incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change”.

“We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

Reports of problems on Downdetector had begun to decline by 9am GMT.

Microsoft initially said it was investigating outage reports “in the Americas,” but later confirmed that the issue apparently affected “Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region”.

Microsoft 365 is the company’s cloud-based subscription service that includes popular applications such as Outlook and Teams.

- AFP

Paul Goldsmith’s life in politics: The inspiring, the bleak, and John Key telling him to ‘shut up’

New Zealand Herald November 13, 2026

Paul Goldsmith pulled down the curtain this week on 15 years in Parliament. He shares his highs and lows, his thoughts on the state of the National Party, and how to fix MMP.

“I’m not going to be Pocahontas.”

That is what Paul Goldsmith told himself as he eavesdropped on the corridor outside his office in Parliament. It was 2020, and new party leader Todd Muller and deputy Nikki Kaye were being grilled about the lack of diversity in National’s shadow Cabinet.

Goldsmith’s ears pricked up when he heard Kaye describe him as “obviously of Ngāti Porou”. He immediately thought of US Senator Elizabeth Warren, a woman as white as he was.

“You might remember at the time that Donald Trump had called her ‘Pocahontas’, because she’d claimed an Indian ancestry,” Goldsmith tells the Herald. “I thought to myself, ‘I’m not going to be Pocahontas.’ I need to nip this in the bud.”

He then emerged to a flurry of journalists’ questions.

“I am not Māori myself,” he clarified at the time. “The Goldsmith family have many connections to Ngāti Porou. My great-great-grandfather had European wives and Māori wives, so I’ve got lots of relatives across the Ngāti Porou, but I don’t claim to be Māori myself.”

The fuss led to Shane Jones shouting “Ngāti Epsom” at Goldsmith in the House later that week, while Tova O’Brien, during her press gallery farewell 18 months later, chose her coverage of the corridor exchanges as her political broadcasting highlight.

Goldsmith was an active participant at O’Brien’s farewell. “I yelled from the backbench, ‘When are we going to hear from the victims?’ All these nice speeches about her career, but nothing from the victims.”

It’s the kind of dry humour for which Goldsmith is well known. He’s also known for his competence, as evidenced by the 10 ministerial portfolios he will now relinquish after failing to return to Parliament.

“That’s life,” he says, a phrase he repeats often during a lengthy phone call with the Herald from his family bach in the Waitakere Ranges.

“It’s surrounded by bush which is all regenerating, and so every year it just gets better. Lots of serenity, which I need after the hurly-burly of the election campaign.”

After 15 years in Parliament, he is in the unaccustomed position of having lots of free time.

“I’m actually going to try my hand at bricklaying. I’m going to make a fireplace outside. How hard can it be?

“Prior to politics, I wrote histories and biographies for a living. I may well get back to doing some of that.”

Maybe a memoir? “Well, who knows?”

Goldsmith entered Parliament in the class of 2011 as one of nine new National MPs. In his maiden speech, he called for a strong economy, small government and an overhaul of the “no questions asked” welfare system.

The former Waitangi Tribunal historian also noted “the special place of Māori within our culture”, while expressing concern about “a tendency to elevate the importance of ethnicity in our political and legal arrangements”.

There was one aspect of life as an MP that he wasn’t prepared for: the long hours.

“My first term of Question Time was a life and death struggle not to fall asleep. It was a running joke among the nine of us who was going to be caught snoring.

“I was snapped once apparently during the Speech from the Throne, fast asleep with my mouth slightly open. I said I was just concentrating. By my fifth term, I didn’t notice it. I suppose there’s an element of conditioning.”

His early days in Parliament were under Sir John Key, who was “inspiring”. Goldsmith recalls having to catch an early flight after a late night of work during a particularly hectic week.

“I was almost catatonic, just putting one foot in front of the other. And I looked up as we were getting onto the plane, and John Key was just glad-handing everybody, chatting away, laughing, cracking jokes.

“That struck me as amazing. He would always tell us that people are watching you, whatever you do. You’ve got to always be good to people, engage, be upbeat. He lived by example.

“I loved working with him.”

Goldsmith once tried to convince Key, with characteristic dry humour, to take him to England as a token ethnic representative from the National caucus.

“He was about to head off to see the Queen. I said to him, ‘Prime Minister, when you go to Korea, you take Melissa Lee, when you go to China, you take Jian Yang, and when you go to Samoa, you take Sam Lotu-Iiga. Now you’re going to Britain. I’m British. Why aren’t you taking me?’

“He just said, ‘Shut up, Goldsmith.’”

From 2014, Goldsmith served as a minister under Key and then Sir Bill English.

“We had great times. Probably my closest mate was Simon Bridges, and we used to go running together. It was very sad when he moved on.”

Their running crew once invited Jason Walls, a Herald reporter at the time.

“I’ll never forget the sheen of sweat and look of desperation on Jason’s face when he realised he’d got himself into something that was way beyond what he’d anticipated. It was very entertaining.”

The crew didn’t last, but a new one emerged with Goldsmith now on the receiving end.

“I ran with Tama Potaka in the last couple of years, but he’s too fast. It’s hard work keeping up with him.”

Goldsmith’s first stint in Opposition, after NZ First formed a coalition with Labour in 2017, was when National was still polling in the 40s.

“We started 2020 in the mid-40s. Simon Bridges was going to be Prime Minister and I was going to be Finance Minister. It was all going to be great.”

But along came the “pretty bizarre” Covid period.

“The thing about politics is that there’s obviously some elements you can control, but there are many elements you just can’t control. You’ve got to be able to cope with that.”

During the early stages of the pandemic, Goldsmith told Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern to “stick to her knitting”. He claims it was a gender-agnostic context. His point was that the Prime Minister, who’d expressed anger at job losses, should be focused on growing the economy.

“Annoyingly, I agreed to do a pre-recorded interview with Lisa Owen on Radio New Zealand, which was predictably robust.

“About an hour after I’d done that, somebody rang in and reminded me that I’d said exactly the same thing about Shane Jones six months before.

“It would have been nice to have had that information when I was talking to Lisa Owen. It’s a bit of a theme in my political life. I always came up with a brilliant answer two hours after I needed it.”

Bridges was rolled as leader within months, but Goldsmith remained finance spokesman leading into the 2020 election. Then came the $4 billion hole in his fiscal plan.

“That was the bleakest moment. I was in a hotel in Queenstown when Robbo [Finance Minister Grant Robertson] dug out another error. It was about day three, and he’d found some other little wrinkle.

“I was sitting there and I distinctly remember thinking, ‘I’m not sure I’m going to get out of this.’”

Goldsmith was stripped of finance in the post-election shuffle, demoted, and given education. Commenting on the history curriculum the next year, he garnered headlines after saying colonisation had been good for Māori, on balance.

“I stand by those comments. When you look at the New Zealand that we’ve created today as a result of colonisation, do we conclude that it is overall a good thing and something to be proud of? Absolutely.

“To say otherwise, that it’s all somehow negative, to me is no way to think of the country.”

He describes the feedback he received at the time as “mixed”. Some were reminders of stolen land.

“But there’s lots of good things. Whole families were created. People fell in love and created new dynasties. That is the history of New Zealand.”

What is the state of Crown-Māori relations today?

“The one thing that sort of irritates me is people going around saying ‘Māori think this’ or ‘Māori think that’, when there are nearly a million New Zealanders who have Māori ancestry, and they certainly do not all think the same. They have a wide variety of views.

“This idea that Māoridom thinks the Crown-Māori relationship can be characterised simply as this or that, I think, is just not a sensible proposition.”

His National Party predecessor as Treaty Negotiations Minister, Chris Finlayson, has been highly critical of the coalition Government’s direction regarding Māori issues.

“The actions of the last three years have been destructive and harmful to the relationship between Crown and Māori,” Finlayson wrote in Facing Up To Our Future, published this year by the Helen Clark Foundation.

“I don’t agree with that,” Goldsmith says. “I just think it carries on being tested in many ways. There’s no one single thing such as the Crown-Māori relationship. That’s the point. There are many relationships.”

He notes several Treaty of Waitangi settlements he brought to conclusion.

“Nobody should kind of expect perfection in any of this, but we continue to talk and engage freely and discuss our history. As long as we keep doing that, that’s good. It’s when you stop talking that the problems arise.”

Finlayson’s view of where the National Party stands on Māori issues had some support this week from outgoing National MP Vanessa Weenink, who lost her Banks Peninsula seat.

“A lot of people in that electorate were telling me, literally, that they hate us,” Weenink said.

“Then other people would say, ’You guys have lost your way, you used to be much more reasonable, and you’re listening far too much to other people in your coalition.’”

Goldsmith doesn’t dispute that Act and NZ First pulled the coalition in a way National might not have otherwise done.

“That is what the people of New Zealand gave us in terms of the outcome of the [2023] election. That is the nature of the democracy that we have.”

Being hated is a part of being an MP, he adds.

“One piece of advice I give to my colleagues is that there’s a certain percentage of the population who will hate you and not be afraid to say it. If you took it personally, you wouldn’t get out of bed in the morning.

“You’ve just got to realise that it’s because you’re a National Party MP. You’ve just got to take it on the chin and recognise that’s part of the job.”

There’s also occasional abuse that can threaten to escalate.

“The one time I thought I was at risk getting bonked on the head was when I was first a candidate in 2005. I was just walking down the street, and somebody pulled over and got out of the car in a very menacing manner.”

A group of people on the street intercepted the agitator, “but for a split second I thought, ‘Oh heck, I’m in trouble here.’ I would have had to run. I always backed myself as a fast runner.”

He’s also a black belt in tae kwon do, but “the first thing you learn in tae kwon do is try not to get into fights, if you can avoid it”.

The “vast majority” of interactions with the public have been positive, he stresses.

“I have actually done quite a lot of door-knocking over the years in Epsom. There are some people who just say, ‘Look, I don’t like your kind’ and close the door politely.

“But it’s very rare that people are actually rude.”

Epsom has been Goldsmith’s shadow electorate since he first stood as National’s candidate in 2011, when John Key had a cup of tea with Act’s John Banks to signal a vote-splitting strategy.

That continued through 2014, when Act leader David Seymour became the Epsom MP, until this election, when Goldsmith tried to win the seat in earnest for the first time.

But Seymour retained Epsom with a 2044-vote majority.

“There’s no point regretting anything, but maybe I should have started a bit earlier. We really only really cranked into it three or four weeks before the election. If we’d started six or eight weeks before ... anyway, that’s life, and I certainly wish David all the best.”

Why didn’t they start earlier? “Well, I was kind of busy. I had a few things on,” he said, alluding to his 10 ministerial portfolios.

Why not try to be the Kaipara ki Mahurangi candidate after Chris Penk quit? “Yes, well, what’s done is done.”

And so is Goldsmith’s political career, despite his being effectively No 3 on National’s list behind Nicola Willis and Chris Bishop (others above him were in safe blue seats).

Done too are Willis, Bishop and Gerry Brownlee. National has no list MPs as a result of its seven overhang seats and a party vote below 30%.

Goldsmith doesn’t consider this a poor result.

“Governments all around the world are unpopular and facing challenging times, when petrol’s expensive and people are grumpy. In New Zealand, there’s been a big property-price correction and a slow economy for a while.

“The fact it looks like the Government’s going to hold on and be able to continue is a considerable success.”

Nor does he think the National Party is in a weakened state, given the loss of such seniority.

“We’ve got seven new MPs, and they’re a very impressive bunch. It requires the next generation to step up, and I have confidence they will.”

Right to his last day, Goldsmith walked to work across the parliamentary forecourt in the morning “with a surge of feeling in my spirit”, saying “this is great, what an honour”.

“My goal in politics was to be a senior minister in a government that made a difference to New Zealanders. I’ve got to do that for the last three years. I would have liked to have carried on, but that’s life.”

He notes fewer victims of violent crime when asked about his achievements (justice was one of his portfolios), but then points to the wider team.

“I don’t overcomplicate things. The most important thing any government can do is just provide a stable, financially sustainable, predictable platform upon which the private sector can build and prosper, and people can live healthy and safe lives.

“I think we achieved that through the John Key era, it came a bit unstuck in Opposition, and we were making good progress to re-establish that under Chris Luxon. And I’ve got every confidence that the next few years will be even better.”

He has one parting shot: MMP.

“It’s got real problems with the overhang strategies that have been employed on both sides

“If we did nothing, in three years’ time it wouldn’t surprise me if we could end up with even more of that, and the system falling over.”

He prefers the Supplementary Member (SM) system, which won only 5% support in the 1992 referendum that presented four options to replace First Past the Post (FPP).

SM would see a fixed number of electorate seats and a fixed number of list seats. Voters would have the same two votes as under MMP: an electorate vote and a party vote.

Electorate seats would go to the candidate with the most votes, and the list seats would be split proportionally, according to the share of party votes.

“Having some electorate seats and the party vote applying to the other seats, I think, is a better system. You could argue about whether it was 60/60 or 80/40, and there’s good arguments both ways, but it would do away with all this overhang nonsense.”

It would also lead to minor parties having a disproportionately smaller share of seats in Parliament, if they had only list MPs. That would mean fewer tails wagging the dog, and smaller chances of a small party holding the balance of power.

“There’s different democratic systems all around the world that are not strictly proportional. We went from one extreme to the other, from FPP to MMP, and I think a sensible thing would be halfway between the two.

“That would be the best of both worlds.”

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

A late-night foodbank service introduced to make support easier to access has uncovered a growing need, often among working Rotorua families.

The Rotorua Salvation Army Foodbank launched a Thursday evening service in August after identifying that new daytime parking charges had become a barrier for some people to seek help.

Community ministries manager Darnielle Hoods said the late appointments at its choice-model supermarket had been fully booked most weeks since, with demand rising and a new group of working families accessing support.

Hoods said asking for help was a “big step” for many families the service supported and it wanted to remove barriers.

“Sometimes we underestimate what $2 means to someone who has very little to begin with.”

The new late appointments run until 7.45pm, allowing clients to access support after work and take advantage of free parking after 5pm.

“For us, accessibility isn’t just about having a service available, but about making sure people can actually access it,” Hoods said.

“We might not be able to change every circumstance that comes through our doors, but we can look at what we can do differently to make things easier.”

Hoods said the response to the service was “encouraging” and had also unearthed new clientele.

“One māmā shared that by the time she dropped her tamariki at school and arrived to book an appointment, we were often already full.

“Another man who worked during the day couldn’t access support during our normal hours but was able to come in during the evening when he desperately needed help.”

Over the first 14 Thursdays with late appointments, the foodbank supported 206 whānau, compared with 174 over that period last year – an 18% increase.

The organisation also supported a further 67 whānau through other services, and had to turn away 24 after appointment limits were reached.

“These figures highlight both the growing demand and the importance of making our services more accessible,” Hoods said.

“Even with extended hours, there are still limits to how many people we can safely and meaningfully support.”

Today, the Rotorua Daily Post launches its annual six-week Christmas Appeal for the Rotorua Salvation Army Foodbank.

Run in partnership with The Hits Rotorua 97.5FM, the appeal rallies the community behind the foodbank in the lead-up to Christmas.

Last year’s appeal had a final donation tally of almost $93,000.

It was made up of more than 11,000 food items that were assigned an average value of $3 each, about $25,000 in cash and vouchers and 776 gifts estimated to be worth about $29,000.

One highlight was The Hits Rotorua’s Fill the Bus collection, which returns on December 3.

Hoods said this year’s appeal centred on the theme “Christmas is Better Shared”, highlighting the idea that everyone had something to contribute.

“When we share our resources, time and responsibility for caring for our community, we can make a much greater difference together.”

She said the festive season added further strain for families already struggling and that “hardship” was not always as obvious as people might think.

“Having a job doesn’t automatically mean someone is financially secure.

“We see whānau who are doing their best to provide for their families, but once rent, power, transport, groceries and other essentials are covered, there’s very little left.”

According to Stats NZ, the cost of living for the average New Zealand household increased 3% in the 12 months to September.

Petrol prices rose 19.1% over the period, accounting for about a quarter of the increase in the annual average household inflation rate.

Hoods said the response to the Thursday late-night service showed why the organisation needed to think differently about who was seeking help.

“Our normal operating hours don’t always work for people who have mahi, are managing tamariki drop-offs or juggling other commitments.”

Donations throughout the appeal are put towards staple foods and other essential items.

“When we share what we have, we are doing more than filling cupboards or putting presents under trees,” Hoods said.

“We are reminding people that they are seen, they are valued, they are not alone, and to us that is what Christmas is really about.”

Rotorua Daily Post editor Kim Gillespie said the Christmas Appeal was an important campaign that brought the community together.

“It’s crucial that locals get behind the foodbank and its vital work, and they will, as they have year after year.

“We’re proud to do our bit to get the word out and help Rotorua help those who need it.”

Newly re-elected Rotorua MP Todd McClay said the appeal highlighted the strength of Rotorua’s community, with residents coming together to support fellow locals during the festive season.

“It pulls the whole community together, people from every suburb, businesses and other associations pitch together to raise money and it shows the best side of Rotorua.”

He encouraged those who could spare a can or make a donation to get behind the appeal, and said the Salvation Army would welcome any support with “open arms”.

“I’ve always found Rotorua to be very generous, and it’s often those that have the least will give the most.”

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell said she was “blown away” every year by the generosity of the Rotorua community.

“This appeal goes a long way towards bringing some relief, dignity and joy to local families during the festive season.”

She said every donation made a difference and that everyone deserved a “full belly” and some “joy” this Christmas.

“Together we can help make that happen for more families in our community.”

Kaitlyn Morrell is a journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post. She has lived in the region for several years and studied journalism at Massey University.

Christmas Appeal: Tauranga foodbank sees families returning for weeks of ongoing support

New Zealand Herald November 13, 2026

For a growing number of Tauranga families, needing help from the foodbank is no longer a short-term setback but a weeks-long reality.

It comes as the cost of everyday essentials leaves some households with little or nothing left for food.

Tauranga Community Foodbank general manager Nicki Goodwin said the service had supported more than 22,000 people over the past year and distributed 8276 food support packages.

This was equivalent to more than 280,000 meals.

She said the number of families now needing a full week’s groceries and ongoing assistance just to get by had grown 105% since 2024.

“This increase is definitely a trend to be concerned about.

“There is no other income available during that [week], and for some, this can continue for several weeks.”

She said the foodbank was seeing more families return for regular assistance through “no fault of their own”, often with little prospect of their situation changing.

“I feel for many who are trying to survive with little hope for the future.”

Each day, an average of 35 households seek help from Tauranga Community Foodbank, and Goodwin said that number would increase over the coming months.

“This is a massive amount of food heading out into the community each day, the only other alternative is that people would go hungry.”

Goodwin said she was aware of other food support services around the country having to limit how many households they could afford or manage each day.

“This is something that we would not wish to have to do, and will continue to manage the high need if we have the support of volunteers and donors.”

Today the Bay of Plenty Times begins its annual six-week Christmas Appeal for Tauranga Community Foodbank.

Supported by The Hits Bay of Plenty 95.0FM, the appeal replenishes the foodbank’s shelves, offers Christmas treats for people who may otherwise have none and boosts the foodbank into the new year.

Last year’s appeal saw $266,031.98 in donations – $176,145.98 in cash and 29,962 food items.

The foodbank values each item at an average of $3, totalling $89,886 worth of food.

“Cash donations go towards purchasing the nutritious kai we offer, and food donations often head out the door the very same day they come in,” Goodwin said.

“All support, no matter how small, matters and makes a difference to someone else.”

Goodwin said traditionally the foodbank would provide four days of groceries to meet the needs of the individual or family.

“What we are seeing now is a growing number of people needing a minimum of a full week’s groceries.”

She said redundancies, illness and unexpected emergency expenses were among the most common drivers behind the need for week-long food support.

“After paying essential costs such as rent, power, medical, and other everyday costs, there is often very little left and in some cases a deficit.”

Goodwin said housing pressures remained a major driver of food insecurity, with power and fuel cost increases placing further strain on stretched household budgets.

According to Stats NZ, the cost of living for the average New Zealand household increased 3.0% in the 12 months to September.

Petrol prices rose 19.1% over the period, accounting for about a quarter of the increase in the annual average household inflation rate.

“Many people run a very tight, inflexible weekly budget which means that even the smallest change in circumstances renders them unable to afford any groceries,” Goodwin said.

She said it was sad that Christmas often added to the pressure many people were already feeling.

“It is meant to be a time of celebration, reflection, and spending time together.”

Tauranga Crossing; the Tauranga CBD, Greerton and Pāpāmoa libraries; Mercury Baypark Arena and the Pāpāmoa Sports & Recreation Centre are drop-off points for non-perishable food donations during this year’s appeal, during normal opening hours.

The Mount Maunganui library is closed for renovations.

Perishables and non-perishables can also be dropped at the foodbank’s depot on Brook St near Fraser Cove.

Financial donations can be made directly to the foodbank’s bank account.

The Hits Bay of Plenty team will also be collecting canned food donations for the appeal next month at two community events as part of the Bower Real Estate and Chuffed Gifts Christmas lights trail.

Bay of Plenty Times editor Kim Gillespie said tough times often brought out the best in people.

“We know plenty of people are feeling the pinch, but we really appreciate those who still give, knowing there are others worse off.

“We’re confident our readers will give generously to our Christmas Appeal, as they have year after year.”

Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale said the foodbank played an important role in supporting people across the community all year round.

“At Christmas, when household budgets can be stretched further, the need for that support is even greater.”

He said the annual appeal brought out the best in Tauranga as individuals, businesses and organisations stepped up to support.

“With demand continuing to grow, every bit of the generosity helps.”

Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell said the Christmas Appeal had brought Tauranga together for more than 14 years, supporting the important work of the foodbank.

“It’s a great example of the generosity and community spirit we have here in Tauranga, with local people, businesses and organisations all pitching in to help others.”

He said Christmas was an expensive time of year for families and encouraged anyone who is able to donate to get behind the appeal.

“Help make Christmas a little brighter for people in our community.”

Financial donations received throughout the six-week appeal are put towards staple foods and help the foodbank get through the New Year as well.

Goodwin said: “My message is for us all to take a moment to be grateful for what we may have ourselves, and then to look outside to see if we have the opportunity to help others.

“Tauranga is an amazingly generous city and truly cares about others; let’s prove that by making things a bit better for someone else.”

Kaitlyn Morrell is a journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post. She has lived in the region for several years and studied journalism at Massey University.

Christmas Appeal: Letter from the Rotorua Salvation Army Foodbank

New Zealand Herald November 13, 2026

Rotorua Salvation Army community ministries manager Darnielle Hoods. Photo / Kelly O'Hara

Every Christmas, people across Rotorua make time to do something for someone else.

Tamariki (children) bring donations to school for Fill the Bus.

Firefighters across Mamaku and Ngongotahā head out on to the streets to collect kai.

Local businesses host different ways of gathering cans, churches and volunteers join in and people add a few extra cans, cereal boxes or treats to their shopping to share.

If you have been part of that in any way over the years, thank you. We see what your generosity makes possible for whānau.

The Salvation Army’s Christmas Appeal theme this year is Christmas is better shared.

Here in Rotorua, we see that ... when whānau come into the choice-model supermarket, they can choose the kai that suits their household.

When you donate, you help us stock the shelves with a range of kai so people can pick what they will actually use and what their whānau will enjoy.

At Christmas, your support also helps put gifts under the tree for tamariki.

Our team meets whānau who are working hard to make ends meet and still find there is not enough left for groceries after the bills are paid.

We know many of the people who give to this appeal are watching their own budgets closely too.

That makes it all the more meaningful when someone chooses to share what they can.

If you are able to give this year, please give. We would love your support.

You might add a couple of cans to your shop, donate a new gift for a child, get behind Fill the Bus or one of the local can drives or give some of your time.

You can also donate directly to the appeal, which helps us buy kai and gifts.

Our team and volunteers then bring all that you contribute together and they fill the Supermarket so whānau in need can choose what kai they need as they head into Christmas.

On behalf of our team at The Salvation Army Rotorua, thank you for thinking of others and for sharing what you can.

It means a lot to us to see Rotorua turn up for one another, year after year.

Meri Kirihimete.

Forestry report: Has Christmas come early?

New Zealand Herald November 13, 2026

Export log prices are at their highest level in 20 months. Photo / Marty Melville

Content brought to you by Stand Forestry

OPINION

It’s amazing how quickly people’s demeanour changes with a run of fine weather and increased temperatures, even with a backdrop of a very negative election campaign by the big players.

While the election results still hang in the balance, the improved demeanour has been buoyed by better economic news, strong farm returns and, as of this month, the highest export log prices in 20 months.

Sort of like Christmas has come early, especially if you’re the leader of the Opportunity Party.

While an increase in export log prices wasn’t entirely unexpected, the magnitude of the increase caught a few off guard.

A-grade short prices in Southern North Island ports have topped $131/Japanese Agricultural Standard (JAS), and there are reports of prices upwards of $135/JAS in some other ports where there is a battle for volume.

Although in many cases the increase may only cover the additional cost of fuel, we are definitely headed in the right direction.

Before we get too carried away and order a new Maserati, it’s important to understand that this increase is not due solely to a supply and demand imbalance and more thanks to reduced shipping costs and foreign exchange.

The holding of the OCR by the Reserve Bank saw the NZ dollar take a popularity dip reminiscent of the Republicans in the mid-terms and, although it has rebounded somewhat, it is still around a cent lower than mid to late October.

Also helping is the strengthening of the yuan against the $US which is now at a four-year high.

Shipping rates have eased thanks to softened demand for Handysize vessels globally although, unfortunately, the Pacific Basin is holding up better than the Atlantic.

Further softening is, however, expected throughout the month.

Current uplift from Chinese ports is running at 65,000m3 per day, which is a solid number, and port inventories have dropped by 270,000m3 from September to 2.3 million m3.

So, on the face of it, we are headed in the right direction but until we get close to a 2.0 million m3 inventory level we are unlikely to see significant increases in CFR sales prices.

New Zealand supply will drop over the Christmas break, potentially creating a hole in mid-February deliveries which times well for the Chinese New Year (CNY) break.

This annual holiday effectively takes a month of demand off the table.

If we can head into the CNY period at a sub-2.0 million inventory level then we will likely look rosy headed into Q2 2027.

However, New Zealand supply generally increases during the summer months (especially with increased export prices), which may scupper this potential.

There’s not much in the way of great economic news out of China.

The Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) dropped into negative territory in October with a result of 49.3 from a slightly positive September number of 50.1.

In addition, the October China Producers Price Index (PPI) was at a 2026 high of 5.7% versus the Consumer Price Index (CPI) of 0.7%.

This indicates that the raw materials and other goods used by manufacturers are rising faster than actual consumer goods which will be putting a significant squeeze on manufacturers’ margins.

Ultimately, if this trend continues, it will lead to inflation; however, they are coming off a rather low base of 0.9% to the year ended September so there’s a fair bit of headroom.

India cargoes continue to be problematic with, in my view, ridiculously long delays to unload vessels at Kandla Port.

In my opinion, in addition to the already antiquated unloading methods that add significant cost, bulk vessels are unloading cargoes such as iron ore destined for Iran on to Kandla Port for reloading on to much smaller coastal freighters (which are less of a loss if they have an unfortunate missile interaction) before heading for the Strait of Hormuz.

Until India drags its port operations into the current century, it is unlikely that this market will be able to play with the big boys both in terms of operational cost and volume throughput.

The local market continues to show more than a few green shoots.

Following strong building consent numbers in August, September also showed a decent lift with an 18% annual increase (compared to 21% in August).

Canterbury still leads the charge with a 35% increase to the end of September, which should come as a surprise to no one.

Non-residential consents don’t paint the same picture unfortunately, with a slight lift of only 2.2% for the same period.

These numbers are lead indicators and don’t necessarily convert into immediate additional timber demand; however, they do point to improved sentiment and generally flow through the system in the following 12 months.

The recent announcement of the MPI ballot for registering forests planted on Land Use Capability (LUC) class 6 land into the ETS saw an oversubscription in the over 100ha class and an undersubscription in the under 100ha class.

Information released by MPI shows that in the over 100ha category there were only about 12,000ha of unique titles submitted which is less than 10% of what was initially reported.

This indicated that many properties were entered multiple times in an effort to improve one’s chances which is less than ideal.

The current NZU spot price has crept up over the $50 mark, with trades currently at $50.90/NZU.

Depending on the make-up of the next Government, there may be price pressure in either direction as each party has a different view on what they want to do with the ETS.

Our hope is that they keep their wee fingers away from it but that’s looking less likely.

So, as we roll ever closer to putting the tinsel on the Christmas tree, the general feeling is a positive one in terms of log prices that will hopefully last past the New Year’s hangover.

Once the deals are done in the Beehive and the new round of MPs are minted into the system we will know how the cards fall and what, if any, lollies are left in the jar for the forest industry.

It would be great to see the Minister of Forestry within Cabinet and preferably at the important end of the table, but generally, in the political lollie scramble, we’re the ones running in from the back with a limp … and that’s before we get ankle-tapped by Federated Farmers.

Angkor Wat may be Cambodia’s greatest drawcard, but these unexpected corners charmed me more

Sydney Morning Herald November 14, 2026

In the streets, villages and corners of Siem Reap, other spectacles are waiting to be discovered.

I think I may have fallen in love with a rat named Gertrude. In the thick afternoon heat of Siem Reap, Cambodia’s second-largest city, I watch the African giant pouched rat scurry across a sandy enclosure. The size of a small cat, with oversized ears and a twitching pink nose, she’s sniffing for explosives, scratching the ground when she detects TNT and earning a treat from her handler.

Gertrude is one of the HeroRATs used by APOPO, a Belgian non-profit that trains the animals in Tanzania, then deploys them in Cambodia and other countries to detect landmines. Too light to detonate the explosives, the rats can search an area the size of a tennis court in less than half an hour, a task that might take a human, working cautiously with a metal detector, four days.

An estimated 1.7 million Cambodians died under the Khmer Rouge in the 1970s and decades of conflict left 4 to 6 million landmines buried across the country. Despite three decades of clearance efforts, the explosives are still claiming victims, with 39 people killed or injured in 2025 alone. Gertrude is a small but mighty solution.

A day earlier, I’d gone looking for wonder on a grander scale. Beneath a swirling monsoonal sky at Angkor Wat, the world’s largest religious monument and the centrepiece of Cambodia’s vast Angkor temple complex, I watched dawn smudge the silhouettes of its five lotus-shaped towers. There was no spectacular sunrise, just diffused light falling over ancient stonework, and influencers posing for photographs against a backdrop of rain-soaked, almost neon-green forest.

It was my third visit to Angkor, and although I appreciate its extraordinary scale and artistry, it’s never given me the tears or goosebumps I often experience when I travel. Maybe it’s the crowds or the weight of expectation, but the awe I keep wanting to feel has always eluded me.

After bidding Gertrude farewell, I head out of Siem Reap, past roadside stalls piled high with fruits, before the countryside opens into rice paddies dotted with candy-coloured stilt houses and hump-backed cattle. I’m with Chhunnin Neat from the Shinta Mani Foundation, the charitable arm of the hotel where I’m staying. We pull up outside a village home, where a small group of women is weaving bags and baskets in the shade using dried water hyacinth, an invasive weed I’d seen choking Tonlé Sap Lake earlier in my trip. Each bag takes four days to finish, the women tell me, as I calculate how many I can squeeze into my suitcase. The work allows them to earn an income without leaving their children to find seasonal agricultural work.

Raised by a single mother who woke at 2am to sell cakes at the market, Neat was encouraged to pursue an education. Now she works to give other women the same chance. “I really want to help women like me,” she says as we drive back into the city. “I’m tired, but when I see the women’s faces, it charges me.”

Back in Siem Reap, I wander through the Made in Cambodia market, running my fingers over colourful, handwoven blankets and admiring shelves of ceramics, crafts with centuries-old roots in Cambodia. My next encounter with Siem Reap’s enterprising women comes with a fresh lotus flower, presented by my tuk-tuk driver the same evening. She works for Tuk Tuk Lady, an association founded by Kim Sokleang, a single mother of two who began driving to support her children, despite being told that women belong at home and driving is men’s work. Her network now includes 25 women, each earning their own income and choosing their working hours.

My driver drops me at Phare Circus, where things take a wonderfully peculiar turn. Beneath the big top, performers scatter rice across the stage, tracing patterns in the grains before launching into dizzying acrobatics as live music swells around them. Rice rains from the ceiling while a painter, seemingly oblivious to the chaos, works on a canvas, revealing his finished painting to thunderous applause. Part Cirque du Soleil, part celebration of Cambodian culture, the circus grew out of a 1994 art-therapy program established by young Cambodians returning from refugee camps.

On my final morning in Siem Reap, I consider returning to Angkor but, instead, follow the Siem Reap River, past shuttered bars and enormous rain trees strung with lights, towards Wat Bo, one of the city’s oldest Buddhist temples. Inside, local families are gathering to make offerings and receive blessings. There isn’t another tourist in sight and, feeling like an intruder, I slip outside into the gardens. There, almost by accident, I discover two long rows of statues of Buddhist monks, their faded saffron robes and golden lotus pedestals forming a silent corridor beneath the trees. I stand before them in the early morning light, goosebumps rising on my arms, and tears finally pricking my eyes.

The writer travelled courtesy of Shinta Mani Angkor and G Adventures.

Matt dug in Patagonia. He made a priceless discovery about Earth’s biggest creatures

Sydney Morning Herald November 14, 2026

A fossil hunt in a remote Argentinian province has revealed a skeleton critical to the story of biology’s grandest experiment.

Dr José Luis Carballido, diviner of bones and hunter of Earth’s most colossal creatures, is an animal of the field. His hide is a navy hardshell jacket, zipped against the unrelenting winds of the Patagonian badlands. A geological hammer – one side blunt for splitting rocks, the other a metal talon – hooks into a fold of his jacket so the handle sticks up from his shoulder for easy unsheathing, like a Viking’s battleaxe.

Striding through the bone-coloured hills of Bryn Gwyn, a 40-million-year-old fossil field in Argentina’s remote Chubut province, he stoops and, with the sharp side of his hammer, conjures miracles from the shale. He flips out a tooth from a cousin of the megalodon shark. Then comes a disc resembling a ring of dehydrated pineapple; a sliver of the ancient shark’s spine. He fills our palms with fragments of mouth plates prehistoric stingrays used to grind up crabs, back when this moonscape, gnarled with thorns as long as toothpicks, was a shallow sea. There are ribs from the ancestors of river dolphins. The fist-sized vertebrae of small whales. Primeval penguin bones.

As Carballido’s hammer has revealed, Argentinian Patagonia is rife with fossils. Carballido’s trick is tracking down where the most complete and enormous lie. “It’s not very scientific,” he grins. “It’s a feeling, like the people who look for water.” He crosses his hammer over his forearm to create an X, mimicking divining rods.

The institution he works for, the nearby Museum of Palaeontology Egidio Feruglio (MEF), frequently receives reports of fossils unearthed by the wind and spotted by the region’s gauchos – Argentina’s beret-doffed horsemasters, who roam these remote plains as shepherds and ranch hands.

Palaeontologists don’t automatically get excited at such reports, especially in fossil-rich Patagonia. But when Carballido visited one of these prospective excavation sites in 2020, north of a nowhere town called Paso de Indios in the desolate steppe halfway between the Andes and the Atlantic, his instinct shivered. The knobbed end of a thick femur jutted from a hillside. Beside it lay a broken tibia – the “shinbone” that joins a femur. The proximity of the bones hinted that what lay deeper in the rock could be a fossil-hunter’s goldmine: articulated dinosaur bones, arranged together as they would have been in life. Rods crossed in his mind. But he didn’t yet dig.

A few years later, Carballido began talking with Dr Matthew McCurry, curator of paleontology at the Australian Museum, while planning the Sydney installation of MEF’s roving exhibition called Dinosaurs of Patagonia. At the centre of the show is Carballido’s blockbuster discovery, the goliath he unearthed and described to global fanfare in 2017: Patagotitan mayorum – a leading candidate for the largest animal to ever walk the Earth. Nine metres tall and more than 30 metres long, the 57-tonne member of the “titanosaur” clade defied gravity and thermodynamics to pose evolution’s fiercest challenge to the limits of physics.

Amid wargaming how the enormous sauropod skeleton would fit into the museum – an issue now solved – the palaeontologists raised the possibility of gathering fresh fossil material to add to the exhibition. Carballido asked if McCurry could help excavate those bones that intrigued him near Paso de Indios in 2020. “It was a little bit nerve-racking, flying somewhere where you don’t speak the language, you’ve never met the people in person, you’re in a remote area,” says McCurry, a blue-eyed, short-bearded paleontological polymath who once earned a living as a mechanical bull operator before dedicating his career to science. “It’s quite heavy work, especially when collecting a really big fossil like a dinosaur. And the scientific outcomes were always a bit high-risk.” Such risks included flying such a long way and finding nothing valuable beneath the surface.

But things quickly became exciting when they began excavating in March last year. The rock layer itself dated to a mysterious phase of the Cretaceous – the final age of the dinosaurs before an asteroid felled their kingdom – which we know precious little about. The bones belonged to a sauropod, the thick-legged, tiny-headed, plant-hoovering behemoths with necks as grand as spires, made famous by Jurassic Park’s majestic brachiosaurus herds.

Carballido realised, from the shape of facets on the vertebrae, that a new species was on their hands – a possible early relative of Patagotitan. The dinosaur died between 110 and 115 million years ago, perhaps in a gentle, braided stream. It was a time when moist oceanic winds nourished a humid forest lush with conifers, ferns and ginkgos, before the volcanically violent rise of the Andes transformed these lands into the arid plains of the steppe.

As the excavation team dug around the 1.6-metre femur, more treasures emerged: an articulated length of the dinosaur’s tail. Parts of its front and back limbs. Most of its pelvic girdle, including the sacrum, a large triangular plate wedged between the wings of the pelvis, also known as the “holy bone” because it shields the reproductive organs and was used in the sacrificial rites of some ancient cultures. It was the first complete sauropod sacrum ever found in the region, and as it emerged, Carballido’s face lit up. “There were a lot more bones than we realised,” McCurry says. “That means it’s a lot more scientifically important.”

The reason Carballido offered to work with McCurry, the Australian expert suspects, is that they’re both “reasonably chill”. Fieldwork is not for the highly strung. It is painstaking, back-breaking, nail-biting and unglamorous. McCurry calls it “type 2 fun”: gruelling in the moment but satisfying when it’s done. McCurry shows a video of the excavation team after a 12-hour day of having their teeth rattled by handheld jackhammers: someone, to lift the mood, is blasting electronica and running a disco light. Coloured orbs skate across exhausted bodies slumped silently against the walls. Type 2 fun.

Extracting fossils can be meticulously slow, but at other times the action unfolds at pace. At the palaeontology field in Bryn Gwyn, we watch a group of trainee field technicians scramble across a hillside, obeying instructions barked in rapid-fire Spanish. Paintbrushes, broomsticks and chisels are at work in the grave of an ancient cetacean (whale or dolphin). The group’s intense focus is sporadically thrown off by a primordial-looking stick insect crawling through the action. The students treat the bug as gingerly as a live grenade; when disturbed, it spews a noxious chemical that fouls the air and blinds the eyes. Just another hazard of working in the badlands.

5:42

Inside the hunt for Earth’s biggest dinosaurs

A fossil hunt in the badlands of Patagonia has revealed a Sauropod skeleton, critical to the story of biology’s grandest giants

Thankfully, the air is sharp with a different scent: nail polish remover. The crew drench the bones in acrylic resin dissolved in acetone, which soaks into and stabilises the porous fossil. Working fast, they layer wet strips of toilet paper over the bone like papier-mâché. Then come buckets filled with a slurry of plaster, which they scoop up in fistfuls and slather over the paper, forming a thick, hard shell. White-crusted fingers pass around a cup of mate (“mah-tay”), the bitter Argentinian tea sipped through a communal straw that seems to fuel a nation. The operation creates a “field jacket”: a giant, white, protective egg built around a fossil so it can be transported safely back to the lab.

The jacket containing the sauropod sacrum, which now lies in the museum ready for analysis, weighed two tonnes. McCurry has returned to Argentina to scan and scrutinise the bones with Carballido to piece together where this creature fits in the story of titanosaurs, the group which gave rise to the biggest land animals of all time. The project holds the potential to shed crucial new light on how evolution pulled off its most extreme experiment.

To understand why Patagotitan’s gigantism evolved, we must look to theropods – the bipedal, carnivorous, vicious killers that include velociraptors and history’s most iconic apex predator, Tyrannosaurus rex. The T. rex didn’t yet exist when Patagotitan thundered the Earth 100 million years ago, but other terrors bloodied the wet Cretaceous forests and marshlands of Patagonia.

In 1995, close to McCurry and Carballido’s recent sauropod site, a monster emerged: Tyrannotitan chubutensis, a massive meat-eater that reached a comparable size to T. rex, at 12 metres long and 4 metres tall at the hip. Living in a world stalked by bus-sized hunters packing skulls crammed with 60 blade-like and replaceable teeth, other dinosaurs had to evolve ways of avoiding Tyrannotitan-mediated murder. They could get really fast. Become excellent at hiding. Develop thick-skinned “armour” and flock in herds. Or grow to the size of gods.

Patagotitan opted for the latter strategy to spectacular effect, but it came at a cost: a body that size is a logistical nightmare. When you’re the weight of 14 African elephants, simple processes become Sisyphean feats. Eating enough food and getting enough oxygen. Not overheating (the bigger your body size, the more difficult it is to relinquish heat). Maintaining the skeletal architecture to withstand the crushing force of gravity weighing on 57 tonnes of flesh and bone. There’s a reason the world’s biggest animals, blue whales – shorter than Patagotitan but heavier by weight – evolved in the ocean, where buoyancy negates much of gravity’s tyranny.

Sauropods had some extraordinary adaptations to cope with being giants. Their lungs were fashioned in the hyperefficient style of modern birds. Unlike our lungs, which inflate with each breath and uptake oxygen only when we inhale, dinosaur lungs were fixed and rigid. Air cycled through in one direction, so fresh air never mixed with stale breath and oxygen constantly gushed into the bloodstream. It’s this “superlung” system that allows birds today, such as the bar-tailed godwit, to span the Pacific Ocean on their death-defying migrations, often in oxygen-poor altitudes. Sauropod lungs also worked in concert with air sacs that honeycombed their skeletons, which made breathing even more efficient, helped shed metabolic heat and significantly lightened the weight of their bones.

Microscopic analysis of mineralised structures within a young titanosaur’s femur reveals a dense web of nutrient-delivering blood vessels, similar to fast-growing mammals such as whales. This, scientists believe, is evidence the titanosaurs grew astonishingly quickly, dashing the idea, imported from reptiles, that the dinosaurs grew slowly over decades like crocodiles. “It’s crazy because when you see an animal so large, people used to think that they lived for 300 years,” Carballido says back at MEF, standing among hunks of titanosaur vertebrae as big as barbecues. “But the oldest one that we know is around 60. Hold this.”

He disappears into the museum’s backstage collection, which holds 42,000 fossils, and I am left manhandling a sauropod egg the size of a soccer ball. Its hatchling couldn’t have been much larger than a chihuahua. And yet, from eggs such as this one emerged babies that swelled to the size of buildings in just 15–20 years. The phenomenal growth rate makes sense, given the goal was to spend as little time as possible with a body small enough to fit between a predator’s jaws.

About 60 Tyrannotitan teeth were found alongside the six Patagotitan specimens Carballido famously unearthed between 2012 and ’15 with colleague Dr Diego Pol. Initially, due to bite marks on the sauropod’s tail, they believed the Patagotitans had been killed by the carnivores. Histological analysis, however, showed the sauropods were young adults, still growing but already the size of semitrailers and too large for Tyrannotitan’s jaws. At that size, only one dinosaur could have posed a threat: another Patagotitan. “They were at the age and at the moment of the year when males fight each other to be the dominant one of the group,” Carballido speculates. “Probably, the specimens that we found were those who lost the fight.” Those Tyrannotitan teeth, then, may have been the result of a scavenging smorgasbord rather than an active kill.

At a similar time to Patagotitan rose Argentinosaurus – believed to be even bigger, but it’s hard to say unequivocally given we only have a handful of their bones. At another site, Carballido is excavating the bones of another new titanosaur that may be 5 to 7 per cent bigger again. Something about this time period, the “Albian” age between about 100 to 113 million years ago, made the gigantic possible. The biggest titanosaurs also only occurred in a restricted band of the mid-latitudes, far from the equator. Carballido believes tropical forests may have been too hot for the giants. McCurry is pondering another theory he’s keen to discuss with paleobotanists: that the latitudes titanosaurs occupied had uniquely phosphorus-rich vegetation, which acted like fertiliser for their fast-growing bones.

Titanosaurs shrank towards the end of the dinosaurs’ reign into species such as Saltasaurus, which grew to 8.5 metres and weighed only 2.5 tonnes; positively pocket-sized, by sauropod standards. The trend violates an idea called Cope’s law. “The idea with Cope’s law is that everything gets bigger through time until there is an extinction event,” McCurry says. “But it’s not the case with sauropods. It seems like it’s happening in a peak during the middle Cretaceous.”

The exact factors behind the giants’ rise and fall remain under scrutiny. But you needed it all for biology to achieve its grandest, meatiest megalith: the perfect climate, ideal latitude, lush vegetation and ferocious predators. Kaboom. Patagotitan.

The new sauropod bones excavated by McCurry and Carballido are spread across the institute’s laboratory, a dusty workshop strewn with bloodthirsty-looking skulls, buckets of ribs and boulder-sized fossils that could crush a Corolla. It’s a place that shows the study of dinosaurs remains a hotbed of discovery. A new dinosaur species is coming from the earth once a week, and cutting-edge technologies are pushing the limits of what fossils can teach us. We learned only recently from preserved pigment structures that Diplodocus sauropods had sensationally speckled skin, and Australian-led research out this month has uncovered fossilised red blood cells in the 115 million-year-old bones of a Brazilian feathered theropod.

Carballido hands over a chevron bone, a Y-shaped structure the length of my forearm and shaped like a crude slingshot, that would’ve carried a rope-like vein down the sauropod’s tail. In a crate nearby are two caudal vertebrae – almighty slabs of the beast’s tail – and its clublike femur, all bound for display in Sydney. The sacrum of the new species lies in the centre of it all, splayed open and demanding reverence like the eldritch slab of an ancient altar.

Over the next week, McCurry and Carballido painstakingly code every bump, curve and knob of these bones and feed the numbers into a phylogenetic character matrix, which converts morphological elements of a skeleton into code. By comparing the matrix to other Gondwanan sauropod species from both Australia and South America, they can calculate where a new species fits on an evolutionary tree.

What they have discovered is not just a primitive Patagotitan relative. They suspect this dinosaur marks the first branch on the evolutionary tree that led to titanosaurs. The critical opening chapter in the odyssey of biology’s grandest juggernauts.

“We need to get a little bit more data into the phylogeny to have it for certain,” McCurry says when we meet up in Buenos Aires after his week of rapid analysis at MEF. “But it’s looking good. There’s all these characters within the pelvis which show it’s probably got quite a wide stance, which is a pretty characteristic titanosaur thing. It’s potentially one of the reasons they were able to feed really efficiently, because they had a large area for their internal organs and stomach.” That wide stance allowed for the sauropod’s engine – the fermentation tank of its gut – to grow fat and supercharged, so it could slowly strip every iota of nutrition from vast amounts of vegetation it gorged upon from the top of the canopy. “It means titanosaurs, when they first evolved, had these traits. And we didn’t necessarily know that.”

Before the palaeontologists can name and describe the new species, they must recover the rest of the fossil. At least a scapula and a humerus remain buried. But funding such expeditions, of late, has been difficult.

In Buenos Aires, a few days after visiting Chubut, traffic is at a crawl. We inch past a protest on the edge of detonation: soon rocks will fly and police will return fire with tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets. The demonstrators are raging against right-wing populist President Javier Milei’s cuts to universities and education. Science funding in Argentina has plummeted by 50 per cent since 2023. Professors’ pay has plunged below the poverty line and world-class experts, such as Carballido, have found themselves kneecapped with little funding for fieldwork.

Meanwhile, Australia’s premier science body, the Academy of Science, has been up in arms over the fact that spending on research and development has crashed to the historic low of 1.69 per cent of GDP, below the 2.7 per cent average among OECD nations.

That’s forced researchers of all stripes to get creative. McCurry and Carballido, for their part, are gunning for funding from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which operates a diplomatic grants program called the Council on Australia Latin America Relations (COALAR). The idea is to run more joint expeditions, cross-pollinating Australia’s analytical know-how with the expertise of Patagonia’s field technicians – and hopefully fund the rest of the sauropod dig on the side.

In Chubut, times in the province are tough as the profits of traditional industries, including sheep farming, wane. Amid the downturn, the paleontology museum has become a beacon of tourism and economic activity, and the institution’s regional city of Trelew has embraced the dinosaur theme with gusto.

A mock fossil site decorates the walls of the baggage claim at the airport and a model raptor snarls in a corner. Walk outside the arrivals hall and on the steppe’s flat, dry horizon, you’ll spy a looming model Patagotitan. Stand beneath it and you can imagine a primordial mammalian part of you quivering with the memory of scuttling around the feet of giants. All around, the Patagonian wind blows, spiriting away sand and time to offer the bones of gods to the air.

Angus Dalton and Louise Kennerley travelled to Patagonia courtesy of the Australian Museum and Adventure World. Dinosaurs of Patagonia opens on November 28.

Surveilled, scared and broke: How Emily’s ex is ruining her life through the Family Court

Sydney Morning Herald November 14, 2026

Emily* has two suitcases filled with hundreds of documents from her years in the Family Court. Her story is far from unique.
