Emily* has two suitcases filled with hundreds of documents from her years in the Family Court.

Over five years and multiple appeals, her ex Liam* – who is subject to an apprehended violence order (AVO) protecting Emily – issued dozens of subpoenas requesting years of information about her, their child and her new partner’s health, travel, expenses, schedule, and conversations with her psychologist.

While the Family Court allows only five subpoenas per party per order, Liam lodged more than double that number in a single month. Emily has sole parental responsibility, which Liam has repeatedly challenged.

The barrage of requests for information has left Emily feeling surveilled and controlled, while the protracted proceedings have left her broke.

Systems abuse, where perpetrators weaponise legal processes to continue domestic and family violence, is endemic. Despite recent reforms, inquiries continue to warn that the Family Court is being used to financially and emotionally exhaust victim-survivors and keep them tied to their abusers.

Eighty-four per cent of parenting cases in the Family Court contain allegations of domestic violence.

Emily has spent half a million dollars on legal fees, forcing her to sell her home and jewellery, liquidate shares and take out loans.

Emily earns too much to qualify for Legal Aid, but can no longer afford a lawyer, and is now self-representing. Her ex, who hired a private barrister for his AVO defence, is self-employed and qualifies for Legal Aid.

“All the money I had saved for my children is gone. It is exhausting and soul-destroying,” Emily said.

“I feel so let down by the system.”

This masthead has spoken with dozens of victim-survivors, advocates, lawmakers and experts about endemic systems abuse in the Family Court system.

Several spoke anonymously, fearing backlash from aggrieved parties or influential judges.

The Federal Circuit and Family Court is one of Australia’s most secretive courts. It is illegal to publish details that may identify parties, witnesses or children involved in a family law case.

Emily’s story is being platformed to launch an investigation by The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age into abuse in the Family Court. We want to understand how systems abuse is taking place. We’d like to hear from you via the survey below. We understand this is sensitive and all answers can be submitted anonymously.

While a range of reforms have been implemented to better protect victim-survivors, researchers and advocates said an urgent overhaul was needed. The court does not release data on the efficacy of these programs.

Funding for several key services supporting survivors has recently been slashed, with legal service organisations reducing eligibility criteria.

Emily thought leaving Liam would end his control. Instead, she said the court enabled his harassment.

Weeks into a new job, Liam subpoenaed Emily’s employer for internal communications, timesheets and drug-testing records. She alleged the move was intended solely to damage her reputation.

He also subpoenaed her bank, the Department of Home Affairs, police and therapists for notes from her and their daughters’ sessions.

“It’s been brutal,” she said.

The subpoenas forced her to explain Liam’s history of domestic violence to her new employer.

“I had to let most of [the subpoenas] through – I couldn’t afford to have representation to object to everything,” Emily said.

She said a redaction error also accidentally revealed her address to him.

The state court failed to hear her request to alter the parenting orders to align with the AVO, forcing her back to the Family Court at a cost of thousands.

Emily said her lawyer described Liam’s tactics as a “scorched earth” strategy designed to drown her in legal fees and paperwork to discourage her from pursuing parenting orders.

She submitted a complaint about Liam’s lawyer to the legal services commissioner, alleging the lawyer facilitated his domestic violence. The complaint was dismissed.

However, the court recognised the burden of Liam’s applications and, in a rare move, awarded Emily costs orders. It’s been two years, and Emily said he had yet to pay a cent.

“The only money I have is in my superannuation,” Emily said. “Every spare cent has been spent on these proceedings.”

A court spokesperson said it did not comment on individual matters, adding that additional subpoenas required the courts’ permission, parties could object, and parties could apply to the courts to have costs orders enforced.

“Misuse of court processes can be a form of family violence … and litigation itself can be used as a form of coercive control,” the spokesperson said.

Former Family Court judge Warwick Neville described family litigation as a “wretched business” that “brings out the worst” in people.

“The system itself is used as an insidious form of domestic violence … a form of payback for leaving,” he said.

Neville said this abuse spanned all income levels, particularly when a perpetrator realised they could not maintain control.

“[They think] I’m going to do whatever is necessary to make sure there’s nothing left,” he said.

“It just becomes a pattern of behaviour: sinister, controlling, coercive – the worst sides of humanity.”

Neville said parties regularly drained savings, borrowed from grandparents or relied on loans as legal fees surged to “eye-watering” amounts.

“Once you’re tied to the litigation chariot, it’s really hard to break that bond because you get dragged around,” he said.

While judges have tools to sanction vexatious litigants, Neville said the legal threshold was high, and costs orders, as in Emily’s case, remained exceptionally rare.

Now working as a mediator, Neville advises parties to negotiate early and avoid the courts where possible.

Melbourne Law School professor Heather Douglas conducted 65 in-depth interviews with women in the Family Court. Thirty-five of them had experienced systems abuse.

Systems abuse can include filing baseless applications – including for non-existent properties – adjournments, appeals, variation applications, false child abuse or drug allegations to trigger investigations, and launching broad subpoena “fishing expeditions”.

She is also aware of cases where ex-partners have given false information to police, causing tactical raids on the victim’s elderly parents, and unsuccessfully launched defamation proceedings over the woman’s court testimony.

“There is a problem with overuse of subpoenas, especially to medical and counselling records, and applications that have no basis,” she said.

Douglas said forcing victims into court for frivolous appearances was not only a major emotional stressor, but meant they had to fund childcare, take time off work, travel and pay legal bills.

Court was often the only venue where a perpetrator could legally see their victim, while inflicting stress serves as an extended form of control.

“All these things demonstrate his continuing control over her as part of the abuse,” she said.

Since 2024, the courts have undergone significant reform, including introducing training for staff and the judiciary, expanding domestic violence screening and referral programs, prioritising child safety over shared parental responsibility in custody orders, and empowering judges to bar vexatious litigants from launching proceedings.

However, the efficacy of these reforms is not known. The courts do not collate or release data on the reform’s implementation. While compliance with goals under the court’s Family Violence Plan is assessed annually, the court does not publicly release this data.

Domestic Violence Commissioner Micaela Cronin in September said some judges still held horrendous views about women, while a 2025 study found Family Court judges reinforced gender bias.

A court spokesperson declined to provide figures on the number of judges and staff who had undergone annual training.

University of Technology Sydney professor and investigative journalist Jess Hill, who is leading an independent evaluation of the reforms, raised concerns that a small percentage of judges resisted the training or did not see it translate into practice, with identical cases yielding wildly different outcomes depending on the judge.

She said some legal practitioners would consider negotiating an agreement, even if it were not ideal, if it were placed before a specific judge, for fear that a judicial decision would be worse.

Just 20 per cent of cases across the courts are decided by a judge, with parties entering mediation and making decisions by consent. Hill said this was true even for cases assessed as being high risk for violence.

“Mediation relies for its success on both parties having basically equal negotiating power,” she said. “In coercive control, the power is totally unequal.”

While exemptions exist for domestic violence, Hill’s research shows those exemptions are incredibly hard to come by.

“In our data set, there were a number of women who said that they had been pressured or forced to consent to orders they believe were unsafe,” Hill said.

“The process makes people, especially victim-survivors, mentally unwell because it keeps them in a state of prolonged hypervigilance and ongoing contact with the perpetrator.”

The threat, complexity, confusion, and inconsistency of the court and the broader family law system could have “dire consequences”.

“If you don’t succeed, maybe your children have to spend time with or live with someone you’re afraid might harm or kill them,” she said.

“There’s no more consequential law system than family law, and people don’t necessarily have a choice whether or not to engage.”

A spokesperson said the courts report on their performance through internal reviews, which are not published, and were working to improve transparency on specific orders, including those barring vexatious litigants.

The spokesperson said family violence can make it “unsafe or impossible to negotiate freely” and said the courts assessed suitability and safety, with most mediations conducted electronically, which helped “manage safety concerns”.

“The courts are working to improve timeliness through early risk identification, active case management, urgent hearing pathways and specialist lists,” the spokesperson said.

Scores of recent parliamentary inquiries, studies and reports have highlighted how the courts are contributing to further harm for people experiencing violence.

A 2025 parliamentary inquiry found the Family Court was not equipped to respond to family violence, with drawn-out and costly proceedings keeping victim-survivors tied to their abusers despite the safety risks, while a recent paper in the journal Violence Against Women found the courts were being used to inflict long-term financial and psychological harm as a form of “post-separation coercive control”.

The issue is so ubiquitous that the domestic, family and sexual violence commissioner called in her annual report, released in September, for the courts to be transformed into a family violence court.

Federal Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said while “incremental change” was being achieved, roundtables showed systems abuse was still a serious concern.

“There is still a long way to go,” she said. “And whilst we are making progress, we’re coming off a base that is a really serious one … That would be small comfort to people who are going through this system.”

Rowland said the government had recently agreed in principle to a 2022 Australian Law Reform Commission recommendation to establish a federal judicial commission as an oversight mechanism.

“The key issue is about accountability … in terms of how the law is being used,” she said.

The government has begun an audit of abuse in Commonwealth systems.

*Names changed for legal reasons.

The National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) offers support for emotional, physical and financial abuse. Support is also available from Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800; Lifeline 131 114; Beyond Blue 1300 224 636.

Too many boundaries are behind the ‘sex recession’, warns Esther Perel

Sydney Morning Herald November 14, 2026

The world-famous psychotherapist on midlife marriage, infidelity and how to manage the tension between love and desire.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Esther Perel pops onto the screen looking exactly as her devoted legions of fans would expect. Her asymmetrical blonde bob is perfectly swept to one side, her silk shirt (black today) is opened just so, revealing one of her favoured drop necklaces from a range called “ladders to bliss”. The twinkle in her eyes is enchanting even in two dimensions.

For the most ardent of Esther Perel’s millions of followers, all of these hallmarks must be as familiar as freckles on their partner’s face.

Women and men have been drawn to the Belgian-raised, French-sounding psychotherapist with cult-like devotion for decades. They come seeking reassurance and reasons for hope when their romantic relationships hit the toughest of times, her charismatic wisdom offering the promise of everything from repair after a seismic betrayal of trust, to advice on returning vitality to garden-variety marriages.

Podcaster, author, TED talker and most recently consultant to Olivia Wilde’s box office hit, The Invite, Perel is such a global star of sex, intimacy and relationships advice that some online dissect her every aphorism. But if Perel, 68, is aware of the weight of the expectations of lovelorn hordes, she wears it as lightly as the hand-harness chain she often sports on TikTok, Instagram or live: it looks as delicate as gold thread but also as steely as chain mail.

For someone attributed with borderline supernatural powers to peer into the heart, her words are down to earth. I open with a question based on the Australia’s recently published longitudinal study, known as HILDA, which examined 17,000 people’s attitudes to their relationships. It exposed a satisfaction gap between genders starting as soon as a couple move in together.

Overall the findings were positive; people in very long-term relationships are highly satisfied. But an odd happiness gap widens between men and women as perceived relationship quality descends until the 24-year mark. That’s when it bottoms out for both, before bouncing back up again as decades advance.

I wonder what insights or solutions the New Yorker who shot to fame 20 years ago with her global bestseller, Mating in Captivity, may add to established understandings of why men seem happier than women, and what it is about midlife that triggers this big dip for both.

“On some level, this is an old finding – that life satisfaction and health increases for men in committed relationships and life satisfaction for women often decreases, and her health for that matter because she’s busy taking care of everybody else’s health, and she forgets her own very often,” she says.

Women are more likely to struggle to maintain a sense of autonomy and individuality because they enter the care-taking and executive role in the family, assuming “a sense of responsibility for the wellbeing of others, the home and the domestic, and they often have two jobs,” she says. “But that doesn’t mean that it’s glorious for the men.”

Experience has shown Perel that “family life and domesticity, and intimate relationships, are challenging in and of themselves”, leading her to conclude that what family life thrives on is also “what eroticism defends against”, as she puts it to Good Weekend. “There is this notion that if you love, you desire,” she says. “But in fact in a long-term relationship, what love wants – which is consistency and familiarity and safety – are elements that are preconditions for desire. But desire basically lives in the space that is more playful, less responsible.”

“If family life wants routine, and consistency and repetition, desire doesn’t want to return to the same spot day after day. So there is an inherent tension in reconciling love and desire in the same place – because it addresses a set of needs that … are actually polarities.”

In a time when far longer life-expectancies mean couplings are expected and required to bridge more decades of challenge and routine – as well as happy stability – mining the daily conflict between excitment, freedom, and a craving for security remains a super-rich seam. At the many women’s conferences where she is invited to speak, Perel is often asked to articulate how those exhausted by demands of work and home can make space to be themselves and regroup.

“When you find yourself mired in tasks and responsibilities and to-dos and lists, it is not so obvious that at the end of the day, and a long list of things, number 27 will suddenly be ‘connect with my desires and my playfulness and erotic self’.”

She cites a study for which men and women in heterosexual couples were invited to write down the family duties they complete between 5pm and 11pm. Men typically had five to 10 on their lists, Perel says, while women had up to 30 – including ensuring their partner carried out his. Men felt more relaxed at night generally because they expected to do fewer tasks, but also felt stressed that their partner was monitoring them: a passion-killing burden by 11pm if ever there was one.

“So then the issue is: How do you create an erotic space where that part of you can express itself?” asks Perel. No wonder her audiences love her when she makes them feel so seen.

Western couples now expect their romantic partner to fulfil all the roles in life that a whole village once sustained, Perel famously says, and this is too much to ask. And she is openly compassionate when addressing the fallout when things go bad, which includes people having affairs.

Perel emphasises the pivotal role of trust in sustaining authentic connection. But she also says that people can decide to effectively “marry each other again” after their original partnership is shattered by betrayal, for example with an affair – effectively a second marriage to the same person, if the damage or disappointment can be overcome. The million-dollar question is how you achieve that – as the stultified couple in The Invite is advised to do by Piña, the luscious and liberated sex therapist character played by Penelope Cruz.

“There is repair after rupture,” says Perel, who has been married to psychologist, family therapist and author, Jack Saul, for more than 40 years. “There is a way to take accountability for hurt and to bring back the good things in the relationship, because not all infidelity is the end of the relationship.”

This idea of a new marriage to the same person was a line Perel actually coined some time ago, after working with many post-infidelity couples. “And from there came this thinking that many of us want something different at a certain point,” she says. “There’s your 24-year mark – we want something different, and 24 years often means midlife.”

“Midlife often means a time when we say, ‘Is this it? Is there more? Is this going to be my life for the next 25 years? I have one more chance for something different, better, more satisfying. My children are gone, my career is somewhat established’,” she says. “And then the question is: Do you need to be with someone else … or can you imagine a new story for the two of you, and is that something you aspire to?”

The “how?” doesn’t turn out to be simple. It can involve any number of changes. Physically moving to a different place. Doing something professionally different. Starting an entirely different life. “Organising one’s life in a different quadrant,” she says, comes with questions. “What is important that I do that brings me joy? What is important for me to learn and grow and give back? It also depends on what happened in the 24 years before.”

The movie Perel heavily influenced happily discusses sex styles enjoyed by the fresh – but still solidly middle-aged – couple who live above our time-worn, married heroes (played by Wilde and Seth Rogen). It traverses practices incorporated into the mainstream from what was traditionally considered porn territory – for example “pegging”.

But surprisingly for someone unflustered by airing so-called taboo topics in her content, Perel’s team advises Good Weekend that asking what she makes of the fact sexual choking has become normalised, especially among younger Australians, is off the table. And the implications of the way women are depicted in commercial porn now (often very demeaningly), aren’t up for discussion either. Even in the midst of a global debate about why so many young men have been caught up in online worlds that warp their ideas of healthy relationships with women and themselves, a question about whether porn can reduce desire is similarly a no-go.

But Perel is happy to discuss the so-called “sex recession” being experienced in the west, and if repeated claims that young people are less sexually active than ever before are really true. The answer is yes, and the reasons complex.

“One of the big shifts or challenges to our romantic pursuits is romantic consumerism. More and more the heart thinks like a market when we look at relationships, we have brought to it the language of optimisation, maximisation,” she says. “It is one big transactional vocab.”

But sex, Perel says, comes with a plot. And the plot is the relationship. “If you don’t approach people, you’re constantly ‘boundarying’ yourself out of living. If you make sure constantly to protect yourself to not be vulnerable … then you are going to have a sex recession. We’ve had a sex recession for quite a while. But it has taken up way more proportions at this point.”

What she wants to discuss is “relational thinness” – the loss of deep connections, and disembodiment – the fact that so much of what was once experienced in person is now delegated to online personas.

“I think we are experiencing a gradual social atrophy where we are less and less connecting to people,” she says. “The big paradox of this moment relationally is that we know from study upon study how important relationships are for a healthier, happier life, and yet we are increasingly avoiding each other and sleep-walking into isolation.”

This may translate as the phenomenon of “stable ambiguity”, which means we now have a whole set of narrow relationships that give us enough contact and consistency not to feel alone, but not too much either, which could make us feel enclosed or lacking freedom.

“What used to be tight knots, now they’ve become loose threads,” she says, “that allow you to get in and out of a loose bond. That looseness means often commitments become very flimsy and people treat each other like magazine subscriptions that they don’t need.”

As our time ticks down, Perel graciously agrees to answer a question from an Australian fan, a friend whose marriage is aged in its mid-twenties, and who listens to Perel’s couples’ therapy podcast, Where Should We Begin.

“How do you stop the little things turning into big things?” my friend wonders.

“Number one is humour,” Perel replies. “Humour demystifies and brings perspective, it reminds you what truly matters. It is an underused art and resource and if one has it, let that person be the one to diffuse.”

Second is good old mindfulness. “Ask, ‘If this was my last day, would I want to remember it based on the squabble about the toothpaste?’ … Things are going to bother you until the day one of you drops dead or leaves, it won’t change. The only thing that will change is your response to it.”

Even so, the perennial argument about the wet towel chucked on the bed or floor is never really about that.

“It’s about control, power, trust, respect, recognition. ‘I’ve asked you one hundred thousand times about the towel, you don’t care about what I say, you don’t pay attention to me, you only think about you.’ That’s the subtext and what makes a fight big is not the wet towel, it’s what it represents.”

Perel brings her live show Strangers, Friends, and Lovers: A Night Out with Esther Perel to Sydney on December 11, Melbourne on December 13 and Brisbane on December 17.

Russell Brand accused of misconduct by six more women, according to report

The Guardian Thu, 12 Nov 2026 23:51:04 GMT

Allegations of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour made against ex-comedian who was jailed on Monday

Russell Brand has been accused of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, according to a report.

The comedian, 51, is accused of having sex with a woman without her consent and then apologising afterwards, an investigation by the Times and the Sunday Times said.

The newspapers also alleged the comedian continued having sex with another woman after she asked him to stop because he was hurting her.

Brand, 51, was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after being convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault at Southwark crown court in London.

The Times reported that a woman said she had an on-off relationship with the actor in the late 2000s after a professional meeting at his London home.

On one occasion, she said they were in bed together when he moved to initiate sex. Having noticed he was not wearing a condom, she said she asked him to stop.

She told the Times: “And then he was very close, on top of me, and sort of pushing – but I knew he didn’t have a condom on and I said: ‘No, stop,’ and I started to sort of try and move. And … that wasn’t happening.”

The woman added she decided at that moment that “I’m not going to fight” because “who knows what he could do”.

After the alleged incident, she said Brand apologised to her in person and by text message. “I justified it in my head by saying to myself: at least he admitted it.”

Another woman who encountered Brand when she was queueing to meet him with a friend in 2007 aged 19 said she told him during sex: “It’s painful”, according to the report.

She alleged he would not stop, adding: “And then it gets worse and it’s really painful. And I say ‘stop’ and he doesn’t stop.”

The woman claimed he said afterwards: “Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn’t want to do.”

Brand is also accused of misconduct by a fan, then in her late 20s, who met him after he performed at The Chapel venue in San Francisco in 2013, who claimed he “manhandled” her and forced his hand down her trousers, telling the Times: “I didn’t resist. I just sort of let it happen.”

Another woman, then in her mid-twenties, said Brand approached her in 2005 at a music festival and told her: “Please I just need to have sex with you, I will pay you.”

According to the Times investigation, Brand is also accused of misconduct by a woman who was in her late 20s when she won a BBC 6 Music competition and was invited as a guest on his show in 2006.

After seeing each other sporadically for the next year, she claimed the comedian told her to lick a toilet seat at his house and “got angry” when she refused, adding: “[He] seemed pissed off that I wouldn’t let him humiliate me.”

Another woman, who worked at a London venue Brand visited regularly in 2015, said a member of Brand’s staff told her there: “Russell wants you” and said: “He’s in the disabled toilets”.

She said when she went in the lights were off and Brand claimed he wanted toilet paper, but grabbed her when she went to hand it to him.

The new allegations could not be reported until his criminal case ended to avoid prejudicing proceedings. The Times reported that “extensive steps” were taken to corroborate the claims and that none of the sources were paid.

The newspapers reported that Brand was approached for comment via legal representatives after his conviction on Monday. His lawyer reportedly said he would consider “injunctive relief” but did not send any response to the allegations despite being given additional time and an agreed deadline passing. Brand has previously denied wrongdoing and claimed all his relationships were consensual.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the media industry needs to “look at itself” and “step forward” to protect women and girls following Brand’s rape conviction and allegations of sexual misconduct made against the comedian David Walliams in an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

Walliams has denied the allegations. Brand’s lawyer was contacted for comment.

A cricketing drama to divide a nation: why the sandpaper scandal is Australia’s Bazball

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 20:00:24 GMT

The sandpaper affair is back, and the reason it has hit Australia so hard is because it is sneaky – or basically quite English

Any plans for the weekend? Personally I’m all set. I will be watching the full Pat Cummins sandpaper denial press conference, filmed live on location in Sydney on Friday morning, and now preserved uncut and un-redacted on YouTube.

I will not speed it up, or flick through impatiently only to find myself bogged down in endless adverts for old fat guys doing military calisthenics, and pills that will dissolve the vile writhing parasites that definitely live in my guts.

This is culturally vital material. As such I will be watching it at least five times, with periods set aside for reflection, notation and, as necessary, stabbing myself in the eyeballs with a sharpened kebab skewer just to dull the pain.

The point is, this is not a task to be undertaken lightly. You will need breaks. You will need a sense of hair-shirt necessity, like forcing yourself to watch a solemnly repetitive arthouse film where people are just always smoking and talking and looking sad. At one hour and eight minutes, the Cummins presser is a bit shorter than Three Colours: White. It’s almost the same length as Battleship Potemkin, and nobody actually wants to watch that.

There are similarities though. The opening sections of Battleship Potemkin are called Men and Maggots, Drama on the Deck and A Dead Man Calls for Justice. So yeah, love that. Elite mate-ship. Battleship Potemkin is also about a heroic worker’s revolt, with the lurking sense that everything here might just succumb to the tide and the forces of history. So yeah, again. Go Team Pat.

It has been said this is a scandal that will make no sense at all to anyone not pre-converted to Test Match cricket. But a quick 20-second explainer: Australian players used sandpaper to rough up the ball to their advantage during a Test Match in Cape town eight years ago, at a time when such outlaw practices were widespread.

The problem is the plan was enacted on the field in full view of the TV cameras. Cricket is a ball-fixated team game. But three Australian players took full responsibility and had their careers derailed. The Cummins press conference was in response to claims in Usman Khawaja’s new book that in fact the entire team was in on it. Subsequent investigations had somehow failed to detect this, but did make the whole thing go away. And: breathe.

The best bit of the one hour, eight minutes is the start. Cummins looks the same: lean, super-handsome, eyes sparkling, like the future cyborg-captain of the intergalactic space fleet. But he is also unusually hyped-up, voice cracking as he gets his prepared lines in at the outset.

Khawaja’s book is, he says, a series of “allegations” that he is still “trying to understand”. Although, to be clear, trying to understand without having actually read it in full. Crucially, Cummins states that if Khawaja is saying “we knew sandpaper was going out on to the field then he’s 100% wrong”. Note how the middle part of that sentence qualifies the ending. Going out on to the field has always been key. Note also the way this replicates the statement by Australia’s bowlers in 2021. Execute. Discipline. Stick to the process.

Cummins shifts on to more general notes. We were part of a team. Usman is a friend. Usman has also betrayed not just me but all of Australian cricket. He then opens up some distance by pointing out he was 24 and playing his 13th Test at the time. Which is true. But then, the entire Cummins persona is also built on presenting himself as the opposite of that moment.

Clearly, this is an attempt at containment. Cummins says he will not be talking about it again. But like it or not, these moments capture you. What we have here is a man trying desperately not to become a meme, while visibly turning into one before our eyes.

What is happening here, really? It is hard to overstate how massive this story is in Australia. At the same time it feels like nothing at all, an entity without content beyond its own emotional hot air. On TalkSport on Friday morning, Alan Brazil asked the editor of Wisden, Lawrence Booth, if the Australian team was ripping itself apart over this, if England might take advantage. Er, actually no. That same day an Australian team with different names was gleefully tearing England apart in Perth, with Mahli Beardman – nickname suggestions: Bob, Jacob, “And Me” – taking six debut wickets.

But then Beardman was 14 years old when this happened and would surely be quite happy if the old lags faded from view. This is key to the sage, and to the sport. In cricket you basically hate your teammates. This is an individual pursuit masquerading as a team sport. You win together. But also, you don’t really. This is hard numbers, independent value, a series of conjoined duels.

Sandpapergate is a public airing of that strange internal dynamic. But it also offers a perfect mini-anatomy not just of Australian cricket, but of Australia itself. A key fact: nobody else actually cares about Sandpapergate. Initially the ICC handed out one-match bans, which seemed fair enough. Meanwhile Australia frothed and blamed, imposed ludicrously one-year exiles from all cricket, and banned David Warner from ever captaining anyone ever again.

At moments like these you remember what a culturally sui generis place Australia is, beautiful as a stage set, cities ranged warily around the coastline, a place that is wealthy, free, unspoilt, and still embracing something while also rejecting it.

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

It might come as a surprise, but English people love Australians. They really do, to the extent it is often a shock to realise this is not always entirely reciprocated. There is an edge there. These are not in fact your fun country cousins, but a former settlement with its own set of deep structural recalibrations still in train.

And of course cricket, that absurd scratchy formal dance, is the perfect sporting vessel. In Australia cricket has been defined by a terse but fraternal conservatism. Cricket is about toughness, resilience, the content of your character. Crucially it is about playing correctly, about being more resolute, more disciplined, more worthy (let us say it: than the English), about presenting yourself to the room, while also being better and more authentic than the room.

One reason Australians hate the sandpaper affair, the reason it hits so hard, is because it’s sneaky. It’s embarrassing. It’s mean, small, pigeon-chested. It’s basically quite English. And cricket is supposed to tell you that you’re the opposite of this, to offer hard, sunlit legitimacy, to answer the questions: are we fine now, are we good, out here still facing westwards from thousands of miles away, still trying to be better, straighter, tougher?

In a way Sandpapergate is Australia’s Bazball, another bizarre cricketing contortion, whose energy was almost entirely inward-facing. Bazball was a simple tactic, the self-congratulatory urge to bash a cricket ball around in a fast-forward, attacking manner. It was only in England that this seemed vital and seductive and profound, in those few giddy months before it dissolved in its own cult-like amour propre. The reason it hit that sweet spot, why it both enraged and delighted, is that cricket in England is about class, privilege, hierarchy, the question of who owns the space, who gets to decide the mood.

And the key quality of Bazball was its deep cultural mnemonic, the gentleman-amateur style, the idea of winning from above the fray, winning while saying, oh you didn’t actually think any of that stuff really mattered, did you, old boy. Even the body language was maddening, Ben Stokes on the balcony, vest, shades, jawline, muscular insouciance, Brendan McCullum with his feet up, oozing careless alpha-dog energy. Even when we lose we win. Because we are us, doing this.

Nobody else out there really gave a toss about all this, beyond the fact it was undeniably annoying to play against, and deeply satisfying to beat it. This was English cricket speaking to itself, and to the way it wants to be seen. Bazball was unearned exceptionalism, faux amateur nobility. Bazball was honi soit qui mal y pense in a daring reverse scoop new-ball hoick. It was also doomed and phoney, unable to progress because it wasn’t really anything but a style.

But that was English cricket’s own psychodrama, in the time of shrinkage and lost edge. And now Australia have this. It is obvious enough what should happen. No more bans. No more hand-wringing. An apology to the players who were over-punished. A rooting out of the administrators who mismanaged this farrago of weirdness when it all went down. Then let’s get on with the game.

Yeah, good luck with that. In reality this can never resolve itself with logic or cold compromise, because it’s about change, identity, what remains and what matters, about seeing a world in a grain of sandpaper. One hour and eight minutes. Frankly, we’re just getting started.

The US supreme court agreed on Friday to consider Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the US-Mexico border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration wants to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications is illegal.

Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the US.

At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say years-long processing times had previously contributed to an influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an attempt to unilaterally “eviscerate” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the US. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, those attorneys argue.

The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank

Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to entice shoppers

The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?

Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.

Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”.

As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust.

“The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says.

While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value.

It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops.

But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person.

In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000.

Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending.

The report, also produced by Cyclehoop, which makes bike storage, calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides.

Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom.

This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits.

The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund.

However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business.

The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade.

“Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets.

“What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away.

Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found.

This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI.

In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy.

The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock.

In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts.

The Council on Foreign Relations suggested selling H200s would “supercharge” China’s future AI factories and strengthen the US’s rival.

Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate he made at least three purchases of Nvidia shares in the days after announcing this, all of them between $250,001 and $500,000.

These trades are among Trump’s larger purchases of Nvidia stock, although he appears to have made dozens of transactions involving the chipmaker’s shares since taking office.

DeKleptocracy wrote in its analysis: “While the country debates how a possible Chinese spy may have manipulated White House policy for one AI company, it must grapple with how Trump’s corruption may have motivated him to deliver the entire AI industry’s technology to China.”

The forestry workers took unusual care as they picked their way through the mossy undergrowth of a Tasmanian forest. They were carrying a small group of furries – humans in animal suits that can cost thousands of dollars – mindful of not letting any tails drag in the mud. Hired as production crew for the day, they were more used to hearing the drone of heavy logging machinery than the moans of animal lust. Once the furries were in place, the director closed the set so that they could film their group sex scene in private.

“They were just adorable. Even when they’re doing adult acts, it still just looks really cute and kind of innocuous,” artist Kirsha Kaechele says.

This fluffy tableau is one of 12 featured in OnlyFerns, Kaechele’s “artwork-cum-economic engine intended to protect Tasmania’s ancient forests”. Known by the Museum of Old and New Art (Mona) as its first lady (she is married to the museum’s founder, David Walsh), Kaechele will be familiar to readers who followed her captivating 2024 discrimination case against the Mona’s Ladies Lounge.

OnlyFerns is similarly headline-friendly: an OnlyFans portal through which people pay to view forest-themed kink videos set in Tasmanian sawmills and forests (private ones, since OnlyFans doesn’t allow the filming of adult content in public places). The revenue is intended to compensate forest workers for not felling trees; instead, Kaechele says, they will be paid to create boardwalks and artwork in the logging coupes of old growth forests, in an attempt to save those sites from destruction.

Mona and Kaechele covered all production costs, including paying the creators and crew for the videos, and producing an accompanying documentary and book. Sawmills will be employed to manufacture the artwork, and paying the loggers is paramount too. “Ensuring that there are no hours lost is critical to the success of the project,” she says. “Most environmental campaigns have set up an us-them scenario, where workers are excluded from protection. That is not pragmatic, it ruffles feathers. And it is inelegant.”

Sustainable Timber Tasmania, formerly Forestry Tasmania, said in a statement that they are “having discussions with Mona about their ambitions in relation to forest management … but we are also mindful that we need to remain within our charter as a Government Business Enterprise.” They praised Kirsha’s project as “an amazing initiative that has brought stakeholders together and created time and space for an important conversation about forests and timber production.”

As for the revenue that will be raised, there’s no way of knowing in advance how many viewers the adult videos will attract. “The scale of what we build will depend on our success (and the generosity of my husband and other philanthropists who may or may not support it by subscribing),” Kaechele says.

And there have been questions raised by environmental groups about collaborating with the logging industry at all.

Kaechele has a knack for a playful bait and switch, with one recent example being Eat the Problem: a feast, cookbook and ABC TV series focused on turning maligned native species into spectacular dishes in the name of environmental sustainability. For OnlyFerns, she looked to the simple premise that sex sells.

Her use of the OnlyFans platform has echoes of the recent collaboration between UK adult entertainment creator Lily Phillip and the climate advocacy film group Yellow Dot Studios, to make erotic content about climate change. Along the same lines, many TikTok creators are using the #GRWM (“get ready with me”) format to discuss complex topics such as abortion rights while applying their makeup.

Around twenty OnlyFans content creators flew into Burnie for their shoots, accommodated by a town local to the sawmills. One creator, Kellie Panther, who has a forked tongue among other body modifications, recalls boarding the small plane and looking around at the other passengers as everyone offered a knowing, “Oh, hey.”

Role playing sawmill workers and dirty, dirty hippies is one way to explore the power dynamics in the long and bloody battle over Tasmania’s forests. In real life, Kaechele says, “both sides are so traumatised” – but she is straddling a line between them that has left some environmental groups unhappy.

OnlyFerns comes out of the Forest Congress, a body which Kaechele formed in 2023 to bring together conservationists, scientists, Palawa elders and representatives from the forestry industry. The work is ongoing – OnlyFerns is but one unfurling off-shoot – but the project has drawn criticism for not going far enough.

In July, upon its withdrawal from the congress, the Wilderness Society released a heated statement against collaborating with the logging industry, who they said had taken “zero steps … to correct their poor commercial and industrial practices”. The Bob Brown Foundation, which boycotted the Forest Congress from the start, called the project a “pro-logging plan”, adding that Kaechele’s agreement with loggers to protect “3 or 4%, labelled ‘old growth’ by the industry, leaves 96% of the forests to be clear-felled and incinerated along with their wildlife.

“Ending this tragedy is not performance art,” the statement continued. “It is a huge and serious challenge for Tasmania and Australia in an age of unprecedented environmental destruction.”

Announcing OnlyFerns on Instagram in April, Kaechele backed the philosophy behind her idea: “Many conservationists speak on the importance of transition, but they are yet to put forward a viable economic model.”

To the Guardian, she justifies the focus on old-growth forests. “We are selecting forests for which there is no doubt [on either side]. This is in the interest of building consensus, and of protecting the most precious irreplaceable and ancient ecosystems. Forests no one wants to see fall.

“Numerous sawmills hosted us, and these are the people who stand to lose,” she says. “If we protect old-growth forests, it’s their timber and their processing hours that’s at stake. So they’re incredibly generous to go on this journey, and I think it’s because I’ve been transparent the entire time. I said: ‘Here’s the deal. I want us to leave these old-growth forests standing. I want you to protect them. I want the villain to become the hero … but I don’t want it to impact you negatively. So how do we do this?’”

The artist’s outsider status is something she’s learned to leverage on her path of “radical diplomacy”. Her mother was an artist, her father a retired aerospace engineer turned Rolfing healer, who moved the family from Topanga Canyon in California to Guam in Micronesia when she was five, and the only white girl.

“I do tend to put myself into the middle of these spaces where I don’t belong, and then I’m so rewarded by making friends with the so-called enemy,” she says. “I like having my beliefs blown open.”

Panther, an OnlyFerns creator who lives in bushland on the outskirts of Melbourne, relished the chance to get involved, having worked as a stripper to fund her degree in environmental science. She was among many other creators walking the red carpet at last week’s opulent Melbourne premiere of a feature-length version of OnlyFerns: 18+, and invitation only.

In a vintage Twin Peaks styling, the scenes were stitched together with the through-line of Kaechele as the receptionist of a sex line at a sawmill, matching punters with their kinks. Panther plays a hippy activist being dragged through the mud by Rebel Roper, a shibari artist. Other characters include a “logger” in hi-vis being fellated among the ferns; and, in a nearby sawmill, a female dominatrix, who pegs an environmentalist amid the woodchips and heavy machinery.

In the cinema, the opening moments from each creator drew whoops of encouragement from the assembled crowd – but even the most seasoned stars fell silent during the more intense scenes. Every now and then a voice called out from the seats to break the tension: “Save the trees!”

In Sarah’s house, David Walliams has been a bedtime staple for years. Her children, aged eight, six and four, have dressed up as his characters for World Book Day – they love the over-the-top, unusual names and illustrations.

Now, all the books are going. “I’ll probably take them away and replace them with other authors,” says Sarah, a mother in west London. “Sooner rather than later, so they don’t realise.” If any of her children ask why, she will tell them “that his choices aren’t great and that I think we should be reading other books”.

This week a joint Guardian and ITV News investigation alleged that the children’s author used his position to pursue young women and girls for sex, including girls as young as 15. Walliams denies the allegations. HarperCollins stopped publishing new Walliams books last December and dropped his entire backlist in September.

For many independent children’s booksellers, the news only confirmed a decision made long ago.

Helen Tamblyn-Saville, owner of Wonderland Bookshop in Retford, Nottinghamshire, stopped stocking him in 2020. “They didn’t fit the ethos and values of my shop,” she says. Walliams’s books “punched down”, she believes, citing what she sees as “themes of racism, misogyny and classism” in his writings.

In 2021, HarperCollins removed a story about a Chinese boy – Brian Wong, Who Was Never, Ever Wrong – from future editions of The World’s Worst Children after complaints that it relied on harmful racial stereotypes.

In 2025, Tamblyn-Saville turned down an invitation to an event with him. “It feels very much as if the golden goose had to be protected, despite the clear red flags.”

Griffin Books in Penarth, south Wales, dropped his books about 18 months ago over “the low quality of the writing and his frequent use of offensive stereotypes”.

The Chicken and Frog bookshop in Brentwood, Essex, has not stocked him for a decade. Urmi, owner of Pickled Pepper Books in north London, has a blunter opinion: “We heard [rumours] about David Walliams at least five years ago and at that point chose to not stock his books,” she says. She believes that “everyone in the industry knew … so anyone that’s only just taking books off the shelf is only interested in profit”.

Mainstream stores have moved quickly. The Works, a budget retailer, said it had removed all David Walliams titles from sale and TG Jones confirmed it no longer sold his books in store or online. Waterstones said it was talking to HarperCollins about returning “the small number of copies which remain in stock in a few of our shops”.

Families are clearing their shelves too. One parent walked past a neighbourhood book-swap box this week and found it stuffed full of Walliams titles. Another mother joked that she would be burning hers, saying Walliams was “a knock-off Roald Dahl anyway”. Sarah hasn’t decided what to do with hers: giving them to a charity shop just puts them “back into the system”.

Walliams’ sales have been falling sharply – but they have not disappeared. Retailers sold 7,497 Walliams books over the past four weeks, worth £48,400, according to NielsenIQ BookData figures reported by The Bookseller.

In the same period last year, when he had a new book out, Walliams sold 102,000. Even so, almost 108,000 copies of his books have been sold so far this year, worth more than £702,000, and his titles have made more than £153m since 2008.

Public libraries are also facing a difficult decision. “This is a very sensitive issue involving deeply disturbing allegations, and some people may find the continued presence of these books upsetting,” said Isobel Hunter, CEO of the charity Libraries Connected.

The Metropolitan police have launched a criminal investigation into David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences.

Walliams, 55, was accused in reports by ITV and the Guardian this week of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. He has denied any wrongdoing, being a sexual predator or breaking the law.

The Met said the allegations it was investigating were separate to those reported by the Guardian and ITV but as “part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences”.

The new allegations made to police are understood to have come from several people. Some date back to the 2000s and are described by police as “non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s”.

It is understood at least some of those who made reports to the police did so this week and had given initial accounts to detectives from the Met’s specialist crime division. Those accounts were enough for the Met to launch a full criminal investigation by detectives specialising in serious and complex sexual offences.

Police declined to detail the alleged offences, or where and when they are alleged to have occurred, saying this was to minimise the chances of the people who had complained being identified. Detectives stressed that those making the allegations were entitled to life-long anonymity.

It is police policy not to name people under investigation, and in a statement announcing the criminal investigation, the force said: “In recent days, the Met has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s.

“Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers.

“The allegations are separate from those reported by ITN and the Guardian. However, as part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences.”

The Guardian and ITV News reported the allegations against Walliams after a court rejected a legal attempt aimed at preventing publication. Walliams has not been arrested and is in a medical facility.

Det Supt Mike Cagney, from the Met’s complex sexual offences unit which is leading the investigation, said: “We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

“We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.”

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the media investigation, Walliams wrote: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

“I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

He added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

Police have not carried out any searches as part of their investigation and one of their central aims is to support and keep the confidence of those who have complained to them about being victims of sexual offending.

The allegations made to the Guardian include accounts from two women who said they first met Walliams when they were 15 years old. Both women, now in their 30s, said they felt they had been groomed by him two decades ago, and that the experience had continued to affect them.

Walliams was accused of abusing his position to pursue women through the family television show Britain’s Got Talent and at his former children’s book publisher, HarperCollins, where he is alleged to have had a sexual relationship with a junior member of staff.

The allegations were revealed in a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News that heard from 30 sources with first-hand accounts of his conduct.

Since the allegations were published, Walliams has been dropped by his literary agency, the BBC has begun to remove his programmes from iPlayer and the Labour party has suspended his membership.

The Met said people could report information to police by calling 101 and providing the reference 4900/10NOV26, or by contacting the complex sexual offences unit on 0207 175 2738.

Popular chaser victorious but ground issues, horses slipping and the low sun are all negatives for Cheltenham

One of the more remarkable career records in jumping was extended again on Friday as Jonbon, one of the most popular chasers in training, won the Shloer Chase for the third time in the last four seasons and maintained his lifetime streak of never having finished outside the first two in 29 starts under National Hunt rules.

On the opening day of Cheltenham’s second-biggest meeting, though, it also felt like a somewhat flat success, out of keeping with the setting and occasion. Jonbon was left with just two rivals to beat after Gidleigh Park, the second-favourite on Friday morning, was ruled out a couple of hours before the race due to concerns about the drying ground.

Nor was Harry Fry’s chaser the only absentee on the card – there were nine in all, including two big fancies for the Listed novice chase – and Cheltenham is facing the prospect of more non-runners in Saturday’s showpiece Paddy Power Gold Cup card.

What with the runners in the Grade Two Albert Bartlett Novice Hurdle later on the card being forced to bypass several obstacles due to the low sun, and horses slipping on the bend into the straight, it was a day when it seemed every possible element – with the sole exception of the Microsoft outage – was conspiring to disrupt the proceedings.

The official going description of good, good-to-soft in places at the start of racing on Friday was changed to good later in the afternoon ahead of Saturday’s card. At the spring festival on the other side of Christmas, Jon Pullin, Cheltenham’s clerk of the course, would almost certainly be able to turn on the taps overnight and put on enough water to maintain the current going, at least.

With the track having been hit by an unexpected overnight frost before Friday’s card, however, it is not an option, as a repeat of Thursday’s overnight temperatures would likely leave the course frozen.

Friday’s going was at least ideal for Jonbon, whose career-long 29-race streak of finishing either first or second remains intact.

It is a remarkable record, for all that – famously or notoriously, depending on whether you backed him – Jonbon has been the runner-up in all four of his starts at Cheltenham’s festival meeting in March.

There was also little sign of advancing years catching up with him this time, as Jonbon, who will be 11 when next year’s festival rolls around, made all the running and jumped with accuracy and enthusiasm on the way to a two-and-a-quarter length success at odds of 1-2.

There is a fair case to be made for a dozen of the 15 runners in the Paddy Power Gold Cup at Cheltenham on Saturday, but second-season chaser Blueking D’Oroux (2.20) has the prominent racing style that tends to prevail over this track and trip and that could tip the balance in his favour.

The seven-year-old was a dual Grade Two winner over hurdles for his former trainer, Paul Nicholls, and finished second in a Grade One novice at Aintree at the end of his novice chase campaign.

Blueking D’Oroux switched to Dan Skelton’s championship-winning stable in the summer with just five runs over fences in the book, and starts the new campaign on a mark that offers plenty of scope for further progress.

Cheltenham 1.10 Joseph O’Brien’s Atomic City posted a decent time under a hands-and-heels ride when making a successful debut over hurdles at Cork last month and will be a tough opponent for the likely favourite, Charles Darnay.

Windsor 1.25 Kildinian Prince is one of the least exposed runners in the field and makes his handicap debut off a potentially lenient mark, not least with the step up to three miles likely to see further improvement.

Cheltenham 1.45 The much-anticipated meeting between Kabral Du Mathan and Old Park Star has been frustrated with Dan Skelton’s runner taken out on Friday evening, while Old Park Star, last year’s Supreme Novice Hurdle winner, is also doubtful. That leaves Henry de Bromhead’s Workahead as the likely beneficiary if the race cuts up as expected.

Cheltenham 2.55 With just five runs over timber at eight years of age, Horaces Pearl has clearly not been easy to train but he goes well fresh and is fairly weighted on his limited form to date.

Andy Burnham urges Labour to ‘rearm’ for Kemi Badenoch comeback

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:20:01 GMT

No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens

Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “rearm” to fight the Conservatives at the next election amid concern inside government that they must take the prospect of a Kemi Badenoch-led recovery seriously.

Downing Street sources said the prime minister wanted Labour headquarters to refocus on the Tories as an electoral threat after more than two years of prioritising Nigel Farage’s Reform and, on their left flank, the Greens.

“Andy is well aware of how volatile electoral support is. Just because the Tories are trailing in the polls now, their trajectory is upwards and they could bounce back ahead of the election. We can’t be complacent about our old foe,” one source said.

The Conservatives took 24% of the vote at the last general election, before support dipped to 18%. But last week this had risen to 25%, according to polling from More in Common, the first time in 18 months they had exceeded their vote share at the time of their record election defeat.

Many Tory MPs who had felt their party’s situation was existential, now believed they had a route back, with Badenoch finally appearing to recognise that the economy, rather than culture wars, presented her with an opportunity, especially among core supporters.

A senior Downing Street figure said Burnham did not want party officials to take their eyes off Reform – which has dipped in the polls amid ongoing scrutiny of party finances – but felt they should be planning for a potential Tory resurgence as well.

A third No 10 insider told the Guardian: “Kemi is running a party base strategy with policies aimed at higher earners, mostly in the south. It won’t be enough to win at the next election but it does put them more in contention. We need to be ready for that. We need to rearm.”

Cabinet ministers including the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, and the Europe minister Hamish Falconer have Tory-facing seats, while Labour MPs across Hertfordshire, Kent and parts of London, including Finchley and Harrow, could also be at risk.

One tactic under discussion is talking up the prospect of a Tory-Reform pact, with MPs suggesting voters would only return in earnest to the Tories if there was a genuine chance they could win a majority, but that they could stay with Labour if they were worried about Farage getting close to power.

Another is to focus on the Tory brand – including the shadow cabinet – more generally. While Badenoch’s personal ratings are relatively strong, the Conservatives overall lag way behind. Only a third of people who told More in Common they believed Badenoch was doing a good job said they would vote for her party.

Labour officials insisted that, as the Conservatives were the official opposition, they still had them in their sights day to day. But they acknowledged they needed to step up their wider strategy.

The party is understood to be preparing to devote more resources to taking on the Tories from January, in the run-up to the May elections. “We did really well at this set of elections last time, so it will be a real test point for whether the Tories have got their act together,” one said.

“Because of the shallow but broad nature of Labour’s support at the last election, there are more seats that could end up being Labour-Tory fights than you might think,” he said, adding that the Tories were also currently taking more votes from the Lib Dems than the other way around.

The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:01:46 GMT

From Cairo to Moscow to Washington, governments are turning up the pressure on media workers

Lina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October, resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month.

Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions.

On Monday, Russia finally succeeded in silencing the famed Novaya Gazeta, which had spent decades battling growing repression. Six of its journalists, including Anna Politkovskaya, paid for their coverage with their lives. But the newspaper continued until, stripped of its newsroom, donation platforms and right to publish, it was forced to turn the lights off. (The separate Novaya Gazeta Europe, founded by many of its alumni, continues.)

These cases are part of a wider pattern. Press freedom is at its lowest ebb for a quarter of a century, Reporters Without Borders said this spring, judging more than half of the 180 countries it surveys to have “difficult” or “very serious” conditions for journalists. The rising tide of war worldwide is also increasing the pressures and dangers: the Committee to Protect Journalists recorded a new peak of 129 deaths of reporters and other media workers in 2025. Unesco said last week that almost nine out of 10 killings of journalists go unpunished.

High-quality journalism has never been more necessary in a world of rising conflict, AI slop and malicious fabrications spreading on platforms run by big tech firms who barely nod to ethical responsibilities. As Ms Attalah herself has pointed out, the disappearance of professional media organisations enlarges the space for conspiracies and disinformation.

Yet while the US previously pressed the case of threatened journalists overseas, sometimes helping to ease their conditions, it is now led by a man who has called news media “the enemy of the American people”, whose FBI raided a correspondent’s home in January, and who is currently pursuing a $10bn lawsuit against the BBC. Donald Trump has also sought to dismantle federally funded organisations which were an important source of independent reporting on many repressive nations.

This week, an appeals court panel ruled that the administration had illegally fired the head of Voice of America. VoA, Radio Free Asia and Radio Free Europe have all struggled on thanks to dedicated staff, though hugely diminished. Recent elections in Serbia, Brazil and the US are evidence that journalism, alongside activism, can stem the erosion of democracy. Thousands of people protested in Turkey last month against Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s media crackdown. Large parts of the public still want the truth and, against the odds, courageous journalists worldwide persist in finding it out and sharing it. That authoritarians target them so relentlessly only testifies to their importance.

The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:00:56 GMT

The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past

“Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize.

Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said.

Set in an unnamed seaside town in an unspecified future, The End of Everything depicts a disintegrating Britain after the invasion of an alien species called the iGhettis, rumoured to have “come out of the internet”. Capitalism, ecological disaster, AI, Brexit – the cause of “the crisis” is unclear. All we know is that “it’s ongoing and unresolved. It never ends.”

Ahead of Cop31, Ed Miliband this week claimed that “the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences”. With news of Microsoft outages, cyber-attacks on supermarket freezers, not to mention national stockpiling, the Booker judges’ decision couldn’t be more timely. As Atwood has said, science fiction is “always about now”.

From Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein to Isaac Asimov’s Robot series to Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (a new film adaptation of which has been panned by critics), writers have been fascinated by non-human intelligence. Science fiction responds to anxieties about the impact of scientific and technological discoveries on society and the human psyche. Harrison’s great hero, JG Ballard, described his move away from classic sci-fi as a rejection of outer space for “inner space”.

Harrison has dismissed science fiction’s world-building as “the great clomping foot of nerdism”. The End of Everything is about a world breaking down, and as rationality and communication have collapsed, he had to break down the rules of fiction, including science fiction. There are no explanations or solutions, no salvation. He wants the reader to feel as confused and destabilised as his characters.

For some, this lack of answers is bewildering, and will confirm the Booker’s reputation for tricky winners. Others have an alien aversion that no amount of fine writing can overcome. The Wasp Factory author, Iain Banks, published his science fiction novels under the name Iain M Banks to distinguish them from his mainstream work. This is no longer necessary.

Whether the novel’s win marks a new frontier for publishing and literary awards remains to be seen. One thing is certain – there will be no shortage of fiction confronting a bleakly precarious future. As Harrison has said, we are living “in an age of fantasy”. The End of Everything is a novel for our times. Today’s polycrisis demands a polyphony of genres. Be it speculative fiction, science fiction, horror, fantasy, satire, dystopia - or a mix – the question of whether such fiction deserves a capital L belongs to a bygone age.
