Maro Itoje warns England not to sleepwalk into clash with Eddie Jones’s Japan

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:00:21 GMT

‘Japan have a distinct way of playing,’ says captain

Steve Borthwick hails ‘weird and wonderful’ Jones

Maro Itoje has insisted England will be ready for any curveballs Eddie Jones may throw on Saturday, warning his side they cannot “sleepwalk” into battle against Japan.

Jones, England’s longest-serving head coach after his stint between 2015 and 2022, has strongly hinted he will set his side up to unsettle his former charges at Twickenham, warning that they do not like “unorthodox” rugby. The hosts are heavy favourites to back up last week’s record win over Australia with another emphatic victory and have never lost to Japan but Steve Borthwick has made 10 personnel and two positional changes, fielding an inexperienced side against that of his predecessor.

“The overarching message this week is that we need to be alive,” said Itoje. “It’s impossible to tick off every eventuality that an opposition might do, especially a team like Japan, who have a very distinct way of playing. They’re very consistent at getting speed into the game. They could do a number of things, so let’s be alive and let’s not sleepwalk into things and think ‘most teams play like this’ because Japan aren’t most teams.

“One, we need to be alive. Two, we need to impose our game. We need to play the way we want to play. Whether it’s unorthodox shapes in attack, things around the set piece. I know they’re going to want to keep the ball in play or come up with ­special unique plays. If we’re alive and we’ve got our house in order then we should be able to deal with what they throw at us.”

Jones gave Itoje his debut in 2016 and oversaw his development into one of the world’s leading second-rows. When the Australian was in charge, England won three Six Nations titles, including one grand slam, and reached the final of the 2019 World Cup in Japan.

“I’m sure [the crowd] will receive him warmly,” added Itoje. “It’s not the first time he’s been back. Most coaches want to keep you thinking. Eddie would throw a whole load of weird and wonderful things at us to keep us sharp and keep us on our toes.”

Borthwick, meanwhile, has a debt of gratitude to Jones, who gave him his coaching break with Japan before appointing him England assistant. “What [Eddie] does really well is maximises the strengths of any team he coaches,” said Borthwick. “So from coaching the Japan team to coaching the England team, two very different teams, both of which he did really well with.

Toxic media industry must face a reckoning

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:53:10 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett in which she questions why it took so long to unmask Russell Brand and David Walliams

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is correct when she talks about the toxic 1990s in the media industry (Why did it take so long to unmask Brand and Walliams? Because noughties culture told girls like me abuse was normal, 11 November). This abhorrent sexualised behaviour from celebrities and channel executives has been going on for much longer.

When I worked in the media as a makeup artist in the 1980s we were warned never to be alone if working with a certain Mr Savile or Mr Harris. Men like those two were the majority, not a minority. They were directly enabled by those managers and directors who sanctioned their behaviour through inaction. If you complained, you were seen as trouble and hounded out.

If the Russell Brand case has taught us anything, it should be that those in power are equally culpable through inaction and refusal to upset the so-called “talent”. Until these enablers are rooted out, the TV industry will remain a ripe hunting ground for sexual predators who are excused because they make money.

I long for that day to come, as it is obvious that the safeguarding laws today are completely ineffective in the face of power, money-making and obstructive management structures.

There are many more of these cases both present and past that will now surface. How offences are reported will influence how the victims are perceived. I cheer from the sidelines each time a vile, entitled abuser is held accountable. It would be far-reaching to hold TV executives accountable, too. Claire Parkman Brighton, East Sussex

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s article gives a thoughtful perspective on young womanhood for those of us who experienced the early to mid-1990s and 2000s as teenagers and young adults.

I would like to add that not only were young women subjected to the appalling lads’ mag culture that no doubt enabled sexual assaults through constant objectification and dehumanising language, but women were also hoodwinked into thinking that mimicking poor male behaviour was somehow empowering, only to find that so-called ladette culture was subjected to harsher judgment.

It often led woman to be complicit in their own dehumanisation and objectification. “We’re only having a laugh, love – have another beer!” What a thoroughly depressing time. Kirsty Lees Mont-Joli, Canada

While it’s true that misogyny and lad culture were applauded and rewarded in the 1990s when I was young, I don’t believe for a minute that my daughter is growing up in a safer, less toxic environment.

In a world where drink covers are available to buy online to prevent your drink being drugged while out, let me assure you that girls and women are still in danger every day, everywhere. Domestic violence is on the rise, and the comments yelled at my daughter and myself are still as vile and threatening as they’ve ever been.

It would be lovely to be able to walk down the street without some man my age saying he wants to F my daughter. It’s great that women are speaking up, but quite often that just makes them more of a target. Ask any female politician or public figure about the abuse they receive on a daily basis. We have a shockingly long way to go. Sarah Wolf Elwood, Melbourne, Australia

I have every sympathy with Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s experiences of growing up with “lad culture” and rape myths. I was born in 1961 and it was all alive and thriving when I was growing up: the miniskirt myth, the “she had it coming” view of rape victims, the trivialising and the jokes. All the more reason to applaud the victims – and the journalists – who challenge the culture that women have endured for too long. Melanie Tuck Abingdon, Oxfordshire

How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:53:05 GMT

An investigator writes that a human-written grievance at least gets to the heart of the issue immediately. Plus letters from Dexter Jandoo and Pete Bibby

Re your article (‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints, 8 November), I’m a complaint investigator for a housing association. I’ve worked here for nine years, and the scope of my job has completely changed within a few months. I am well-versed in policy and legislation, and I love my job, but it can be unbearable sifting through hundreds of pages of extremely wordy complaints.

You only need to look at the awful case of Awaab Ishak to know how important it is that a housing provider’s complaints process is accessible to tenants, but AI-generated complaints don’t help with this. Sending a complaint can be intimidating and time-consuming, and using AI can give someone confidence, but when we speak to customers in person or over the phone, and reference the same technical language that’s in their AI-generated complaint letter, they often don’t understand what we are saying.

It is much better to receive a human-written complaint (even with spelling mistakes and expletives), because at least it comes from the person, and gets to the heart of the issue. It means we can help you to the best of our ability, because you have told us exactly what you need. Additionally, AI enables our regular complainants.

“Frequent flyers” are part of any complaints role, but receiving multiple, massive, AI-generated complaints a month from someone makes us feel as if they don’t see us as people worthy of respect. Our organisation is considering classing this as a form of harassment, and it can’t come soon enough. Name and address supplied

I am wholly unsurprised at the AI clog phenomenon, though I view it through a different lens. Using AI as an assistant to seek support or remediation for crumbling public services should not be seen as a nuisance. It is the democratisation of recourse for wrongs that would normally be reserved for those with the time and resources to pursue them. Public bodies, especially councils, need to face their problems and start using AI assistance (with a human in the loop) to work through the likely legitimate complaints, regardless of how they are written. Dexter Jandoo Transformation consultant, London

The fact that AI has been used to write a complaint doesn’t necessarily invalidate it. It might be that AI enfranchises those who by reason of lack of education or inarticulacy have until now been unable to express a grievance. The “clog” might just be a metric of previous powerlessness. Pete Bibby Sheffield

Monty Don was the best teacher and presenter imaginable

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:52:52 GMT

Saul Abbott says his pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him, Jane Bates values Gardeners’ World immeasurably, while Joe Mackenzie shares a poignant memory

I started my professional gardening career in 2004, a year after Monty started presenting Gardeners’ World (‘It’s the final goodbye’: Monty Don bows out with a blissful last Gardeners’ World, 6 November).

To say this great man taught me much of what I have learned since is a gross understatement. Not just about the principles and practices of gardening itself, but the understanding in a greater sense of what a garden is, what it gives to us both in bounty, tangibly, and nourishment of something far greater, internally.

His pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him. I truly believe he has been the greatest presenter of a TV show in a generation.

I had a tear in my eye at the end of his final episode. As a novice, I would sit and watch the show with a pencil and pad every Friday night and make notes of every plant shown and every method of gardening, so that I could go to work the next week and put that newfound knowledge into practice. My friends couldn’t believe that I was giving up Friday nights out for a gardening programme. Honestly, I wouldn’t change that for all the Camellia sinensis in China.

I can’t express how much I will miss him on the show. Thank you, Monty, for being the best teacher imaginable. Saul Abbott Saul Abbott Garden Design, Essex

Monty Don’s struggle with depression has always been a part of his presenting of Gardeners’ World. The programme hasn’t focused on mental health, but it has always focused on the benefits that gardening, fresh air and plants bring to anyone experiencing the ups and downs of living.

Friday nights with Monty and his team of gardening experts have given me an hour every week to look at what is real and relevant to my own internal life and enjoyment. My life is decidedly the better for it. I value the programme immeasurably and look forward to its continuation in a new form for years to come. Thank you, Monty. Jane Bates Macclesfield, Cheshire

I was sad to hear about Monty Don’s last episode on Gardeners’ World, not that I was an avid watcher. In fact, I only learned about the show during Covid when I was quarantined with my granny, who watched it religiously. She was an avid gardener herself, regularly took part in her village flower competitions, and in the summer of 2020 spent more time outside than in. She wasn’t that interested in TV, but she never missed Gardeners’ World. I think it was Monty (who I’m sure she had a huge crush on) who inspired her to allow part of her garden to grow into a wildflower meadow to attract bees and insects.

The week of my wedding, my granny went into hospital, and the night before, worrying about her and the big day, I turned on the TV in our hotel and Gardeners’ World was on. My granny died a week later, so she got to see the flowers from my wedding, but not Monty’s final episode. Joe Mackenzie Lewisham, London

The folly of just-in-time supply chains

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:52:48 GMT

Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose

The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence (The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November).

The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences.

The same thinking has shaped public services and national defence. Hospital beds, experienced staff, strategic stockpiles and redundant infrastructure can all appear wasteful when measured against immediate demand. Yet their value lies precisely in their availability when circumstances cease to be normal.

Europe’s dependence on American military capabilities provides a particularly troubling example. What appeared financially efficient in peacetime has created strategic vulnerabilities as the reliability of US commitments comes into question.

The fundamental error is not optimisation itself, but optimising the wrong objective. A system designed to minimise expenditure may succeed brilliantly at doing so while becoming progressively less capable of fulfilling its actual purpose. Resilience is not inefficiency. It is a form of insurance. Like all insurance, the value only becomes apparent when it is needed – usually in a crisis. Hannah Walker Wymondham, Leicestershire

No 10 considering expanding under-25s benefits overhaul to older age groups

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:43:26 GMT

Exclusive: Plans to replace key disability benefits for young people with work and training could affect adults

Downing Street is considering whether plans to replace key disability benefits with work and training for people under-25 should be expanded to older age groups, the Guardian has learned, in a move that risks reigniting Labour tensions over welfare changes.

Andy Burnham and other cabinet ministers are looking at applying the idea of “participation first” to all people of working age, meaning spending billions more on support to enter the workplace while cutting or removing some disability benefits.

The move would be politically risky given the difficulties that Keir Starmer faced in getting changes to health and disability benefits past the Labour parliamentary party last year, with a rebellion leading to a major U-turn.

The government is preparing to accept recommendations from its adviser, Alan Milburn, next week on overhauling the benefits system for young people.

In his report, Milburn will propose that under-25s should get training and support instead of the universal credit health element. Under the plans, young people with disabilities will also lose their personal independence payment (Pip) but will be able to apply to a local fund for specific short-term expenses and equipment, rather than an ongoing payment. Those with the most extreme needs who cannot work will have their entitlements protected.

This week, cabinet ministers looked at whether the arguments could be applied more broadly to over-25s, and were considering an intervention from the prime minister or Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, to make the case that the principles should apply to all. This could happen within weeks of both the Milburn review and the Stephen Timms review into disability benefits being published.

Some government sources said they believed the idea of expanding the welfare changes to over-25s would ultimately not survive given the probable backlash from some parts of Labour. Others said they believed Milburn had successfully made the case that the system needed to change and that the public were behind his efforts.

Burnham has repeatedly said the changes would not be “crude cuts”, but some backbenchers have said they are sceptical and worried about the impact on young disabled people.

If the changes were expanded to the over-25s, it could yield more savings as the cohort is much larger than the under-25s and the level of support needed to get people back into employment would probably be lower.

Ministers have said they believe any system for the over-25s would need to reflect the different circumstances of older people, many of whom had families or caring responsibilities, and more complex health needs. However, there was a belief that many of the core problems, including detachment from the workplace and a need to encourage greater participation, were the same for under- and over-25s.

A government source said: “The support offer and benefit changes Alan has set out were devised for young people and the specific circumstances they face. But the Timms review has set out that Pip is no longer fit for purpose, and the government will respond to that review when it reports.”

Milburn, a cabinet minister under Tony Blair, has promised his report is about giving billions more in support to young people to help them into work. The Guardian has learned there has been consternation within some government departments – including the Department of Health and the Department for Education – that the upfront funding for Milburn’s extra support will come from within their budgets.

Some estimates have put the cost of Milburn’s proposals at around £6bn. However, it is understood the report will not commit to a level of spending that high, even though it will provide some costings for the upfront funding needed and a trajectory for projected savings.

Milburn told the Guardian this week that the support for young people outlined in his report would create 440,000 employment and education opportunities by 2036 and raise the net incomes of young people by more than £2bn.

He said the main finding of the review was not a lack of ambition from young people but a lack of opportunities. “I have not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet [not in education, employment or training]. Not one. They want independence, they want to earn their own money and they want someone to give them a chance,” he said.

The Guardian revealed last month that ministers were working up sweeping plans for welfare changes, including scrapping key disability benefits for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.

Charities are nervous about how the proposals will affect young people. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation said the proposals could significantly weaken the safety net for hundreds of thousands of young people with a disability or health condition, leaving many of those on universal credit living on a basic rate of support of about £80 a week.

“Cutting someone’s income when they’re already struggling to afford food or the bus to college makes it harder for them to stay in education or find work,” said Iain Porter, the charity’s senior policy adviser.

More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities have warned ministers against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.

In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.

Polling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe that tackling the root causes of joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people, including Neets but not children, about 2.5%.

A government spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews are due to be published shortly, and we will respond to their recommendations in full.

“We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work. But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure.”

Don’t just blame the culture for keeping powerful men’s dirty secrets. Blame the law too

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:43:03 GMT

It is important to understand just how effectively perpetrators of abuse have used lawyers as their shields. A challenge to that can’t come soon enough

There will be empty shelves in many bedrooms this weekend, where the David Walliams books once stood. For parents of a certain era, there was no escaping that particular publishing-industrial complex, and I certainly did my share of wearily reading Gangsta Granny or Mr Stink on repeat. At his peak, Walliams was the bestselling children’s author in Britain for 100 weeks straight, to say nothing of the spin-off theatre productions, Christmas specials, countless World Book Day costumes, and that family-friendly stint as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent during which we now learn he was reportedly inviting teenagers to his dressing room.

“What I try and do most of all in my books is encourage reluctant readers,” he told breakfast TV’s Lorraine Kelly in 2024, the year before publisher HarperCollins finally dropped him after allegations over his behaviour towards junior female staff. But it’s parents who would have been reluctant to bring his books anywhere near bedtime had we known earlier about the young girls claiming that Walliams exploited his fame to prey on them, and then threatened legal action if they tried to speak out.

One 19-year-old was left “shaking” in fear by a missive from Walliams’s lawyers, Schillings, warning that she risked committing a serious civil offence if she talked publicly about her experiences with him, and requesting a signed legal undertaking not to do so. (Schillings maintains it was acting on its client’s instructions that she might sell “untruthful” stories to the press.) If it takes an agonisingly long time to bring some stories to light – the Guardian has been investigating Walliams since 2022, while the Sunday Times started piecing together its separate case against Russell Brand in 2019 – then don’t underestimate the herculean effort required now to build the evidence and to win the trust of frightened young women. They are not just afraid of having to relive a trauma in court, or being outed and harassed on social media, but of being personally sued for everything they have.

This isn’t just about Walliams, who denies the allegations and was eventually named after failing to secure an injunction against publication sought on the grounds that he might attempt suicide, however. Shortly afterwards, Private Eye reported that another male celebrity accused by multiple women has secured an injunction preventing the magazine from publishing. And even now, some women are still reportedly gagged by so-called non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) from sharing what they know about the convicted rapist Russell Brand. Publicly and privately, in our increasingly angry conversations about how exactly toxic men get away with it, women are starting to ask some very pointed questions about the law’s role in protecting them.

Twenty years ago, celebrities facing embarrassing stories about their sex lives might have asked their PRs to lean on a friendly tabloid editor and get it spiked. But that doesn’t work in an era of girls whistleblowing independently on TikTok, which means reputation management is increasingly now the preserve of lawyers, and in particular privacy specialists.

Why risk suing for libel in open court, if you can stop things long before that? Five times as many women as men have signed NDAs, according to the campaign group Can’t Buy My Silence – whose co-founder, Zelda Perkins, bravely broke her own to help get her former boss Harvey Weinstein convicted of rape – while Slapps (so-called strategic lawsuits against public participation, essentially designed to intimidate and exhaust the target rather than necessarily to win in court) are becoming increasingly common in allegations of sexual misconduct.

Even better than hushing things up afterwards, meanwhile, is ensuring confidentiality before they have even happened. The celebrity stylist Lou Teasdale posted on Instagram this week that it’s now routine in television for girls left alone with male stars to be asked to sign NDAs and surrender their mobile phones first. Though ostensibly to protect the celebrity from sneaky recordings, an agreement “to remove the woman’s voice and the device that would keep her safe” hardly incentivises men to behave well, Teasdale argued.

Everyone, of course, should enjoy the right to protect themselves against malicious claims, libellous gossip and unjustified intrusion into private life. But that doesn’t explain why two years ago, an inquiry by parliament’s culture, media and sport select committee accused the music industry of using NDAs to get victims of sexual harassment to leave quietly, while keeping the perpetrators in their jobs.

It doesn’t explain the rape victim bound by a gagging order that stopped her even discussing the attack with medical professionals, whose case was raised in parliament by the then backbencher (now cabinet minister) Louise Haigh during her successful campaign to curb the worst abuses of NDAs. It doesn’t explain the solicitor-turned-MP Sarah Russell’s memories of dealing with companies where everyone knew the boss to be a pervert but “the board can give the women 20 grand to go away, they sign an NDA and that is the end of that”.

And it certainly doesn’t explain the late Harrods boss and serial rapist Mohamed Al Fayed’s routine use of NDAs to silence and intimidate his victims. (Though legally such orders can’t stop someone reporting a crime, women were warned that Harrods’ feared head of security, John Macnamara – a former Met police officer – would find out if they contacted the police. Alison Kervin, author of a book about Fayed’s crimes, heard of one survivor who emerged from giving a police statement to find Macnamara waiting outside.)

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

At long last, the tide may be turning. The equalities minister, Bridget Phillipson, is considering new curbs on NDAs, to prevent “a system where rich and powerful men are able to silence women”. Later this month, parliament will debate the former Tory minister John Whittingdale’s backbench bill aiming to stop the weaponisation of Slapps against journalists and whistleblowers.

But nine years on from the mass reckonings of #MeToo, both its successes and failures are now clicking into sharper focus. Young women are thankfully far more vigilant for predatory behaviour than my generation was, and as Brand discovered, so increasingly are juries. (Though still too low, rape conviction rates are rising, with completed prosecution rates at their highest for a decade.) What we didn’t foresee when the old barriers crumbled, however, was that new ones would rise so fast. It’s true there has been for too long a culture of impunity for powerful men, and shame for women. But it isn’t just “the culture” – that vague, amorphous soup for which nobody is clearly responsible – that keeps men’s dirty secrets: sometimes, it’s also the law. Too bad for predators, then, that the latter is by far the easier to change.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Microsoft scrambles to fix global outage affecting Teams and Outlook

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:41:15 GMT

Tech firm says it is ‘deeply sorry’ for disruption and has now addressed the underlying issue

Microsoft outage hits UK hospitals, GPs, schools and police

Microsoft outage – live updates

Tell us: have you been affected by the outage?

Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.

The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began Thursday evening, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover just before midday GMT on Friday. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier on Friday, it said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels” as it brought back services. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, according to the company.

On Friday, government agencies worldwide, from municipalities in France to the US House of Representatives, reported problems with Microsoft services. The issues were patchy, with some but not all users reporting problems with services including Microsoft Teams and Outlook email.

The outage website Down Detector showed an increase in Microsoft 365 problems at about 6pm GMT on Thursday, with nearly 130,000 reports of problems in 74 countries affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. Copilot was also affected.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.

Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

The Microsoft outage also hit connectors used by ⁠OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI ⁠services.

OpenAI said it was investigating a problem with Microsoft connectors in which new connections might be broken and tools were not working as ⁠expected. Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider ​affecting its Microsoft 365 ​connector.

The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.

In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

Some schools in the UK notified parents that reporting attendance or absence issues had to be done via phone. National Rail, which provides information across the UK network, warned people might not be able to access tickets that had been emailed to them.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

Multiple cities, including the City of Tampa, Florida, posted notices on their municipal websites to say that they were affected by the outage. Law enforcement offices across the US were also affected, with one sheriff’s county in Colorado saying it was unable to process bond payments because Outlook email was down, and requesting that anyone who needed to post bond do so in person.

When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.

The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted.

In financial markets some portfolio managers have been unable to check emails, making it hard to access on some trading platforms.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

Microsoft last month reported an ​outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected a ​suite of productivity software ‌and a range ​of industries worldwide.

Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University in Melbourne, said the outage appeared to be affecting the network layer in Microsoft’s systems, and was potentially similar to the configuration issue that brought down Optus’s network in 2023.

He said that when some of the servers had configuration issues, it meant customers were forced to share a smaller pool of servers to access the cloud services.

“If you lose part of that pool, then all of the users are trying to access the remaining servers, and that overloads them. And then they go down. And so you end up with a cascading problem. Then it takes time to find the underlying problem, in this case, a misconfiguration in the network layer.”

Gregory said businesses reliant on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options.

Mohammed Alfatih rearrested over alleged plot to target Israelis in Europe while detained for attack on bailiff

A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in Germany for allegedly plotting to murder Jewish people.

Details of the alleged plot can now be reported after Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was found guilty on Friday of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his home in Birmingham.

The 40-year-old was found guilty by a majority verdict of unlawful wounding, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.

He was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit when he attacked the bailiff last year.

Alfatih, the son of a senior Hamas official, could not be named during his trial because of reporting restrictions.

He had been photographed working for a former leader of Hamas before being granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.

While detained for the attack on the bailiff in Birmingham, he was rearrested after authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged plot to attack Israeli targets in central Europe.

Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK, with his connection to Hamas stated in the German extradition request.

German prosecutors charged seven suspected Hamas members in September over an alleged plot to target Jews or Israelis in Germany or Austria around the second anniversary of the 7 October attack on Israel.

They said “Mohammed A” played a prominent role in transporting and storing weapons but was being prosecuted separately after UK authorities arrested him in London and noted he had not yet been returned to Germany.

German authorities said he was connected to Hamas’s leadership and was said to have produced a video in advance to take responsibility for the attack on its behalf.

The attack was disrupted by Germany’s domestic intelligence service after a tipoff from the Mossad, Israel’s secret service.

During a two-week trial at Birmingham crown court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October 2025.

Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:10:23 GMT

The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world

For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.

Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.

That’s where things get tricky. Last month Burnham’s government approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, dismaying climate activists. Soon there will have to be a decision on Rosebank, the much bigger proposed new oilfield northwest of Shetland. There are also signs that ministers are preparing to weaken the targets set for the car industry to shift to electric vehicles. And this week, the chancellor, John Healey, declared himself fully “behind building a third runway at Heathrow”. Small wonder that campaigners are talking of hypocrisy and the government’s “crumbling” credibility.

What is Burnham to do? He has Healey in one ear, telling him that a thriving airport is an engine for economic growth, doubtless alongside the oil, gas and car industries. And in the other he has the climate scientists, reminding him that global carbon emissions are at record levels and the planet is getting hotter every year. What option does he have, except to keep putting off the moment of choice, buying himself time by saying, for example, that Rosebank is a “quasi-legal decision” that cannot be hurried?

Naturally, there are advocates for each of the binary options, whether it’s green activists demanding he put the planet first, regardless of the impact on jobs or prices, or business leaders insisting it be the other way around. But he is in a different position from each of those warring sides – because he has to come up with something both can live with. The answer might just be an arresting blend of pragmatism and radicalism – both, and at the same time.

Such an approach would begin with saying a couple of things campaigners might not want to hear. First, that the most reliable route to reducing the use of fossil fuels lies not with curtailing supply – blocking production – but with slashing demand. Or as Michael Jacobs, who served as the climate and energy adviser to Gordon Brown in Downing Street, told me this week: “We need to destroy the demand for oil and gas.” On that goal, there has been remarkable progress, whether measured in the shift to renewable sources of power, such as wind and solar, for the generation of electricity or the move to electric vehicles: last month just under one in two new cars registered in the UK were either fully electric or plug-in hybrids.

The second message Burnham might deliver to a wary, green audience would be: symbols matter, but they should not obscure the thing they are meant to symbolise. In that context, and given that destroying demand is more important than curbing supply, he could argue that the green light he gave to Jackdaw should not be overplayed. That project is relatively small and has an expected lifespan of only about 10 years. Yes, it became a signifier, but the bigger picture is what matters.

It would be much harder to make that argument for Rosebank, which is bigger than Jackdaw and set to last for 25 years, and harder still for Heathrow, not least because emissions from aviation are stubbornly difficult to reduce: you can’t shrink demand for aviation fuel, because, as of now, there are few readily available alternatives. So a third runway means a serious increase in the UK’s emissions of CO2.

But what if Burnham felt he could not rebuff the growth lobby on Heathrow and Rosebank, especially if he also stands firm on his electric vehicle targets despite the howls of protest from UK carmakers? Is there a bone he could throw them, while not enraging the climate-concerned voters he needs to keep on side?

One option would be to grant reluctant consent to Rosebank – but follow it with a blanket policy that says any fossil fuel production in the North Sea must engage in carbon capture and storage, or CCS, essentially sending the equivalent amount of carbon that will be released by burning the extracted oil or gas back into the ground from which it came. It’s an expensive process, with vehement critics, and such a move would have to be phased, but it is possible. Norway has been running a CCS operation at the Sleipner field in its part of the North Sea for 30 years.

The UK government has set aside about £21bn to subsidise CCS, but here’s where the radicalism comes in. Healey should tell the fossil fuel companies, whatever the decision on Rosebank, that if they want to drill in the North Sea, they will have to pay to capture and store the carbon themselves. It’s the most elementary principle: the polluter pays. What’s more, it will free up that £21bn to be spent on schools, hospitals, defence – anything more worthy than subsidising the fossil fuel industry.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I’m told such a move is under “live” consideration by ministers and so it should be, not least because government estimates suggest CCS would create about 50,000 UK jobs in the 2030s, many more than lie in further extraction. It would represent a one-two punch of pragmatic radicalism: granting consent for some fossil fuel extraction, such as Jackdaw, while limiting the wider industry’s impact on the planet. Sure, it lacks the purity and simplicity of a wholesale ban that would keep fossil fuels in the ground – but it would be the next best thing, keeping an increasing amount of carbon deep in the earth. If it worked, Jacobs believes the likes of the EU or Norway might follow suit, imposing a similar CCS demand on their own oil and gas producers – thereby making good on Burnham’s promise of a “new era of British leadership”.

It’s just one example of a possible approach for a government that needs to find a way through the dilemma that confronts it – and governments like it across the globe. If it can’t say no to every move that entails emissions, then it must not say yes to all of them either. It will have to explain its logic on each specific case – even as it makes the broader argument about the necessity of preventing a climate breakdown and the most effective ways to do it.

It won’t be easy, not least because there are always more novel, more eye-catching issues to discuss. Climate breakdown at least used to have the market in existential, apocalyptic threats to itself – now it has to compete for that attention against the menace of AI. Charting a path ahead and having the public follow will require a nimble, trusted communicator, unafraid of nuance and complexity. It could be one of Andy Burnham’s biggest tests.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

She gets 16 pelvic exams a day – so yours don’t hurt

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:00:20 GMT

Molly Callahan, a gynecological teaching assistant, helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams

On her busiest days, Molly Callahan, has 16 speculums inserted into her vagina. She works full-time as a gynecological teaching assistant (GTA) – a layperson who helps medical students practice pap smears and breast exams before they work with actual patients.

It’s not as unpleasant as you might think. In fact, the point is to help students learn how to do it without causing discomfort. Contrary to common belief, pap smears – tests that screen for cervical cancer – don’t have to be painful.

“I don’t ever really feel physically in pain even after the longest week of work,” she said. “If [your] reaction to my job is that it sounds like torture, I hope you feel scammed,” added Callahan, 30, who is also the president of an international association for GTAs and MUTAs (male urogenital teaching associates). “I hope you go fire your gynecologist.” (While students practice speculum exams with her throughout the day, she says that the actual pap smear – the collection of cells from the cervix – is a little abrasive and she “definitely could not do 16 of those in a row”.)

Pap smears have reduced cervical cancer–related deaths by 86%, but many women avoid them due to confusion around guidelines, perceived lack of symptoms and, most commonly, speculum discomfort and embarrassment. One large study of US cancer statistics data found that from 2005 to 2023, 32% of women aged 21-29, and 15% of women aged 30-65, had never had a pap smear.

The negative association isn’t surprising. Looking at the cervix for indications of cancer became more common in the early 20th century, said Dr Kirsten Gardner, director of medical humanities at the University of Texas San Antonio, and methods centered innovation over comfort.

“So much of that conversation [on pap smears] was about the medical possibilities, not about the impact on the female patient,” said Gardner. “And when it did talk about impact, it was very much in the language of early cancer detection. It was never in the language [of]: ‘How does a woman feel? Is this painful? What can we do about the pain?’”

GTAs exist in part to answer that question. Pelvic exams and pap smears were historically performed on anesthetized patients until the 1970s, when GTAs became more commonplace in an effort to improve the ethics and educational quality of such exams. While GTAs teach medical students the basics, they also provide real-time reactions and feedback.

“They center the patient’s voice,” Gardner said. “Getting an experience with the GTA just reminds practitioners that they can talk to patients.”

Currently, more than 90% of medical schools in the US and Canada utilize GTAs – Callahan, who lives in Queens, teaches at 30 universities and hospitals. But despite the flexible schedule and pay rate – almost $100 per hour – Callahan estimated that there were only about 40 GTAs in the tri-state area, where there are more than 15,000 medical students.

GTA trainees learn anatomy and the tactics of breast and pelvic exams: how to swab the cervix, check for abnormalities, find the ovaries. They practice on a qualified GTA, then each other. It requires two months of training and a final test to ensure they are able to teach the exam to medical students.

Callahan became a GTA because of her mother, an actor, director and producer who was looking for additional income when a friend suggested it. Eight years ago, Callahan, who also went to theater school, was cobbling her life together after graduation. “She was like: ‘You’d be so good at this,’ which is a strange thing for a mom to say to a daughter,” said Callahan.

One stormy evening, I went to Teaneck, New Jersey, to observe Callahan teaching two labor and delivery nursing students from Fairleigh Dickinson University. Inside a fluorescent-lit classroom, Callahan sat upright on an exam table wearing a patient gown.

“I talk a lot about preserving people’s modesty and privacy as much as possible,” she said. “But to me? No, I don’t really care. It’s just parts. It’s just my meat suit.”

Callahan spent a few hours with the students – likely their only lesson on pelvic and breast exams during school, as is common for nursing students. First, she talked them through breast exams; the students doused their hands with sanitizer and sat at the base of the table. Callahan dropped her gown and explained that since appointment times are often short, they would be focusing on the areas of the breast where malignancies are most common: the outer tissue and in the underarms. They took turns gently pressing their fingers in a circular motion on Callahan’s chest.

“Don’t tell patients they look ‘good’ or ‘perfect’,” said Callahan. “Use positive but clinical language.”

She moved on to pelvic exams, holding a small mirror so she could see their movements. The student cautiously placed the back of her hand on Callahan’s inner thigh, a gesture Callahan teaches for consent and calming the patient before proceeding.

Then Callahan issued instructions: First, place two fingers on the labia and check for redness. Gently expose the clitoral hood to check for adhesions, which can indicate infections or skin diseases, and check the vestibular glands for cysts. Insert fingers, nail side down, to gauge speculum size. Explain what you’re doing at every step; if the patient winces, you are causing pain.

A proper exam is a collaboration that begins even before the appointment starts, Callahan said. For patients, it can be helpful to know the intricacies of a pap smear and what evidence-based care looks like. Patients can read guidelines and recommendations from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) to stay informed on key information like how often to get a pap smear. There is also knowing your own body: what does your vulva look like? Do you experience pain during sex? Is your breast tissue naturally firm?

This is important because you may change providers between exams, or a provider may not remember you, Callahan said. By tracking any differences over time, “you can tell when something’s changing and not healing so you have really concrete [information]”.

One of the best things people can do is think about their own experiences with providers, especially negative ones, and identify what would make it better and more comfortable, said Callahan. Then ask for what you want at the beginning of an appointment.

“If you, the patient, know that there’s a certain part you really hate – like speculum exams are really painful – could you ask for the smallest size possible?” she said. (Speculums come in different sizes: small, medium, large and pediatric.) Larger speculums are sometimes used by default simply because “the more tissue you push away, the more you can see”, said Dr Corey Babb, medical director of the Haven Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Additionally, patients may request a blind swab, which omits the speculum, or to insert the speculum themselves.

For additional comfort, Babb said, speculums can be warmed and should be well-lubricated. Patients can also ask to be put under nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, if available.

A provider who makes you comfortable and is invested in your wellbeing is worth holding onto, Callahan said. And if the experience is negative, you can provide feedback, or file a complaint for more distressing cases.

On one of her days off, I met Callahan at Hex House, a members-only warehouse in East Williamsburg, where she sometimes conducts GTA training. In her studio, Callahan gestured toward a three-tier cart full of medical books.

“I love this one,” she said, pointing at a 1981 publication called How to Stay Out of the Gynecologist’s Office, by the Federation of Feminist Women’s Health Centers.

“Going to the gynecologist was such a nightmare [at the time]. So it guides you through doing a self-pelvic exam, how to treat yeast infections, how to do a vacuum-assisted abortion,” she said, flipping through images. “Full bush, obviously.”

Gynecology emerged in the 20th century as a male-dominated field that displaced midwives, Gardner said. In the 1950s, biologist and sexologist Alfred Kinsey conducted a study that became known as the Kinsey report. In his research, he gently stroked the cervix of patients with a cotton probe, which only 5% of 878 participants could feel. When he tried a larger object, 84% reported feeling a sensation. Yet only the former result made it into the final draft, and he concluded that the cervix was insensitive. J Marion Sims, “the father of gynecology”, practiced on enslaved women and never used anesthesia. Body parts like fallopian tubes, Bartholin’s glands and the G-spot were named after male doctors.

“They think they discovered these things,” said Callahan, who prefers location-based names, such as “uterine tubes” and “vestibular glands. “Give me a break.”

At the end of the teaching session, the two nursing students admitted that neither of them had ever experienced a slow, gentle pelvic exam themselves. Callahan put her clothes back on as the students waved goodbye.

Once home, Callahan said, she would let a hot stream of water wash away the long evening of being touched – her hips and back get stiff from all the sitting, and the work can be exhausting. It can be taxing to unteach conventions of the past.

“It’s wonderful to be a good example for all of the students,” she said. “The healthcare providers assume everyone hates this, and it’s so horrible and it’s so weird – and it doesn’t have to be that way. I think it’s really great to show them that you can treat [physical exams] with consideration and respect.”

Carmen Rising is a writer based in Brooklyn

‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet,’ UN chief tells Cop31 in farewell speech

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:00:14 GMT

António Guterres says climate action central to every aspect of UN’s work, as leaders depart Cop31 and talks go on

Tackling the climate crisis is central to all of human life and must be at the forefront of global governance, the outgoing UN secretary general has said in an emotional farewell address at the Cop31 climate summit.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” António Guterres said at his final climate press conference as secretary general on Friday. “You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends.”

Guterres has been the most forthright secretary general yet on the subject of the climate, returning to it again and again to castigate fossil fuel companies and recalcitrant governments.

He leaves office at the end of December and his successor is still unknown after Donald Trump tried to interject his preferred choices into the process. There are widespread fears that the next incumbent will downplay the climate crisis in favour of other issues.

In a clear message to his successor, Guterres spelled out why the UN must continue to place the climate at the top of the global agenda. “Climate change does not stay in its lane,” he said. “It drives anger and displacement around the world. It wipes out development gains built over decades. It pushes countries deeper into deficit. It aggravates competition for land and water.

“It fuels instability. And increasingly, it threatens the very existence of communities and countries. For all these reasons, I have never viewed climate action as just one of many other issues. Climate action is central to every aspect of the work of the UN.”

Guterres was one of the few world leaders left at Cop by Friday afternoon as most of the more than 90 who had attended returned to their capitals, leaving negotiators to get down to tackling issues such as the electrification of the global economy and a just transition out of fossil fuel industries for workers.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, flew out after hosting a meeting between major international investors and Australian renewable energy companies, followed by a meeting with Taneti Maamau, the president of the low-lying Pacific nation of Kiribati. Albanese made raising the plight of his country’s Pacific neighbours a major part of his two and a half-days at the talks.

The Australian co-presidency of the 31st “conference of the parties” to the UN framework convention on climate change issued a list of “reflections” that encapsulated the proposals countries had expressed since the talks began on Monday. This will form a loose basis for a first draft of the “cover decision”, the final negotiated document gavelled through at the end of the summit, which is likely to be the central outcome of Cop31.

Recent cover decisions have produced significant progress: at Cop28, in Dubai in 2023, the cover decision included a global pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, and at Cop26, in Glasgow in 2021, a cover decision produced a requirement to “phase down” coal.

This year, hoped-for resolutions include a target of deriving 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035, seen as one of the most important ways of decarbonising the global economy, and pledges to cut methane emissions, make progress on the phase-out of fossil fuels, and ensure adequate finance for developing countries hit by climate disaster.

The “reflections” document gave a clear sense of how difficult it will be for Australia – which, in an unusual sharing arrangement, is presiding over the negotiations while Turkey hosts the talks – to forge an agreement before the scheduled end next Friday night.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and the president of the negotiations, said: “We are making sure parties are being listened to as we progress negotiations. The reflection text is not a negotiating text. Nothing in it is prejudged, locked in or necessarily to be included in the final decision.”

Countries will have until late on Saturday to respond, with an official draft cover decision text not expected until early next week.

More than 100 companies and groups linked to fossil fuels were present at the talks, research revealed on Friday, despite efforts to clamp down on the presence of lobbyists in recent years.

Prakash Dalal, of Pro Public/Friends of the Earth Nepal, criticised their presence. “Big polluters have caused loss of livelihood, emotional damage, trauma and survival challenges for our people,” he said. “We cannot tolerate the disproportionate space given to them compared to civil society and our country delegations.”

There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino’s news conference at US Soccer’s national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks – they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.

“I think [the decision was],” Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, “one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much.”

The news conference read very much as a farewell to Pochettino, but there is still work to be done. The Argentinian will guide the USMNT through a pair of Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. In the meantime, the future United coach did his best to address questions about his departure and what comes next.

“These moments are not easy decisions,” a reflective Pochettino told the media. “Normally it’s the opposite. Normally you get sacked and you cry because you want to stay and you’re sacked by [the club]. It’s a tough decision but at the same time we are excited for the next step forward.”

Pochettino characterized United’s interest and negotiations as having come together at the last minute, essentially, with contact between the two sides first made Sunday.

“We cannot underestimate the staff and the players. When things became big and big and big, the players are very sensitive and the staff are too – they start to feel things as well. [Everything] was so quick, because we arrived here last Friday and Sunday afternoon this situation started to appear and some contact. We were very transparent, we were talking with [US Soccer CEO] JT [Batson] and the federation.”

Details were quickly ironed out between the sides, with the club and federation agreeing Pochettino would remain with the US through the upcoming matches.

“[Thursday], when things were positive in the way the agreement was, we had a meeting and I communicated to the players and the whole staff. I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation and they know us – how committed we are for the next two games. The decision between the federation and Manchester United, to agree that we’ll continue with our job in the camp; [nothing] can change our commitment and how important the next two games are.”

Pochettino and the US federation touted his contract renewal in August as the start of something new and significant, with the coach given a larger role in the overall direction of the US men at every level. That went by the wayside when United came knocking.

“They know that there are not too many opportunities that can happen in your career like [this one with Manchester United],” Pochettino said. “When they arrive, it’s difficult to turn down. But I want to make it clear, when we decided together to [stay another four years], it was always the commitment for the federation, too. Maybe the four games [in the September/October window] if we lose them, maybe you start to put pressure [on me]. And maybe something can be in a different way.

“Or even in the future,” he continued, “Things can happen. The federation and maybe new people arrive or don’t, or maybe have different ideas and you say, ‘We are thinking in different directions’ and maybe they say ‘Mauricio, maybe you need to go home.’ We cannot think in these extremes – I think we were very committed and never thought this would happen so quickly.”

‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:38:27 GMT

Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems

The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.

After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.

The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”

Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.

In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.

In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.

“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.

“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”

after newsletter promotion

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.

Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.

The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.

“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”

Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”

In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].”

Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”

Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”

Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

Branding it like Beckham: how Jude Bellingham is future-proofing his fame

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:03:19 GMT

From Calvin Klein to British Vogue, the Real Madrid man is leading the way when it comes to football’s foray into fashion. But is he playing it safe?

This Sunday, Jude Bellingham will line up with his England teammates for a match against Spain. But the footballer has been hitting the headlines way beyond the pitch recently – thanks to fronting a Calvin Klein underwear ad released this month, and becoming the first footballer to appear solo on the cover of British Vogue.

It’s a savvy move for the 23-year-old, future-proofing himself as a power player both on and off the pitch. This is a roadmap carved out by David Beckham, who since retiring in 2013 has become a brand and personality that transcends sport. Beckham – together with his wife, Victoria – became a billionaire this year.

The Calvin Klein ads, which feature Bellingham in underwear, sometimes in his signature Christ the Redeemer pose, have caused a stir since appearing in London and New York, with passersby stopping to take selfies. The popularity of a billboard in Soho, New York also cements his celebrity status in the US after this summer’s World Cup.

Of course Bellingham is a bona fide star on the pitch. Mark Borkowski, a public relations consultant, says this factor is pivotal to the footballer’s crossover appeal. “Bellingham is an exceptional sporting talent, and his brand value is understandably enormous,” he says. “But fashion doesn’t create that value, football does. Fashion merely provides another means of exploiting it.”

This buzz is working out well for Calvin Klein. The fashion data firm Launchmetrics said in 48 hours the Calvin Klein campaign generated $35.8m (£27m) in media impact value, the metric that works out the monetary value of social media posts. The fashion platform Lyst reports that searches for Calvin Klein underwear have risen by 25% since the campaign was released.

Bellingham has a savvy team around him, with his mother, Denise, a former HR executive, working as his personal manager. Some are wondering if his 21-year-old brother, Jobe – in the England squad for the first time this month – might do similar campaigns, increasing the rise of the Bellingham brand.

So far Bellingham – and his management team – have been strategic with his brand choices. As well as Calvin Klein, Bellingham works with Adidas, Kim Kardashian’s underwear brand Skims and Louis Vuitton.

Daniel-Yaw Miller, in his influential SportsVerse newsletter, compared him to Beckham. “It’s very intentional,” he says. “What [Bellingham is] doing is aimed at the higher tier of the market but at the same time, a big part of his personality is very relatable.”

Bellingham is also a heart-throb, with looks that, in another life, could belong to a boyband. Vogue have amped up this factor: the magazine comes with a pull-out poster. “It helps that he’s incredibly good-looking,” says Miller.

Sign up to Fashion Statement

Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved

after newsletter promotion

Bellingham is not the only male footballer to work with the fashion industry. Bukayo Saka and Son Heung-min were in Burberry’s autumn campaign, Kylian Mbappé worked with Christian Dior, and Declan Rice is on the cover of GQ this month. “The earnings that they can get during their football career are obviously huge,” says Miller. “But what sets them up for life beyond that is being brands and businesses in their own right. It’s not only just a money thing. It’s about cementing a legacy and securing their profile in the game long term, commercially and culturally.”

Not everyone is impressed by Bellingham’s foray into fashion. Felicia Pennant, the editor of the football and fashion magazine Season, says if he is following Beckham’s business model, the older footballer pushed the boundaries more, appearing in edgy photoshoots covered in (fake) blood for The Face magazine in 2001, and in artwork by Sam Taylor-Johnson. “Beckham was the subject of art and he was the art rather than selling the art,” she says. “I think what Jude’s doing feels quite transactional … there’s nothing that directional about anything he’s done so far.”

Borkowski sounds a note of caution going forward. “Fame surrounds exceptional young athletes with people whose livelihoods depend on telling them how wonderful they are. That can become a very dangerous echo chamber,” he says. “The football makes the myth. The business can preserve it. But hubris can destroy both.”
