Young men were key to the blue wave. Our research offers a reason why

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:00:21 GMT

Amid concerns over the influence of the manosphere, our findings show that young men are concerned about caregiving

When young men helped propel Donald Trump into the White House in 2024, the administration doubled down on a brand of toxic masculinity popular in the so-called manosphere.

They touted high testosterone, male supremacy, and a “biblically-based family” where men work and provide, and deferential women stay home to bear children and care for others.

In a complete reversal, on 3 November, young men powered the blue tidal wave that swept away Maga’s hold on political power. Men 18 to 29 shifted nearly 40 points to help Democrats capture both Houses of Congress, flip seats in state legislatures, and win some unexpected governorships.

Turns out, young men may not be so toxic after all. So what do they want?

The election results made clear that young men want financial stability at a time when the cost of living is soaring and jobs have become precarious, disposable and threatened by AI. But they also want time to give care.

That’s according to recent research we produced with NORC at the University of Chicago on men’s attitudes and experiences with care, based on a nationally representative survey of more than 3,000 Americans, with an oversample of young men 18-29.

We found that more than six in 10 young men value caregiving as much as paid work, even though many of them are not yet fathers or caring for a loved one.

Thirty percent of young men identify as caregivers, including 44% of young Hispanic men, who swung for Democrats by 47 points from 2024. Nearly six in 10 young men who have worked while giving care have reduced their work hours. Providing care while still earning enough to live is a major concern.

“Everything is so expensive these days that a young person can’t even consider taking care of someone, as they can barely take care of themselves,” a 23-year-old male caregiver from Ohio shared in the survey.

Eight in 10 say that being an involved father is an important part of being a man. Seven in 10 say they’d be at least somewhat interested in being a stay-at-home parent if they had the choice.

In fact, six in 10 young men, compared to about four in 10 young women, said they’d be at least somewhat interested in being a full-time caregiver – hardly the answers politicians pandering with UFC fights on the White House lawn might have expected.

Abdul, one of our survey respondents, began caring for his chronically ill father at age 19 because no one else in his family was available, and they couldn’t afford the high cost of paying for care. He missed classes, quit his job, and moved in with his extended family in order to care for his father until his death.

“It was always nice for me to be there for my father, because he was there for me when I was young,” Abdul, now 26, told us. “I have no regrets. I would do it again.”

Our survey did find that some young men hold traditional views on gender.

Men ages 18 to 29 are nearly three times more likely than women of the same age group to say that it’s OK for men to do some care work, but women are better suited to do most of it (32% versus 12%). Young men are also more likely than young women to say that men’s role in the family should be providing financial support while women run the household (32% versus 14%).

Still, these are minority viewpoints. More than 70% of young men say that care should be divided equally between men and women. Sixty percent said mothers and fathers do an equally good job of caring for a newborn, compared to just 52% of men over 30. And young men are more likely than young women to say gender does not play a role in who is best suited to care for an adult.

Half of young men said they are “somewhat” or “very” likely to need paid leave from work to care for a child in the future, about the same share as young women, and 44% anticipated needing leave to care for an adult family member.

Among young fathers who took paid leave to care for a child, 70% said having access to paid leave through their employer or state was a major reason they took it.

And when we asked men who wanted to take caregiving leave from work, but didn’t, the most common reasons were that they couldn’t afford it, worried their careers would suffer, or that their workplaces weren’t supportive. Just 5% said taking leave wasn’t “manly”.

Nearly one-third of young men say they have “no control” over their work schedules, and while 33% work from home at least some of the time, 68% would prefer to, a 35-percentage-point gap between what young men have and what they want.

Perhaps what young men want is what we all want: good work with living wages that ensure the ability to have and care for a family.

Instead of disgruntled Republicans working to thwart Democrats at every turn in the next Congress, policymakers would do well to raise the minimum wage, help all families cover the high cost of care, and pass federal paid family and medical leave, and measures to give workers more flexibility and control over their schedules.

Evidence suggests young men are moving beyond toxic masculinity and the politics of division.

If they want to stay in power in 2028 and restore hope for the future, it will be up to policymakers to deliver instead on what the newly elected Texas senator James Talarico calls the politics of love.

Brigid Schulte is an award-winning journalist for the Washington Post and the Washington Post Magazine and was part of the team that won the 2008 Pulitzer prize. She is director of the Better Life Lab at New America

Haley Swenson is a PhD social scientist and senior Writer and researcher at New America’s Better Life Lab

Eleanor Donaldson, wife of former DUP leader, placed on sex offender register

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:48:02 GMT

Judge imposes three-year treatment order on Donaldson for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her husband, Jeffrey

Jeffrey Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has been placed on the sex offender register for five years for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her disgraced husband.

Eleanor Donaldson appeared via remote link at Newry crown court to hear the order on Friday one month after her husband, the former Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, was convicted of abusing two women when they were children.

The 60-year-old bowed her head and cried as Judge Paul Ramsey imposed a three-year supervision and treatment order as well as placing her on the sex offender register. Asked if she understood the court order, she nodded and said yes.

In June her husband was convicted of 18 sexual offences, including one count of rape, spanning 1985 to 2008. The case stunned Northern Ireland and destroyed the career and reputation of a politician who had been the leading voice of unionism. In October he was sentenced to 15 years.

His wife faced a trial of the facts after being deemed unfit to participate in a conventional trial on mental health grounds. A jury found that she had aided and abetted her husband’s abuse.

She could not be given a prison sentence, only a hospital order, a supervised treatment order or a discharge. Two experts, one for the prosecution and one for the defence, told the court that a supervised treatment order was the most appropriate option.

The victims, known as complainants A and B, were in court for the hearing on Friday. The prosecutor, Rosemary Walsh KC, told the court that “pain permeated” their statements.

Donaldson’s three-minute appearance on screen was the first time she had been seen in court since 2025. Wearing a black jumper, and with close-cropped hair and two cuts on her forehead, she cast her eyes down and held a tissue.

The judge told the court the medical evidence about her was unchallenged and that a supervision and treatment order was “inevitable”. Donaldson would be under the supervision of a social worker from the Craigavon community mental health team for three years, he said.

This would require attending appointments, treatment and home visits, said Ramsey. She will be subject to the notification provisions of the sex offender register for five years.

Bronagh Muldoon, the assistant director for the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children Northern Ireland, said aiding and abetting abuse required consequences.

“It is right and important that the role she played in these terrible crimes has been recognised in court today. The women involved in this case have shown incredible bravery in coming forward to ensure the Donaldsons have both been held accountable,” Muldoon said.

The former DUP leader is appealing against his convictions and his wife is appealing against the jury verdict.

After the Guardian revealed the gift, Harborne said it was intended “to support Nigel’s security not just now but for the rest of his life”.

The party refused to answer questions about whether Farage had spent any of the £5m on security costs to date. It also refused to address questions about why Farage had refused the offer of a taxpayer-funded package.

The Guardian understands that the party makes a distinction between security required as a result of its leader’s political activities, which it pays for, and his potential longer-term personal security needs, which the gift was intended to provide for.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Nigel Farage’s excuses over his secret £5m ‘gift’ have fallen apart. You can’t trust a word he says. Zia Yusuf, Reform’s spokesperson for home affairs, complained publicly that the party was having to seek fresh support from donors to meet Farage’s security costs in October 2025.

Harborne gave Farage £5m shortly before he stood as an MP in the 2024 general election. On becoming an MP, Farage was offered and accepted taxpayer-funded security, which he used until autumn 2025.

Harborne had been the dominant party donor in recent years until he was joined by his fellow crypto tycoon Ben Delo in donating a further £36m each in September.

Marlon Brando cool to Jensen Huang joke: how the black leather jacket became a meme

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:17:09 GMT

Once the ultimate symbol of Hollywood rebellion, the former Nvidia chief’s signature look is now being mocked as a midlife crisis cliche

For nearly two decades a black leather jacket has been a key part of Jensen Huang’s look. Now it has become a punchline.

As the founder and chief executive of Nvidia resigned this week after reports of multiple affairs, his affinity for a leather jacket, an item of clothing typically associated with a man in midlife crisis mode, has become widely mocked.

The Cut ran a story suggesting a clear line between his penchant for a luxury leather jacket and his extramarital affairs. “Jensen Huang’s leather jackets confessed before he did” read the headline. Writing in the New York Times, the author Anand Giridharadas asked “is an expensive leather jacket on a middle-aged man the new symbol of a honeypot victim?”

Meanwhile, the internet is rife with memes, including an AI-generated image of a leather jacket flying at half mast outside Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. There was also another fake image, this time of Huang in a studded leather jacket, that many people believed was real.

Elsewhere, there are plenty of divorced dad jokes doing the rounds. “Jensen leather jacket discourse reminds me of the time two years ago when I wore my beloved moto jacket to a party and my good friend said “great jacket, sorry you got divorced”, wrote one user on X.

Similar to Steve Jobs’s black rollneck and jeans or Mark Zuckerberg’s Latin-sloganed T-shirts, Huang’s black leather jacket has become a visual trademark. He likes to pair a leather jacket (always black) with a black T-shirt and black jeans.

In September, in an interview with CBS, Huang explained he had 30 to 40 leather jackets. He credited his wife, Lori Huang, with choosing them. They vary from motorcycle-inspired jackets with a tighter fit and plenty of zips to collarless croc-embossed jackets and clean-cut tailored versions. He has worn them to trade shows, to parties and to give keynote speeches at developer conferences. In 2021 he appeared on the cover of Time magazine in a black leather jacket from Tom Ford. In July, another Tom Ford jacket worn and signed by Huang sold at a charity auction at Sotheby’s for $960,000, more than 10 times its original price.

“The leather jacket is Huang’s way of borrowing some cool,” says Peter Bevan, a writer and stylist. Bevan points to the leather jacket’s “rebel history” as part of the appeal.

Marlon Brando led his biker gang wearing an asymmetric zip jacket in 1953’s The Wild One; James Dean zipped around off-screen in a similar style while following his Berlin era; David Bowie wore a black leather jacket on the cover of his Heroes album in 1977. Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing, John Travolta in Grease and Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones also made a leather jacket an enduring symbol of Hollywood style.

By choosing a black leather jacket rather than a corporate suit, it suggests that Huang is unconventional, a leader rather than a conformist.

“It’s basically Huang saying: ‘I’m not a regular billionaire boss, I’m a cool billionaire boss’,” Bevan says.

When asked by CBS in October why he wore a leather jacket day in, and day out, Huang said it helped him avoid decision fatigue. “Black is the absence of choice,” he said. “It’s nice to wear the same thing every day because no surprises. For everybody else, they probably have to make three or four decisions. I took that off my plate. The moment I wake up, I could be thinking about important things.”

It’s a look that has not gone unnoticed by his fellow tech giants. In 2024, Zuckerberg posted a photo of Huang swapping jackets. Later in the year, at a Siggraph conference in Colorado, Zuckerberg presented him with another jacket. “It’s black and leather and shearling,” Zuckerberg said describing the coat. “It’s a vibe. I mean, get this guy a chain.” In return, Huang gave him the black leather jacket he was wearing, explaining that Lori had bought it for him to commemorate that year’s conference. “This is worth more because it’s used,” Zuckerberg said as he slipped it on.

Bevan says that while Huang’s choice of designer jackets are “the kind that most fashion insiders would rate”, a box-fresh leather jacket “feels try hard” and as a result, “tips into midlife crisis territory fast”.

The biggest mistake men make when buying a leather jacket Bevan says is choosing one that is “too shiny, too new and too tight.”

The list of those who get it wrong is long – including Jeremy Clarkson, who likes to wear a black leather jacket with bootcut jeans.

For Bevan, the men who have mastered a leather jacket are those who “look like they’ve owned it for ever”.

Lenny Kravitz who, like Huang, is in his 60s, prefers a battered leather jacket. John Malkovich, who is a decade older, likes a brown oversized leather jacket, while the rapper A$AP Rocky, who is in his 30s, has made a bomber leather jacket his style staple.

For those without youth or “rock-star DNA” on their side, Bevan suggests ditching a leather jacket for a cotton Harrington style that he describes as “having the same cool but none of the leather-clad midlife baggage”.

As for Huang, he may have to reconsider his default wardrobe for next week. While he managed to pull off a leather jacket at tech conferences, it may be harder to pull off at a congressional testimony.

Why Chelsea and Manchester City’s WSL clash is not as season-defining as you think

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:05:44 GMT

Neither side have lost in the league yet but a more competitive division should take title race to the wire

There was a time when the games between the top three – traditionally Chelsea, Manchester City and Arsenal – were title-deciders. Where every point taken off a title rival was key. Such was the gap in investment and quality between those teams and the rest of the Women’s Super League, it was extremely rare that points would be dropped to teams outside that elite clique.

As the WSL has grown in investment, profile and size, that narrative has started to shift a little. The investment gap is still large from the top to the bottom of the league. But increased investment among the best of the rest and even among those teams further down the table, as well as an increase in high-quality coaches with the tactical and technical vision to get more from players, is having an impact.

That’s a roundabout way of saying that when Chelsea welcome the title holders and current league leaders to Stamford Bridge on Saturday lunchtime, counterintuitively, the three points isn’t the most important takeaway. Instead, based on the state of play, it’s the momentum, confidence, belief and bragging rights that are critical.

Naturally, should Chelsea win and thus leapfrog Manchester City, then the title race will be considered wide open. If Andrée Jeglertz’s City extend their lead over Chelsea from two points to five, even at this early stage, they will be considered favourites for the title in May, but it will be said with a little less confidence than it might have been in previous years.

The WSL is more and more competitive year on year. There have been only two occasions, in the 15 years since the first WSL season was played (after it was launched to replace the FA Women’s Premier League National Division), when the title winners have lost more than two games in a season. Both of those have come in the last three years, with Chelsea the first to do so in 2023-24 and then Manchester City last season.

You could say that because wins are less consequential in the games between title rivals, those games are less thrilling, but the reality is that the growing unpredictability of almost every match across the WSL means that every game becomes a must-watch.

At Stamford Bridge on Saturday, the remaining two unbeaten teams have the opportunity to inflict a first defeat. Neither side has looked infallible this season. City have kept just two clean sheets in their 13 games in all competitions, while Chelsea stuttered last weekend, with their second draw of the season allowing City to move above them.

Arguably, there has been a momentum shift between Sonia Bompastor’s and Jeglertz’s teams, with the former having dropped points against Everton before a 0-0 draw with the Swedish side Häcken in the Champions League while City earned a 5-0 win over West Ham and picked up a first win in Europe, after three draws, with a 4-1 defeat of Inter.

Jeglertz said that moving top had changed nothing before this clash. “We’re still early in the season. We want to win all games. That’s our focus this weekend,” he said. “Nothing has changed from that point of view and I don’t think it will have for them either.”

Chelsea have been defensively strong, and are the only WSL team to still be in single figures for goals conceded, on five to City’s 10, and they have kept nine clean sheets in their 13 games in all competitions (not including Champions League qualifying).

However, the key to the west London side’s ambition of drawing first blood between the two teams this season will probably centre around how well they cope without Lauren James.

They may lead the way in goals scored too, 28 to City’s 27, but against Everton the absence of the England forward’s creativity was keenly felt and Chelsea’s attack looked a little predictable. Everton nullified the impact of the wide players Ellie Carpenter and Sandy Baltimore and Chelsea struggled to find another way through.

“My job is to make sure I find solutions when some players are not available and not playing for the team,” Bompastor said last week.

While Chelsea have to cope with the absence of James, who has a hamstring injury that Bompastor says means they “won’t see her until the end of this block” – up until at least the international break at the end of the month – City have players returning.

Rebecca Knaak is fine after a knock to the head against Inter and Vivianne Miedema, Beth Mead and Niamh Charles are on their way back. “All three of them, actually, were in the session today and I hope that they will be available for Saturday,” said Jeglertz. Advantage City then, just.

In a way, that it is unlikely that this result decides either team’s season makes it a more interesting and exciting contest, because players are free to play uninhibited by the pressure of how catastrophic a loss could be and, with the two dominant teams going head to head, we’re in for a show.

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 13:48:13 GMT

Singer, 76, was in Manchester with his band for penultimate UK show of his Songs in the Key of Life anniversary tour

When Stevie Wonder’s team just called to say: “Can we all come to your restaurant in Stalybridge at 11pm on a Sunday?” Ryan Robinson, of course, said yes.

First the band turned up, and then – at 12.30am – the man himself arrived. Hours later, staff at the Cafe Continental were sharing a £1,000 tip.

It was, the co-owner admitted, “all a bit mad”, as he praised Wonder as someone who was happy to chat to everybody, and the team around him as down to earth and extremely polite.

Wonder, 76, was in Manchester with his band for the Sunday night gig at Co-op Live on his Songs in the Key of Life 50th anniversary tour.

It was the penultimate night of a 13-date European leg of the tour in which Wonder performed all 21 songs from his most celebrated album, which includes Have a Talk With God, Sir Duke, Joy Inside My Tears and Isn’t She Lovely.

Robinson told the Manchester Evening News that some of the musicians on the tour had already been in a few times, “as they often tour with other artists”.

“Every time they’ve visited, they’ve been like: ‘Stevie might come’, and we were always just thinking that it would be amazing but we never expected anything from it.

“His band visited again on Saturday and then we got the call to say they wanted to come again with Stevie’s youngest daughter after their show in Manchester, and they said again that Stevie might come. We stayed open late for them, and then he turned up – it was all a bit mad!

“We normally just do a roast service on Sunday, so it was a bit of a scramble to make it all happen and ensure we had the full menu ready for them, but everybody was so lovely. Stevie is actually a really nice guy and was happy to pose for photographs and have a chat.”

Among the late-night diners was Wonder’s daughter Aisha, for whom he wrote Isn’t She Lovely when she was a newborn. Robinson said: “His daughter, his family, and his entire team are just all down to earth and very polite. You wouldn’t think they were these massive global superstars. I just kept looking over being like: ‘Is this actually happening?’ We’ve still not come to terms with it now!”

Robert Pattinson has emerged as the favourite in the race to succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond, according to a credible film-industry source.

The casting process for the new Bond film, the 26th in the official series, has become very public in recent weeks, with industry reports suggesting that three actors – Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor – were on the producers’ shortlist, and two weeks later that two others, Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult, were also being tested.

Each contender will have been offered terms before the test process began – what Belloni calls “test deals” – and Belloni surmises that producers must not have been fully happy with the original three-strong shortlist, to allow more established names to join the process.

Bond 26 will be the first film made by the series’ new owner, Amazon MGM, which has “creative control” of the franchise after striking a deal with its previous producers, Eon, in 2025.

Producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal are overseeing the project, while Dune’s Denis Villeneuve will direct and Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight is writing the script.

After participating in a number of successful franchises, including Twilight, Harry Potter, The Batman and Dune, as well as appearing in acclaimed dramas such as Bel Ami, Cosmopolis, The Lost City of Z and The Lighthouse, Pattinson is the most high-profile of the contenders – something that would have likely gone against him when Eon was still in control, whose credo was that Bond was a bigger star than any actor.

Belloni suggests that in the current media landscape, that may no longer hold: “No franchise is bulletproof any more – everything is vulnerable and most can be helped by a value-add element, like an established star.”

If you’re wondering what a Reform government might look like, just look at its chaotic record in Wales

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 13:35:49 GMT

As the main opposition in the Senedd, the party should be taking politics seriously. Spoiler alert: it’s not

In May 2026, Reform UK became the official opposition inside the Welsh Senedd. It was the best result the party had ever received in a national parliament – and since that time it has been a wild ride. Given that its leader, Nigel Farage, claims he expects to one day lead the UK government, how it performs in Wales matters more than just for the people of Cymru; it gives the rest of the UK a sense of what it could expect if Reform does well in the next general election.

Just to give you a taste, here are two developments. In September, Reform’s leader in Wales, Dan Thomas, resigned after he was arrested and released on bail on suspicion of assault and coercive or controlling behaviour. (Thomas said that he had done “nothing wrong” but resigned to avoid becoming a “distraction”.) It has also lost one of its members in a bizarre defection from the rightwing Reform (which has been sceptical about even the existence of the Welsh parliament) to the leftwing Plaid Cymru (which wants more devolution and ultimately an independent Wales).

To mark six months of Reform holding more than a third of seats in the Senedd, two colleagues and I decided to undertake a deep-dive investigation into the party in Wales, which we published on my newsletter. We spoke to several Senedd members and staffers who all agreed to speak to us on the condition of anonymity. They took us inside Reform WhatsApp groups and revealed a world of paranoia, leader worship and an obsession with “disruption”, rather than a party of serious opposition or government in waiting. Our findings flew in the face of the Reform UK Wales deputy leader’s claim in September to be the “most effective, professional and united opposition the Senedd has ever seen”.

Our investigation found that out of 100 Senedd committee meetings held between 8 May and 21 October, there have been 31 times when at least one Reform MS has been absent. For context, here are the figures for the other parties: Plaid, eight times; Labour, nine; the Tories, nine; the Greens, six; and the Lib Dems, one. Committee meetings are a key way for MSs to hold the Welsh government to account, and the number of Reform MSs to have missed meetings is almost as many as all the other parties’ absent members put together.

But what was most striking was the total aversion to scrutiny and the dictatorial way that the party’s MSs are managed. According to the members we spoke to, there is a “banned list” of organisations and journalists whom Reform Senedd members are forbidden to talk to. These include Oxfam and the Books Trust charity. I must now admit a certain amount of professional pride that I too have managed to make the list.

For example, back in the summer I sat inside the Senedd canteen eating lunch. The number of MSs increased by more than 50% at the last election, so space is at a bit of a premium. There was a seat free on my table and a Reform MS came up with his tray and asked: “Do you mind if I join you?”

“Please do,” I said.

He sat down and we ate our food in silence. After a minute he looked up at me, paused, and said: “You’re Will Hayward.”

I replied: “I know.”

He then looked panicked, like a man who had just clicked on a link in a phishing email. “I am not allowed to be here or talk to you,” he said.

I said: “You are a grown man and an elected representative on £80,000 a year, you are allowed to talk to who you want.” He stood up, glanced around and squeezed his way on to a packed table elsewhere.

But is it surprising that they behave like this? Sources told us that there is a large picture of Farage on the back of the Reform group’s office door in the Senedd. More significantly, the power of the leader is captured by the fact that the Welsh Reform constitution states that he must give permission for the Reform group to work with any other party.

However, the fear of journalists within the party pales into insignificance compared with how paranoid the Reform higher-ups are about Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain. As one MS told us: “Everything the party is doing is about countering Restore. HQ are obsessed.”

This drive to defend their right flank has manifested itself inside the Welsh parliament in just the past week, when the Reform MS Joe Martin made claims that white British people were being “replaced” and would be a minority in the UK by 2063 (the definition of “white British” used by Reform is so narrow it would exclude King Charles).

The speaker in the Senedd told Martin that he would not be called to speak again until he apologised for his comments. This prompted one of the most surreal press conferences I have ever attended where Reform’s leader in Wales, Helen Jenner, said that the rest of the party would be boycotting the Senedd in solidarity.

And if you really want to know what a large Reform group could be like in Westminster, look no further than the WhatsApp message Jenner posted when talking about attending a group in the Senedd established to develop policy to tackle the issues affecting women in parliament and wider society.

“Sort of makes me feel like we should go along and disrupt,” she wrote.

By the way, I put everything we found out in our investigation to Reform UK to comment. They said, “These claims are blatantly outlandish, ridiculous and unsubstantiated.” We sought clarification on which of the 13 different points we put to them they were referring to. Despite repeated attempts, they did not reply.

At a time when Wales is crying out for a credible and serious opposition, we are left with disruption for disruption’s sake. To quote Succession’s Logan Roy, these “are not serious people”.

Will Hayward is a Guardian columnist. He publishes a regular newsletter on Welsh politics

‘You can’t train to be chucked in a box full of rats!’ Ade Adepitan on fear, facing down sharks and being I’m a Celeb’s first wheelchair user

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 13:00:19 GMT

His upcoming appearance on I’m a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here! is already causing a huge stir. As he heads to Australia, the paralympian talks leeches, evil taxis – and snakes round his nether regions

‘If you spend enough time in the TV industry, at some point you’re going to end up in the jungle, eating animal genitalia, with Ant and Dec watching you!”

Paralympic medallist and TV presenter Ade Adepitan is in the building, and he’s ready to cause a stir. The 53-year-old is set to become the first wheelchair user on I’m a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here!. His participation has already ignited a social media maelstrom, drawing ableist ire – from accusations of “cheating” due to the jungle being adapted for him to outright crowing that a disabled person should not be on a primetime show as it is ostensibly “box-ticking”.

A wheelchair user for most of his life, Adepitan has keenly felt the weight of responsibility of being “seen” in a disabling world ever since he acquired his disability. Born in Lagos, he contracted polio as an infant; an accomplished wheelchair basketball player, he has since moved into TV presenting, largely covering sport as well as the natural world and the climate crisis. Taking part in Shark! Celebrity Infested Waters brought him to the attention of I’m a Celebrity’s producers.

To adapt the show for Adepitan, he was flown out to look at the camp site and advise the producers on disability access. Changing types of terrain, small pathways and transferring out of his chair to move around the site were all potential problems. His access needs mean he will use different wheelchairs, crutches and other mobility aides. A niggle at the back of his mind has been that this would be seen as an “advantage”, yet having a disability, he says, is like starting a race – or a marathon – five miles behind anyone else.

Being in the jungle is not so different to moving around his home city of London, or using the tube as a wheelchair user: “There’s a few more trees, a few more leeches, but it’s that kind of thinking and problem solving that we, as people with disabilities, have to do all our lives.” In fact, London has been at the heart of the problems he has encountered: from broken lifts trapping him in train stations to black cabs refusing him a ride. But Adepitan refuses to give in to the despair of a world built from barriers. He cycles from acerbically funny to a kind of charismatic vulnerability when detailing his experiences as a disabled man of colour.

Setting foot in school as a child in callipers meant “I had all eyeballs on me”. The weight of preconceptions had to be dispelled: “Even as a five, six-year-old child, I recognised that. I’ve carried that weight all my life knowing that I have to, like, change people’s perspectives.” And yes, he has felt like an outsider as a result. There are people with extreme views on what it means to be disabled and taking part in a reality show, he notes with a smile. Had his childhood self seen someone like him in the mainstream, Adepitan wonders what that would have done for his self-esteem. After all, later on being introduced to Ian Dury from the Blockheads, someone with the same disability, was a revelation. There was such power in seeing someone in a similar situation refusing to be hidden away.

“It’s almost like society is ashamed of us and it’s almost brainwashed us into being ashamed of ourselves as well,” he says. But regardless of the issues or fears he will face on I’m a Celebrity, it will be worth the effort to spark a conversation on disability, he says.

Asking Adepitan what he is most scared of in the infamous trials gets a spectacularly comical response: “Hell no, I’m not telling you my fears! Why am I going to tell you my fears? I tell you my fears, you write them down.” He assumes an “airs and graces” type of voice: “And the people from I’m a Celebrity [will be] like: ‘Ohh, noted, this is what Ade doesn’t like!’”

His previous experience as a contestant on Shark! Celebrity Infested Waters doesn’t necessarily mean he’s “good” with sharks, either: “It’s not like I’m gonna jump into the ocean and be like: ‘Oi, shark … that’s your pint mate! I know a few of your mates in the Bahamas. Fist bump?’”

It’s been suggested that a background as an athlete will stand him in good stead for the show – something he roundly rejects. “Mate … who has trained to be chucked in a boxful of rats or eat a cow’s udder?” He describes himself as having the skills to shoot basketball hoops, “not to have a snake wrapped around my nether regions. While Ant and Dec do a countdown!”

He impersonates the Bushtucker Trials, mimicking the hosts: “Come on Ade, you can do this! 10 seconds, 10 seconds! Eat it! Shove it up there, do that!”

As a disabled person who has been in the public eye for decades, Adepitan is acutely aware of progress around perception and care – and there are tiny signs of it actually happening. “Being disabled is hard. And the nonsensical thing about it is, constantly – because I’m old and I’ve been around for a long time, and we’ve watched and seen how the Paralympics have evolved and there’s more people with disabilities with [a] profile – I’m always told: ‘Haven’t you come a long way? Things have moved on so much!’”

after newsletter promotion

Back in the day, taxi drivers wouldn’t even stop for him. “I would have to hide behind the corner, and dangle my good old-fashioned two-legged friends in front as bait!” There’s something of the Del Boy about him as he details his routine to flag down a cab: “They would hail it down then I would appear from nowhere and leap into the back! That was the only way I could get a taxi.” So yes, says Adepitan, some things have gradually changed.

But like so many, Adepitan has a few grim tales of being left stranded by drivers, regardless of what the law may state. It’s an experience that happens “regularly”, he says, often from misconceptions around the size of, or just not wanting to “take” his wheelchair in their vehicle. Another case saw him in court, where a driver eventually lost his job for such a refusal; Adepitan spoke out about the experience on an Instagram Reel, with many other people noting the exact same experience.

What Adepitan wants people to understand is that it is not his wheelchair that makes him disabled, nor a body chronically seen as a “problem” in need of correction. It is the physical and emotional barriers a society has decided to choose that are the disablement. And it can turn just as quickly: “When things go wrong in society, when things get tougher, we are one of those groups that are going to be the scapegoats.”

And just as quickly, we’re back to a different serious conversation. He is keen to “pay it forward”, as a salute to the sacrifices made by his parents. They were both from Nigeria, where he lived before coming to the UK.

“They gave up everything to bring me and my sister over here. They never went on holidays. They did, like, three jobs each, as well as studying. And we lived in a council house with damp everywhere, but everything they did was for us.” Their sacrifices, he says, are something that can be shown as having been “worth it”.

The point, says Adepitan, is that taking part in a show such as I’m a Celebrity is bigger than just himself. It’s not a desire to represent every disabled person – that is impossible, of course – but this will be something of a landmark first. He smiles, almost wistfully, expressing his big hope: “To make my parents proud if they’re watching from up there.”

I’m a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here! starts on Sunday at 6pm on ITV1.

The dark side of reselling apps: ‘If you include your pants, I’ll pay more’

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:54:16 GMT

Ministers consider banning under-16s from online marketplaces amid reported misuse of messaging functions and users’ photos

In June, Hannah* listed her seven-year-old daughter’s pink swimming costume for sale on Vinted, hoping other parents surfing the reselling site would snap up the £1 offer. Her inbox pinged.

“So a little girl wore this yh [yeah]?” wrote a user with a male handle.

“She did yes,” Hannah replied.

“Naked?”

After sending back a barbed “What do you think?”, Hannah swiftly blocked the user and reported the incident to Vinted. She described the exchange as “disgusting” and “disturbing”.

Her experience is just one of the many innocuous listings of children and young people’s secondhand clothes on reselling apps that are attracting sexualised comments through their direct messaging function.

The Children’s Society has said some young users of resale sites are increasingly being asked for indecent photos in exchange for money or gifts. Some photos of young users posted on the platforms have been AI deepfaked into nudes without their consent.

In response, ministers are considering banning under-16s from platforms such as Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to the Sunday Times, over mounting fears that their private messaging functions are the latest frontline in child exploitation. Vinted, which has a minimum age of 18, would have to join the other sites in gating access with strict age verification features.

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said on Sunday that the government was “looking seriously” at expanding the under-16s social media ban to include online marketplaces. It is understood the regulations were sent for cabinet signoff this week, with Nandy expected to present them to parliament in December.

Young women have posted on TikTok and Reddit about their concerning interactions with buyers. Those exchanges include asking the seller if the item will come with used underwear if they buy it, or unsolicited sexual comments about their appearance.

Lucy* started reselling her pre-loved clothes on Depop when she was 15 and has been subject to many unsettling experiences. Once, she listed an item of clothing for about £10 and a user requested to raise the price. “The person had changed it to £30 and said: ‘If you include your pants I’ll pay more’,” she said. “That made me feel like, oh my God, awful.”

She then discovered that images of her taken when she was under the age of 18, posted to advertise her clothes, had been scraped from Depop and were circulating on Reddit.

“These pictures are actually still being resurfaced on these Reddit pages, which is quite frustrating,” she said. “It would be me at 17 trying to sell a bikini, and these men have screenshotted these images … It’s not just me, it’s hundreds of other girls.”

About two years ago, Lucy came across another social media platform, Discord, where she found users had stolen her old Vinted and Depop photos and manipulated them using AI to make deepfakes of her “fully nude”. She said: “It’s deplorable that people think it’s acceptable to take people’s images and make them into AI porn – I felt really, really upset.”

Vinted says minors can only access the site under the supervision of adult account holders, while Depop says users must be aged 13 or over to set up an account, and over 18 to use PayPal and the Depop payment systems. However, the UK communications watchdog, Ofcom, has found that 15% of eight to 14-year-olds use Vinted each month, while another report has suggested that some children are able to bypass checks and access age-restricted online services.

Some child safety campaigners have expressed fears a sweeping social media ban could exclude children from the internet entirely. Karen Garland, the head of policy at the Marie Collins Foundation, a charity that supports victims of technology-assisted child sexual exploitation, said: “We need to make spaces for children and young people that are safer by design. And so, in some ways, extending a ban into other spaces may not be the best route overall.”

Despite her experience, Lucy is conflicted about the ban. “It’s a real shame because there are probably very young girls that maybe are from different backgrounds … that maybe really need that money.”

However, she acknowledged that there could be “extremely dangerous” consequences to selling clothes on Vinted. She said that as she was now 25 and has continued to find sexualised images of herself online,, the risk did not end at 18.

A Vinted spokesperson said: “We have zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content and use a combination of dedicated moderation teams and detection tools to spot and remove activity that breaks our rules. When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities.”

An eBay spokesperson said: “We have clear policies and safeguards to protect our community, including encouraging people to keep conversations on eBay, avoid sharing personal contact details and report any suspicious or inappropriate behaviour. Where we or our customers identify policy violations, we take appropriate action.”

Depop said: “Using someone’s images without their permission is a violation of our terms of service, which explicitly prohibits users from using or sharing another user’s content without their consent, whether on Depop or elsewhere. We take the safety of our community extremely seriously and we have robust policies, controls and processes in place to protect our users.”

Brendon McCullum has backed Kevin Pietersen to help educate England’s batting lineup before the “­specialist mentor” he hired in the summer leaves the tour of Australia after Sunday’s second one-day ­international in Adelaide.

The collapse to 131 all out for a seven-wicket defeat in Perth on Friday naturally brought back memories of the first Ashes Test 12 months ago. But more relevant is what it means should a similarly fast, bouncy surface – such as at the Wanderers in Johannesburg – be encountered during next year’s 50-over World Cup in southern Africa.

McCullum said he would outsource the post-match debrief to Pietersen, before the 46-year-old departs for India on Monday to speak at a YouTube conference. Having originally planned to return for the T20 leg of this tour, Pietersen’s next assignment with England is now expected to be the ODIs in South Africa in January.

“It all happened pretty quick,” England’s white-ball head coach told TNT Sports. “We weren’t quick enough to adapt to the conditions. We talked extensively leading into the game about the surface. It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline, there are certain shots that are very difficult to execute.

“Overall we’re disappointed but there are some good lessons for us. If you look towards the World Cup in South Africa there’s going to be some pitches there that will test us from a bounce point of view. We need to be able to adapt to conditions a bit more, we need to scrap a bit more.

“KP has got such a nice manner about him. He sees his role to get the talent to perform on the world stage. His message will be measured but firm – adapting to conditions, what could we have done, trying to drive the ball on the up is not wise. Next time we hit a surface like this we have to try and work it better.”

After an encouraging summer that returned series wins over India and Sri Lanka, England’s 50-over side has endured a disappointing start to the winter. Four defeats and just one dead-rubber victory during the recent tri-series in Pakistan has underlined the scale of their task over the next 11 months.

One noteworthy feature during this run – albeit not exactly telling here in Perth – has been the leg-spinner Adil Rashid, England’s second highest ODI wicket-taker and a pillar during their past success, losing his spot to Liam Dawson.

As was the case in Pakistan, the one-day captain, Harry Brook, insisted this particular selection call was solely down to conditions although whether this reason holds in Adelaide, usually a more batter-friendly pitch, remains to be seen.

Brook added: “We knew that the surface here today was going to be seam-friendly and spin wasn’t going to play a massive part, hence why we went with Daws [who is] probably a better batter than Rash at the minute. ‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 11:31:21 GMT

As Amazon MGM Studios prepares to announce the next 007, much rides on how the news is broken. From double bookings to health and safety embarrassments, we look back at how not to do it

And then there were five. While nothing has been officially announced, it is widely understood that the shortlist to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond is now down to a handful of actors: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult.

The hunt for a new Bond comes at a propitious moment for the franchise as a whole, 25 films in (not counting the two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983). After Daniel Craig stood down from the role after completing No Time to Die (in which Bond appeared to be killed in a missile strike), Amazon MGM Studios paid over $1bn to acquire “creative control” from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the British-American heirs to the series’ original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.

Amazon has lost no time in indicating that it aims to change direction, hiring Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight to write the script and Denis Villeneuve to direct; it’s consolidating the franchise’s move away from the safe-pair-of-hands directors that Cubby Broccoli preferred, and the writing contributions of Neal Purvis and Robert Wade, who have screenplay credits on the last seven Bond films. A new lead actor will send the clearest signals of their intentions for the future for what is the sixth most lucrative franchise in cinema history, having accrued more than $7.8bn in box office returns since 1962.

Six actors have previously been given the role, and Amazon MGM will be looking for certain qualities in its new lead. Robert Sellers, who comprehensively researched the Bond casting process in his 2024 book The Search for Bond, says the balance between sophistication and brutality is vital. “You have this man, Bond, who can hang out in casinos but can also get down and dirty and take out half the Russian army. If you read the novels, Bond is dangerous, he’s a killer. So as a Bond, you need that roughness, but also that debonair touch. I think this is where Daniel Craig scored so highly – he had that street fighter element.”

Once the decision is made, the way it is communicated to the outside world is a key moment in the process – not just for the franchise but also in the transformational effect it has on the life of the actor concerned. In 1962, it was a low-key affair: a 15-line article in trade magazine the Daily Cinema announced “Meet James Bond …”, accompanied by a photograph of a fresh-faced Sean Connery holding a cigarette. Compare that to events 43 years later in 2005, when Daniel Craig was sent bombing down the Thames on a Royal Marine speedboat, followed by a press conference at HMS President, a shore unit of the Royal Naval Reserve.

But things don’t always go to plan. Safety regulations meant that Craig had to wear a lifejacket – non-debonair optics that were widely ridiculed in the media – and at the subsequent press call he appeared somewhat intimidated by the attention. It was an experience that Craig himself later described as “a fucking train wreck … I was terrified”.

It now appears that at least part of the reason behind Craig’s inauspicious introduction was that the producers were concerned that the secret of his casting was on the verge of getting out. A senior film publicist familiar with the Daniel Craig announcement told the Guardian: “The PR company involved were scrambled at short notice to help pull together the press conference because there had been a significant leak. A logistics company were brought in to do the whole coming down the Thames on the speedboat bit – he had to wear a lifejacket and the tabloids decided to go to town.”

The publicist added: “Daniel had been properly prepped but when the music comes on and he walks down the gangway to the front you can see he’s gone a bit rabbit in the headlights. All those questions he had been prepped for were getting fired at him – and he just clammed up.”

Craig soon put that to rights in the first few minutes of Casino Royale, in which his Bond administers a brutal beating to a corrupt fellow agent in a Prague gents’. Fortunately, however, Craig’s publicists never had to deal with anything like the interview Connery gave shortly after his casting announcement, one of several intended to introduce him to a wider audience. In an encounter that, if it happened now, would likely kill the entire franchise stone dead, Connery expounded on his theories of when and how it was acceptable to hit women, throwing demonstration punches at Sunday Express writer Susan Barnes. Presumably this display was designed to lean into what Connery called the “cruel, sadistic” elements of the Bond persona.

By the time George Lazenby was given the nod to take over the role after Connery resolved to leave, the unveiling of the new actor took place in 1968 at what became a Bond tradition: a press conference at an expensive London hotel. When Roger Moore finally got the gig in 1972 – after being ruled out in 1961 and 1968 with prior commitments to TV shows The Saint and The Persuaders respectively – he was photographed enjoying a fat cigar on the roof of the Dorchester, an image that set the tone for his segment of the Bond series.

Control of information is another issue with Bond: in the 1980s and 1990s, the series was still big news, even if box office returns were at a low ebb (Licence to Kill, in 1989, is the least successful Bond film at the box office, adjusted for inflation). Pierce Brosnan was offered The Living Daylights in 1986 but, ironically, the resulting buzz motivated NBC to renew his then-dormant TV show, Remington Steele, and thereby preventing him from taking the role. The press ferreted out the name of his replacement, Timothy Dalton, while Dalton was still working on another film in Puerto Rico, where he was besieged by reporters. In what now appears an amazingly behind-hand move, Dalton was first presented to the outside world at a press call in Vienna, well after filming on The Living Daylights had begun.

In the 2020s, the media landscape is vastly different, even from Craig’s debut two decades ago; Amazon MGM may feel it doesn’t need the traditional press call, and announces the new Bond via a social media post to trigger what is likely to be a tsunami of engagement. The senior film publicist says: “It’s a cliche, but we all like it, all the photographers and the pictures, the news journalists and entertainment journalists, and now influencers and other things that are patched in. I would love to see a good old-fashioned Bond press conference with whoever it is.

“It’s what Bond represents: a sense that everything else might change, but the Bond movies haven’t. The fact that it’s reported across every platform on a daily basis right now is huge. It transcends politics, leftwing and rightwing. It doesn’t matter, everybody’s got a an opinion.”

Rugby League World Cup glory again for England’s wheelchair champions

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 10:39:08 GMT

England prevail 50-38 over France in Wollongong final

Joe Coyd scores four tries in successful title defence

England men’s wheelchair rugby league team completed an historic defence of their World Cup title, defeating their great rivals France in a thrilling final in Wollongong which underlined the overwhelming positives of the sport.

The English and the French have been the two dominant nations in the wheelchair game, sharing the previous four World Cup titles between them. On the field, they have produced thunderous and often controversial encounters but off it, there is great respect in a sport that allows disabled and able-bodied athletes to compete alongside one another.

The two nations served up another classic in Australia on Friday, with England emerging victorious to back up their win on home soil against France four years ago. The winning margin may have been 12 points but the contest was much closer for almost the whole match, with a late second-half flurry of points from the English proving decisive.

Joe Coyd, the brother of England’s head coach Tom, was one of the stars for the world champions. It was his two tries which put them into an early 10-0 lead before the French responded with four unanswered tries of their own. Now 22-10 ahead, the momentum looked to be with Cyril Torres’ side, but England struck in style as half-time approached.

Jack Brown and Rob Hawkins both scored, with Coyd also completing his hat-trick courtesy of a world-class team try to give the English a six-point advantage at the interval. That lead was wiped out shortly after the restart when the impressive Dany Denuwelaere scored for France and, as four years ago when England won by only four points, the final looked to be going the distance.

But Hawkins, this week crowned the winner of the Golden Boot and named the world’s best player for a record-breaking third consecutive year, acrobatically responded with a try almost immediately before Coyd scored his fourth and Brown crossed on two more occasions to complete his own hat-trick.

Denuwelaere offered the French brief hope with a second after Coyd’s fourth but by the time he scored his hat-trick in the final minute, the damage had been done and time had run out for France. The sound of the full-time hooter sparked jubilant and emotional celebrations among the England squad.

Perhaps the most important moment from this thrilling game is the one you did not see, though. Four years ago, England’s Finlay O’Neill was watching from home, inspired to get involved with wheelchair rugby league after being told he could not play the running version of the game any more, for health reasons.

The new star of English rugby league may have ignited the same feelings for others sitting at home on Friday morning, inspiring them to get involved thanks to the heroics of the world champions. And while the World Cup means so much, that glimmer of hope for people who need it the most undoubtedly means more.

Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 08:00:14 GMT

For all the supposed improvements, inspectors still obsess over statistics and adjectives, but surely school success depends on teachers and parents

The government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards, which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty.

The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey that showed more than half of headteachers in England polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are now considering early retirement as a result of the experience. This sense of misery was also illustrated in a poll conducted by the National Education Union one year on from the introduction of the new framework, with 65% saying it is the same as or worse than before.

It is no wonder that the leader of the National Association of Head Teachers, Paul Whiteman, has called for an immediate halt to Ofsted’s visits. “The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it,” he said. “It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life.” Even the new education secretary, Lucy Powell, has said she takes the reaction to the inspections “incredibly seriously” and said she wanted to see a system that was “more supportive” to staff. We have yet to see what that means.

Schools used to be local institutions that belonged to the community. Bringing state-maintained schools under central government control in England and Wales began in 1988 with Thatcher’s national curriculum reforms. In 1992, John Major created Ofsted to enforce it. He also began a national league table of secondary schools, which were to be judged by their exam results. It is hardly surprising that the whole dynamic of secondary education became “to teach the exam”. Sports, art, music were shamelessly sidelined.

By the time of Tony Blair, the resulting avalanche of Whitehall regulations was said by a teacher friend to fill a wheelbarrow every school term. Vocational and technical education were demoted in favour of academic and university-oriented subjects. The nation’s performance in the international Pisa league tables became as competitive as the Olympic Games.

Now, Ofsted inspectors descend on schools, usually once in four years, with usually just 24 hours’ notice. They are armed not with advice or money but with exam statistics and adjectives. They have reduced the teaching profession to a production line.

The trauma experienced by staff has been an inevitable consequence. Perry’s sister says she has been contacted by 12 other heads saying they too have felt suicidal after glib dismissals of their work. How could such a brief inspection take account of considerations as important as a child’s health, the local job requirements and tutoring resources? An inspector merely needed to sniff the air, decide “not good enough” and stroll back to Whitehall. Would we judge our doctors, lawyers or bankers that way?

The naivety of the inspection regime is a classic of overcentralised government, of the relentless search for standardisation. I can find no evidence that relates a pupil’s or a school’s exam results to an individual’s wealth or happiness in later life. They are measuring for measuring’s sake.

The one great fault of comprehensive education in Britain from the 1960s onwards was its devoting so much of the secondary syllabus to academic subjects. Powell has already shown herself open to reforming this. She has banned GCSE preparation from the first two years of secondary school, and is determined to end the denial of vocational education for those who fail maths GCSE. Her proposal to teach subjects such as health and social care is welcome. So too is her enthusiasm for oracy and verbal confidence. If Powell means what she has said, she must put an end to Michael Gove’s generation of ministers and their obsession with academic league tables and to preparing pupils for university.

Possibly Britain’s currently most disgraceful statistic is that since the outbreak of Covid about 20% of children in England in year 9 – their mid-teens – are “persistently absent” from school. We need look no further for the cause of the current Neets crisis. The failure is glaring.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The success of a school, primary or secondary, is largely a function of its relationship with its local area. It depends on the reputation of its staff and their collaboration with parents. When schools were locally owned and run prior to Thatcher’s nationalisation these relationships were built into their governance. A school’s success was a feature of local pride. Of course this meant some worked better than others. But I find it significant that the UK was recently rated only the 16th “happiest country” in Europe. In part I sense it reflects its distant and heavily centralised public sector.

Nobody needs Ofsted. Andy Burnham should move to devolve schools to the communities they serve and on which they should in future depend. Inspecting the professional quality of their work should be a local matter. We need only to look abroad to see that this works.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 08:00:13 GMT

After wittily blending pop and politics on their debut, the Belgians are now processing their personal lives. We join them for a mindbending tour of their home city of Ghent

Boris Kor Tom Zeebroek is staring up at a grey gothic building in the centre of Ghent, squinting through the late September sun that is covering his home town in a cloak of unseasonal warmth.

Zeebroek is encouraging his bandmate Charlotte Adigéry and I to crane our necks towards the Mammelokker, an 18th-century Flemish relief on the top of the building. It’s a gruesome bit of stone, which sits above the town square and depicts a daughter suckling her own father. The pair are taking me on a tour of their medieval home town, and this disturbing architectural decoration is part of our itinerary.

“Would you breastfeed your own father?” Zeebroek asks me, while still staring skywards. I’m about to tell him I’ve never really thought about it, but he and Adigéry start to cackle uncontrollably. “You might have to one day,” he adds. “Think about it.”

This is part of my initiation into the oddball, utterly fascinating world of Zeebroek (who goes by the stage name Bolis Pupul) and Adigéry, who used the Mammelokker as inspiration for the video to their single Googoo Gaga, perhaps the funkiest ode to child-rearing ever recorded.

In the video, Adigéry takes on the role of wet nurse, breastfeeding an elderly white man who could represent the Mammelokker – or is it an allegory about the Belgian state’s notoriously extractive practices in the Congo? The duo’s work isn’t ever quite what it seems: part joke, part social commentary, but always packaged as pop with dance music DNA.

The pair pick me up outside my hotel on a pair of cargo bikes that they use to cart around their young families. Zeebroek tells me to hop in the front of his and we weave through the cobblestone ginnels of Ghent, dodging fellow cyclists and the tourists who litter the streets. First, we head for coffee, then a quick look at the Van Eyck brothers’ recently restored Lamb of God altarpiece, then the Mammelokker.

Walking or cycling around Ghent with Zeebroek and Adigéry can only be done at a glacial pace: it’s impossible to move 50 metres down the street without someone from their past popping up. Zeebroek’s old babysitter cycles past us, before we turn a corner and bump into Adigéry’s best friend from primary school who happens to be visiting from the US. Another well-wisher turns out to be the original drummer from Belgian rave-rock titans Soulwax.

“You see that guy in that cafe?” Zeebroek says, waving at a tall Belgian in a yellow jumper. “He was one of the lead actors in Belgica,” the 2016 film about a hedonistic club, which featured both Zeebroek and Adigéry on the soundtrack. During the course of four hours, we’re stopped by more than 20 people. Have they set this up? “You’re in the Truman show!” jokes Adigéry.

Adigéry and Zeebroek both grew up in the city, but didn’t meet until 2013. Both were drawn into the orbit of Soulwax (AKA David and Stephen Dewaele), the brothers who helped to put Ghent on the musical map with the notorious mashups made by their alter egos 2manydjs in the early 00s. It was the Dewaeles who suggested Adigéry – a vocalist who they’d worked with on the soaring electro track The Best Thing – should team up with Zeebroek, who was playing in local bands and helping the brothers to catalogue part of their 70,000-strong record collection.

The first album by Adigéry and Zeebroek – 2022’s Topical Dancer – was perhaps the smartest, deftest artistic response to the Black Lives Matter movement. They ridiculed language policing (Esperanto); wrote a certified banger about fitting in as an Afropean (Blenda) and crafted an ode to the limits of new puritanism (Hey). Overall it was a knowing send up of race, colonialism and the performative allyship of the BLM era – “us observing our world and the internet as millennials”, says Adigéry – and often hilarious. It was written on the road, with the pair plucking song ideas out of thin air; they were once travelling to a gig and heard a song riddled with cliches on the radio so they decided to write a riposte – Ceci N’est Pas un Cliché – a Magritte-referencing, ESG-esque single that got the remix treatment by Soulwax.

Their second album – Mainland Madinina, out in February – is different: much more personal, rooted in their collective grief. Zeebroek lost his mother in between the two records, and Adigéry’s father, who had Alzheimer’s, also died. “We wanted it to be more introspective and more vulnerable,” Adigéry says.

To write it, the pair decamped to Martinique, the tiny Caribbean island Adigéry’s parents moved to Belgium from (Madinina is the original Arawak name for Martinique and the name of her mother’s now-closed cocktail bar; “Mainland” is a nod to Zeebroek’s Hong Kong heritage). When visiting as a child, Adigéry says she found the island’s energy inspiring and all-consuming, but on this trip with Zeebroek the pair rented an Airbnb on a quiet hillside, got out an acoustic guitar and produced a bunch of stripped-back demos. “It was a little cringe,” says Zeebroek, mimicking plucking a guitar, after we sit down to talk at a restaurant. “‘Hey, does this chord sound good?’”

But what started to form was a deeper version of their sound. There’s still the humour in Googoo Gaga, the glam-rock stomp of Stepmother and the maniacal funk of Losing My Shit, but overall this is a record about growing older and raising children, all while processing the loss of loved ones. “Looking back at those four years,” says Zeebroek, in between mouthfuls of steak tartare, “there were some darker things happening and we had to digest them.”

The album is bookended by opener Restless, and closing tracks Rite of Passage and I’m Lost – a song in which Adigéry breaks down while sing-talking about finally throwing away flowers from her father’s funeral. It’s raw, visceral and beautiful songwriting, and was cathartic as the singer tried to come to terms with her grief. “When you become a parent, I think it’s such a mirror,” says Adigéry. “What’s the trauma from my parents or my grandparents? What do I want to leave behind? I don’t want to be a bag lady with all this baggage.”

The most ambitious track is the eight and a half minute From Healer to Dealer, a piss-take of wellness culture and therapy speak, with the pair performing a dramatic vignette in the middle of the song as alter egos: Ruben and Grace. What starts as an apparently compassionate conversation descends into absurdist mud slinging of buzzwords and bullshit: “You love-bombing, breadcrumbing, emotional dumping, energy-draining mess!”

The song was partly inspired by a pair of not-exactly-zen club bouncers they knew who became life coaches. “I think this holistic approach to health and mental health is good,” says Zeebroek. “It’s great to see that a lot more people think of meditation and how to heal yourself, but then there’s also this obsession with healing. It creates a blind spot … and it’s all very superficial.”

After our meal we make our way to the Deewee studio, the cavernous monochrome lair of Soulwax, which was designed by local architect Glenn Sestig. Its exterior is an obsidian black block with a small embossed Deewee logo: the only real clue about what goes on beyond its walls. Once inside, I’m led to a recording booth which looks like the hideaway of a Bond villain with a taste for analogue synths: an audiophile’s dream, where Adigéry and Zeebroek honed Mainland Madinina. “They keep on buying gear,” says Zeebroek. “It is never ending.”

The Soulwax duo co-produce everything on the Deewee roster, and Zeebroek describes them as being musical “chiropractors”, able to nudge their music joints into position or give their ideas a high-fidelity rubdown. “Whenever we’re stuck they know when to push,” says Zeebroek. Adigéry adds that they often ask “what’s the real intention behind what you’re writing now?”, pushing them to add extra layers to their songwriting.

Zeebroek remembers first seeing how their music could be a Trojan horse for bigger ideas. On their first UK tour, an up-for-it Manchester crowd began screaming the chorus to their bouncy 2022 single Blenda. Witnessing a couple of hundred Mancunians shout “Go back to your country where you beloooooong!” was a pinch-me moment for the duo, who had hoped that politics and pop could in fact mix and audiences were smart enough to get the joke.

“It really brought tears to my eyes,” says Zeebroek. “That was the first time I felt like we were the Beatles or something. My monitors were being overpowered by the shouting.” Manchester gets it; hopefully the rest of the world is ready.

Mainland Madinina is released on 5 February via Deewee. Googoo Gaga and From Healer to Dealer are out now

Progressives are still so pessimistic, but why? The populist right can and will be defeated

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 06:00:12 GMT

From the US midterms to Brazil and Hungary, extremists are floundering yet the left still overestimates their power. Reality is on our side

From Brazil to Hungary and Britain to the US, why are so many people so surprised by the right’s election defeats? Flávio Bolsonaro, Viktor Orbán, Reform UK, the Tories and a vast array of Republican candidates have all been rejected in national or local contests this year, even in usually reliably conservative Mississippi. Apparently impregnable incumbents and populist insurgents alike have been beaten, often by big margins. The supposedly ascendant global right has been out-organised, out-thought, outmanoeuvred and outnumbered.

Yet each time this happens – which is more often than the usual gloomy narrative of our politics allows – many liberals and leftists absorb and share the good news almost with wonderment. Rightwing governments such as Donald Trump’s may have been struggling for many months, having made countless impossible or incompatible promises and strategic blunders, and opinion polls may have been consistently pointing towards a meltdown, but their actual election defeats are seen as miracles: unexpected moments of joy in the morning news, often followed over subsequent months by a creeping conviction that the right’s supremacy will inevitably return.

A similar progressive pessimism follows the right’s victories, whatever their scale. The 52% vote to leave the EU in the 2016 Brexit referendum set off years of centrist and leftwing soul-searching about why the right supposedly had a better understanding of the whole country. Boris Johnson’s 2019 general election win with a medium-sized majority of 80 seats – less than half the size of Tony Blair’s in 1997 and 2001 – was widely described as a “landslide” and a sign the Tories would stay in office for many years to come.

Then came Trump’s hugely hyped 2024 presidential victory. Despite him having run against a last-minute, less than compelling Democrat candidate, being ahead by just 1.5 points in the popular vote, and achieving an electoral share below 50%, his win was seen as signalling a profound shift to the right, not just in politics, but in American culture and society, from how young men thought to whom Latino voters supported. A brash but socially conservative, confrontational but entertaining counter-revolution was said to be surging in the US and far beyond, ideally suited to the online world.

The midterms haven’t made this movement disappear. But they are the latest evidence that its strength has been overestimated. Some of that error originates in the ultra-confidence of rightwing populists. Especially when amplified by a powerful rightwing media, it can convince some voters for a while, as the blustering Johnson’s relative popularity from 2019 to 2021 demonstrated. In democracies riddled with doubt and with a recent history of tentative leaders, the performance of certainty can be seductive – until its bluffing and self-delusions are revealed.

Many voters and journalists want to see politics in clear narratives. Believing that the right, or the left, is dominant is simpler and more emotionally resonant than acknowledging that many western democracies are closer to political stalemate, and have been for a long while. Over the past 50 years, the Republicans have won the US presidency seven times and the Democrats six, with the 2000 Republican win achieved only through a highly contentious ruling by the supreme court – itself a symptom of deadlock.

In truth, the battle for power in any democracy is much more complex and multi-dimensional than national contests suggest. Electoral politics happens at many different speeds and scales. Then there are public protests such as marches, riots and strikes; elite private lobbying operations; slow but potent changes in popular attitudes; culture wars in the media and other institutions; battles between ideas in books and online; shifting power dynamics within personal relationships; and evolving assumptions inside people’s heads.

If an ideology or political party significantly shapes many of these processes simultaneously, then it has achieved hegemony, as the term was understood and refined by the still influential Italian thinker Antonio Gramsci during the 1920s and 1930s. This century’s recurring transatlantic tendency to see the right as establishing a new era of dominance is a misapplication of this theory: a mistaken belief, across the political spectrum, that modern conservatism has come up with a formula as potent as those of the right’s last two hegemonic leaders, Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher, almost half a century ago. Yet unlike them, the right’s current icons such as Trump, Nigel Farage and the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, only seem able to achieve a year or two of decisive political momentum at a time, and even then never manage to shed their deep unpopularity.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

With national elections looming in two important countries where the populist right is currently strong – France and Spain – it’s possible the movement will finally start reshaping societies for the long term. But even if the populists get into office, it feels more likely that their governments will quickly become incoherent and intensely disliked, as Trump’s has. Scapegoating migrants, “woke” elites and minorities can be an effective campaign strategy, but doesn’t solve a country’s cost of living problems.

The modern overestimation of the right also has consequences for left-leaning governments. It can make them too cautious, as if they are impostors who believe that society’s natural rightwing rulers will soon replace them.

So far, Andy Burnham has largely avoided this psychological trap, clearly relishing being prime minister, referring to Reform and the Tories strikingly little in his speeches, and ambitiously promising a 10-year plan, to be revealed next month. However, in some of his policies, such as on immigration and prisons, a deference towards the populist right and its worldview can still be discerned.

Successful centre-left politicians, from Blair to Bill Clinton to Burnham, have always argued that their illiberal moves are responses to voters’ concerns. But where do those concerns come from? Often, from the right’s fear-mongering about modern life, its exaggerations about migrant invasions and the extent of crime. This dystopianism needs to be called out by conservatism’s opponents, and the association of the right with realism – social, economic or electoral – needs to be broken, or at least weakened. After years of failed rightwing governments all over the world, it’s well past time.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist
