As housing protests sweep Portugal, police and politicians here seem bent on making the crisis worse

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 05:00:11 GMT

While Spain, Germany and the UK have all introduced laws protecting renters’ rights, Luís Montenegro’s centre-right government is empowering landlords

As Storm Charles reached Portugal’s shores this week, flights were aborted, schools were closed, and the global Web Summit in Lisbon was forced to cancel a whole day of lucrative events. But even the promise of some very bad weather was not enough to deter housing protesters from setting up camp for another night on the streets.

Since 14 October, echoing recent eruptions over housing in Spain, and the fierce student-led protests in France, Lisbon and Porto have become the focus for encampments and daily protests drawing people in their thousands. Almost one month later, they show no sign of disappearing.

The breadth of these demonstrations is as wide as the housing crisis that has provoked them. At the protests you might find architects, waiting staff, high school graduates, philosophers, young mothers, professional politicians, projectionists, security guards, graphic designers and master’s students. I met thirtysomething professionals still living with their parents, separated couples having to sleep under the same roof, and families torn between cramped living conditions in the city and moving far away from their jobs, schools and communities.

On the days I spent at the protest camps, the mood was both animated and serious. There was a “people’s university”, a canteen serving free meals and people dropping by after work, university or school. A number of discrete social and housing movements from both cities have joined together. Some have come out to protest against their appalling living conditions, others are fighting eviction orders, and many more have found it impossible to move on with their lives because they can’t move home. In Paris they burned cars, while in Barcelona they built barricades; in Portugal, the most provocative act of the encampment was a giant spooning sleepover. There were also clowns, a dedicated group of supportive “camp mothers”, singalongs, and performances from pop singers Mayra Andrade and Ana Moura.

The government’s responses have only made matters worse, ranging from the farcical to the outright repressive. Prime minister Luís Montenegro called the demonstrations “selfish”, and suggested they were a “foreign import”. Protesters have noted that he owns at least six properties across Portugal, as well as extensive land. Lisbon’s mayor, Carlos Moedas, complained about the impact protests would have on an upcoming German-style Christmas market. Meanwhile, the police reaction has been shocking and aggressive, with Lisbon’s police attacking peaceful protesters while they were sleeping.

According to the Público newspaper more than 160 people have been injured – including some who were shot in the face with rubber bullets – and 99 arrested in Lisbon and Porto. Videos show police actively attacking protesters as they flee. The police brutality and impunity has provoked an outcry. More than 200 lawyers have signed a letter alleging disproportionate force and illegal measures, and demanding an inquiry. Amnesty International issued a statement accusing the police of “beatings and excessive force … causing physical harm and hospitalisations. This response is a choice. It can – and must – be stopped by the Portuguese authorities.”

Why, then, is the government going to such lengths to avoid addressing what is one of Europe’s very worst housing crises? Access to decent, affordable housing has long been an issue that has afflicted low income – and, in particular, racialised – communities in Portugal; but it has become something that now affects even the professional middle classes.

The numbers are so extreme, they seem impossible to ignore. Since 2015, house prices nationwide have increased by 169%; in Porto, that figure rises to 180%; in Lisbon, it is 186%. Meanwhile, wage growth has failed to keep pace. Portugal has the highest discrepancy in the entire EU between house price and income.

This state of crisis did not arrive overnight. The deregulation of Portugal’s housing market was set in motion following the 2011 bailout administered by the Troika (the European Commission, European Central Bank and International Monetary Fund) in the aftermath of a national financial crisis. The bailout conditions restricted government spending and borrowing, prompting the centre-right government at the time to seek new sources of private and foreign capital, making urban development increasingly dependent on private investment rather than public funding. It was also during this period that rental laws were relaxed to favour landlords, stoking a profit-driven rental market. Since then, huge swathes of land and property have become the target of speculation.

A recent tourist boom has further inflated the profits being generated by property in Portugal. Tourism has become a significant driver of economic growth, but it has come at a different kind of cost. In Lisbon and Porto, the proliferation of short-term lets from sites like Airbnb has pushed rents and property prices up across dozens of neighbourhoods, forcing communities out as a consequence.

Demonstrations about housing in Portugal have become increasingly frequent over the past five years, but have fallen on deaf ears. And while Spain, Germany and the UK have all recently implemented laws to protect renters’ rights, Portugal’s centre-right government is now introducing legislation to give greater powers to landlords to raise rents, demand larger deposits and evict tenants more quickly.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Since the protests began, Montenegro has made no signs of considering any concessions. His apparent public indifference has been accompanied by a series of attempts by elected officials to discredit and criminalise protesters. Moedas claimed that cleaning graffiti on Rossio square had cost the disputed sum of €138,000 (£115,000). Meanwhile, the police have been dreaming up some creative new means of repression; on 1 November they announced they would fine motorists €60 for tooting their horns in support of protesters – though they were forced to withdraw the measure within 24 hours.

The response of Montenegro’s government can be understood in the context of Portugal’s current political tensions. Facing a serious challenge from the far-right Chega party, Montenegro’s Social Democratic party – a rightwing party, perhaps contrary to its name – is attempting to bring voters onboard through aggressive rhetoric around public policing and immigration.

These bullying tactics are reminiscent of Portugal’s recent past. The chants frequently aimed at the police over the past month – “It reeks of dictatorship” (“Cheira a ditadura”), or “we are all anti-fascists” (“Somo todos anti-fascistas”) – serve as a reminder that the country’s long imperial dictatorship (1926-1974) is still in living memory. But so is the spirit of resistance that eventually brought it crashing down.

The Portuguese housing crisis isn’t going anywhere without radical interventions. The protesters in Portugal’s streets deserve more just and dignified solutions than to be ignored by politicians and beaten by police.

Ana Naomi de Sousa is a documentary film-maker and journalist

Why New England’s Republican Governors Withstood the Blue Wave

The New York Times November 12, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The low-key approach modeled by Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont and Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire may gain new relevance as their party looks to recover from a national drubbing.

By Jenna Russell

Reporting from Brattleboro, Vt.

Peter Gallagher, a voter in liberal Townshend, Vt., filled in the ovals for Democrat after Democrat at the polls last Tuesday. But when it came to the race for governor, Mr. Gallagher, 67, made a notable exception: He voted for the Republican incumbent, Gov. Phil Scott.

So did Joanne Davis of Putney, who said she appreciated Mr. Scott’s low-key persona: “He’s a normal person. Not crazy, not scary.”

Vermont voters helped drive the blue wave that stunned the country, casting out two dozen Republicans from the state Legislature and replacing them with Democrats, who regained supermajorities in both chambers. But enough also stuck by Mr. Scott, a soft-spoken moderate, to deliver him a record sixth term, in a state that favored Vice President Kamala Harris over President Trump in 2024 by one of the widest margins in the country.

Mr. Scott’s success in a liberal New England state — and the success of Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who was re-elected last week in neighboring New Hampshire — offer a glimmer of hope for a party freshly battered by rejection. In different ways, the two governors have survived by leaning into an old-school strain of Republicanism, melding fiscal pragmatism with a moderate approach on social issues. Mr. Scott, in particular, has also explicitly separated himself from President Trump.

“He’s the only Republican I’ve ever voted for,” Mr. Gallagher said of Mr. Scott as he loaded groceries into his car outside a supermarket in Brattleboro, Vt., last week. “I like the way he crosses the aisle and works with people — that’s the biggest thing.”

Both governors fit a prototype with deep roots in New England, a region better known for liberalism. In Massachusetts, voters have frequently sought to keep liberal legislators in check by electing moderate Republican governors like William Weld and Charlie Baker.

New Hampshire was long known for a “leave-us-alone type of Republican, with a kind of libertarian flavor to it, and a focus on the small footprint of government,” said Dante Scala, a professor of political science at the University of New Hampshire.

As the national Republican Party shifted toward a new model over the last half century, courting socially conservative and religious voters, the influence of New England’s fiscal conservatives waned, he said. Now, the moderate, compromise-seeking approach modeled by Mr. Scott and Ms. Ayotte may gain new national relevance.

Ms. Ayotte, who was first elected governor in 2024, appears to have endured in part by showing restraint on social issues that Republicans elsewhere have gone to battle over. She vetoed legislation this year that would have rolled back discrimination protections for transgender people. And she has kept a campaign promise to leave New Hampshire’s relatively permissive abortion laws alone.

“She said she would put those issues on the back burner as governor, and she has done that,” Dr. Scala said. “It’s a key question for the Republican Party, whether they continue to put culture wars and social issues at the center of the party’s future identity.”

Both Ms. Ayotte and Mr. Scott faced serious challenges this year from Democrats whose campaigns gained unexpected momentum as the national mood turned against incumbents. Ms. Ayotte won, 51 to 47 percent, after hammering her opponent, Cinde Warmington, for her brief stint as a pharmaceutical lobbyist. In Vermont, Mr. Scott won, 52 to 46 percent, — the closest race of the six he has run for governor, against Amanda Janoo, a progressive Democrat.

New Hampshire and Vermont are the only states in the country where governors’ terms are two years instead of four.

Ms Janoo, in her first run for office, won 71 percent of votes in the state’s largest city, Burlington. One of her main proposals was to raise taxes on Vermont’s highest earners to help pay for universal primary health care. Mr. Scott, who called for cutting taxes, won by a similarly wide margin in the state’s traditional Republican strongholds: its rural western edge and towns along its remote northern border.

Ms. Janoo, whose background is in economics, argued that Mr. Scott’s trickle-down model had failed to deliver on affordability, and proposed that the state instead “build its economy from the bottom up” rather than relying on outside investors.

But even some Vermont voters who longed for change gravitated back to the familiar instead. Michelle Mortimer, a registered nurse and small business owner from Williamsville, felt that Mr. Scott had served long enough. She watched three debates, hoping to be persuaded that Ms. Janoo had a solid plan to rein in health care costs.

“I was begging her to say something to make me vote for her, but she had nothing concrete,” said Ms. Mortimer, 56, who ended up voting for Mr. Scott. “Her answers were soft and squishy.”

Mr. Scott was also helped by voters like Anne Wheeler, 44, of Putney, who until last week had never voted for him. Ms. Wheeler, who works in a factory doing quality control, said she voted for Mr. Scott out of frustration with the state’s high cost of living. She increasingly believes that “progressive liberals are hurting, not helping, Vermont.”

“Vermont is only for the rich or poor,” she said outside the grocery store in Brattleboro. “There are no jobs or housing for the working class. It’s getting harder and harder to stay here — I don’t want to work two or three jobs to survive.”

Mr. Scott has long talked about affordability, and he blamed rising taxes on the Democrat-controlled legislature. Voters rebelled two years ago, ousting two dozen Democrats in the wake of a staggering property tax increase. Last week, they reinstated many of the same Democrats.

The governor’s bipartisan appeal dates to his early days in state government, said Paul Dame, chairman of the Vermont Republican Party. Mr. Scott was elected lieutenant governor in 2010, and served under Gov. Peter Shumlin, a Democrat.

His understated manner, and roots in blue-collar Barre, made Mr. Scott a natural choice for working-class voters. So did his weekend passion for stock car racing and his winning record at the Thunder Road racetrack in Barre.

“While the Democratic Party was becoming more elite, he was connecting with working-class Democrats and building that coalition,” said Mr. Dame.

Mr. Scott also let it be known that he voted for President Biden in 2020 and for Ms. Harris in 2024. But he did so without drama. “He doesn’t go on cable news shows,” said Jason Maulucci, his policy director and campaign manager. “He doesn’t go out of his way to antagonize or attack. People in Vermont value that.”

(Mr. Scott did not commit to an interview for this article; Ms. Ayotte did not respond to requests for comment.)

Mr. Scott’s brand — unflashy dependability — is not exciting. But he leaned into his image as “Governor Dad,” as some have called him, during the campaign, warning voters that the last two years of the Trump administration would be “incredibly chaotic” and asking them: “Who do you want at the wheel?”

Even as she made the case for change, Ms. Janoo recognized the tempting solace of the status quo.

“I think we’re all pretty traumatized,” she said on Wednesday. “In that context, I understand holding onto what feels secure.”

Jenna Russell is the lead reporter covering New England for The Times. She is based near Boston.

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Search and rescue operations were continuing after the riverboat, which was docked and had 129 people aboard, was struck by a cargo ship on Friday afternoon, the authorities said.

By Rebecca Chao and Ishani Desai

Search and rescue efforts were underway in New Orleans after a cargo ship struck a docked riverboat with nearly 130 people on board on Friday afternoon, the authorities said.

An asphalt tanker crashed into the riverboat, the American Heritage, around 12:30 p. m. on Friday, Kimberly Curth, a spokeswoman for the Port of New Orleans, said in a statement.

The riverboat had been docked for two hours on the Mississippi River outside of 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, Ms. Curth said, and was just beginning to unload passengers.

After the boat was struck, those on board were brought inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triaging.

Local news video showed a capsized boat leaning against a dock.

A representative for the City of New Orleans said in a statement that search and rescue efforts were ongoing, and that multiple individuals had been rescued.

It was not immediately clear how many people had been rescued or their conditions.

“We are in close coordination with the U. S. Coast Guard and local authorities,” a spokeswoman for American Cruise Lines, which operates the boat, said in a statement. “Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved. We will share more information as it becomes available.”

Gov. Jeff Landry said on social media that his office was aware of the crash and that he was headed to New Orleans.

The American Heritage can accommodate up to 150 guests, according to American Cruise Lines. It has a glass-enclosed restaurant, guest lounges and a fitness center.

“Public safety agencies are coordinating response efforts, with the immediate priority being the safety and rescue of those involved,” the New Orleans statement said. “This remains an active and developing incident.”

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U. S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel are on scene, officials said.

This is a breaking news story. Check back for more developments.

Jeffries Leaves Nothing to Chance in Push to Lock Down Speakership

The New York Times November 13, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Facing resistance from the left but no challenger, the Democratic leader is sewing up support from key coalitions as his allies say he deserves a unanimous vote.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from the Capitol

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, is pressing to wrap up his nomination to be speaker next week quickly and overwhelmingly, leaving potential detractors little room to maneuver around him even as some of them complain about an undemocratic process.

His allies this week began asking Democrats to sign a letter publicly signaling their backing for Mr. Jeffries ahead of the House Democrats’ closed-door leadership elections on Wednesday. Some of them think he deserves to be elected unanimously during that session, bypassing a vote by secret ballot that would give any dissenters a chance to register opposition. It would be a show of overwhelming unity and support, although Mr. Jeffries has not yet indicated whether he is seeking it.

But his allies are soliciting group endorsements to lock in backing from large factions, effectively shutting down any conversation about other options in an implicit sign that his nomination is inevitable. The New Democrat Coalition, a group of 114 center-left House Democrats and at least 40 members-elect, issued one such statement in support of Mr. Jeffries this week.

Mr. Jeffries has been meeting privately both with incumbents and new members to make his case, although he has yet to reach out to every newly elected member of the House. He is set next week to attend the Congressional Progressive Caucus board meeting, according to two people familiar with the plans, and his goal is to be in direct contact with every member by Wednesday.

The quiet campaign comes as Mr. Jeffries, in line to be the first Black speaker after presiding over sweeping Democratic victories and winning a historic majority, is facing some resistance from an energized left clamoring for a new face at the helm of the party for the new Congress. No one has stepped forward to challenge him.

But several Democrats elected last week would not commit during their campaigns to backing Mr. Jeffries for speaker. And many members are receiving an influx of calls and emails from progressives who say they are fed up with the Democratic Party establishment and see the leader, a reserved moderate, as an avatar of the status quo who is beholden to corporate interests.

Mr. Jeffries has publicly shrugged off the dissent — “You think I don’t have the votes nailed down?” he told a reporter this week, flashing a smile — but said that he takes “nothing for granted” and that part of the process was laying out “our vision for the future.”

At the same time, his allies are privately working to ensure any lingering resistance to Mr. Jeffries cannot derail him.

“There is an accurate sense of confidence that the votes are overwhelmingly there, but there’s an active whip operation underway to take no chances,” said Representative Jared Huffman, a progressive California Democrat who is part of Mr. Jeffries’s whip operation. He and other supporters of the leader are reaching out to each other and to other Democrats and “making sure this thing is airtight,” he added.

The push has alienated some incoming members who are openly chafing at what they view as an unfair process meant to engineer a predetermined outcome.

Representative-elect Don Leonard of Ohio has said he wants votes on ending U. S. aid to Israel and a constitutional amendment to overturn the Citizens United ruling that struck down limits on spending in politics. He said his first hours in Washington were an introduction to the hardball tactics.

In a video he posted online, Mr. Leonard said that unnamed “senior House Democrats” had threatened to make his life a “living hell” if he did not support Mr. Jeffries for speaker.

“We kind of knew this stuff was coming,” Mr. Leonard said in his video. “It’s a whole other thing when it’s in person, by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you but expect you to wear the team jersey and be a team player.” He later said that he had spoken with Mr. Jeffries and had expressed his concerns to him privately.

Some of Mr. Jeffries’s allies said that if new members wanted to kick off their congressional careers by opposing the first Black speaker, that was their prerogative but it would make little difference.

“Hakeem deserves it to be by acclamation,” said Representative Josh Gottheimer, Democrat of New Jersey, referring to a unanimous voice vote. “That said, if winning in places we’ve never won before and having a historic majority isn’t good enough for a few of our members, then let them vote ‘no.’”

Mr. Jeffries’s top lieutenants helping to shore up the vote said that despite some squeaky wheels, overall the process is lacking in real drama.

“I’ve been in a lot of whip organizations,” Representative Joseph D. Morelle, the New York Democrat overseeing new member orientation, said in an interview. “This is by far the easiest.”

Mr. Morelle said he had spoken to almost all of the new members and asked whether they had any concerns they wanted him to share with Mr. Jeffries. So far, he said, nobody had told him they planned to stand in the way.

That has not stopped some progressives from seeking to use the moment to press their agenda with Mr. Jeffries. Representative Pramila Jayapal, Democrat of Washington and a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said she was angling for a promise of a committee markup next year on a Medicare for All bill.

Ms. Jayapal conceded that with no one challenging Mr. Jeffries, her leverage to secure any concessions from him is minimal, but she argued he had plenty of incentives to embrace the liberal agenda.

“I’ve been explaining to people, you can’t beat somebody with nobody,” she said. “He knows he needs us, and we can be the wind behind his sails.” She would not say whether she would support Mr. Jeffries if he did not give her what she asked for.

“I’d like to believe we’re going to get a ‘yes,’” she said.

That’s an impression Mr. Jeffries has been leaving with other progressives, who said he appeared to be approaching conversations with an open mind.

Representative Delia Ramirez, Democrat of Illinois, told Drop Site News that she had met with Mr. Jeffries about bringing to the floor the Block the Bombs Act, which would withhold certain offensive weapons from Israel. She said that he did not give her a “no.”

Mr. Jeffries’s political challenge is the inverse of the one faced by his predecessor, former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, when she was working to round up the votes to be elected speaker in 2018. Back then, it was moderate Democrats who did not want to elevate the liberal congresswoman from San Francisco.

This time around, it is the progressives who are raising concerns. Mr. Jeffries has been steadfast in the face of criticism.

“Our track record of success, decisiveness and a historic victory over MAGA extremism speaks for itself,” Mr. Jeffries said in an interview last week. “There’s nothing else for anybody to say when it comes to what this House Democratic leadership team has been able to accomplish.”

Mr. Huffman, himself a senior member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said the sniping from the left has been mostly noise.

“For now, there’s this little tempest,” he said. “I will wager that you’re going to see a surprisingly small number of protest votes.”

Even the new members who have complained that they are being steamrolled have not gone so far as to say they will not vote for Mr. Jeffries.

“It has been disappointing how undemocratic this process has felt,” Representative-elect Melat Kiros, a democratic socialist from Colorado who defeated an incumbent in the primary, told CNN. “I fiercely believe in the importance of competitive elections. It feels like a lot of our class are just coming in and being told: ‘This is what the leadership is going to be.’ ”

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

Lauren Boebert, a MAGA Favorite, Loses Her Re-election Bid in Colorado

The New York Times November 13, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Boebert’s loss to Eileen Laubacher in a conservative House district represents a significant victory for Democrats.

By Bayliss Wagner and Kellen Browning

Representative Lauren Boebert, a hard-line Republican, on Friday narrowly lost her bid for re-election in a conservative Colorado district, according to The Associated Press, an outcome that showed just how deeply Democrats encroached into Republican territory this year.

Ms. Boebert, a fiery favorite of the MAGA movement, switched congressional districts a few years ago after her old seat in Colorado grew more competitive. But the change was not enough to keep her from being ousted by Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat and a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Ms. Laubacher declared victory on Monday, and was leading by more than 3,000 votes when the race was called on Friday. Ms. Boebert, who amplified President Trump’s false claims of a stolen election in 2020, has not yet conceded. Her lawyer suggested last week that Ms. Boebert would request a recount.

Democrats flooded the airwaves in the district with more than $7 million worth of ads, outspending Republicans by more than 23 to 1, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Many of the ads fixed on Ms. Boebert’s polarizing nature and past scandals, with one calling her “uniquely unfit.” Another ad contrasted Ms. Laubacher’s profile as a Navy veteran and mother of five with headlines about Ms. Boebert.

“Lauren Boebert flips out over ‘Beetlejuice’ groping footage,” the chyron read in one clip, referring to Ms. Boebert’s ejection from a Denver theater in 2023. Another showed Ms. Boebert cursing at the person filming.

“Like so many of us, Eileen is done with the extremists in both parties,” a narrator said in the ad, which was run by Ms. Laubacher’s campaign. “Maybe the best way to break through the noise is a little less talking and more listening.”

Democrats had viewed Ms. Boebert as vulnerable in the closing stretch of this year’s race, as her once-close alliance with President Trump became a liability among voters who blamed his administration for high gas prices and other affordability concerns.

Ms. Boebert, first elected in 2020, broke with Mr. Trump at times during the past year, particularly over her calls to release files related to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. And she drew the president’s anger by campaigning for Representative Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who became a nuisance for Mr. Trump.

After the election, Ms. Boebert declined to blame Mr. Trump for Republicans’ blowout losses, though she said she was “very frustrated with the war.” She told reporters this week that the Trump administration should have gone further to deport immigrants who were in the United States illegally and that Republican lawmakers “could have done a lot more.” Ms. Boebert did not respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Laubacher ran on a centrist platform but hammered Ms. Boebert for her votes against resolutions directing Mr. Trump to end the war in Iran or seek congressional approval. She also centered a promise to protect rural hospitals in the wake of Medicaid cuts.

Ms. Laubacher served in the National Security Council for two years during the Biden administration, and earlier in her career she worked as a Navy intelligence officer and served in the Navy Reserves. She was promoted to the rank of rear admiral in 2018.

“I don’t answer to a political party,” Ms. Laubacher said in a statement declaring victory on Monday. “I answer to the people of the 4th district and I’ll work with anyone and everyone, including President Trump, Republicans, and Democrats to get things done for Colorado.”

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Kellen Browning is a Times political reporter based in San Francisco.

N. Y. C. Officials Expand Collapse Inquiry as Families Demand Answers

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Building Collapse in Brooklyn

Advertisement

Supported by

The Department of Buildings has also hired an engineering firm to provide an independent report on what caused the three-story building to collapse, killing eight people.

By Claire Fahy

The outcry over a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn this week has zeroed in on possible systemic failures as city officials examined other building sites connected to the companies in charge of a neighboring construction site.

The building, at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, crashed down into a pit where construction crews were excavating next door on Wednesday afternoon. Eight people were killed, including two children, and 18 others were injured.

On Friday, at an unrelated news conference with Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the buildings commissioner said the city had hired an engineering firm to produce an independent report on what happened.

The commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, also said the city was looking into 160 building sites connected to the companies in charge of the project, without specifying which ones. Mr. Mamdani reiterated his message since the collapse that “if we find anyone that has violated the law, we will hold them fully accountable.”

At the same time, other city officials and affected families were holding their own news conference, demanding answers and accountability.

“Since Wednesday afternoon, our community has been living through a nightmare,” said Farah Louis, the City Council member representing the district where the collapse happened. Her voice cracked as she noted that children had died — cousins, ages 9 and 10 — and said that she had spoken to a man whose pregnant wife was pulled from the rubble. “It’s a painful reminder that these families lost everything,” she said.

Ms. Louis broke down in tears as the New York attorney general, Letitia James, urged her to be strong.

“Grief without accountability is not enough,” Ms. Louis continued, her voice growing stronger. “Buildings do not simply collapse without systemic failures, especially when records show a building with nearly 100 open violations sitting next to an excavation site, cited for violating a stop work order.”

The Brooklyn district attorney, Eric Gonzalez, has already said that his office was working with the Department of Buildings and the Department of Investigation on a criminal investigation.

Surveillance video footage obtained and verified by The New York Times from a business across the street shows the apartment building suddenly begin to lean before crumbling into a cloud of dust.

Julie Menin, the City Council speaker, who was at the news conference with the families, emphasized how young many of the victims were. They ranged in age from 9 to 31.

“We will ensure that their names are never forgotten,” Ms. Menin said. “We also will ensure that we strengthen the building codes, the building rules and regulations.”

Zariah Coleman, 13, who lived in an adjacent building that lost a wall in the collapse, said at the news conference that her family had long felt shakes in the building during the nearby construction.

Ms. James embraced Zariah, smoothing her hair as the girl cried. Ms. James said that she was monitoring the internet and social media for scams looking to take advantage of the situation and also called for setting up a fund to support the victims.

“The families in this community deserve answers about what led to this collapse,” Ms. James said. “I have faith that the investigators will follow the facts and that anyone found responsible will be held to account.”

Ms. James said that elected officials would support a budget increase if the department needed to hire more investigators. Ms. Menin noted that the Buildings Department had over an 8 percent vacancy rate and said the city had to make sure that those roles were filled.

“We must meet this moment,” Ms. Menin said.

Jeffery C. Mays, Maria Cramer and Kaja Andric contributed reporting.

Claire Fahy reports on New York City and the surrounding area for The Times.

Russia Revives Demand That NATO Retrench to Secure Ukraine Deal

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

The hard-line position of Russian officials in closed-door negotiations about ending the war thrusts European security into the heart of the talks.

By Anton TroianovskiAndrew E. KramerJeanna SmialekDavid E. Sanger and Eric Schmitt

Two months before Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, it issued a series of far-reaching demands, including that NATO pull its troops back to positions they held in 1997, before the Western alliance expanded toward Russia’s borders.

Now, in closed-door negotiations with President Trump’s envoys this week about how to end the war in Ukraine, the Russians have revived that stance — in some cases word for word — in an effort to attain a larger victory after five years and hundreds of thousands of deaths.

Moscow’s unyielding position was laid out in a paper that Russian officials circulated this week, according to a copy obtained by The New York Times from a person involved in the talks.

The paper, whose authenticity was confirmed by another person with knowledge of the negotiations, shows that President Vladimir V. Putin has scarcely budged on his core objectives after more than 20 months of diplomacy by the Trump administration to end the conflict.

Russia’s demands that NATO pull back forces from its eastern flank in Poland and the Baltics thrust the question of European security into the heart of the negotiations over Ukraine. And they detail the objective behind Mr. Putin’s public statements. The Russian leader has continually insisted that what he calls the “root causes” of the war — Russia’s wide-ranging grievances with both NATO and Ukraine — be addressed before he stops fighting.

The document also underscores how the economic inducements that Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have offered Mr. Putin have yet to secure concessions from Moscow. To critics, the United States risks enabling Mr. Putin’s long-running attempt to reassert a Soviet-era sphere of influence as far away as Central Asia.

Russia’s decision to stake out this expansive position comes as Mr. Putin is set to sit down with Mr. Trump next week in Shenzhen, China, at an annual meeting of the Asia-Pacific regional economies. It will be the second time the two men will have met in Mr. Trump’s second term.

The Russian document, dated Nov. 10, provides new details on the hard-line stance that the Kremlin took in this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. It was the first time since February that U. S., Russian and Ukrainian officials had all met face-to-face, and the first such session since the Trump administration mounted a new push this fall to address Russia’s demands over European security in the Ukraine negotiations.

The document represents Russia’s opening position, and Russian officials in the talks signaled that Mr. Putin could still be flexible, according to the two people involved in the talks, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the sensitive discussions.

But Russian officials in Abu Dhabi made clear that they saw the Cold War, and the Soviet-led alliance at the time known as the Warsaw Pact, as a model for how Europe could look after the war in Ukraine ends. In the decades after World War II, Europe became the focal point of confrontation between nuclear superpowers, with the threat of war hanging over the continent.

But the Russians argued in Abu Dhabi that the separate U. S. and Soviet regions of influence of that era, and the communications and understandings that went along with that arrangement, actually reduced the risk of conflict, according to people present for their remarks.

It remains to be seen how far Moscow will get with that argument.

A U. S. official said that Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner had told the Russians that much had changed since December 2021, when their country demanded a new treaty that would end most NATO military activity across much of Eastern and Central Europe.

The Americans urged the Russians to look toward the future, according to the U. S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the negotiations. Mr. Trump’s envoys, the official said, are open to new proposals from Moscow that would include concrete steps by Russia to reduce tensions.

A spokesman for Mr. Putin did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.

Mr. Trump’s envoys are now working to allay fears that they will negotiate a sweeping deal with Mr. Putin over the heads of Europe and Ukraine.

After the Abu Dhabi meeting, Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff traveled to Moscow to meet with Mr. Putin on Thursday.

There, Mr. Kushner told Mr. Putin in the on-camera portion of the meeting that Russia, Ukraine, Europe and the United States had already made progress on “long-term security” issues. But Mr. Putin later told the Americans that Russia’s 2021 proposal for a NATO pullback still reflected “our vision of the pillars of an indivisible security architecture,” Yuri Ushakov, the Russian president’s foreign policy adviser, told reporters after the meeting.

From Moscow, the U. S. envoys went to Dublin on Thursday, where they debriefed President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine. Afterward, Mr. Kushner said that “we cannot conclude this deal without Europeans being at the table.”

But the fact that Russia’s opening position on European security this week remained virtually unchanged from five years ago illustrates the scale of the challenge of finding a compromise that will get Mr. Putin to end his war.

This week’s paper spelling out Russia’s position carries no letterhead or signature — it is a “non-paper,” in diplomatic parlance, meant to lay out one side’s views unofficially. Echoing Russia’s December 2021 demands, it says NATO countries must rule out the further expansion of their alliance and as well as “any military activity” in Ukraine and elsewhere in “Eastern Europe, in the South Caucasus and in Central Asia.”

The document shows that if anything, Mr. Putin has doubled down on some of his positions. In 2021, Russia wanted NATO to drop its “nuclear sharing” arrangements that had long allowed U. S. allies in Europe to benefit from the protection of American nuclear weapons. Now, the paper shows, Russia also wants France and Britain to rule out the possibility that they would use their nuclear weapons to protect other European countries, a concept that has been actively discussed in Europe in the past year, partly because of concerns about Mr. Trump’s willingness to come to NATO’s aid.

The paper also seeks to choke off aid to Ukraine, foreseeing an end to “the supply of any type of Western weapons and military equipment and products to Ukraine.” Russia would only approve of Ukraine’s joining the European Union, it says, if Ukraine does not participate in the bloc’s common defense policy.

And, mirroring Russia’s 2021 demands ahead of the invasion, the paper says Russia wants NATO to pull back its troops and bases to the alliance’s 1997 borders, before it began to expand into Central and Eastern Europe — a step that would weaken the ability of the alliance’s most vulnerable members, such as Poland and the ex-Soviet Baltic countries of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to defend themselves.

In recent days, as word of Russia’s hard-line positions rippled out of Abu Dhabi, some European leaders were quick to reject them as nonstarters. Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland said on Thursday that “accepting Russia’s conditions would mean a direct threat to Poland’s security.”

“It is clear that they are unacceptable not only to Ukraine but, above all, to Europe, and certainly to countries such as Poland,” Mr. Tusk said in Dublin.

The talks in Abu Dhabi also included Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, the top American military commander in Europe. General Grynkewich, who is also the senior NATO commander, had a lively back-and-forth with Russian officials during the talks, pushing Russian officials to explain their concerns in Europe, according to two people in the room.

Capt. Arlo Abrahamson, a spokesman for General Grynkewich, said the general had attended the talks in his capacity as the head of U. S. European Command to provide military advice for U. S. leadership, but declined to comment given the sensitivity of the negotiations.

The revived Russian demands have come as Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner renewed their push in recent months to fulfill Mr. Trump’s promise to end the war in Ukraine. In doing so, the envoys have deepened talks about possible business deals with Russia and decided to engage with Mr. Putin’s longstanding efforts to negotiate a new European “security architecture.”

Previously, Ukraine’s supporters have said they were only willing to hold such negotiations with Russia after it ended its invasion.

But the circumstances have changed. Luc Frieden, the prime minister of Luxembourg, said in an interview that it was “natural” for the Americans to talk to the Russians and Ukrainians together.

“But they also talk about the future of Europe,” he went on. “We say, ‘Well, you cannot talk about the future of Europe without us being at the table.’”

Steven Erlanger contributed reporting.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Andrew E. Kramer is the Kyiv bureau chief for The Times, who has been covering the war in Ukraine since 2014.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U. S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Jensen Huang Lost His Job. Wall Street Lost Its Biggest Prize.

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

The ousted Nvidia chief executive was the consummate dealmaker leading the trillion-dollar A. I. build out.

By Maureen Farrell and Rob Copeland

With Jensen Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia, Wall Street has lost its most powerful and profitable dealmaker.

As Mr. Huang built Nvidia from a regional chipmaker into the world’s largest company, he dispensed with the usual careful, corporate hand-wringing. He personally directed splashy deals and complicated financing structures that pumped hundreds of billions of dollars into would-be competitors, suppliers and customers.

If that made him, in the public eye, a face of the global A. I. build out, on Wall Street he represented something else: manna. His deals produced billions of dollars in fees for banks, asset managers and advisers, and Nvidia was, up until this week, spending or promising money at a speed and magnitude of little precedence.

Now Wall Street bankers, traders and even some of Nvidia’s competitors are wondering and worrying about whether Mr. Huang’s departure will slow the breakneck pace of Nvidia’s investments.

Some say that the fundamentals of Nvidia’s power are still intact, like its extreme control of the global supply of chips, the A. I. boom’s scarcest resource, the company’s deep cash coffers and the Trump administration’s warm support for the industry’s regulatory agenda. But Mr. Huang was the leader who harnessed all of those assets into a deal-making machine.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A. I.,” said Michael Edwards, director of Forum Markets, an A. I.-focused merchant bank. “Imagine the Fed without a chairman.”

Mr. Huang’s financial footprint is stamped all over the A. I. movement.

He steered tens of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s cash into bankrolling smaller A. I. companies — including Anthropic and OpenAI, helping them boom into the two behemoths of the space.

In August, Nvidia agreed to spend as much as $105 billion to back a giant data center in Ohio that is being built by SoftBank Energy and will be leased to OpenAI. At the time, Nvidia said it would offer financial guarantees for other data centers.

Through billions of investments, it has become part-owner of data-center companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren.

Nvidia has also struck deals to buy or effectively buy smaller competitors. Late last year, it said it would spend roughly $20 billion to license the technology of the chip start-up Groq and hire its top executive. In September, the company said it would buy Hugging Face, a library of open artificial intelligence models, for $12.9 billion.

Deals like that are the lifeblood of the financial world, producing fees for bankers and lawyers who charge thousands of dollars per hour. And Nvidia was increasingly reloading to do even more; this summer, with the help of three big banks, it completed its first bond offering in five years.

In turn, Wall Street firms were so enthusiastic to ingratiate themselves with Mr. Huang and Nvidia because he could mobilize other firms to spend hundreds of billions of dollars too, or at least promise to.

In one illustrative deal, Mr. Huang rang up David M. Solomon, Goldman Sachs’ chief executive, and others, with the idea that the bank and rivals assemble a joint consortium to lend to companies in need of expensive chips. Not a dime had been raised and even some inside the companies were unaware of it when Mr. Huang nonetheless corralled the firms’ top brass in August to appear on CNBC and announce a half-trillion dollar target. Wall Street’s titans said they would do practically anything to help Mr. Huang keep the money rolling into A. I.

“This is calling all precincts” is how Apollo’s president, Jim Zelter, repeatedly described the effort during the CNBC appearance.

That financing initiative is in flux, according to three people involved in it but were not permitted to discuss the matter publicly. No loans have closed, and at least one of the six lenders that had agreed to it was on Thursday discussing dropping out, one of the people said.

That effort was signature Mr. Huang who, at seemingly every opportunity and with showmanlike style, carried the banner against technological doomerism and fatalism, arguing to continue to ratchet up the staggering pace of A. I. investment, a trend that became perhaps the singular underpinning for the stock market and broader economy.

With his trademark leather jacket, Mr. Huang consistently positioned himself and Nvidia as the industry’s model citizen and defender of A. I.’s importance to national security and America’s future.

He wasn’t shy to boast to financiers about his company’s importance. In March, after his company reported a $43 billion quarterly profit, Mr. Huang told an audience at Morgan Stanley that it was “the best quarter of earnings in the history of earnings,” and then a moment later expanded the time frame to “the history of humanity.” It was a lot of money, but not a record.

During his second administration, President Trump welcomed Mr. Huang and his policies into the White House. The two men have become close allies and used that alliance to bolster their respective agendas.

Still, not all hope has been lost on Wall Street. While Mr. Huang’s departure has prompted a sell off in Nvidia’s stock, stripping more than $1.5 trillion from its valuation, bankers and investors said that would not necessarily have negative implications for the initial public offering of the A. I. giant Anthropic still on track for next week.

Investors, optimistic market watchers said, did not sell all artificial intelligence stocks this week. Instead, they appear to be looking to diversify their A. I. investments away from Nvidia, potentially freeing up hundreds of billions of dollars to invest in Anthropic’s I. P. O.

The banks representing Anthropic on its I. P. O. are poised to generate more than $500 million in fees from its $1 trillion-plus listing.

Maureen Farrell writes about Wall Street for The Times, focusing on private equity, hedge funds and billionaires and how they influence the world of investing.

Rob Copeland is a finance reporter for The Times, writing about Wall Street and the banking industry.

Connections Coach

Now there are only two practicing members of the last active Shaker community in the United States. Sister June was 88.

Sister June Carpenter in 2014. “I am the last and the least of the community,” she said, “and I’m very happy in that position.”Credit... Sean Alonzo Harris

Supported by

By Penelope Green

Sister June Carpenter, a gentle librarian and one of three practicing members of the last active Shaker group in America, a Christian community of celibate pacifists, died on Nov. 3. She was 88.

Her death was announced by her community in a social media post that said she had been struggling with health and mobility issues, but did not provide further details.

At Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in New Gloucester, Maine, there are 18 lovely brick and clapboard buildings bounded roadside by a white picket fence, set on a lake and 1,800 acres of farmland, woods and wetlands. But there aren’t legions of Shakers in residence.

At this point, there are only two: Brother Arnold Hadd, 70, and Sister April Baxter, who joined last year and is around 60.

Reports of the group’s extinction are a constant source of irritation to them. The oft-used newspaper headline, “The Last Shaker This or That,” particularly grates.

Most inquiries from the news media are politely declined because of reporters’ tendency to focus on the dwindling population. In one instance, media coverage may have exacerbated the situation. In 2006, after The Boston Globe published a story about the community headlined “The Last Man Standing,” one of its members, Brother Wayne Smith, fell in love with the reporter and left.

Yet the public is welcome; one never knows who might be a prospective convert.

The Shaker ideology of pacifism, celibacy and communal living — and of a loving God who embraces both genders, or a Mother-Father spirit, as it is called — beckons many these days. Would-be novices are not uncommon. As Stacey Chase, the Boston Globe reporter, noted in her story, the village can receive as many as 70 inquiries a year. But not many applicants can commit.

Perhaps that is why Sabbathday Lake has such a robust community of Shaker-adjacents and friends: paid workers and volunteers who maintain the museum, help with the farm work — there are some 200 sheep and a few cows — tend to the herb garden and its harvest, offer workshops and preside over the sales of packaged herbs, teas, yarn, furniture, candles and other goodies in the gift shop and online store. Sunday services at the Meeting House are open to all, not just the members.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

A bit of history: The Shakers landed in North America in 1774 after fleeing England, where they had been persecuted for their separatist beliefs — notably their opposition to the hierarchy of the Anglican Church — and their concept of a dual-gendered God. They earned a reputation as the Shaking Quakers because of the ecstatic movements they practiced in their worship. It was a slur, but the name stuck. Those swirling dances went out of favor decades ago, though Shakers still clap and stomp a bit, as various hymns require, during the Sunday meeting.

The Sabbathday Lake community, established in 1783, was one of 11 Shaker orders in the U. S. The numbers soon swelled to 15, with some 5,000 members spread among them. In the mid-19th century, the Sabbathday Lake family, like other Shaker communities, adopted a spiritual name for itself, Chosen Land. At the time, as Jeannine Lauber wrote in “Chosen Faith, Chosen Land: The Untold Story of America’s 21st-Century Shakers” (2009), it was the smallest and poorest of all the communities. Yet it outlasted them all.

When Ms. Carpenter first visited the village in the summer of 1988, she was 49; a friend took her to the dedication of its new library. In college, she had been drawn to stories of people who had religious vocations, and she felt that she, too, wanted to give her life to God. When she learned that the community needed help cataloging its archive for the new library, she volunteered to help, and felt so at home that she asked to be considered for membership.

After Sabbathday Lake’s head curator, David Richards, interviewed her, he declared, “If the meek are to inherit the earth, she will get the whole thing!”

Sister June may have been shy, but she had a quiet, arch sense of humor and, as the announcement of her death noted, a vast knowledge of the British royal family. In addition to working as a librarian, she tended the gardens and assisted in the kitchen.

Jere DeWaters, a retired professor of photography at the University of Maine at Augusta, spent eight years at Sabbathday Lake, starting in 1986, documenting the family. He recalled Sister June’s work at the renovated library — once the village’s schoolhouse — cataloging its extensive collection of manuscripts, photographs, journals and other written material that is a treasure trove for scholars.

“She was naturally shy, but had a wonderful smile when she looked up at the camera,” Mr. DeWaters said. “Not an outgoing person at all, but she did not miss a beat. One of the quiet ones, I think the old saying goes.”

As Sister June told Ms. Lauber, “I am the last and the least of the community at the moment, and I’m very happy in that position. If I get into a position where I’m head of something, like when I was head cataloger at the library where I used to work, I feel uncomfortable and insecure. But I can cope with being little and low. It helps with the humility that we are striving for.”

The Shakers are known for their faith, their furniture and their vast hymnody: “Simple Gifts,” often referred to by its opening line, “’Tis a gift to be simple,” is one of the best-known Shaker hymns. Sister June said she related most to another one:

Great I, little i, Great I can see.

Little i is pretty i, so little I will be.

June Carpenter was born on June 15, 1938, in Boston, the only child of Florence (Blanchard) Carpenter and Sydney Carpenter, a lawyer in private practice who went on to serve in the State Legislature.

She grew up in Brookline, in a religious family. They were regulars at the Federated Church, which combines a number of Protestant denominations, including American Baptist and Congregationalist.

One day, on a trip to Boston, she recalled having a spiritual awakening as she observed the crowds. “I could see that God was within each of them,” she told Ms. Lauber. “I’ve always remembered that — that God must be inside everyone in some way, whether they realize it or not.”

The feeling faded, she said, but the insight did not: “You can’t stay on the mountaintop forever. Like the Shakers say, ‘You have to come down into the valley,’ that’s where most of life is.”

After studying library science at Simmons College (now Simmons University) in Boston, she earned a master’s degree in 1964 and then went to work as a librarian for the Brookline Public Library.

Her father had died when she was 15, and she lived with her mother until her mother’s death in 1985.

Shakers are buried without individual markers, though fellow members note the deaths in the journals they keep of their daily lives. The cemetery at Sabbathday Lake has just one gravestone. It reads simply, “Shakers.”

Sister June, with typical modesty, requested no funeral service or visiting hours.

The Shakers are one of the oldest American religious orders (though they originated in England) and one of the most progressive: They believe in pacifism, celibacy, communal living and a loving, dual-natured God, a Mother-Father spirit. Their historic village in New Gloucester, Maine is a vibrant, robust community of volunteers and paid workers helping with the farm, tending to and harvesting the herb gardens -- did you know that Shakers were the first to use paper seed packets for sale and distribution? -- as well as offering workshops and presiding over the sales of packaged herbs, teas, yarn, furniture, candles and other goodies in the gift shop and online store. Sunday services at the Meeting House are open to all, not just the members. The lifestyle beckons, and many would-be novices apply, though not all can commit. The Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village, where Sister June lived until her death, is perhaps one of the longest running, and most successful utopian experiments in this country. Have you been? Would you like to? I certainly would.

Penelope Green is a Times reporter on the Obituaries desk.

Microsoft’s Global Outage and Fixes: What We Know

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The company described “encouraging” progress on efforts to overcome a second day of disruptions to its email, messaging and other services.

By Michael Levenson

Microsoft is reporting widespread improvements to its services after a global outage took them offline on Thursday, disrupting communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world. The company, headquartered in Redmond, Wash., said on Friday that it was seeing “encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure.”

“We remain focused on addressing residual impact and ensuring reliable service restoration,” the company added.

Here’s what to know as of Friday afternoon.

Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of users, according to Downdetector, an outage-tracking site.

Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working.

Microsoft said in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A. I.” agents.

The company has yet to provide a clear answer, although it has promised to make public a full report that identifies the “root cause” of the outage.

In statements on Thursday and Friday, it provided some details.

Microsoft said on Thursday that “a portion of infrastructure” was experiencing “elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” That could mean that increased stress on its network was caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company said.

Microsoft said the servers were failing health checks — periodic, automated assessments that ensure they are functioning correctly and efficiently. It said the failed health checks “may originate from a specific component that’s responsible for processing server health.”

On Friday, Microsoft said the problem had been introduced to the system “during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.” It said it had addressed the underlying issue, allowing its tools and apps to begin to function normally again.

“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” it said. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

Luca Arnaboldi, an assistant professor of cybersecurity at the School of Computer Science at the University of Birmingham in England, said the outage was a reminder that when people use “the cloud,” they are actually relying on servers, which have finite resources.

“In this particular case, as servers became unavailable, capacity on the remaining servers increased, leaving fewer machines to handle the traffic,” he said in a statement. Even after some of the original servers came back online, he added, “the ones currently under strain now fail, creating a constant catch-up.”

Parents struggled to contact their children’s schools, some government services faltered and many office workers could not access email.

The outage affected parts of the federal government, including the U. S. House of Representatives, according to Samantha Carter, a spokeswoman for the office that oversees House operations.

“We have seen improvements to Outlook’s functionality this morning, but will continue to monitor the situation until all issues are resolved and full functionality is restored to all Microsoft applications,” Ms. Carter said in an email on Friday.

Elsewhere in the world, Britain’s National Health Service said the outage was having a “disruptive impact.” The National Pharmacy Association of Britain said the issues at the N. H. S. were making it difficult for pharmacies to communicate with doctors and some patients, which could cause delays in filling prescriptions. The Metropolitan Police in London said its online contact forms weren’t working.

In Australia, intelligence and police forces said that their operations had been affected. Singapore told taxpayers that email had been disrupted, and the Supreme Court of the Philippines and the European Court of Human Rights said the outage could cause delays in its work.

Reporting was contributed by Isabella Kwai, Karla Adam and Adeel Hassan.

Michael Levenson covers breaking news for The Times from New York.

Reflecting on 2024, Joe Biden Finds No Faults of His Own

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Nonfiction

The former president’s new memoir trumpets his achievements while justifying his decision to run for a second term and his embrace of Israel’s war in Gaza.

By Jennifer Szalai

When you purchase an independently reviewed book through our site, we earn an affiliate commission.

PROMISE ME, AMERICA, by Joe Biden

Joe Biden wants you to know that he is proud of himself — and if his new memoir is any indication, he thinks everyone else should be proud of him, too. “Promise Me, America” begins with soaring declarations about the “long sweep of history” and the “fundamental goodness” of the United States, before turning into a minutely detailed account of his presidential accomplishments. The result reads like a mix of cover letter and campaign speech — one that’s more than 400 pages long.

Save to your reading list:

It didn’t have to be this way. The post-presidential memoir is an uneven genre; to engage in sustained reflection requires some humility, a quality for which former presidents aren’t typically known. And Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, can legitimately lay claim to a raft of domestic policy feats at an extraordinarily difficult time. Pandemic relief, infrastructure, clean energy, semiconductor manufacturing: He understandably wants to chronicle the hard work behind these achievements, and more.

But enumerating the wins is easy. The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not. He is so preoccupied with burnishing his legacy that he gets awkward and defensive when addressing the two issues many readers will be most curious about: his handling of the war in Gaza, and his decision to run for a second term.

From the first chapter, “History Comes Knocking,” the book runs on two tracks: steady pragmatism and accelerating grandiosity. Biden takes pains to show how, as a 78-year-old commander in chief, he assembled a “great team,” and he is plenty willing to give credit where credit is due. He makes sure to name-check his staffers, dedicating entire paragraphs to simply listing the people who traveled with him or attended a meeting. Such compilations are generous, if narratively fatal. It’s hard to sustain momentum amid a blizzard of names.

Not that the book’s trajectory is ever in doubt. It begins on Jan. 6, 2021, when Trump supporters stormed the Capitol. (Biden unhesitatingly calls the event an “insurrection” that “should follow” Donald Trump “to his grave.”) It ends with Trump back in power. When announcing his run for a second term, Biden says, he chose to emphasize that his opponent was a threat to democracy: “He said he’d be a dictator on Day 1. He was planning to invoke the Insurrection Act, which would allow him to deploy troops on the streets of America. He was calling those who opposed him ‘vermin.’ He talked about the ‘blood' of America as being ‘poisoned,’ echoing the language used in Nazi Germany.”

Why, then, did Trump win?

Biden has his ideas. His own policies, he argues, couldn’t have had anything to do with it. (Regarding Kamala Harris, he “was proud of her and the campaign she ran.”) “We had accomplished so much,” he says. He decided to run again because he “wanted to finish the job.” In addition to describing his legislative victories, the book includes an appendix to hammer this point home. “Laws Signed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr.” lists a “selection” of the “more than 600 bills” he signed into law.

As for his age and his health, he repeatedly contends that these weren’t a problem either. He believes that Americans supported him, casting a primary win in New Hampshire as “a resounding vote of confidence.” Instead, he blames “the press and pundits” for pushing a “narrative” and “salivating” at the prospect of his humiliation. “Yes, people could point to moments when I mixed up names or lost my train of thought or had a weak voice or walked slowly,” he writes, grudgingly. “But they could never point to something presidential that I failed to do.”

Reminiscing about his victory in 2020, Biden complains about increased scrutiny: “Now it was four years later, and the noise about my age had grown louder” — as if he hadn’t also grown four years older. Even he cannot wholly disavow his abysmal debate performance against Trump in 2024, and so he shrugs it off as no big deal.

“Lots of presidents had bad debates,” he says, pointing to Barack Obama’s first debate against Mitt Romney. “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me.”

The sulking at the end of that quote is telling. Biden’s voice gets passive; he portrays himself as the helpless victim of events. He gets similarly defensive when recounting the war in Gaza. “I repeatedly sought to restrain the Israelis,” he says, citing multiple instances when he gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a stern talking-to amid the escalating Palestinian death toll. Reassessing America’s unconditional military aid to Israel was apparently out of the question. Biden offers no explanation why, other than to say that he had “always felt an affinity” for the country.

“Too many innocent Palestinians were killed,” Biden allows. “Too much pain was inflicted on people with no connection to Hamas. Too little food and water and medicine and fuel got into Gaza for too long.” Again, note the passive voice. In the same chapter, titled “October 7,” he writes with moving specificity about the suffering of Israeli civilians, referring to several by name. When writing about Palestinian civilians, however, he includes no names, and depicts their suffering in only the most general terms, calling their plight “a tragedy.”

Biden maintains he would have “prevailed” at the 2024 Democratic National Convention. He says he eventually relented to pressure and bowed out of the race for the sake of “party unity.”

In May 2025, he learned he had Stage 4 prostate cancer. He mentions this in his epilogue, though he says nothing about how such a development could have affected him and presumably the country had he gotten his way and been granted another go as president. You have to marvel at such formidable powers of compartmentalization: Biden still wants us to know that he could have won.

PROMISE ME, AMERICA | By Joe Biden | Little, Brown | 465 pp. | $42

Jennifer Szalai is the nonfiction book critic for The Times.

Wall Street Braces for Anthropic’s Aggressive Spending

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The company’s financial picture may get murky as it deals with employee stock compensation and the growing costs of artificial intelligence.

By Cory Weinberg

Reporting from San Francisco

Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, introduced his artificial intelligence company to potential stock market investors this week with a sublime vision. He predicted the end of cancer and mental illness within a decade, and a transformation of cognitive work. “If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles,” he said in a marketing video for Anthropic’s initial public offering.

Wall Street is grappling with how much it may cost to get to utopia.

Stock analysts at Goldman Sachs, the investment bank leading Anthropic’s I. P. O., have told investors privately this week that they forecast the company will burn through more than $65 billion next year, and another $41 billion in 2028, said two people familiar with those discussions. Those totals would make Anthropic’s spending among the most aggressive corporate bets on funding the giant A. I. infrastructure build-out.

“We are in aggressive investment mode,” Krishna Rao, Anthropic’s chief financial officer, said in the video, without discussing specific spending forecasts.

That spending would create a drastically different financial picture than Anthropic has shown recently. The company generated cash from its business in the first nine months of this year, its I. P. O. prospectus shows, a feat in the expensive business of A. I. model development. It has barely spent the $141 billion it raised privately from investors.

The listing on Nasdaq, expected next Thursday, could value Anthropic at $1.4 trillion. It would not only cement its status as one of the world’s most prominent companies but hand it additional firepower to help it pull further ahead of well-heeled rivals like OpenAI and Alphabet. The I. P. O. would deliver Anthropic an additional $100 billion to spend, and make it easier to raise even more money to fund those huge commitments.

But Anthropic’s public debut will lead to costs that don’t appear today. It said in the prospectus it anticipated about $40 billion of expenses in the coming years tied to preexisting stock grants it has given employees that haven’t yet hit its accounting books.

The company’s investor prospectus pegged the size of the future bill that Anthropic has run up for chips, power and other computing infrastructure to help it develop more advanced A. I. models at $900 billion over the next two decades.

Stock pickers and analysts said the prospectus is missing more granular details about the spending, like how much is going toward A. I. training and research, serving customers and the company’s own internal uses of its A. I. service Claude.

“There’s definitely a desire to keep the focus on the massive, broad huge opportunity ahead of us, rather than go into the specifics,” said Ashley MacNeill, managing director at the private equity firm Vista Equity Partners.

Ms. MacNeill, a former investment banker who worked on high-profile tech I. P. O. s, added that she didn’t think Anthropic was “trying to hide the ball” but said the lack of disclosures “creates a vagueness on how they will run this company from a cost perspective going forward.”

Investors are bracing for Anthropic to run up the bill regardless. The size of the existing financial commitments the company laid out “is likely going to be meaningfully short of what Anthropic ultimately needs,” analysts at the investment bank William Blair wrote to investors this week.

The report characterized Anthropic’s pace of constantly releasing new versions of Claude as a “model treadmill.” The analysts wrote that the company’s potential valuation was attractive but added that “we empathize with investors that call out the risk of a company in a 4-year-old industry.”

Part of investors’ challenge is determining exactly what kind of business they’re signing up to support. Anthropic’s ascent has been dizzying. In one year, the company grew quarterly sales from about $1 billion, roughly the size of the dating app Tinder’s parent company Match Group, to $17 billion, the size of more-than-century-old stalwarts like Pfizer and IBM.

Anthropic executives have stressed that they have a lot more room to grow. Its focus on corporate customers, rather than consumers, has helped it leapfrog the ChatGPT maker OpenAI in sales this year. Its success has largely been thanks to heavy adoption by software developers. Next, they’re going after a wider range of white-collar employees to automate more of a variety of work tasks.

“To most workers, Claude is still just a chatbot,” Nicholas Lin, an Anthropic employee, said in an interview on Monday. The company is trying to change that. On Tuesday, it introduced new tools for people to include Claude as a participant in a work meeting or a spreadsheet.

The company will need those products to catch on. Goldman Sachs, in its private forecast to investors, predicted that Anthropic would surpass $440 billion in annual revenue by 2029, more sales than Apple generated last year. That surge would help Anthropic generate enough cash to cover its costs by that year, according to the forecast. The Financial Times earlier reported on the investment bank’s forecast.

But Anthropic’s customers aren’t locked into long-term contracts, and the vast majority of the company’s revenue is generated by versions of its A. I. models it released in the last six months, according to the prospectus.

Shivaram Rajgopal, a professor of accounting and auditing at Columbia Business School, said that could be a problem if Anthropic can’t gain enough customer loyalty and keep prices high.

In a worst-case scenario, the company could have similar business dynamics to Netflix, which has to continue spending heavily on producing shows to keep subscribers. “That’s a business model risk,” Dr. Rajgopal said. “These are slow-moving disasters.”

Anthropic, for its part, said the computing bills to develop new A. I. models will pay off. The spending, it argued, creates a reinforcing cycle that will help it keep its lead in the A. I. race, and eventually generate profits. Executives say customers have kept spending on Claude because its new model versions keep getting better, and the company can also keep costs down for customers and itself as models improve.

The company considers itself the ultimate beneficiary of its own creation, as it uses Claude to automate and speed up its model development.

Anthropic published a report last month that suggested its A. I. agents, or tools that can complete work tasks like writing code or creating spreadsheets, worked six times as many hours in a week as its human employees. “Our pace of discovery is speeding up, and a lot of that acceleration comes from Claude itself,” Sam McCandlish, an Anthropic co-founder and chief architect, said in the investor video.

Many investors weighing the deal haven’t seen Claude transform their work in the same way. “There’s an anxiousness and disconnect you see within A. I. believers and nonbelievers,” Ms. MacNeill said. “We’ve only sat with this technology for a few years.”

An earlier version of this article misstated Ashley MacNeill’s position at the private equity firm Vista Equity Partners. She is managing director, not managing partner.
