Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.

By Jeanna Smialek

Reporting from Dublin, where European leaders are meeting, and from an airfield near the city where Americans and Ukrainians debriefed on Thursday night.

European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.

Instead, they decided on six.

European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E. U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.

In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U. S. envoy, said earlier this week.

Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations, though, and that many voices must be represented.

“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.

“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

Mr. Kushner and his fellow U. S. negotiator, Steve Witkoff, pushed this week to add Europe to the talks after Russia insisted during discussions in the United Arab Emirates that postwar security in Europe be a topic of negotiation.

Russian negotiators made it clear during the talks with Ukraine and the United States that as a condition for ending the war, they want Europe to change how it protects itself. Russia has a record of pushing to pare back NATO operations near its border. European officials have rejected those suggestions, insisting that the continent, not the Kremlin, decides its security.

“I don’t want someone to talk about our European house, if they are not living in that house,” Luc Frieden, the prime minister of Luxembourg, said in an interview on Friday.

Because Europe’s fate is on the table, Europeans want a seat.

On Thursday, Mr. Kushner told reporters at an air base in Dublin, after a meeting with the Kremlin, that President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia had been asked about having European negotiators at the table and was “willing to give it a try.”

Naming negotiators could give Europe a voice in discussions about its own future, and the speed of the E. U.’s decision may avoid the appearance of discord at a high-stakes moment.

How the Ukraine war is settled could reverberate across Europe for decades — either containing the threat of Russian expansionism or emboldening it.

“Europe really needs to pay attention,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine warned dozens of leaders from across the continent who assembled in Dublin for a broader summit on Thursday.

Mr. Zelensky had pushed Europe to choose someone quickly.

Europe’s plan to join the negotiating fray comes as tensions are running high. Ukraine’s domestic intelligence service, the S. B. U., said on Friday that the country’s forces had attacked a Russian warship this week. Analysts placed the warship in the Gulf of Finland, in northern Europe.

The team is meant to balance various tensions.

Smaller nations in the European Union do not always trust the biggest ones to reflect their interests. Britain and Norway, which have a financial and security stake, are not part of the union. And eastern nations bordering Russia doubt that western ones understand the depth of the menace they face.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland said on Thursday, “Under no circumstances will we allow new security rules for this part of the world to be established over our heads, without Poland or Europe having a say.”

The grouping gets around many of those challenges: Smaller countries are represented by the E. U. institutions, Poland is there to represent nations geographically close to Russia, and Britain has a voice.

António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, has long argued that the European Union must be represented in discussions because the bloc controls a large set of sanctions against Russia, which Moscow wants rolled back. Another factor is Ukraine’s potential E. U. membership, which Kyiv wants as a security guarantee.

When Mr. Costa’s office tried in June to reopen lines of communication with Russia, though, France and Germany criticized him for overreaching.

But the chance of sitting at the table now is both more real — and more pressing.

Among other things, Europeans are nervous about America’s positioning. Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, warned on Friday that this could be another “Anchorage moment” — referring to a summit where President Trump alarmed Ukraine and its European allies with sympathy toward Russia.

Europe is hoping to insist upon a key set of values: Territorial integrity, respect for borders and respect for international law.

“If we give up those principles, I think there’s a high risk that other European countries might be attacked in the short or medium term,” Mr. Frieden from Luxembourg said. “And that would be a disaster for Europe.”

Andrew E. Kramer contributed reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

Trump Signals New Strategy on Iran: A Waiting Game

The New York Times November 13, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

The administration appears to be moving toward a long-term economic pressure campaign as President Trump expresses little urgency in securing a nuclear agreement.

By David E. Sanger

David E. Sanger has covered five American presidents, and written on the efforts to contain the Iranian nuclear program for more than two decades.

President Trump says he is leaning toward a new solution to the Iran nuclear crisis: Declare it is over, even if not much has changed.

Mr. Trump and his team have taken to asserting that they have the Iranians right where they want them. They say they no longer need a new nuclear agreement that would remove potential bomb fuel from the country, or to limit Iran’s missile capability, two of the leading reasons the president cited 10 months ago for going to war.

Mr. Trump appears — at least for now — to have rejected a series of military options that would involve intense, if time-limited, attacks on military installations, nuclear sites and even some energy infrastructure.

All the talk this year of sending in commandos to seize roughly 970 pounds of uranium from the country, enriched to a near-bomb-grade level of 60 percent purity, has been abandoned, albeit for the moment. So has the detailed analysis of whether America’s biggest bunker busters are powerful enough to get deep into Pickaxe Mountain, a site U. S. intelligence believes — but is not sure — is the location of advanced centrifuges that can purify uranium into bomb fuel.

In comments to reporters this week in Paris, where he was attending a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 7, Secretary of State Marco Rubio described an approach best characterized as strategic patience: waiting for sanctions on Iran to take their toll and ultimately crack their government.

“At this point, the economic campaign and the pressure and the devastation that our economic campaign is having on the Iranian regime is working so well that the president really doesn’t have any need to conduct major combat operations,” Mr. Rubio said.

If Iran “crosses certain red lines” the United States could intervene, he added, because it has “the most capable military in the world.”

The new approach was underscored on Thursday when Mr. Trump announced that he was redirecting Vice President JD Vance away from his efforts to engage in direct negotiations with Iran’s top security official, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and a former commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

The vice president, who has blamed the war for the widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections, had previously positioned himself to play a key role in bringing the conflict to a negotiated end.

Now Mr. Trump seems to think that a negotiation would be a waste of Mr. Vance’s time. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Mr. Trump wrote in a social media post. “Those days have long since passed.” He said it was more important for Mr. Vance to investigate cities and states run by Democrats, and to hunt down wasted federal funds.

Meanwhile, he asserted that he had all the leverage over Iran he needed. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars,” he wrote, overstating the amount of Iranian assets held by the United States and its allies, “and we’ve got their Strait!” (While estimates differ widely, there may be upward of $100 billion of Iranian funds frozen in various accounts around the world, but only $2 billion or so in the United States.)

The Strait of Hormuz, which Iran disrupted within days of the initial attack, catching the United States flat-footed, has only partially reopened. Each day is a game of cat and mouse as the U. S. Navy tries to guide oil tankers out of the strait.

Despite Mr. Trump’s claims, there are no signs that the United States is packing up and going away. The naval blockade that has prevented Iran from shipping oil remains, officials say, and there is no immediate plan to end it. That suggests a continued, large-scale military presence in the region — exactly what Mr. Trump and his allies said in the spring they wanted to avoid.

Mr. Trump’s hope seems to be that with time, Iran will seep off the front pages as a major issue, and the regime, under greater and greater economic pressure, will crack. But it may not be that simple.

“The president may be finished with Iran, but Iran isn’t finished with him,” Suzanne Maloney, an Iran expert at the Brookings Institution, said on Friday. While the Navy now has oil shipments coming out of the Persian Gulf “near prewar levels,” she noted, it comes “at high cost and considerable uncertainty about its sustainability.”

Tehran will continue to disrupt transit through the strait, rebuild its missile and drone stockpiles, and reconstitute its nuclear program. And as Iran’s economic conditions deteriorate, its leadership is likely to escalate in an effort to relieve the pressure. So the United States remains mired in a stalemate in the Gulf that is likely to intensify rather than fade away.

And there is the nagging issue of that 60 percent enriched uranium. The near-bomb-grade fuel was the No. 1 reason Mr. Trump cited when he ordered the beginning of American attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. Now he sounds unconcerned about the stockpile.

“They have nothing,” Mr. Trump said on “60 Minutes” on Sunday, when Ross Douthat pressed him about the fuel. “It’s buried under thousands of tons of rock,” he said, noting that American spy satellites are watching it.

Of course, it has been sitting under that pile of rock since June 2025, when American bombers first struck three major Iranian nuclear sites: Fordo, Natanz and Isfahan.

At the time, the president said Iran’s nuclear capacity had been “obliterated.” It was an overstatement, experts said — the material was still there, intelligence reports assessed, but the attack certainly made it hard to retrieve.

While the fuel remains exactly where it was, apparently untouched, Mr. Trump’s arguments about it have shifted to match his current needs. He has said he ordered the strike in 2025 because Iran was “two weeks from being able to make a bomb.” It was not; if the fuel had been recovered, it might be two weeks away from having that uranium boosted to bomb-grade material. Fashioning it into a warhead would have taken months or years more.

Now he says it is nothing to worry about. But Mr. Trump’s latest declaration raises the central question: If the nuclear material is not a threat, sitting exactly where it was in February, why did America go to war?

“Trump began the war thinking he would be a hero,” said Karim Sadjadpour, an Iran expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “He’s now trying to figure out how to end the war without looking like a loser.”

“He started with maximalist goals: ending Iran’s nuclear program, its missile production, its regional proxies and potentially the regime itself,” Mr. Sadjadpour added. “He now seems to be preparing for a minimalist outcome: accepting that the nuclear material is still there, as long as it’s buried under rock.”

Should Mr. Trump decide to give up and go home, he would presumably leave it to the Gulf allies, and perhaps the Europeans, to deal with what is left behind. The worry of many officials in the region is that Iran, to forestall a future attack, will decide it should find a way to produce a nuclear weapon — exactly the outcome Mr. Trump said he was determined to prevent.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

OpinionGuest Essay

Credit... Damon Winter/The New York Times

Supported by

By Michael Grunwald

Mr. Grunwald is a contributing Opinion writer. He wrote from Miami.

Democrats around the country are now asking the question weird-crime aficionados and real estate analysts have been asking for years: What is happening in Florida?

The anti-Trump stampede that trampled Republicans in blood-red bastions like Kansas, South Carolina and Texas on Nov. 3 somehow missed President Trump’s adopted state, where Republicans held on to a U. S. Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and every other statewide office. The Democratic candidate for governor, David Jolly, came just over one heartbreaking percentage point of breaking the G. O. P.’s 27-yearlock on Tallahassee.

Now the finger-pointing has begun, with Florida Democrats blaming suboptimal candidates, dubious strategies and especially the national donors who in recent years stopped investing in this former super-swing state. Florida was once the ultimate expression of America’s 50-50 politics, with eight races for governor, Senate and the presidency decided by roughly a point or less from 2000 to 2018, and frustrated Democrats believe their latest razor-thin losses prove that it can be again.

But that deep-purple Florida is gone, and it isn’t coming back anytime soon. The simple reason Democrats lost here last week is that an awful lot of Republicans have moved to Florida since the Covid pandemic, and those newcomers really like the way Republicans are running it. Gov. Ron DeSantis has remained quite popular, despite Mr. Trump’s struggles, and his vision of a “Free State of Florida” — where taxes are low, vaccines should be optional and masks are for woke losers — has become a magnet for some of the nation’s most reliable G. O. P. voters.

In 2000, when Al Gore lost the presidency to George W. Bush by a mere 537 votes in Florida, registered Democrats outnumbered Republicans here by nearly 400,000 voters, a four-point gap. But Republicans took a narrow registration lead after the pandemic in 2021, and conservative baby boomers have continued to flock here ever since. There are now 1.5 million more Republicans than Democrats, a gigantic 11-point gap, and they vote.

There’s no reason to think the trend will reverse, because a majority of Florida’s growth is happening in sprawling Republican boom towns like Lakeland, Cape Coral, Sarasota and the Villages, not already crowded Democratic urban centers like Miami and Fort Lauderdale. Of the 40 fastest-growing counties in Florida, in 2024 zero chose the Democratic nominee, Kamala Harris, over Mr. Trump. Only four voted for Mr. Jolly against the Republican candidate, Representative Byron Donalds, this year. Mr. Donalds won the new Florida, and Mr. Jolly won the old Florida.

It’s true that Mr. Jolly might have managed to win if Mr. Donalds hadn’t raised six times Mr. Jolly’s total or if the Republican state party weren’t so much better funded and better organized than its Democratic counterpart. But that’s to be expected in a red state that keeps getting redder.

Winning begets winning, and corporations and donors have poured money into the G. O. P. throughout the 27 years it’s controlled state government. Losing begets losing, and national Democrats have understandably shifted their resources to less expensive and, it turns out, more winnable states, driving even more losses and depressing morale among party volunteers.

It’s also true that Florida Democrats might have had a less disappointing night with better candidates and better strategies. Their Senate candidate, the left-wing firebrand Angie Nixon, ran a dynamic campaign that (along with Mr. Trump) helped drive solid Democratic turnout, but her membership in the Democratic Socialists of America and harsh criticism of Israel were a bad fit for a conservative state with so many socialist-hating Cuban Americans and pro-Israel Jews.

Mr. Jolly, a mild-mannered former G. O. P. congressman, had a better chance to persuade skeptical voters that he was a different kind of Democrat. But he ran on a conventional Democratic agenda, ignoring those who urged him to distance himself from his party’s brand. And Trump voters clearly saw him as a fairly generic Democrat. He performed only slightly better than Ms. Nixon did in her race, despite her radical politics. In Martin County, an upscale enclave full of the kind of moderate Republicans he used to be, he didn’t even do as well as Ms. Harris did in 2024.

Mr. Jolly also missed something important about the way Florida has changed. He complained more about Mr. DeSantis and his culture wars against rainbow-themed crosswalks and diversity, equity and inclusion than he did about Mr. Trump. When I asked Mr. Jolly about high gas prices last spring, he said he didn’t talk about it much because it wasn’t a Florida issue and he didn’t want to focus on Mr. Trump in a state that had backed the president three times.

But polls suggest Florida voters now disapprove of Mr. Trump by about 10 points, while approving of Mr. DeSantis by a similar margin. Mr. Donalds is a Trump ally who never received Mr. DeSantis’s support in the G. O. P. primary, but the most prominent pro-Donalds ads highlighted his DeSantis endorsement in the general election, warning that Mr. Jolly would undo the governor’s work.

The uncomfortable truth is that a majority of voters here appreciate the DeSantis brand of state government that doesn’t force you to conserve water or build your house outside a hurricane zone or pay a lot of taxes to support people who aren’t you. On Election Day, Floridians overwhelmingly approved a referendum to slash property taxes even though local governments warned that it would gut services; the boomers moving here were fine with that. Most of them don’t want funding to go to electric-car charging stations or racial sensitivity training or Medicaid health services for the working poor.

I wish that weren’t true. Republican rule has left Florida on an unsustainable and unaffordable path of environmental destruction, traffic congestion and political corruption. It’s been a festival of short-term gratification over long-term investment, and there are already signs that the bill is coming due. The growth machine is slowing. The insurance market is in crisis.

Companies are struggling to find skilled workers, and workers are struggling to find affordable housing. The next big hurricane could create an economic cataclysm. And a lot of the DeSantis vision is just wrong: Vaccines work, climate change is real, and weed would be legal in a truly free state.

But it’s easy to see why some Republicans now see Mr. DeSantis as a 2028 presidential nominee after they got drubbed just about everywhere except his state. He’s thrilled conservatives by severely restricting abortion, executing record numbers of inmates and cramming immigrants into a detention center in the Everglades. He didn’t impose tariffs, suppress the Epstein files or start the war in Iran; that was all the guy at Mar-a-Lago.

Maybe someday, there will be a revolt against the excesses of entrenched one-party rule in Florida, just as there was last week in Texas. Maybe loads of new cash would help Democrats turn it back into a swing state. But when they’re already winning races in typically less expensive red states like Ohio, Iowa and even Mississippi, they shouldn’t make Florida their top cash priority anytime soon.

The fact that it’s now an outlier rather than a bellwether state is actually good news for Democrats. The election showed that as goes Florida, so goes Florida. The Republican migration that’s made it redder has made the rest of America a little less red, and the popularity of Mr. DeSantis here no longer necessarily translates into popularity with mainstream America.

The really good news about Florida for Democrats is that they won’t need it to win back the White House in 2028. They have easier targets.

What surprises me most about Florida's affinity for the Republican Party is its extreme vulnerability to climate change-related impacts like accelerating sea level rise and hurricanes. You would think that the thought of aligning oneself with a political party that thinks that climate change is a hoax would be a nonstarter for Floridians.

Lifelong Democrat here. I totally disagree with this article. Dems lost the senate race because they put up a DSA candidate in a conservative state. Had they put up a centrist candidate, like Dem candidates in Mississippi and South Carolina, they would have won that seat. Byron Donaldson was way more charismatic than David Jolly. Had the Dems nominated a candidate with command-the-room presence they would have won that race. In my opinion, if the Dems field better candidates, Florida is still in play.

Michael Grunwald is a contributing Opinion writer and the author, most recently, of “We Are Eating the Earth: The Race to Fix Our Food System and Save Our Climate.”

Jensen Huang’s Leather Jacket Comes Back to Bite Him

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

Critic’s Notebook

The Nvidia founder’s signature look branded him as a maverick. Does that image read differently now?

By Jacob Gallagher

Jacob Gallagher covers men’s fashion, political style and more.

Just before Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday from Nvidia, the Silicon Valley chip juggernaut he founded three decades ago, an uncanny photo of him made the internet rounds: Huang, in what appeared to be a haute-punk Saint Laurent jacket.

It wasn’t strange to see Huang in a leather jacket. After all, rare is the public appearance where Huang doesn’t wear one. He wore one on the cover of Time in 2021 and at Nvidia’s keynote in March. In a 2016 Reddit AMA, he described himself as “the guy in the leather jacket.” (A flat descriptor that sounds as if it could be applied to a video game avatar or a cartoon character.)

But this one was well beyond his typical style: drenched in studs, with fat flapped lapels. It was also, to fashion collectors, a coveted jewel, stemming from Hedi Slimane’s tenure at the French luxury house.

Alas, it was an artifact of A. I. fakery. (Nvidia confirmed that the photo had been doctored.)

To the many gawkers who followed the chronicle of his affairs this week, the executive’s more over-the-top Billy Idol-esque leather simmered with midlife crisis energy — the clothing equivalent of a new Porsche. The studded jacket in the A. I.-generated image seemed to declare “you can’t tame me!” as his company’s stock price, and reputation, crumbled. People ate it up, even as it was debunked.

Still, the photo brought into focus how perhaps even Huang’s leather jackets — the real ones — were an indication of a man branding himself as too much of a renegade.

People who pick a signature-item outfit are often searching for a memorable shorthand to distill their broader tastes or temperament. It’s a Silicon Valley self-branding hack, much like Steve Jobs’s turtlenecks and Mark Zuckerberg’s drab-fab T-shirts.

That Huang chose a leather jacket and not, say, a blazer or windbreaker, was significant. It taps into all our cultural connotations of “go their own way” guys: Tom Cruise in “Top Gun,” Marlon Brando in “The Wild One,” Peter Fonda in “Easy Rider.” It’s a garment for a conqueror: You’re wearing another living thing’s skin, after all. It can be evocative, even a bit sexy.

Just about every profile of Huang in the past decade mentions his jackets. He could count on interviewers to ask about them, granting him an easy opportunity to talk about something other than computing power.

In a 2023 interview with HP, Huang demurred when the host described him as a “style star,” crediting, as he had before, his daughter and his wife, Lori, for dressing him like a tech-world Terminator. That styling credit was seized on by online commenters this week as evidence of Huang’s closeness with his wife of more than 40 years.

In the interview, Huang wore, of course, a leather jacket. It appears to be the same glossy Tom Ford number that Sotheby’s auction house sold for nearly $1 million this year. The house described the jacket as “a symbol for the vision at the forefront of the A. I. revolution.”

When Nvidia was on the rise, the leathers helped accentuate the idea of Huang as a maverick whose company was poised for our present A. I. boom.

This week, as details emerged about Huang’s affair with a Chinese businesswoman, and the revelation that he had a second extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, the leather jacket began to seem less rebellious than reckless.

Jacob Gallagher is a Times reporter covering fashion and style.

Silicon Valley Start-Ups Face a Future Without Jensen Huang’s Money

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Huang championed start-ups, with Nvidia holding $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July.

By Erin Griffith and Cory Weinberg

Reporting from San Francisco

For years, Jensen Huang was a frequent presence at Silicon Valley start-up events, networking with founders, judging pitch competitions and showing up at “demo” days.

The Nvidia chief executive became a godlike figure in the start-up ecosystem, not just because the industry idolized him as one of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs. Mr. Huang, 63, also made it his mission to help start-ups gain a foothold against the industry’s biggest and most powerful tech companies, providing funding and computing power.

“As many good ideas as we have, you don’t have all the world’s good ideas,” he said on the Acquired podcast in 2023.

So Mr. Huang’s abrupt resignation from Nvidia on Thursday has investors and start-up founders nervous that they have lost a powerful ally.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A. I. and all of a sudden, the Fed chairman is out,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at Theory Ventures, which funds young start-ups.

Nvidia held $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including large stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July, according to securities filings. It more than doubled its start-up investments in six months.

Perhaps more critically, Nvidia has provided start-ups and small companies with access to A. I. chips that would have been difficult for them to obtain otherwise, offering $165 billion in lease guarantees and other backstops for cloud computing to start-ups and other companies, according to securities filings. The company has a venture capital arm and a program called Inception that provides tens of thousands of start-ups with training and guidance on how to access chips and computing power.

Mr. Huang has also been the industry’s most vocal advocate for “open source” and “open weight” technology, which makes underlying A. I. technology freely available for anyone to use, which benefits start-ups. Nvidia shelled out nearly $20 billion to buy two open source-focused companies in the last year.

Mr. Huang’s departure adds more uncertainty to an already jittery market. Investors fear A. I. is in a bubble that could burst. And the tech industry also faces potential regulation and a slowdown in data center construction ushered in by the results of the midterm elections. Nvidia controls the vast majority of the world’s market for the computer chips that A. I. companies need to build and service their technology.

The change in leadership could make it more difficult for smaller companies to access the chips and cloud computing power they need to compete against well-funded tech giants like Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft. More practically, it throws a number of investment deals Nvidia has in the works into limbo.

Mike Volpi, an investor at Hanabi Capital, a venture capital firm that backs A. I. companies, said he expected Nvidia to take a more conservative approach to backstopping so many smaller cloud companies.

“My expectation is that we will see some turbulence and some of Nvidia funds coming out of the market in the short term,” he said.

The A. I. industry relies so much on Nvidia that commentators have started to caution against the risks.

Speaking to a standing-room-only audience of software developers in San Francisco last month before Mr. Huang came under fire, Dylan Patel, who runs SemiAnalysis, an A. I. research firm, warned that struggling young data center companies were having no problem securing revenue guarantees from Nvidia. That allowed the companies to then take on debt they otherwise wouldn’t have gotten.

“This is sort of a quite a risky proposition,” Mr. Patel said. “We’ll see what ends up happening there.”

Mr. Huang’s pro-start-up stance has delivered cash windfalls to venture capital investors over the past year, especially with Nvidia’s purchases of start-ups. The company bought the technology and hired employees from chipmaker Groq for roughly $20 billion last December and the A. I. open-source platform Hugging Face for about $14 billion in September.

“Jensen Huang, we have yet to meet, but bravo!” Joseph T. Hasselmann, a start-up investor who backed Groq, wrote on LinkedIn after the deal was announced.

Samantha Lau, who manages a tech stock portfolio at AllianceBernstein, an investment firm, said Mr. Huang’s exit would probably eliminate a key source of financing for companies like the young data center firms that have been planning public offerings, and dampen overall market enthusiasm.

“The god of circular financing is going into hibernation,” she said, referring to the A. I. industry’s many interconnected deals.

Sujay Jaswa, a partner at Wndr, a venture capital firm that has hosted Mr. Huang as its events, compared his resignation to the death of Steve Jobs.

“It’s a gigantic loss for all of us,” he said.

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Dario Amodei, the company’s chief executive, publicly frets about the dangers of artificial intelligence and has made enemies of his peers along the way.

Credit... Timo Lenzen

Supported by

By Kalley HuangMike Isaac and Cecilia Kang

Kalley Huang and Mike Isaac reported from San Francisco, and Cecilia Kang from Washington.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, was becoming a nuisance for his fellow technology industry executives.

Anthropic and OpenAI, the leading artificial intelligence companies, were lobbying the White House to prevent some A. I. models from being developed and widely shared because, they argued, they were too dangerous. But companies like Nvidia and Microsoft saw those A. I. models as a big business opportunity.

At the end of July, Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft, and Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, intervened. They emailed each other drafts of a letter saying those A. I. models should remain open, according to four people familiar with the discussions. When they asked other technology executives whether they’d like to sign on, two dozen companies quickly agreed before the letter became public. Over the next week, 200 more companies — including a chastened OpenAI — signed onto the letter.

Dr. Amodei refused.

Dr. Amodei has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A. I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A. I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A. I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever later this month.

Along the way, Anthropic — which has cultivated an image as a company that tries to do the right thing — has also gained a reputation for playing hardball with customers and competitors. It has cut some off from its service and lobbied against other companies’s free alternatives to its A. I.

Over the last year, other technology companies and investors have organized to push back, according to more than 20 people in the technology industry, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve their relationships with Anthropic.

They have tried to show a united front to counter Dr. Amodei’s warnings about A. I. They have leaned on their ties to President Trump to keep regulators away. They have publicly complained about Anthropic’s business practices. They have even spoken with another Anthropic executive about Dr. Amodei scaring people with his rhetoric.

But the message on A. I. safety from Dr. Amodei, who appears unbothered by criticism from other executives, is breaking through. A. I. agents going rogue and attacking websites have become increasingly common. And in the midterm elections, the threat of job losses from A. I. and data center construction were significant issues for voters in both parties.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Anthropic started with a split. In 2020, a group of OpenAI employees led by Dr. Amodei left the company amid disagreements over how to safely develop A. I. Those employees founded Anthropic in San Francisco the next year.

Its founders’ ties to effective altruism — a philosophy where donors try to measure and maximize the benefits of their philanthropy — created a foundation for the company, particularly its approach to A. I. safety.

But Anthropic played second fiddle to OpenAI, which made everyday use of A. I. tools mainstream with the release of ChatGPT in 2022.

That changed in February 2025, when Anthropic surprised competitors with a preview of Claude Code, an A. I. coding tool. Software engineers started using the tool to generate computer code instead of writing it themselves. Anthropic’s revenue exploded.

Then, its critics say, Anthropic got tough with customers.

A start-up called Windsurf had talks to sell to OpenAI, and those negotiations became public in April 2025. Anthropic later cut off Windsurf’s direct access to its models, which the start-up used to power its own A. I. coding tool.

“I think it would be odd for us to be selling Claude to OpenAI,” said Jared Kaplan, one of Anthropic’s founders and its chief science officer, in an interview in June.

The move crippled Windsurf and potential customers went elsewhere, according to three people familiar with the discussions. Even as Windsurf’s talks with OpenAI broke down, Anthropic kept Windsurf cut off.

Windsurf struck a licensing deal with Google in July 2025. But the message was delivered to the rest of the start-up world: Their businesses were being built on Anthropic’s models, but they had to stay in the good graces of Anthropic to maintain that access.

“Somehow, in the United States, we’ve convinced ourselves that innovation should be in the hands of a few organizations,” said Manos Koukoumidis, chief executive of the A. I. start-up Oumi, in an interview.

Last February, about a year after Anthropic previewed it, Claude Code was on track to make $2.5 billion in annual revenue. In a financial filing, Anthropic disclosed overall revenue of $17 billion in its most recent fiscal quarter.

In early 2025, Dr. Amodei ruffled feathers at Nvidia by backing U. S. trade restrictions on chip sales to China. That June, Mr. Huang said he disagreed with Dr. Amodei on almost everything.

“He believes that A. I. is so scary that only they should do it,” Mr. Huang said of Dr. Amodei and Anthropic at a conference in Paris. (Mr. Huang stepped down from Nvidia on Thursday under pressure from his board of directors.)

Anthropic responded: “Dario has never claimed that ‘only Anthropic’ can build safe and powerful AI.”

But industry leaders worried about public sentiment turning sharply against A. I. and asked Anthropic to tone down the doomsday talk.

Over the summer, Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, of the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, met with Tom Brown, a co-founder of Anthropic. Anthropic was scaring the public with its predictions of extreme job loss, Mr. Andreessen and Mr. Horowitz said, and should cool it down, according to three people familiar with the discussion.

Mr. Andreessen then took out his phone, where he had pulled up one of Dr. Amodei’s television appearances. The text below Dr. Amodei’s face summarized his prediction of a white-collar blood bath and mass unemployment. Mr. Brown appeared taken aback by the confrontation.

Then, last June, Anthropic released Fable, a version of its most advanced model. The company said it would make the model less effective if it thought Fable was being used to research or develop A. I. But Anthropic wouldn’t tell a user it was degrading the performance, infuriating some researchers.

“It is a very real sign of concentration of power that businesses can make such obviously user-harmful behaviors and still lead in the market,” said Nathan Lambert, a co-founder of Trillium Labs, an open-source A. I. nonprofit, in a social media post.

Within a day, Anthropic walked back the policy. Now, if it thinks Fable is being used to research or develop A. I., it switches to a worse model, and then tells the user.

“We made the wrong trade-off,” Anthropic said at the time.

Anthropic also said it would store the data of those using its most advanced models for 30 days “to support our safety work.” In a sign of how paranoid Silicon Valley had become about Anthropic, the change stoked fears that the company could train its models on customer data, and then compete with those customers, according to four people familiar with the changes.

In September, Anthropic started allowing customers to store their data on their own cloud computing services. Danielle Cohen, a spokeswoman for the company, said it treats customer data as confidential and, by default, prohibits training on it.

At the end of July, Silicon Valley’s anger toward Anthropic peaked as Anthropic and OpenAI lobbied the White House to act against open-source A. I. models. Their campaigning came after OpenAI said its A. I. had gone rogue and hacked into other companies, including a start-up called Hugging Face.

So Mr. Huang and Mr. Nadella shared the letter supporting open-weights A. I., which make the rules that govern a model publicly available. It opened the floodgates against Anthropic, according to five people familiar with the discussions. So many companies asked to sign the letter that Microsoft set up an email address so it could accept signatures for the letter more easily. They included Amazon and Google, which are both investors in Anthropic.

OpenAI eventually signed the letter, but Dr. Amodei said he disagreed with parts of it and Anthropic didn’t sign it. He said in a blog post that all A. I. models, no matter how they are developed and shared, “should go through mandatory safety testing.” He said he believed bad actors would exploit open-weights A. I. models.

Silicon Valley’s executives continued discussing how to present a united front on safety concerns, mostly keeping Anthropic involved in those discussions. In calls and texts, executives from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI kicked around ideas, according to five people familiar with the discussions. Some had informal discussions about making a joint statement or commitment on slowing A. I. development. Others brainstormed regulatory proposals.

But in September, three days after an Anthropic employee quit over A. I. safety concerns and the issue burst into the mainstream, Dr. Amodei ran ahead of the other companies and made his own call for the industry to slow down.

About three weeks later, Dr. Amodei struck a different tone at the White House during a lunch with Mr. Trump and more than 30 other technology executives, venture capitalists and politicians.

Seated near the end of a long table, Dr. Amodei said the United States had to win in A. I., and that the technology should be built with maximum speed, according to two people familiar with the discussions.

It was, other guests thought, the opposite of what he had been telling the world.

Cade Metz contributed reporting from San Francisco.

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering Apple and the technology industry.

Mike Isaac is The Times’s Silicon Valley correspondent, based in San Francisco. He covers the world’s most consequential tech companies, and how they shape culture both online and offline.

Cecilia Kang reports on technology and regulatory policy for The Times from Washington. She has written about technology for over two decades.

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Boss Tweed used New York as a personal piggy bank. The Times brought him down, ushering in a new era of muckraking journalism.

Credit... Matt Dorfman

Supported by

By Matthew Purdy

Matthew Purdy is an editor at large for The Times and a frequent contributor to The Times Magazine.

This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

From the scrappy neighborhoods of New York arose a politician of considerable girth and charisma with an insatiable appetite for power and self-enrichment that he shamelessly sated at the public trough.

William Magear Tweed, the swaggering and grandiose Boss of Tammany Hall, 19th-century New York’s most powerful political machine, originated the now-familiar role on the American political stage: self-proclaimed champion-of-the-little-guy turned self-aggrandizing champion-of-self.

As with all transactional politicians, you got what you paid him for and the train of corruption was kept on track with more corruption — from rampant patronage to appointing friendly judges.

With New York City’s immigrant population exploding after the Civil War, the Democratic Tammany organization harnessed the power of these newcomers, turning them into citizens and then loyal voters. This electoral power allowed Tweed and his cronies to control City Hall, the police and the state capital in Albany in the late 1860s and early 1870s.

The men of Tammany were defined by a creed immortalized by their devoted foot soldier George Washington Plunkitt: “I seen my opportunities and I took ’em.”

Tweed saw opportunities everywhere. And he took them all. Far from squirreling away his slice of the public pie, he flaunted it. He adorned his shirtfront with a 10.5-carat diamond pin. His city home was lavish, his Greenwich estate sprawling. He was one of the city’s largest landowners. He had not one, but two steam-powered yachts. Not bad for a former chair and brush maker whose official job was the city commissioner of public works.

If Tweed’s wealth was showy, the mechanics of his thievery was hidden — that is, until a freak accident on a wintry night in 1871.

James Watson, Tammany’s loyal county auditor, was in his horse-drawn sleigh when an oncoming horse panicked and ran into his team. In a tangle of horses and hooves, Watson sustained a fatal stomp to the forehead.

At the time, Watson had been handling a delicate negotiation for his boss, City Comptroller Richard Connolly, whose shenanigans earned him the moniker “Slippery Dick.” A bookkeeper had surreptitiously copied Connolly’s records, which pointed to Tammany’s financial misdeeds, and had passed them in a thick envelope to a former sheriff named James O’Brien.

O’Brien was stewing over Tammany’s denying him what he saw as his share of the corruption bounty. In a bit of gentlemanly blackmail, he suggested to Tweed and others that the incriminating documents could remain secret for a price. Watson’s mission had been to strike a deal with O’Brien — to, as Tweed said later, “stop his tongue.” The errant horse hoof put an abrupt end to the negotiations. A few months later, a frustrated O’Brien showed up at The New York Times with the explosive envelope under his arm.

The July 22, 1871, edition of The New York Times rolled off the presses blaring the headline: THE SECRET ACCOUNTS.

The Times had published smaller accounts of what it called “municipal rascality” that month. But this was the first in a succession of front pages that documented the ludicrously inflated expenditures for work on city buildings.

The exposés included $1,447,999 paid for “repairs and furniture” for city armories, including over $200,000 in a single day — or a total of about $35 million today. Another $170,729 went for chairs, which The Times said could buy “17 miles of chairs.”

The Times delivered the news of corruption with a verve and voice hardly befitting the newspaper later known as The Gray Lady.

One article noted a single month’s payout of $360,751.61 to a carpenter named G. S. Miller. It said, “as G. S. Miller is the luckiest carpenter in the world, so Andrew J. Garvey is clearly the prince of plasterers. His good fortune surpasses anything recorded in the Arabian Nights.” Garvey’s two-month haul: $945,715, or a whopping $24 million in today’s dollars.

In testimony later given to city aldermen, Garvey said he originally had an agreement to kick back 15 percent of all contracts to Tweed and his cronies, “but they gradually raised it from 15 to 40, 45, and, finally, in 1867 or 1870, it was raised to 65 percent.”

The inflated city contracts ballooned the cost of constructing the municipal courthouse on Chambers Street from its budgeted estimate of about $250,000 in 1858 to its ultimate price tag of $13 million, or over $331 million today. The building, with its soaring interior rotunda and its marble and stone edifice (some sourced from a quarry partly owned by Tweed), still stands as a monument to both 19th-century civic architecture and civic rot.

Without irony or shame — or perhaps much collective memory — the old New York County courthouse that now houses the city Board of Education is mostly just called the Tweed courthouse.

But at the time, the Tweed Ring could not escape the storm touched off by The Times’s exposés. Not only were the facts explosive, the publication of leaked records was unheard-of.

The material was put in the hands of a young Scottish-born reporter named John Foord. He went on to become editor of The Times and to write dispatches from Asia, but as his 1922 Times obituary said, “The Tweed exposures were Foord’s greatest news job.”

“Nothing like it had ever appeared before in an American newspaper,” Kenneth D. Ackerman wrote in his 2005 biography, “Boss Tweed.”

The exposés appeared decades before the work of muckraking journalists of the early 20th century, such as Ida Tarbell, who investigated John D. Rockefeller and Standard Oil, or Lincoln Steffens, author of the iconic “The Shame of the Cities.”

If investigative reporting was in its infancy, corruption at all levels of government was in full bloom in the years after the Civil War. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner’s 1873 satirical novel “The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today,” coined the phrase to describe a deeply unequal system gilded by a shiny veneer of wealth accumulated by unscrupulous tycoons.

When The Times, then an avowed Republican newspaper in its 20th year of operation, took aim at Tweed and the Tammany organization, it stood largely on its own as other city newspapers were politically aligned with the regime or on its payroll. The Times’s coverage joined what had been a lonely crusade by the biting cartoonist Thomas Nast, whose drawings for Harper’s Weekly took full advantage of Tweed’s made-for-cartoons corpulence.

Nast portrayed Tweed as “our modern Falstaff,” as the sinister vote-counter at the ballot box, as a man with a moneybag for a head over the caption “The ‘Brains.’” Tweed and his cronies were depicted as fat cats feasting as the poor suffered, and as a literal ring of men, each pointing to the next with the caption: “Who stole the people’s money? T’WAS HIM.”

Nast’s cartoons got under the boss’s skin. Tweed was famously quoted saying, “I don’t care so much what the papers write about me — my constituents can’t read; but damn it, they can see pictures.”

The Times’s presentation — front pages filled with line after line of exorbitant payments presented its own kind of indelible picture, a mosaic of malfeasance.

And like Nast’s cartoons, they landed with readers. A July 29, 1871, Times special supplement entitled “How New York Is Governed: Frauds of the Tammany Democrats,” wrapping together all its revelations, sold a half-million copies, an enormous number considering the paper’s daily circulation was then around 25,000.

The paper also published a version in German, catering to the city’s second largest immigrant population. New York’s German-language press supported Tweed, perhaps because German immigrants were among those courted by Tammany in amassing loyal voters, an effort that involved fraud and vote buying. As Tweed testified later about elections: “The ballots made no result; the counters made the result.”

Tweed, like corrupt leaders before and after him, saw an independent press as a threat and turned on The Times.

The Tammany crew starved the paper of revenue from public notice advertising, doling it out to loyal papers and to their own printing company, set up to siphon more public money. They tried to seize the Times Building, claiming the property had been bought fraudulently. They tried to buy outstanding shares of the Times Company. They even arranged for loyal newspapers to print the home addresses of Times leaders — an early form of doxxing.

Throughout, George Jones, The Times’s publisher, was defiant. As The Times began unleashing some of the leaked financial records, City Comptroller Connolly met with Jones and floated a $5 million bribe in exchange for stopping publishing. “I don’t think the devil will ever make a higher bid for me than that,” Jones said.

The confrontation became legend. In 1933, Columbia Pictures made a nine-minute feature film, long buried in the Library of Congress, that depicts Tweed dispatching Connolly to bribe Jones.

“Well, everyone has his price,” said Tweed, played by Charles Coburn.

“Not George Jones,” the actor playing Connolly responds.

Indeed, when the actor playing Connolly tells the actor playing Jones that with $5 million, “Why, you could live like a prince,” the bookish publisher stands face to face with Slippery Dick and says, “I certainly could, but all the time I’d know I was nothing but a cheap crook.”

He exits, with a plunge of the dagger: “The New York Times will publish the facts.”

Back in real life, those facts triggered a 19th-century version of the future investigative dictum: Follow the money. The records gave supporting evidence to the suspicion of the fledgling reform movement that the Tweed Ring was fleecing taxpayers on a grand scale. The tide turned quickly against the machine as reformers showed how city funds were laundered through fictitious accounts to Tammany leaders.

In short order, banks declined to lend the deeply indebted city more money, and a judge — once a Tammany loyalist — froze city payments. The governor, another former Tammany supporter who saw how the winds had shifted, authorized an investigation.

Within three months, Tweed and three others were charged with fraud and embezzlement and Tweed was arrested.

The Tweed tale turned operatic. In what was surely an inside job, the comptroller’s office was burglarized and records that likely attested to Tammany crimes were burned. Tweed was tried and convicted in the very courthouse — unfinished at the time — that was the source of much of his wealth.

When an appeals court significantly reduced his conviction and punishment, Tweed’s rival, Samuel Tilden, who was then New York’s governor and a future presidential candidate, arranged for him to be immediately re-arrested on civil charges.

Tweed was granted unusual freedom at the Ludlow Street Jail and he took advantage. He escaped first to New Jersey, then Florida, Cuba and eventually Spain, where he was caught. Despite an assumed name (“John Secor”) and a disguise (wig, glasses, no beard), Spanish agents identified him using a Nast cartoon.

Tweed returned to the Ludlow Street Jail, broken, broke and sick. He tried without success to be set free in exchange for his testimony before aldermen investigating the Tweed Ring.

Tweed’s matter-of-fact acknowledgment of his crimes, memorialized in the voluminous transcript of his testimony, underscores how the outlandish can become ordinary.

On ballot manipulation: “I don’t think there is ever a fair and honest election in New York City.”

On passing legislation in Albany: “I found it was impossible to do anything there without paying for it.”

On being asked to say which city leases involved improprieties: “Well, there were illegal practices about most all of them.”

The aldermen concluded that “the city had been, during a considerable period of time, persistently robbed by an organized band of official thieves, to an extent never before equaled in municipal history.”

The Times reported Tweed’s conviction as a victory for “honest people throughout the country,” with a flowery but poignant reminder of the salving effect of justice.

“It is not the conviction of the individual which produces the general rejoicing,” the paper wrote, “but the vindication of the principles outraged by his crime, and the restoration of confidence in law and its administration, which many were induced to think were nullified in the presence of political and monied influences.”

Exploring Boss Tweed and The Times’s role in his undoing was a fascinating journey back to 19th-century New York and the roots of investigative reporting in American journalism. On the one hand, the corruption of Tweed and the “Tweed Ring” was brazen, but on the other, the seemingly invulnerable political machine collapsed like a house of cards once it was exposed.

It’s a story of great drama — purloined documents, a fatal collision between two horse-drawn carriages and an attempted bribe of an editor. It’s also a warning about the seductions of power and testament to the role of a press. And it shows what can happen if you follow the money.

5 Muscles to Strengthen as You Age

The New York Times November 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

We all know we need to strength train to move well and feel strong. But which exercises are the most important?

By Keith Mulvihill

As the years tick by, our body’s machinery starts to lose a little of its power. Muscles weaken, tendons tighten and movements that once felt effortless can become more difficult. The best way to maintain strength and mobility is through exercise, especially weight training.

But what are the most important parts to train? With more than 600 muscles in the human body, where should you focus your attention as you age?

We put that question to physical therapy and rehabilitation experts and asked them which muscles you should prioritize as you get older.

The most important muscles for aging are the ones that drive us through everyday movements, like getting out of bed and climbing stairs. Asked to pick one muscle group, experts said glutes were probably the most important, because they keep your pelvis level when you walk and help recover your balance when you stumble, particularly when you need to step sideways.

“I come at this as a physical therapist and somebody who specializes in fall prevention, so that’s what I’m thinking about,” said Odessa Addison, a professor of physical therapy and rehabilitation science at the University of Maryland School of Medicine.

Most people who exercise regularly are familiar with the largest of the gluteal muscles, the gluteus maximus, and target it with classic movements like squats and dead lifts.

But the ones along the side of your hips — the “hidden butt muscles” — need more focus as you get older, said Dr. Addison. As many people age they tend to move side-to-side less, she said, and thus don’t use them as much.

“If your hip abductors aren’t working well, then the entire chain of movement below doesn’t work well,” Dr. Addison said.

Keeping quads strong is also critical because they help in standing up from a chair, moving forward and your mobility in general. To test yours, try to stand up from a chair as many times as you can in 30 seconds without using your hands.

There are many exercises that hit both the quads and glutes at the same time. In addition to squats and dead lifts, target side-to-side and rotational movement with clamshells, monster walks and lateral lunges.

The rhomboid muscles, between your shoulder blades on your upper back, help you keep your spine more upright and your shoulders down and back. As you age, gravity and everyday habits, like looking down at your phone, can gradually cause you to hunch forward and round your shoulders.

This chronically poor posture has consequences: It compromises shoulder mobility and has the potential to increase stress on the tendons and surrounding tissues in your shoulder joint. This can contribute to neck and shoulder pain and headaches, said Nathan LeBrasseur, a physiology and rehabilitation professor at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minn.

Over time, being hunched over can also start to restrict how your rib cage moves and your ability to breathe as you walk. Lastly, leaning forward over time shifts your center of gravity, making it harder to maintain your balance; it could even cause you to fall, said Dr. Erin Futrell, associate professor of physical therapy at Springfield College, in Massachusetts.

Strengthening the rhomboid muscles, an integral part of your scapular retractors, which keep you upright, can help reverse this and change your posture. Experts recommended engaging in any simple rowing movement. Try single-arm rows to target the rhomboids one side at a time while also engaging your core to keep your torso stable.

Experts were quick to point out that walking speed can be a predictor of longevity and mortality. Our calf muscles help propel us forward when we walk or run and provide power when climbing stairs. They are also important for your balance as you age.

But the calf muscles are often overlooked as we get older; even people who exercise regularly tend to neglect muscles below the knee, Dr. Futrell said.

We know the big calf muscle gets weaker as you age, so training it to maintain strength is important, said Dr. Addison. The experts recommend calf raises and variations like deficit heel raises.

The core, as the body’s stabilizing center, is a critical component of healthy aging. It provides proper body alignment and positioning, allowing your larger muscles to work effectively.

However, many of the core muscles work in tandem with other muscles, making it difficult to isolate just one during exercise. Dr. Addison went with the belt of muscle that wraps around your trunk, known as your transversus abdominis, which plays a major role in keeping you steady and upright when you’re moving.

“It’s your deepest abdominal muscle,” she said, “like your built-in corset to support the rest of your body.” She recommended gently drawing your belly button in when lying on your back, doing pelvic tilts and then trying bird dogs to really activate it.

Because the core muscles largely work as a team, Dr. LeBrasseur recommended front and side planks. These activate much of the core, engaging both the front and the back of the body.

While all the experts agreed that these five muscle groups are important, each had their own pet favorite as well. Dr. LeBrasseur made a strong case for the muscles that support the head, which can be responsible for “tech neck.” He recommended a chin tuck with a head lift: lie flat on your back, tuck your chin and lift your head up and hold for 10 seconds. As you progress, increase the duration to a minute.

Dr. Addison had a particular love for the tibialis anterior, the primary muscle on the front of your shin. This muscle is critical for balance and mobility. It helps lift your foot and toes upward as you walk, keeping you from tripping over a rug, and helping you go up the stairs.

And lastly, Dr. Futrell said that the intrinsic foot muscles, a network responsible for the foot’s fine motor actions and arch support, will always hold a special place for her.

“I’m a big proponent of strengthening your feet, which I think is very neglected in all age groups. Strong feet can help with the whole body,” she said.

If you’re hoping to cut your cell phone bill by switching providers and maybe get a new device as a carrot, check out Mint Mobile right now. The popular budget carrier is offering a limited-time $500 discount on several new Android phones, including the Google Pixel 11 series and Samsung S26 series. To get the deal, you will need to sign up for a 12-month unlimited plan for $180, which breaks down to $15 a month. (Mint requires full payment up front, plus taxes and fees.) Another catch? You have to be a new customer. Phones are only getting more expensive, so discounts like this are worth exploring.

Unfortunately, the list of phones is limited and doesn’t include Apple’s iPhones. On the bright side, the phones aren’t low-quality; in fact, many are on our recommended lists. The unlimited plan also throttles down speeds after 50 GB per month, but it includes 20 GB for hot spot connections. Mint will offer an additional credit of $400 or more when you trade in an eligible unlocked phone (iPhone 16 or higher, Galaxy S25 or higher, Z Flip7 or Fold7 or higher, or Pixel 10 or higher).

Mint rarely offers deals or coupons because its plans are priced lower than traditional carriers, and you would have to pay full price for a new phone; while you’ll still have to shell out to cover the balance for the device, it is still more economical than the phone deals offered by the big carriers.

Silicon Valley Is Still Defending Jensen Huang

Wired November 12, 2026

News of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security was first met with a muted response in Silicon Valley—including inside Nvidia itself. Huang’s resignation, after news of two other alleged romantic relationships with Nvidia staffers, has left both the company and the broader AI industry stunned.

As revelations about Huang’s initial affair came out earlier this week, rank-and-file Nvidia employees at first pursued business as usual, according to two current and three former employees at the chipmaker, speaking anonymously to protect relationships at the company. They trusted the board to investigate and act accordingly, but few workers thought Huang would actually leave.

Nvidia’s roughly 60,000 employees are loyal to the point that its global turnover rate is reportedly among the lowest in tech. Workers say they have heard it called having “green in your blood” or being “green-pilled” or on “team green,” referring to the company’s signature color. Huang was the company’s soul and the founder who stuck with it through challenges for 33 years. Employees appreciated that he kept layoffs rare and red tape sparing.

“In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” one employee said. One former employee insisted in Huang’s defense that something “more sinister” must have been in play, and that affairs alone shouldn’t have led to his departure.

Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley echoed that sentiment, remaining vocal in their support of the embattled CEO even after his ouster. “One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership and contribution in building NVDA,” venture capitalist Antonio Gracias wrote on X earlier this week, using the company’s ticker symbol.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang has also had an extramarital affair with a vice president at Nvidia, and Reuters revealed on Thursday a second “intimate relationship” with an employee. Before those alleged affairs became public, multiple industry executives told WIRED that Huang is “irreplaceable” and that his biggest mistake, aside from his relationship with Alice Huang, was admitting the affair in writing to the whole company.

That appears to still be the prevailing sentiment. “A founder who has spent 30 years building such a unique company so capably has earned the presumption that he should keep leading it,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X after Huang resigned, and a few hours before the Reuters report.

Authorities and Nvidia’s board have yet to formally accuse Huang of wrongdoing in his interactions with the businesswoman and suspected intelligence asset Alice Huang, and China has denied that she’s a spy. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the FBI “is looking into it.” Nvidia’s board has stated that it doesn’t believe Huang compromised any secrets, but it has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate.

Add to all that, some corners of Nvidia had already been whispering about the relationship with Alice Huang; one venture capitalist who declined to be named recalled a recent dinner where an Nvidia executive claimed there had been rumors about Jensen’s romantic relationship with a young Asian woman.

On Monday, the venture capitalist had estimated a “less than 10 percent” chance Huang would lose his job at the top of the world’s most valuable company. “The wind’s going to blow over on this,” they said. “People are going to hate him for three months, and forget this ever happened.”

Huang’s resignation left them in shock.

The big anxiety in Silicon Valley remains the possibility that instability at Nvidia will burst an AI bubble, but analysts aren’t so sure.

The chief executive of one AI company, who spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to affect business relationships, says Nvidia’s recent bankrolling of AI startups and even buying companies such as model-hosting provider Hugging Face has helped prop up the need for chips. A “new professional CEO won’t do any of that,” meaning “systemic risk for the AI trade and AI bubble increases substantially,” the entrepreneur says.

Between bubble talk and Huang rumors, Nvidia shares in recent days have sunk to their lowest point in more than a year. Nvidia reports its latest quarterly earnings next week.

Inside Nvidia, meetings, projects, and the company’s aggressive culture are rapidly pressing ahead with what’s left of Huang’s vision.

Additional reporting by Will Knight and Zoë Schiffer.

Walmart+ gets you free delivery on orders over $35, free shipping, access to Peacock or Paramount+, gas savings, and more. You can try it for 30 days for $1, which may be worthwhile if you plan on doing some shopping at Walmart for the holidays; Just keep in mind that you'll want to manually cancel your membership if you decide it's not for you after 30 days, otherwise, it's $13 per month (or $98 per year). (Note that qualifying government assistance recipients can get this plan for 50 percent off.)

Ecoflow

Walmart

This extremely portable power station is actually pretty easy to tote around, unlike some other gadgets we've tested in this category. Coming in at 17 pounds with a convenient grab handle on the back, it has a massive 768-watt-hour capacity and recharges in just over an hour. The port selection has everything they'll need to stay topped off on a camping trip or for a few days without power. If your prepper friend loves hoarding power banks, this will be greatly appreciated.

Beats

Walmart

The Beats Solo 4 are a little older now, but in a world rife with noise-canceling earbuds and expensive over-ears, these still have a place. The on-ear cups are pretty comfy, especially if your giftee's noggin isn't too big, and they have the iconic Beats sound with a little less overt bass than their predecessors. They don't have noise cancellation, they don't automatically pause, and they aren't dust- or water-resistant. But for the right person, this price isn't bad. They might also be a good pick for teenagers who want cool over-ears.

Apple

Walmart

We've seen this deal pretty consistently for this excellent Bluetooth tracker, which can add anything to your Apple Find My app. Use it to track down your luggage, your pets, your keys, or your wallet. I personally keep one in my car so I can remember where I parked it when I haven't moved it for a few days. The battery is replaceable, and it has a built-in speaker, so you can ping it to find it if needed. It would make a great gift for your scatterbrained friend.

Glocusent

Walmart

This is one of the best prices we've seen for this wearable reading light that any bookworm would appreciate.

Ikarao

Walmart

We think this little karaoke machine makes a great gift, especially for couples.

Workpro

Walmart

Editor and handywoman extraordinaire Kat Merck says this is a “knockout deal” for everything you get. From pliers and screwdrivers to wrenches, bits, and a tape measure, it's hard to beat for an at-home tool kit. It comes with most of the non-power-tools you'd need for basic home projects. You'll probably still want a drill or other specialty tools, but this would make a great gift for a new renter (or for yourself if your tool kit currently consists of random Allen keys in a junk drawer).

Petkit

Walmart

This is a solid discount on the very best automatic litter box we've tried. It strikes a great balance between budget and features and should work well with most one- or two-cat households (provided your kitties aren't too oversize). It doesn't have AI or a camera inside, but it is easy to use, easy to keep clean, and it even sprays a deodorizing mist as needed to keep things smelling fresh. If your cat's litter box is a source of marital strife, perhaps it's time to employ a robot.

Grownsy

Walmart

This is the best bottle washer we've tried thanks to its quiet operation and continuous sterilization. It's perfect for new parents.

Petkit

Walmart

This over-the-top litterbox has more features than necessary, but the price is still better than normal.

Levoit

Walmart

We love this self-emptying cordless vacuum. It's efficient at cleaning (though it works best on carpet) and has an auto-cleaning and auto-charging station. It's especially good for pet parents since it can convert into a hand vacuum and includes several attachments for detailed cleaning tasks. I'm at the point in my life where a vacuum is a genuinely exciting gift prospect; perhaps someone on your list is, too.

Birdfy

Walmart

This adorable smart nesting box has an internal hygrometer and thermometer as well as two cameras (one interior, one exterior). It lets you witness the entire cycle of bird birth with an up-close and personal view of nesting parents. It's easy to set up and use, and while the app doesn't always identify everything correctly, it can still help you make sense of what you're seeing. And the built-in solar panel helps ensure that everything keeps operating with minimal input from you. Kat Merck says it makes an excellent gift.

Jensen Huang Didn’t Name His Own Replacement as One of Tech’s Most Powerful Women

Wired November 12, 2026

The most powerful woman in tech at this very moment is Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia—but her predecessor, Jensen Huang, failed to mention her in a recent back-and-forth about the topic.

Earlier this fall, WIRED published a feature story exploring the complex topic of power for women working in an industry traditionally dominated by men. We questioned why Silicon Valley doesn't have an Elon-esque or Jensen-like female hero (or villain) and determined that the rubric of power still looks different for women, whether they manage to hold significant financial capital, flex their political prowess, dictate cultural norms, or run intellectual circles around the industry.

We also determined there wasn’t just one singular impressive woman in tech, but a whole lot of them: Lisa Su, Gwynne Shotwell, Laurene Powell Jobs, and dozens more. Kress, then-CFO of Nvidia, was also given a nod.

As part of the reporting process, WIRED wanted to include the insights of a few established men in Silicon Valley. So we emailed Huang directly to ask for his thoughts.

He responded that “[Meta’s] Dina Powell, [Google’s] Ruth Porat” came to mind, because he “see[s] them when I’m in DC.” After some prompting, Huang also agreed that Shotwell, the president and COO of SpaceX, was impressive.

Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure.

As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy.

Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls.

Major Microsoft Outlook Outage Leaves People With Email Jobs Unable to Email

Wired November 12, 2026

It’s not just you. Microsoft’s 365 business and enterprise services suffered a major outage on Thursday, preventing users of its popular cloud suite from accessing their accounts.

Around 10:40 am ET on Thursday, Microsoft posted on its 365 status page on X that it was “investigating reports of users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America.” By just before 1 pm ET, it said it was aware of “issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.”

Microsoft later said that its network was also “experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors,” but that the issue was related to servers going offline, not due to increased traffic.

Around an hour later, Microsoft said it had “begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load” and was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.”

“We've paused all deployments. We're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service,” Microsoft wrote.

In an update on its status page, Microsoft said impacted services may include Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, and Microsoft Defender XDR.

“We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson tells WIRED in a statement. “We appreciate our customer's patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.”

Outage reports on the service uptime tracking website Downdetector began falling around 1:15 pm ET after a large spike in users reporting issues with Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products around noon.

It is currently unclear when the outage may be over or what its cause may be. In a status update on X posted just before 3 pm ET, Microsoft said “a problem” was “causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable” but that it was attempting to reboot its systems to hopefully bring them back online.

Outages in cloud services occur frequently, and their causes can vary. Configuration errors, resolution issues with the Domain Name System, and cyberattacks can all cause connection errors. There is currently no indication that a cyberattack caused the current Microsoft outage.

While major Microsoft outages are relatively rare, they are far from unprecedented. In July 2024, a corrupted update from the security firm CrowdStrike caused the “blues screen of death” on Windows machines around the world, while a separate but nearly simultaneous outage knocked out Microsoft Azure services for hours, causing untold millions of dollars in lost revenue due to companies’ inability to function as normal.

Updated 11/12/2026 at 3:05 pm ET: Added comment from Microsoft.

Updated 11/12/2026 at 5:20 pm ET: WIRED updated the article to clarify that the Azure outage was unrelated to the CrowdStrike-related issues with Windows in 2024.

Additional reporting by Matt Burgess.
